subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text: A PDA with states q1,q2, alphabet {a,b}, stack alphabet {a,b,Z}, initial state q1 and stack Z accepts nonempty even palindromes by empty stack. Stack top is at the right. Given δ(q1,a,Z)={(q1,Za)}, δ(q1,b,Z)={(q1,Zb)}, δ(q2,a,a)={(q2,ε)}, δ(q2,b,b)={(q2,ε)}, δ(q2,ε,Z)={(q2,ε)}, fill the two alternatives in each of δ(q1,a,a) and δ(q1,b,b). Discuss whether the displayed list is sufficient.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase with reconstructed code/netlist where needed; linked reproductions remain original-fidelity uncertain.
solution:
In state q1, the machine is guessing and storing the first half. On a matching input/top pair, it has two nondeterministic choices: push that input as another first-half symbol, or treat it as the first symbol of the reversed second half and pop the matching top while entering q2. Thus the displayed blanks are (q1,aa) and (q2,ε) for input a/top a, and (q1,bb) and (q2,ε) for input b/top b.

Those fillings alone do not recognize all even palindromes. Both reproductions omit the mixed push transitions δ(q1,a,b)={(q1,ba)} and δ(q1,b,a)={(q1,ab)}. With rightmost stack top, ba means retain b and push a. For example abba requires pushing b over a; it is rejected if the missing transitions are absent. This is a defect in the printed specification, not an additional blank that can be silently filled.

With these two additional rules, q1 pushes an arbitrary nonempty first half. It switches to q2 only while reading and popping a matching character, then q2 can only pop further matching characters. Finally it removes Z by ε. Acceptance requires both empty stack and exhausted input. subject: 04-data-structures
question_text: An n×n integer array is intended to increase along every row and every column. Where is its minimum? The reproduction quantifies both inequalities only for i,j∈[1,n−1], which is narrower than full row/column sorting.

Under the standard partially sorted matrix interpretation, A[1,1]≤A[i,j] for every cell: move downward from (1,1) to (i,1), then rightward to (i,j), using monotonicity at each step. With strict comparisons and n>1 this makes A[1,1] the unique minimum; the requested blanks are i=1 and j=1. For n=1 the only cell is trivially the minimum.

For n=2, the matrix [[1,2],[3,−100]] satisfies the printed comparisons 1<2 and 1<3, yet its minimum is at (2,2).

subject: 04-data-structures
question_title: Restore a sorted matrix after insertion
question_text: Delete the smallest element of an n×n row- and column-increasing array. Insert x, smaller than every item of the last row and last column, in O(n) time. Complete: i:=1;j:=1;A[i,j]:=x; while (x>blank or x>blank) do if A[i+1,j]<blank then begin A[i,j]:=A[i+1,j];i:=i+1 end else begin blank end; A[i,j]:=blank. Assume the intended full monotonicity and distinct inserted value.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase with reconstructed code/netlist where needed; linked reproductions remain original-fidelity uncertain.
solution:
A complete hole-moving version is:
i:=1; j:=1; A[i,j]:=x;
while (x>A[i+1,j]) or (x>A[i,j+1]) do
begin
  if A[i+1,j]<A[i,j+1] then
  begin A[i,j]:=A[i+1,j]; i:=i+1 end
  else
  begin A[i,j]:=A[i,j+1]; j:=j+1 end
end;
A[i,j]:=x.

Treat the current cell as a hole until the final assignment. If both children are greater than x, x belongs there. Otherwise the smaller of the downward and rightward neighbors is the smallest candidate that can fill the hole without violating either row or column order. Move it into the hole, advance to its old position, and repeat. Along the moved path, predecessors remain smaller than the element shifted into place; untouched cells preserve their old comparisons. The terminal hole receives x.

Each iteration increases i+j by one, hence there are O(n) iterations and O(1) extra storage. The given strict upper bound on x prevents the hole from entering the last row or last column: a boundary neighbor is greater than x and cannot be the smaller neighbor selected while the loop is true. Thus the two neighbor accesses are safe for n≥2. Without that promise use explicit bounds or +∞ sentinels.

Distinct x is a sufficient extra condition for preserving strict order. Without it the guarantee can fail: consider [[0,10,40],[20,30,50],[60,70,80]] with x=10. Here x is below every last-row/column entry, yet the procedure stops with adjacent equal values in the first row. Equal entries can sometimes occupy incomparable cells, but strict preservation is not guaranteed by the printed promise. If duplicates are allowed, interpret sorted as nondecreasing instead. Finally, the literal source quantifier omits boundary comparisons, so the algorithm relies on the intended full row/column definition discussed in part (a).
derived_answer: Compare x to A[i+1,j],A[i,j+1]; choose their minimum; shift it up/left; advance i or j; finally write x.

subject: 04-data-structures
question_text: Insert K,R,P,C,S,N,Y,T,J,M in that order into slots 0,…,9 using linear probing and h(x)=(ord(x)−ord('a')+1) mod10. The input is uppercase while the formula uses lowercase a; distinguish alphabet-position normalization from literal uppercase ASCII. Which insertions collide?
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase with reconstructed code/netlist where needed; linked reproductions remain original-fidelity uncertain.
solution:
With alphabet positions (equivalently lowercasing each character before applying the formula), the home slots are K1,R8,P6,C3,S9,N4,Y5,T0,J0,M3. The first eight insertions find empty slots. J collides at 0 with T and at 1 with K, then occupies 2. M collides at 3,4,5,6, occupied respectively by C,N,Y,P, then occupies 7. Thus J and M are exactly the insertions that encounter collisions.

The final normalized table is 0:T,1:K,2:J,3:C,4:N,5:Y,6:P,7:M,8:R,9:S. Every character appears once and all ten slots are filled.

For literal uppercase ASCII with the printed lowercase 'a', ord(uppercase)=ord(lowercase)−32. Therefore each home slot is shifted by −32≡−2 modulo10. Linear probing is circular and the whole table rotates by the same amount. Homes become 9,6,4,1,7,2,3,8,8,1, and the final table is 0:J,1:C,2:N,3:Y,4:P,5:M,6:R,7:S,8:T,9:K. J and M still collide. This literal result uses mathematical nonnegative modulo; a language whose remainder operator returns negative values needs normalization before indexing. Neither reproduction resolves the case/encoding convention, so both answers are disclosed rather than silently changing the formula.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_text: A complete undirected graph on vertices 0,1,…,n−1 has weight w(u,v)=|u−v| for distinct vertices. Draw a minimum spanning tree.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase with reconstructed code/netlist where needed; linked reproductions remain original-fidelity uncertain.
solution:
Every edge joins distinct integers, so its weight is at least 1. A spanning tree on n vertices contains exactly n−1 edges. Consequently every spanning tree has total weight at least n−1.

Connect consecutive vertices: (0,1),(1,2),…,(n−2,n−1). This is a connected path with no cycles, so it is a spanning tree. Each of its n−1 edges has weight 1, giving total n−1 and attaining the lower bound. Text diagram: 0 --1-- 1 --1-- 2 --1-- … --1-- (n−1), where the labels between dashes are edge weights.

For n≥2 it is also the unique MST. Achieving the lower bound requires every selected edge to have weight 1, and the only weight-1 edges in this graph are exactly the consecutive pairs. There are n−1 of them, so all must be selected. Alternatively, for the cut {0,…,k}|{k+1,…,n−1}, edge (k,k+1) is the unique minimum crossing edge and is mandatory by the cut property. When n=1 the empty tree has cost0; the same n−1 formula applies.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_text: A complete undirected graph on vertices 0,1,…,n−1 has weight w(u,v)=u+v for distinct vertices. Draw a minimum spanning tree.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase with reconstructed code/netlist where needed; linked reproductions remain original-fidelity uncertain.
solution:
For each vertex v>0, consider the cut separating v from every other vertex. Its incident edges have weights v+u, with u≠v. The smallest possible u is0, so (v,0) is the unique minimum-weight edge across this cut. By the cut property every MST must contain it.

Doing this for every v=1,…,n−1 gives exactly the star centered at0. These n−1 edges connect all vertices and have no cycle, so the mandatory set itself is a spanning tree. Its weight is Σ_(v=1)^(n−1) v=n(n−1)/2. Text diagram: center0 with a spoke to each v; spoke (0,v) has label v.

A second lower-bound proof roots any spanning tree at0. Each nonroot vertex v has one parent p(v)≥0, so its parent edge costs v+p(v)≥v. Summing over all nonroot vertices gives total at least Σv. The star attains equality by taking every parent to be0. This argument also shows uniqueness for n≥2: equality requires all parents0. For n=1 there are no spokes and the minimum weight is0. The complete graph assumption guarantees that every required spoke exists.

subject: 03-programming-in-c
question_title: Failure conditions of a binary search
question_text: For N>1, the following Pascal-like program searches an array a[1..N]: initialize i=1,j=N; repeatedly set k=floor((i+j)/2), then if a[k]<x set i=k, otherwise set j=k; stop when a[k]=x or i>=j. Finally print success if a[k]=x and failure otherwise. Determine when it fails. For the intended binary-search interpretation assume a is sorted in nondecreasing order. GFG prints the success message correctly; GateForum instead prints failure in both final branches.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase, with source defects explicitly distinguished from proposed repairs; original fidelity unverified.
solution:
The defect is that the lower update keeps the already examined element: i=k instead of i=k+1. When j=i+1, integer division gives k=i. If a[i]<x, setting i=k changes nothing; j also stays unchanged, a[k] is not x, and i<j remains true. The loop repeats forever.

In fact the final array position N is never examined: while i<j, floor((i+j)/2)<j<=N, so k<=N−1. On a nondecreasing array, the exact classification is: every x occurring among a[1],...,a[N−1] is eventually found; every x<a[1] terminates with failure; every x>a[1] absent from a[1..N−1] loops forever. The latter includes absent values between array entries, values above the maximum, and x=a[N] when that value occurs only at the last position. Duplicates matter: x=a[N] is found if the same value occurs earlier.

For example a=[1,3], x=3 gives (i,j,k)=(1,2,1) forever. With x=0, the first iteration instead sets j=1 and terminates correctly. For a=[1,3,5], x=3 is examined immediately and succeeds. These examples distinguish the actual bug from the inaccurate claim that all unsuccessful searches fail.

A robust repair uses while i<=j, tests equality first, then sets i=k+1 when a[k]<x and j=k−1 otherwise, reporting failure after the interval becomes empty. This also permits examining N. Separately, the literal GateForum reproduction reports failure even after a successful equality test, because its success string is misprinted; that text defect does not cause the nontermination.
derived_answer: Loops when x>a[1] and x is absent from positions 1..N−1; in particular a unique last-element match is missed. GateForum also misprints the success message.

question_text: Global b is set to 3 and test1(b) is called. Procedure test1(a) sets a=5, prints “point 1:” followed by a,b, calls test2, then prints “point 2:” followed by a,b. Procedure test2 sets the global b=10. After test1 returns, the main program prints “point 3:” followed by b. Assume the displayed lexical scope and determine the output with a passed by reference.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase, with source defects explicitly distinguished from proposed repairs; original fidelity unverified.
solution:
A reference parameter is another name for the caller's variable, not a private copy of its value. Here the actual parameter is the global b, so a and b designate the same storage throughout test1. Initially that cell contains 3. Executing a:=5 updates the cell itself, which means both a and b now read as 5. Consequently the first output is point 1: 5 5.

Next test2 executes b:=10. It refers to the global b by the displayed lexical scope; this is the same cell already aliased by a. Therefore both reads at the second output produce 10, giving point 2: 10 10. Returning from test1 requires no copy-back for a reference parameter. The global value remains 10, and the final output is point 3: 10.

The important reasoning is storage identity: a:=5 changes b immediately, and test2's assignment to b changes what a observes immediately. The procedure nesting does not create a second b or hide the global declaration. Spaces and line breaks may depend on Pascal's output formatting; the value sequences, in order, are (5,5), (10,10), and (10).

question_text: Global b is set to 3 and test1(b) is called. Procedure test1(a) sets a=5, prints “point 1:” followed by a,b, calls test2, then prints “point 2:” followed by a,b. Value-result creates a separate local parameter cell. At entry to test1, the current actual value b=3 is copied into a. The assignment a:=5 changes only that private cell; the global b remains 3. Thus the first output is point 1: 5 3.

The call to test2 then assigns 10 to the global b. It does not refer to the private parameter a of its caller, so a stays 5. The second output is consequently point 2: 5 10. This is the observable difference from call-by-reference: a is not an alias for b during the call.

At normal return from test1, the result phase copies the final local a back to the original actual parameter location b. That overwrites test2's value 10 with 5. The main program therefore prints point 3: 5. The chronological storage states are (a,b)=(3,3) at entry, (5,3) after assigning a, (5,10) after test2, and b=5 after copy-out. No conflict among multiple value-result actuals arises because the procedure has just one parameter. If it were ordinary call-by-value instead, there would be no final copy-back and point 3 would show 10; the word “result” is essential.

question_text: Use the SDTS E→E+E {print “+”}, E→E*E {print “.”}, E→id {print id.name}, E→(E) {no action}. An LR parser executes a production's action immediately after reducing by it. Draw the parse tree and give the translation of (a+b)*(c+d).
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase, with source defects explicitly distinguished from proposed repairs; original fidelity unverified.
solution:
The root production is E→E*E. Its left E derives (E), whose inner E derives E+E with identifier leaves a and b. Its right E derives (E), whose inner E derives E+E with identifier leaves c and d. Thus a textual description of the full parse tree is E(E('(',E(E(id a),'+',E(id b)),')'), '*', E('(',E(E(id c),'+',E(id d)),')')). Parentheses are terminal children of their E→(E) nodes, not emitted characters.

Actions run on reduction, after the right-hand-side subexpressions have been recognized. Reducing id a prints a, reducing id b prints b, and reducing their addition prints +. The parenthesized left operand therefore emits a b +. The E→(E) reduction emits nothing. Similarly the right operand emits c d +. Only after both operand E nodes exist can the root multiplication reduce and print the dot specified by its action.

The literal complete output is a b + c d + ., or ab+cd+. when concatenated without separators. The final dot is an emitted multiplication token, not sentence punctuation. It is postfix notation: each operation follows its operands. As a check, a postfix evaluator pushes a and b, combines them by +, pushes c and d, combines them by +, then multiplies the two resulting values. The grammar is ambiguous in general for unparenthesized mixed operators, but these explicit parentheses fix the intended tree for this particular sentence. The enlarged GateForum p16 action explicitly prints a dot, and the GFG p9 action also shows a dot. Conventional postfix ab+cd+* expresses the same multiplication, but it is not the exact string emitted by the printed SDTS and must not replace it silently.
derived_answer: Literal output ab+cd+. (final dot is emitted); root multiplication with two parenthesized addition subtrees.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text: fork L creates a new process starting at label L while the original continues. join V atomically decrements V and terminates the arriving process unless the new value is zero. For N=2; M=2; fork L3; fork L4; S1; L1: join N; S3; L2: join M; S5; goto next; L3: S2; goto L1; L4: S4; goto L2; next:, draw the precedence graph for S1..S5. The goto next after S5 is present in GFG but omitted in GateForum.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase, with source defects explicitly distinguished from proposed repairs; original fidelity unverified.
solution:
After the two forks there are three branches. The original executes S1, the L3 branch executes S2, and the L4 branch executes S4. There is no synchronization among those three statements, so they can occur in any order or overlap.

The S1 and S2 branches both reach join N. Because N starts at 2, the first arrival changes N to 1 and terminates; the second changes N to 0 and survives. Exactly one process therefore continues to S3, and S3 cannot start until both S1 and S2 have finished. This gives edges S1→S3 and S2→S3. The identity of the surviving process is irrelevant to the statement ordering.

The branch completing S3 and the branch completing S4 both reach join M. The same counting argument, with M initially 2, permits S5 exactly once, after both predecessors finish. Add edges S3→S5 and S4→S5. These four edges form the transitive reduction: draw S1 and S2 feeding S3, then S3 and S4 feeding S5. The additional transitive relations S1→S5 and S2→S5 need not be drawn.

This finite five-statement interpretation uses GFG's explicit goto next after S5. In the literal GateForum listing, the survivor instead falls through into L3 and executes S2 a second time, then decrements N from 0 to −1 and terminates. Its execution is not captured by the intended one-node-per-statement DAG. Omitting the jump is a material control-flow variant, not harmless punctuation.
derived_answer: Edges S1→S3, S2→S3, S3→S5, S4→S5, using GFG’s goto next.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text: Three processes P0,P1,P2 share resource types R0,R1,R2. Maximum total claims are P0=(4,1,2), P1=(1,5,1), P2=(1,2,3). Current allocations are P0=(1,0,2), P1=(0,3,1), P2=(1,0,2), and Available=(2,2,0). Show that this can be a state admitted by the Banker’s algorithm.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase, with source defects explicitly distinguished from proposed repairs; original fidelity unverified.
solution:
The table heading “Maximum Need” gives total claims, not outstanding requests. Subtract each allocation to obtain remaining Need: P0=(3,1,0), P1=(1,2,0), P2=(0,2,1). The total resource vector is Available plus all allocations, namely (4,5,5); every maximum is individually within this total.

Run the safety test with Work=(2,2,0). P0 cannot finish yet because it needs 3 units of R0 but only 2 are free. P2 cannot finish because it needs one R2 while none is free. P1 can finish since (1,2,0) is componentwise at most (2,2,0). After it finishes, Work increases by its current allocation (0,3,1), yielding (2,5,1). Adding allocation, rather than maximum, is correct: its extra temporary requests are returned too, leaving the net increase equal to the allocation it already held.

Now P2's need (0,2,1) fits, so its completion releases (1,0,2) and Work becomes (3,5,3). Finally P0's need (3,1,0) fits; releasing (1,0,2) yields (4,5,5). Thus P1,P2,P0 is a safe sequence, proving that all claims can be satisfied in a suitable order. Safety does not assert that every possible future request is immediately grantable; it establishes at least one completion schedule from the current allocations.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text: Three processes P0,P1,P2 share resource types R0,R1,R2. Maximum total claims are P0=(4,1,2), P1=(1,5,1), P2=(1,2,3). Current allocations are P0=(1,0,2), P1=(0,3,1), P2=(1,0,2), and Available=(2,2,0). Determine what happens when P0 requests one unit of R1.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase, with source defects explicitly distinguished from proposed repairs; original fidelity unverified.
solution:
The request vector is R=(0,1,0). First check R<=Need0=(3,1,0), so the request does not exceed P0's remaining claim. Also R<=Available=(2,2,0), so the requested unit is physically available. These necessary checks alone do not justify granting it.

Tentatively allocate the unit. Available becomes (2,1,0), P0's allocation becomes (1,1,2), and P0's remaining need becomes (3,0,0). The other needs remain P1=(1,2,0), P2=(0,2,1). Begin the safety test with Work=(2,1,0). P0 cannot finish because 3>2 in R0; P1 cannot finish because 2>1 in R1; P2 cannot finish because it needs 2 R1 and 1 R2, while only 1 R1 and 0 R2 are free. No process can be the first in a guaranteed completion sequence.

The tentative state is therefore unsafe. The Banker rolls back the tentative change and makes P0 wait, preserving Available=(2,2,0) and the original safe allocations. This is not a claim that the request is invalid or that an actual deadlock has already occurred. It is a refusal to enter a state from which completion under all declared maximum claims cannot be guaranteed. The one free unit's availability is precisely why a full safety test, rather than a simple availability check, is needed.
derived_answer: Defer P0’s request: tentative Available=(2,1,0) is unsafe although the unit is available.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text: A one-level file system uses 4K-byte disk blocks. Disk block 0 contains a FAT with one 8-bit next-data-block address entry per data block. Disk block 1 is a directory with one 32-bit entry per file. Disk blocks 2,3,... are data blocks 1,2,... . Take K=1024. Find the maximum possible number of files.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase, with source defects explicitly distinguished from proposed repairs; original fidelity unverified.
solution:
The directory occupies one block, so its storage is 4×1024=4096 bytes. A directory entry uses 32 bits=4 bytes. Hence it contains 4096/4=1024 entries and can name at most 1024 files. This is a directory-capacity bound; the FAT entry count must not be substituted into this division.

Attaining that many named files does not require one data block for every file if zero-length files are allowed. Empty files can occupy directory entries without owning data blocks, so the customary directory-capacity interpretation gives 1024 files. If instead the question requires every file to be nonempty, the result also depends on the number of addressable data blocks and the unspecified pointer conventions. Under a uniform 8-bit data-block address convention with all 256 patterns usable, at most 256 one-block nonempty files fit, and reserved FAT markers reduce that number.

There is a related source-design omission: a 4096-byte FAT can physically hold 4096 one-byte entries, but one-byte next pointers cannot name all 4096 positions under a uniform address scheme. Thus table capacity, pointer addressability, and directory capacity are three distinct quantities. The problem does not specify empty-file policy, reserved values, or actual disk capacity; 1024 is the unambiguous maximum directory entry count, not a proof that 1024 nonempty files can simultaneously occupy the disk.
derived_answer: 1024 directory entries/files when empty files are permitted; nonempty-file capacity is additionally data-block limited.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text: A one-level file system uses 4K-byte disk blocks. Disk block 0 contains a FAT with one 8-bit next-data-block address entry per data block. Disk block 1 is a directory with one 32-bit entry per file. Disk blocks 2,3,... are data blocks 1,2,... . Take K=1024. Find the maximum possible file size in data blocks.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase, with source defects explicitly distinguished from proposed repairs; original fidelity unverified.
solution:
A FAT-linked file is a chain: its directory entry identifies the first data block, and each block's FAT entry identifies the next. With a uniform 8-bit data-block addressing convention there are 2^8=256 possible address values. If all values are usable data-block identifiers and termination is represented separately (for example by known file length), a file can traverse at most 256 distinct data blocks. It would occupy 256×4096=1,048,576 bytes. This is the conventional intended pointer-width answer.

The 4KB FAT itself has room for 4096 one-byte entries, but room to store an entry is not the same as enough pointer bits to address its block. Therefore 4096 blocks is not justified merely by dividing FAT size by entry size. A pointer width of at least 12 bits would be required to name 4096 data blocks uniformly.

The literal question does not define end-of-file encoding or whether addresses refer to physical disk blocks or data-block ordinals. Reserving one of the 256 values for EOF leaves at most 255 usable uniform data-block addresses. If physical block numbers 0 and 1 are also excluded as metadata locations, the usable range changes again. These are specification choices, not values established by the reproduction. Accordingly 256 blocks is conditional on the standard all-patterns-usable data-block model; an exact implementation-level maximum cannot be certified without the address and termination conventions. The directory entry's 32 bits do not by themselves repair the short next pointers.
derived_answer: Conventional answer: 256 data blocks (1 MiB), conditional on uniform 8-bit identifiers without reserved codes; literal exact bound depends on unspecified encoding.

subject: 01-digital-logic
question_title: State diagram of an XOR-feedback register
question_text: A synchronous circuit has three D flip-flops with common clock. Q1 feeds D2, Q2 feeds D3, and Q2 XOR Q3 feeds D1 through the feedback gate. State Si denotes the binary value i of Q1Q2Q3, so S0=000,...,S7=111. Draw its state-transition diagram.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase, with source defects explicitly distinguished from proposed repairs; original fidelity unverified.
solution:
A D flip-flop takes its next output from its D input on the common active clock edge. All three updates use the old outputs simultaneously. Reading the circuit wires gives Q1(next)=Q2 XOR Q3, Q2(next)=Q1, and Q3(next)=Q2. In particular, do not feed the newly computed Q1 into Q2 during the same clock edge.

Evaluate the equations for every state:
S0: 000→000, hence S0→S0.
S1: 001→100, hence S1→S4.
S2: 010→101, hence S2→S5.
S3: 011→001, hence S3→S1.
S4: 100→010, hence S4→S2.
S5: 101→110, hence S5→S6.
S6: 110→111, hence S6→S7.
S7: 111→011, hence S7→S3.

To draw the diagram, put a self-loop on S0 and draw the separate seven-state directed cycle S1→S4→S2→S5→S6→S7→S3→S1. There is no external input, so each state has exactly one outgoing edge and there are no input labels to choose. The zero state is a fixed point because shifting zeros and XORing zeros still gives zeros. As a consistency check, the listed targets contain all eight states once; the transition function is invertible, since the old Q1 and Q2 are read from the new Q2 and Q3 and old Q3 is recovered by XORing new Q1 with new Q3.

subject: 01-digital-logic
question_title: States unreachable from the initial register state
question_text: A synchronous circuit has three D flip-flops with common clock. Q1 feeds D2, Q2 feeds D3, and Q2 XOR Q3 feeds D1 through the feedback gate. State Si denotes the binary value i of Q1Q2Q3, so S0=000,...,S7=111. Starting at S4, identify all unreachable states.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase, with source defects explicitly distinguished from proposed repairs; original fidelity unverified.
solution:
The next-state equations are (Q1,Q2,Q3)→(Q2 XOR Q3,Q1,Q2). Begin with S4=100 and repeatedly apply them. The successive states are S4=100, S2=010, S5=101, S6=110, S7=111, S3=011, S1=001, and then S4=100 again.

Once a deterministic state repeats, its subsequent trajectory repeats too; there is no input capable of taking a different branch. Therefore the reachable set is exactly {S1,S2,S3,S4,S5,S6,S7}, including the initial state itself at time zero. The only member of the eight-state space not visited is S0=000. It is unreachable from S4, although it is a perfectly valid state and would remain at zero forever if chosen as an initial state.

One can verify the exclusion algebraically. If the next state were 000, then new Q2=old Q1=0 and new Q3=old Q2=0. New Q1=old Q2 XOR old Q3=0 then forces old Q3=0. Thus only 000 can transition to 000; no nonzero state can enter it. The enumerated seven-state cycle proves that no additional state is excluded. GFG labels this subpart separately as question 73, but it is part (b) of original question 24 and shares that question's circuit and five-mark group allocation.
derived_answer: Only S0 is unreachable; the seven nonzero states form the cycle containing S4.

subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_title: CPU overhead of continuous DMA transfers
question_text: A 50 MHz processor uses DMA for a disk transferring 2000 Kbytes/s continuously. The average DMA block is 4 Kbytes. Each transfer needs 1000 processor cycles for setup and 500 processor cycles for its completion interrupt. What fraction of CPU time is consumed by disk handling?
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase, with source defects explicitly distinguished from proposed repairs; original fidelity unverified.
solution:
First count transfers rather than bytes: 2000 Kbytes/s divided by 4 Kbytes/transfer is 500 transfers/s. The same meaning of K occurs in both quantities and cancels, so decimal versus binary K does not change this rate.

The processor performs 1000+500=1500 cycles of administrative work for every transfer. At 500 transfers/s this costs 750,000 CPU cycles/s. A 50 MHz processor supplies 50,000,000 cycles/s, so the fraction used is 750,000/50,000,000=0.015, or 1.5 percent.

An equivalent time calculation checks the units. Each processor cycle lasts 1/(50×10^6) s=20 ns. Setup takes 20 microseconds and the completion handler takes 10 microseconds, totaling 30 microseconds per transfer. Transferring 4K bytes at 2000K bytes/s takes 0.002 s=2 milliseconds; 30 microseconds/2 milliseconds again equals 0.015. The transfer uses DMA, so the CPU is not charged for executing an instruction per byte. The calculation counts only the specified setup and completion overhead; additional bus-contention stalls, queuing effects, or other driver costs are not given and should not be invented. The statement that the disk transfers continuously fixes the block rate at its full throughput.

subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_title: Choosing hierarchy sizes with model caveats
question_text: A three-level hierarchy has level-1 access time 50 ns/byte and options 8KB (hit .80), 16KB (.90), 64KB (.95); level-2 access time 200 ns/byte and options 4MB (hit .98), 16MB (.99), 64MB (.995); level 3 has access time 5 microseconds/byte, size 250MB, hit 1.0. Use the GFG table; GateForum has inconsistent duplicated tables, KB/MB units and 250/260MB labels. The question does not explicitly state whether lower-level access times include earlier failed probes. Choose minimum level-1 and level-2 sizes giving average access time strictly below 100 ns.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase, with source defects explicitly distinguished from proposed repairs; original fidelity unverified.
solution:
If the tabulated times are complete service times for a hit at the corresponding level, and h2 is conditional on missing level 1, then T=h1·50+(1−h1)h2·200+(1−h1)(1−h2)·5000. Try the smallest options first: h1=.80 and h2=.98. Their mutually exclusive outcome probabilities are .80, .196, and .004, summing to one. Hence T=40+39.2+20=99.2 ns, strictly below 100. Since 8KB and 4MB are individually the smallest listed sizes, this pair is componentwise minimal in that model.

A different standard convention treats 50,200,5000 as incremental sequential probe times. Then every access pays 50, every L1 miss pays another 200, and a miss in both pays another 5000: Tseq=50+(1−h1)[200+(1−h2)5000]. The same 8KB/4MB pair gives 110 ns and fails. At 8KB, increasing L2 to 16MB gives exactly 100 ns, still failing the strict inequality; 64MB gives 95 ns. At 16KB, the smallest L2=4MB already gives 80 ns. Thus the nondominated feasible pairs in the sequential model are (8KB,64MB) and (16KB,4MB); neither is smaller in both coordinates. Minimizing total installed bytes selects (16KB,4MB), whereas minimizing L1 first selects (8KB,64MB).

Therefore the familiar 8KB/4MB answer requires the complete-service-time interpretation. Without specifying the timing convention, the literal question has no single model-independent answer. The lower-level hit ratio is also taken as conditional, not as an additional unconditional probability.
derived_answer: Complete-service-time model: 8KB L1 and 4MB L2 (99.2 ns). Sequential probing gives different feasible minima; see solution.

question_text: Relations are USERS(User#,UserName,HomeTown), BOOKS(Book#,BookTitle,AuthorName), and ISSUED(Book#,User#,Date). Natural joins match the identically named key attributes. One-sentence answer: It returns user number 6 together with the titles of books recorded as issued to that user.

The projection π_User#,BookTitle retains just the user identifier and title, discarding names, dates, book identifiers and author names. Finally σ_User#=6 keeps only rows whose user identifier is 6.

Selection occurs after projection here without losing its input attribute, because User# is explicitly retained. It could equivalently be pushed earlier to restrict the user or issue records before the joins. Under ordinary set-based relational algebra, projection removes duplicate pairs: borrowing the same titled book more than once does not produce multiple identical (6,title) rows, and distinct books with the same title also collapse at this projection. No return-date or current-loan condition exists in the schema, so “recorded as issued” is more precise than claiming these are necessarily the user's currently unreturned books. The query yields titles with the fixed identifier 6, not a count of loans, author names, or all users who borrowed the same books.

subject: 09-database-management-systems
question_title: Interpreting authors read by a hometown group
question_text: Relations are USERS(User#,UserName,HomeTown), BOOKS(Book#,BookTitle,AuthorName), and ISSUED(Book#,User#,Date). Natural joins match the identically named key attributes. Explain in one English sentence the query π_AuthorName(BOOKS ⋈ σ_HomeTown='Delhi'(USERS ⋈ ISSUED)). Use the projection and natural-join symbols visible in GFG; GateForum misprints/degrades these operators.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase, with source defects explicitly distinguished from proposed repairs; original fidelity unverified.
solution:
One-sentence answer: It returns the names of authors having at least one book recorded as issued to a user whose hometown is Delhi.

The inner natural join USERS ⋈ ISSUED matches each issue to its borrower through User#. Selecting HomeTown='Delhi' retains issue records belonging to Delhi users; the condition describes the borrower's hometown, not the author's residence or the book's publication place. The join with BOOKS matches Book# and adds the author of each surviving issued book. Projection onto AuthorName then discards every other attribute.

Under set semantics each distinct author name appears once, even if several Delhi users borrowed that author's books or one user borrowed several such books. The condition is existential: one qualifying issue suffices. It does not require that all books by the author have been issued, that every Delhi user has read the author, or that the author is popular by any numerical threshold. Likewise nothing in the given schema tests whether a book has since been returned. If no Delhi user has any issue record, the result is empty. Two different people who happen to share AuthorName are not distinguished by this schema and projection; the result is a set of names rather than necessarily unique real-world author identities. GateForum's apparent σ before AuthorName would not be a well-formed selection predicate; the GFG π supplies the coherent reading.
derived_answer: Names of authors with at least one book issued to a Delhi-hometown user.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_text: Rain probabilities are 0.5 today, 0.6 tomorrow, and 0.7 for at least one of the two days. Find probability of both.
question_text_status: Self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and task; complete reproduced options/figures linked, original fidelity unverified.
solution: Let A and B denote rain today and tomorrow. Inclusion–exclusion gives P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B). Thus P(A∩B)=0.5+0.6−0.7=0.4. This is D. Multiplying 0.5 by 0.6 would assume independence, which is not stated and is inconsistent with the given union probability. The word either is interpreted as inclusive or, as required by the standard union reading.

question_title: Newton iteration from a negative start
question_text: Apply Newton–Raphson to x²−2=0 starting at−1. Does it converge to−1, +sqrt (2), −sqrt (2), or fail?
question_text_status: Self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and task; complete reproduced options/figures linked, original fidelity unverified.
solution: Newton’s update is x_next=x−(x²−2)/(2x)=(x+2/x)/2. From−1 it gives−1.5, then approximately−1.416667. Negative iterates remain negative. Put u=−x>0; then u_next=(u+2/u)/2. After the first step u≥sqrt (2), and this iteration decreases toward sqrt (2), since its only positive fixed point is sqrt (2). Hence the original iterates approach−sqrt (2), C, rather than crossing to the positive root.

solution: The determinant of an upper-triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal entries. This follows by expanding repeatedly along the first column, whose entries below the diagonal are zero. subject: 04-data-structures
question_text: Which standard representation permits O(1) concatenation: singly linked, doubly linked, circular doubly linked, or array list?
question_text_status: Self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and task; complete reproduced options/figures linked, original fidelity unverified.
solution: A circular doubly linked list exposes its tail as head.prev. For nonempty lists with heads h1, h2 and tails t1, t2, set t1.next=h2, h2.prev=t1, t2.next=h1, h1.prev=t2. Only four links change, so concatenation is O(1), C. Empty-list cases need only pointer assignments. A head-only linear list requires traversal to find its tail, but an explicitly stored tail pointer also makes singly or doubly linked concatenation constant-time. Thus uniqueness of C depends on the usual representation metadata, not merely the link direction.
derived_answer: C with head-only representations; stored tails also suffice

question_text: Grammar X→X⊕Y|Y, Y→Z⊙Y|Z, Z→id. Determine associativity of⊕ and⊙.
question_text_status: Self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and task; complete reproduced options/figures linked, original fidelity unverified.

Therefore⊕ is left associative and⊙ right associative, A. The lower nonterminal level also makes⊙ bind more tightly, but precedence and associativity are distinct properties.

subject: 04-data-structures
question_text: Which structure is essential for efficient infix-to-postfix conversion: operator stack, operand stack, both stacks, or parse tree?
question_text_status: Self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and task; complete reproduced options/figures linked, original fidelity unverified.
solution: Operands can be emitted directly to the postfix output. Operators must wait until higher-precedence operators and parenthesized subexpressions are resolved, so a stack stores pending operators and delimiters. When an operator is popped, it is appended to the output. Thus the standard shunting-yard conversion needs an operator stack, A, not an operand-value stack. An operand stack is used later to evaluate postfix, and an explicit parse tree is an alternative representation rather than a requirement of this direct conversion.

subject: 07-compiler-design
question_text: A language permits arrays whose sizes are unknown at compile time and requires efficient memory use. Can it be compiled using static allocation, dynamic allocation, or only interpreted?
question_text_status: Self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and task; complete reproduced options/figures linked, original fidelity unverified.
solution: The compiler can generate runtime code that evaluates an array’s size, allocates that much storage and records its address and dimensions. Dynamic allocation therefore handles unknown compile-time sizes while avoiding allocation for an arbitrary worst-case bound, giving C. Interpretation is not necessary: compilation can defer particular operations until runtime. Static allocation alone cannot efficiently reserve exactly the required unknown sizes in the general case.

subject: 07-compiler-design
question_title: Why a language needs heap storage
question_text: Choose the feature motivating heap allocation: recursion, dynamic data structures, dynamic scope, none.
question_text_status: Self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and task; complete reproduced options/figures linked, original fidelity unverified.
solution: Recursion normally creates nested activation lifetimes, which a stack handles. Dynamic scope concerns name lookup and does not itself force arbitrary object lifetimes. General dynamic structures such as linked nodes may be allocated and released in an order unrelated to calls and returns, so they need storage managed outside a strict activation stack: the heap, item 2. This is the conventional distinction. Particular bounded or region-scoped structures could use specialized pools, so “required” refers to supporting general dynamic lifetimes, not every individual dynamic object.

subject: 10-computer-networks
question_title: Purpose of an asynchronous start bit
question_text: Does an RS232-style start bit synchronize each received byte, a whole byte sequence, provide parity, or synchronize only the last byte?
question_text_status: Self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and task; complete reproduced options/figures linked, original fidelity unverified.
solution: Between asynchronous frames the line is idle. The start-bit transition tells the receiver that a new character frame has begun, allowing it to align sampling instants for that frame’s data bits. This resynchronization occurs for each byte, A. It is not a parity check and does not establish one permanent clock phase for an unlimited sequence. Strictly RS232 specifies electrical/interface aspects; the question refers to the familiar asynchronous framing used over that interface.

subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_text: An N-bit adder uses 4-bit 74181 ALUs and 4-bit 74182 carry generators, with N divisible by 4. What is best asymptotic addition delay?
question_text_status: Self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and task; complete reproduced options/figures linked, original fidelity unverified.
solution: A four-way carry generator combines propagate/generate information for four lower-level groups. Cascading these in a balanced hierarchy reduces the number of groups by a factor of four per level. Therefore carry information traverses O(log₄ N)=O(log N) levels, followed by constant local sum-generation work. B is the best bounded-fan-in architecture among the choices. A serial chain would take linear time, but is not the best organization; constant delay would require unbounded fan-in or a different physical model.

question_text: On all integers define n*m=max (n, m). Is this a monoid, Abelian group, group, or none?

On a set with an added−∞ element, that element would be an identity, but it is not an integer in the stated domain.

question_text: Hasse chains are f<e<b<a, f<g<a, f<d<c<a, with no further covers. How many complements does e have?
question_text_status: Self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and task; complete reproduced options/figures linked, original fidelity unverified.
solution: The bottom is f and top is a. A complement z must satisfy e∧z=f and e∨z=a. For each of g, d, c, the only common lower bound with e is f and only common upper bound is a; all three qualify. The remaining elements do not: f has join e, a has meet e, e meets itself at e, and b has meet e. Therefore exactly three complements exist, B. Complements need not be unique in a nondistributive lattice.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text: Over{a, b}, which is uncountable: all finite strings, all languages, regular languages, or Turing-recognizable languages?
question_text_status: Self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and task; complete reproduced options/figures linked, original fidelity unverified.
solution: Finite strings can be enumerated by length and lexicographic order, so Σ* is countably infinite. All languages form its power set P(Σ*), which is uncountable by Cantor’s theorem. In contrast, finite automata and Turing machines each have finite descriptions over a finite alphabet, so there are only countably many of either and hence only countably many languages they describe. Thus B. The distinction is between elements that are strings and arbitrary sets of those strings.

question_text: A page reference always repeats the previous page, is likely among recently used pages, always hits resident memory, or always faults.
question_text_status: Self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and task; complete reproduced options/figures linked, original fidelity unverified.
solution: Temporal locality is the tendency to reuse recently accessed data or instructions, for example within a loop. Hence the next page reference is likely to be among a recent working set, B. A program can move to a new phase and access a different page, and whether that page is resident depends on available memory and replacement history. Thus the three statements containing always are too strong.

solution: The handler’s action depends on the event. An ordinary completed-I/O interrupt may simply update device state and return, while a fault or trap requiring an unavailable resource may block the current process and allow another to run. This uses interrupt broadly enough to include synchronous traps/faults; a narrow device-only definition would need more careful distinctions about why the interrupted process blocks.

question_text_status: Self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and task; complete reproduced options/figures linked, original fidelity unverified.
solution: Thrashing occurs when processes repeatedly fault because their active working sets do not fit in available frames. The system spends excessive time moving pages rather than executing useful instructions, so C describes it. It increases rather than reduces paging traffic and degrades performance. solution: A dirty bit records whether a page has been modified since its backing-store copy was synchronized. subject: 05-algorithms
question_text: T(1)=1 and T(n)=2T(floor (n/2))+sqrt (n) for n≥2. Choose O(sqrt n), O(n), O(log n), none.
question_text_status: Self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and task; complete reproduced options/figures linked, original fidelity unverified.
solution: At recursion depth j there are roughly 2^j subproblems of size n/2^j. Their combined nonrecursive work is sqrt (n)·2^(j/2), increasing geometrically toward the leaves. Summing through depth about log 2 n gives O(n), and there are Θ(n) leaves each contributing constant work, providing Ω(n). Hence T(n)=Θ(n), so B. Equivalently the Master theorem has n^(log 2 2)=n and toll n^(1/2), which is polynomially smaller; rounding does not change the asymptotic order.

subject: 04-data-structures
question_text: A priority queue is used to implement a LIFO stack. PUSH inserts an item with a chosen integer key; POP deletes the minimum. Should keys be nonincreasing, nondecreasing, strictly increasing, or strictly decreasing?
question_text_status: Self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and task; complete reproduced options/figures linked, original fidelity unverified.
solution: The newest live item must have the smallest key so it is returned first. Assign successively decreasing keys, for example 0, −1, −2, …; then delete-min exactly follows last-in-first-out order. Strict decrease prevents ties whose unspecified resolution could return an older item. Thus D is the standard sufficient choice. A merely nonincreasing sequence permits equal keys and does not guarantee LIFO without an extra tie rule. Keys need only outrank still-live items, so global decrease is a simple implementation policy rather than the only possible schedule-aware assignment.
derived_answer: D as the sufficient unambiguous scheme

subject: 07-compiler-design
question_text: For expression prefix (a*b)*c op…where op is+, *, or exponentiation, which operators permit the accumulated product to remain in one register?
question_text_status: Self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and task; complete reproduced options/figures linked, original fidelity unverified.
solution: After computing a*b, the single accumulator holds that intermediate value. If op is+or*, ordinary precedence and left associativity allow completing the multiplication by c before moving to the following operation; the accumulator can be reused without spilling a*b. If op is exponentiation, the c-power subexpression binds more tightly and normally must be computed before multiplying by the held a*b, creating a second live intermediate. Thus A in the stated compiler-evaluation model. The omitted suffix and machine instruction set are not fully specified; recomputation or different schedules can change storage requirements, so this is not an architecture-independent impossibility theorem.

question_text: Vertices 1…100 are adjacent when their difference is 8 or12. Count connected components among 8, 4, 12, 25.
question_text_status: Self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and task; complete reproduced options/figures linked, original fidelity unverified.
solution: Every allowed difference is divisible by 4, so a path preserves residue modulo 4. There are at least four components. Each residue class contains 25 vertices; after rescaling by 4, its edges connect indices differing by 2 or3. These 25 indices form a connected graph: all odd indices connect by 2, all even indices connect by 2, and the edge 1–4 of difference 3 joins the two chains. Hence each residue class is one component, proving exactly four, B. The boundary argument is necessary; a gcd observation alone would only prove the lower bound for a finite interval.

question_text: Which regex describes binary strings with no substring 100? Choice D is 0*(10+1)*.
question_text_status: Self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and task; complete reproduced options/figures linked, original fidelity unverified.
solution: Any leading run of zeros is harmless and is covered by 0*. After the first 1, there cannot be two consecutive zeros, or the preceding 1 followed by those zeros would form 100. question_text_status: Self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and task; complete reproduced options/figures linked, original fidelity unverified.

CFG nonemptiness is found by marking variables that derive terminal strings until a fixed point. TM language equivalence is undecidable: if decidable, it could compare any TM with one recognizing the empty language and thereby decide TM language emptiness, an undecidable semantic property. question_title: Deterministic recognition with a middle marker
question_text: Which language is deterministic context-free: {wcwR:w∈{a, b}*}, unmarked even palindromes over{a, b, c}, {a^n b^n c^n}, or all palindromes over{a, b, c}?

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text: Three processes each may require two units of one resource. Minimum units guaranteeing no allocation deadlock among 3, 5, 4, 6?
question_text_status: Self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and task; complete reproduced options/figures linked, original fidelity unverified.
solution: With only three units, each process can hold one and wait for a second, creating deadlock. With four units, if all unfinished processes hold at most one, at least one unit remains available to give some process its second. It can finish and release its units, after which the argument repeats. Therefore four is sufficient and three can fail, so C. This is the standard worst-case incremental-allocation guarantee with eventual completion and no other resources; a restrictive admission policy could safely serialize processes with fewer units.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_title: A process signals instead of waiting
question_text: Nine processes repeat P(mutex);critical section;V(mutex). A tenth replaces its initial P by V. What maximum number can be inside simultaneously?
question_text_status: Self-contained paraphrase of essential givens and task; complete reproduced options/figures linked, original fidelity unverified.
solution: The faulty process never consumes a permit when entering and adds permits both before entering and after leaving. With a counting semaphore, it can complete enough loops to accumulate at least nine permits while the others wait to run. Then schedule all nine correct processes through P and pause each inside its critical section. Finally let the faulty process enter too: all ten are inside. Ten is the absolute upper bound because only ten processes exist, so it is attained. Even a saturating binary semaphore can be repeatedly reopened by the faulty process to admit more peers before they leave. Thus D.

subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_text: An 8085 must drive a one-bit output port at I/O address FF hexadecimal through a D flip-flop. The transferred bit is D3, and the output must clear at power-on. Using exactly one ten-input NAND gate, one inverter and one D flip-flop, give the interface circuit. State clock/reset polarities explicitly.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase with reconstructed code/netlist where needed; linked reproductions remain original-fidelity uncertain.
solution:
The eight-bit I/O address FFH is all ones. In an 8085 I/O cycle, that address is duplicated on the high address bus A15…A8, so these eight nonmultiplexed lines can be decoded without adding an address latch. Do not use AD7…AD0 directly throughout the write: those pins carry the data during the data phase.

Let /WR denote the active-low write strobe and IO/M=1 denote an I/O cycle. Use the one inverter to form W=NOT(/WR). The ten-input NAND receives A15,A14,…,A8,IO/M,W. Its output is
CLK = NOT(A15·A14·…·A8·IO/M·W).

A complete connection list is:
8085 D3 → D input of the flip-flop.
A15…A8, IO/M, NOT(/WR) → the ten NAND inputs.
NAND output → positive-edge-triggered CLK.
RESET OUT → active-high asynchronous CLEAR.
Q → the one-bit output.
Any asynchronous preset input is tied inactive.

For FFH on an I/O write, CLK goes low while /WR is asserted and rises when that write ends. The positive edge captures D3 while the data is valid. For another port, a memory cycle, or a nonwrite cycle, at least one NAND input is zero and the clock remains high. Asynchronous clearing makes Q=0 during the power-on reset independently of clock activity.

The flip-flop's clear polarity matters. The above netlist chooses an active-high CLEAR so the 8085's active-high RESET OUT connects directly. With an active-low /CLR device instead, connect the same active-low power-on /RESET IN net that resets the CPU to /CLR. Do not connect RESET OUT directly to /CLR and do not silently use a second inverter. The edge and reset assumptions are explicit because the question does not specify a particular flip-flop part. This is an ideal bus-timing design, assuming normal setup/hold timing and no wait-state or reset anomaly.
derived_answer: D←D3; CLK←NAND(A15,…,A8,IO/M,NOT(/WR)); asynchronous clear from reset; Q is the port output.

subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_text: An 8085 must drive a one-bit output port at I/O address FF hexadecimal through a D flip-flop. The transferred bit is D3, and the output must clear at power-on. Write an 8085 program producing equal ON and OFF intervals of seven bus/machine cycles each.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase with reconstructed code/netlist where needed; linked reproductions remain original-fidelity uncertain.
solution:
Only accumulator bit 3 affects this one-bit port. Complementing the entire accumulator is therefore enough to toggle the output: bit 3 alternates between 0 and 1. One program is

        MVI A,00H
LOOP:   CMA
        OUT FFH
        JMP LOOP

CMA takes one machine cycle, OUT takes three, and an unconditional JMP takes three. Between the end of one OUT and the end of the next OUT, the processor executes JMP, CMA and OUT. The total is 3+1+3=7 machine cycles. The same instruction path is used whether D3 is changing from 0 to 1 or from 1 to 0, so both steady-state half-periods are equal. At the FFH output port, values FFH and 00H alternate, but only their D3 bits are stored.

The initialization MVI is outside the loop and does not contribute to repeated periods. Power-on clearing ensures the initial output is low; the interval from reset release to the very first transition need not equal a later half-period. Interrupts and inserted wait states must be absent if exact timing is required.

Here “bus cycles” is interpreted as the 8085 machine-cycle count, not seven clock T-states. The instructions take 4+10+10=24 T-states in a normal execution, so a complete square-wave period is 14 machine cycles, or 48 T-states. Counting instruction bytes or taking “7” as seven T-states would give the wrong timing model.
derived_answer: MVI A,00H; LOOP: CMA; OUT FFH; JMP LOOP. Each steady-state half-period is 1+3+3=7 machine cycles.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_text: The vertices are the n² integer lattice points (x,y), 1≤x,y≤n, n≥2. Distinct vertices are adjacent when BOTH |x1−x2|≤1 and |y1−y2|≤1; an edge has Euclidean length sqrt((x1−x2)²+(y1−y2)²). This is the GateForum p11 adjacency, including the second-coordinate bound omitted in GFG. Find the minimum spanning-tree weight.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase with reconstructed code/netlist where needed; linked reproductions remain original-fidelity uncertain.
solution:
There are n² vertices, so every spanning tree has exactly n²−1 edges. Distinct integer lattice points are at distance at least 1; hence every spanning tree has weight at least n²−1.

This bound is achievable without using any diagonals. In each row, connect its n vertices consecutively with n−1 horizontal unit edges. This uses n(n−1) edges and leaves n connected row paths. Connect consecutive rows by vertical unit edges along the first column, using n−1 more edges. The result is connected and has n(n−1)+(n−1)=n²−1 edges; equivalently, joining the disjoint row trees by a path cannot create a cycle. Its weight is exactly n²−1, matching the lower bound.

For n=2 this construction has three unit edges and weight 3. Using a diagonal would replace a unit edge by one of length √2 and cannot improve the minimum.

The source variant matters for the companion maximum-weight question: GFG prints only |x1−x2|≤1, permitting long changes in y. For this minimum, however, the same answer remains valid under that literal variant. All distinct vertices are still at least unit distance apart, and the unit-edge construction is still allowed. Thus this particular answer is robust even though the reproduced graph definitions differ.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_text: The vertices are the n² integer lattice points (x,y), 1≤x,y≤n, n≥2. Distinct vertices are adjacent when BOTH |x1−x2|≤1 and |y1−y2|≤1; an edge has Euclidean length sqrt((x1−x2)²+(y1−y2)²). This is the GateForum p11 adjacency, including the second-coordinate bound omitted in GFG. Find the maximum spanning-tree weight; also distinguish the literal GFG graph that constrains only |x1−x2|≤1.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase with reconstructed code/netlist where needed; linked reproductions remain original-fidelity uncertain.
solution:
In the stated king-move grid, every edge is either horizontal/vertical with weight 1 or diagonal with weight √2. We therefore want as many diagonal edges as a spanning tree can contain.

Color vertex (x,y) by the parity of x+y. A diagonal changes both coordinates by one, so it preserves this parity; a horizontal or vertical edge changes it. Both parity classes are nonempty for n≥2. A connected spanning tree must consequently include at least one unit edge to join the two classes. Since it has n²−1 edges in total, its weight is at most (n²−2)√2+1.

To attain the bound, observe that the diagonal-only graph has exactly two connected components, one of each parity. Here is a constructive connectivity argument. Repeatedly use an upward diagonal to reduce y until reaching the first row; at a side boundary choose the inward direction, always possible because n≥2. On the first row, vertices of a fixed parity can move two columns at a time through a vertex of the second row. Thus all vertices of each parity are connected by diagonals. Take a spanning tree inside each diagonal component. Together they use n²−2 diagonal edges. Add any unit edge between the components. This produces a spanning tree attaining the upper bound.

For n=2 the two diagonals, joined by one side, have weight 2√2+1. That is the answer to GateForum's full adjacency rule. Under GFG's literal omission of the y-bound, longer edges are allowed when n≥3. Its maximum is instead

(2n−2)√(1+(n−1)²) + (n−1) + nΣ_(j=2)^(n−1)√(1+max(j−1,n−j)²).

Here is a separate optimality proof for that literal graph. Call vertices on y=1 or y=n boundary vertices. For each interior vertex at row j, select an edge to a farthest boundary row in an adjacent column. Such a column always exists for n≥2. Its length is √(1+max(j−1,n−j)²), a maximum edge across the cut isolating that vertex. Add these edges while each interior vertex is still isolated; all chosen parents are boundary vertices, so no cycle arises. By the maximum-spanning-tree cut property, each addition is safe.

Next add all 2n−2 boundary diagonals with |dx|=1 and |dy|=n−1. They are globally maximum edges, each of length √(1+(n−1)²), and form two disjoint alternating-row paths on the 2n boundary vertices. Interior attachments do not join those paths. Finally join them by a same-column edge from y=1 to y=n, of length n−1. Every competing cross-component edge with an interior endpoint is at most √(1+(n−2)²)<n−1 for n≥3. Remaining boundary cross-edges have length at most n−1, so this last edge is also cut-safe. At n=2 there are no interior vertices and the bridge length is 1.

The safe selections form a spanning tree and give the displayed sum: n equal-length interior attachments for each row j, 2n−2 boundary diagonals, and one bridge. Thus both materially different printed graphs have an explicit maximum and a proof, rather than silently restoring a bound in GFG.

subject: 03-programming-in-c
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase with reconstructed code/netlist where needed; linked reproductions remain original-fidelity uncertain.
solution:
Pass by value gives every call its own local x, but all calls still share the same global z. It is important not to copy z into each activation or to overwrite a caller's x with its child's final x.

On descent, no assignment z:=x+10 has executed yet: it comes after the recursive call. Therefore z stays 10 while the successive calls enter with x=10,20,30,40,50. Entered x=30, saved updated x=40: assign z=50.
Entered x=20, saved updated x=30: assign z=40.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text:
Use the GFG grammar with start symbol S:
S → bSe | PQR
P → bPc | ε
Q → cQd | ε
R → dRe | ε.
Terminals are b,c,d,e. Generated words are b^i c^j d^k e^m with nonnegative integer exponents. GateForum instead prints S→bSc and mistakenly gives nonpositive exponents; those literal variants must be distinguished.
What condition on i,j,k,m characterizes the generated language?
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase with reconstructed code/netlist where needed; linked reproductions remain original-fidelity uncertain.
solution:
Let t be the number of uses of S→bSe before S→PQR. Let p,q,r be the numbers of recursive productions used by P,Q,R. Their contributions are P⇒b^p c^p, Q⇒c^q d^q and R⇒d^r e^r. Combining them with the outer b/e pairs gives

i=t+p,  j=p+q,  k=q+r,  m=r+t,
where t,p,q,r are nonnegative integers. Adding opposite equations yields the necessary relation i+k=j+m.

To prove sufficiency, assume all four exponents are nonnegative and i+k=j+m. Choose any integer t satisfying max(0,i−j)≤t≤min(i,m), and put p=i−t, q=j−i+t, r=m−t. These parameters are nonnegative and reproduce every exponent, including k=j−i+m. Such a t always exists: i−j≤m follows from k≥0, while i−j≤i follows from j≥0. Thus the equality, together with nonnegativity, is also sufficient.

GateForum's visibly different rule S→bSc cannot silently be substituted. Its full generated form is b^(t+p)c^(p+q)d^(q+r)e^r c^t, with a trailing block of c symbols after the d/e blocks. For example S⇒bSc⇒bPQRc⇒bcdc is possible, contradicting that reproduction's claim that every generated word is in b*c*d*e*. Restricting to words of the claimed block form forces either t=0, or q=r=0 so no d/e lies before the final c. The t=0 case gives i=p,j=p+q,k=q+r,m=r, hence i+k=j+m and j≥i. The other case gives only b^i c^i, already included in that subset. Thus the block-form subset has that extra inequality, but it is not the whole literal GateForum language. The word be belongs to GFG but not GateForum.

Finally, GateForum's printed i,j,k,m≤0 is inconsistent with arbitrary nonempty strings of repeated terminals. Taken literally as string exponents, only zero exponents are meaningful, leaving ε; the language intended by the grammar is not that singleton. This solution uses nonnegative counts, as explicitly printed in GFG, and discloses both source differences.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_text: A hash table has n≥1 buckets, uses external chaining, and is initially empty. K distinct keys are inserted. Each key hashes uniformly to one of the n buckets. Under the standard additional assumption that different keys hash independently, find the probability that bucket 1 is empty after K insertions.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase with reconstructed code/netlist where needed; linked reproductions remain original-fidelity uncertain.
solution:
A single inserted key avoids bucket 1 with probability (n−1)/n=1−1/n. Bucket 1 is empty after K insertions exactly when every one of those K keys avoids it. Under independent hashing, multiply the K probabilities to obtain

P(bucket 1 empty) = (1−1/n)^K.

The table may have collisions in other buckets; they do not affect this event. External chaining allows arbitrarily many keys in a bucket, so K need not be at most n. For K=0 the probability is 1, including the n=1 case, by the empty-product convention. For n=1 and K≥1 it is 0, because the only bucket must receive every key. For n=2,K=3 it is (1/2)^3=1/8.

The independence qualification is substantive. The source supplies the uniform probability for any individual key, but marginal uniformity alone is not enough to multiply events. For example, choose one uniformly random bucket U and send all keys to U. Every key is marginally uniform, yet bucket 1 remains empty with probability 1−1/n for every K≥1, rather than (1−1/n)^K. The displayed answer uses the usual independent-uniform hashing model and is not claimed under that correlated alternative.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_text: A hash table has n≥1 buckets, uses external chaining, and is initially empty. K distinct keys are inserted. Each key hashes uniformly to one of the n buckets. Under the standard additional assumption that different keys hash independently, find the probability that none of the K insertions causes a collision.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase with reconstructed code/netlist where needed; linked reproductions remain original-fidelity uncertain.
solution:
After j collision-free insertions, exactly j buckets are occupied. Conditional on that event, the next independently hashed key must choose one of the n−j empty buckets, which has probability (n−j)/n. Multiplying from j=0 through K−1 gives

P(no collision in K insertions)
= 1·(n−1)/n·(n−2)/n·…·(n−K+1)/n
= n! / ((n−K)! n^K), for 0≤K≤n.

For K>n the probability is zero by the pigeonhole principle. Do not extend the factorial formula to a negative factorial. At K=0, the empty product is 1; at K=1, no collision is possible and the result is also 1. For n=3,K=2 it is 2/3, because only the second key can cause the first collision.

An equivalent counting argument considers n^K equally likely ordered bucket-choice sequences. Collision-free choices are injective assignments of the K ordered keys to the n buckets, numbering n(n−1)…(n−K+1). The keys are distinct, but that does not make their bucket values distinct automatically.

This derivation needs independent uniform hashing, not just equal marginal bucket probabilities. Under the correlated scheme that sends every key to one common randomly chosen bucket, the probability is already zero at K=2 despite uniform marginals. That source-model limitation is stated explicitly rather than hidden in the multiplication.

question_text: A hash table has n≥1 buckets, uses external chaining, and is initially empty. K distinct keys are inserted. Each key hashes uniformly to one of the n buckets. Under the standard additional assumption that different keys hash independently, find the probability that the first collision occurs on insertion K.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase with reconstructed code/netlist where needed; linked reproductions remain original-fidelity uncertain.
solution:
The event consists of two parts: the first K−1 insertions are collision-free, and the Kth key hits one of their occupied buckets. Given the first part, there are exactly K−1 occupied buckets, so the conditional probability of the second part is (K−1)/n.

For 2≤K≤n+1, the requested probability is therefore

[n(n−1)…(n−K+2)/n^(K−1)]·(K−1)/n
= n!(K−1) / ((n−K+1)! n^K).

The upper endpoint n+1 is legitimate: the first n keys could fill all n buckets without a collision, after which the next key certainly collides. Its probability is n!/n^n. For K=1 the event is impossible because an empty table has no occupied bucket. For K>n+1, a first collision must already have happened, so the probability is also zero.

As a check, write p_j for the probability of no collision after j insertions. Then P(first at K)=p_(K−1)−p_K. Summing from K=2 to n+1 telescopes to p_1−p_(n+1)=1, as required. For n=2 the probabilities are 1/2 at K=2 and 1/2 at K=3. These arguments all use independent uniform bucket choices; the source's uniform marginals alone do not determine the distribution of the first collision.

question_title: Count injections into a larger set
question_text: Let F be all one-to-one functions from {1,…,n} to {1,…,m}, where m≥n≥1. How many functions belong to F?
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase with reconstructed code/netlist where needed; linked reproductions remain original-fidelity uncertain.
solution:
Choose the values of the function in domain order. There are m choices for f(1). Once it is chosen, injectivity excludes that value for f(2), leaving m−1 choices. In general f(i) has m−i+1 choices after the preceding i−1 images have been fixed. The multiplication principle gives

|F| = m(m−1)…(m−n+1) = m!/(m−n)!.

Another way is to choose the n-element image set, in C(m,n) ways, then assign its distinct members to the n labelled domain elements, in n! ways. Hence |F|=C(m,n)n!, the same result.

The distinction between a function and an image set matters: C(m,n) alone discards the order in which the n selected values are assigned to 1,…,n. For n=2,m=3, the image set {1,2} supplies both f(1)=1,f(2)=2 and f(1)=2,f(2)=1. There are six injections overall, not three. At n=1 the answer is m, and at m=n it is n!, the number of permutations, providing simple boundary checks.

question_title: Count injections whose image contains one
question_text: Let F be all one-to-one functions from {1,…,n} to {1,…,m}, where m≥n≥1. How many f satisfy f(i)=1 for some domain element i?
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase with reconstructed code/netlist where needed; linked reproductions remain original-fidelity uncertain.
solution:
Because f is one-to-one, the codomain value 1 can occur at exactly one domain position if it occurs at all. Choose that position i in n ways. The remaining n−1 domain elements must receive distinct values from the other m−1 codomain values, giving (m−1)!/(m−n)! assignments. Thus the total is

n·(m−1)!/(m−n)!.

There is no double-counting: each satisfying function has a unique preimage of 1, so it appears in exactly one of the n cases. Equivalently, choose its image set to contain 1 and n−1 other values, then order the n image values over the domain. This gives C(m−1,n−1)n!, equal to the first expression.

As a probability check, divide by all m!/(m−n)! injections. The fraction whose image contains a specified codomain value is n/m, consistent with an image set containing n out of m values symmetrically. At n=1 there is only one satisfying function, f(1)=1. At n=m every injection is a bijection, so all n! functions qualify. These checks also show why simply multiplying the total by 1/m would be wrong: any of n domain positions, not a fixed one, may map to 1.

question_text: Let F be all one-to-one functions from {1,…,n} to {1,…,m}, where m≥n≥1. GFG asks for f(i)<f(j) for ALL 1≤i<j≤n; GateForum asks for this for SOME pair. Give the count for each printed variant.

For the GFG universal condition, f(1)<f(2)<…<f(n). Choose any n distinct codomain values. There is exactly one way to place them in increasing order on the ordered domain. Consequently the number is C(m,n). Choosing the set contributes all the freedom; multiplying by n! would wrongly include orders that violate monotonicity.

GateForum prints an existential condition: there must be at least one pair i<j for which f(i)<f(j). Count its complement. Failure means f(i)≥f(j) for every i<j. Since f is injective, equality is impossible, so failure is exactly strict decrease: f(1)>f(2)>…>f(n). For each n-element image set there is one decreasing order, giving C(m,n) failures. Subtracting from all injections gives

m!/(m−n)! − C(m,n).

For n=1, the universal statement is vacuously true and all m functions count; the existential statement has no available pair and counts zero. Both formulas reflect this difference. For n=3,m=3, there is one universally increasing permutation, while five permutations have at least one increasing pair; only 3,2,1 fails the existential condition. For n=2 the two numerical answers happen to coincide, which can conceal the wording discrepancy in small checks.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_text: Let R be a reflexive and transitive relation on a set A. Define E={(a,b):aRb and bRa}. Prove that E is an equivalence relation.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential problem paraphrase with reconstructed code/netlist where needed; linked reproductions remain original-fidelity uncertain.
solution:
We must check the three equivalence-relation axioms on the same set A.

Reflexivity: for every a∈A, reflexivity of R gives aRa. Both required directions in the definition of E are then the same true statement, so aEa.

Symmetry: if aEb, the definition supplies both aRb and bRa. Reversing their order immediately gives bEa. No symmetry assumption about R is needed; taking its mutual part creates symmetry.

Transitivity: suppose aEb and bEc. Then aRb and bRc, so transitivity of R yields aRc. We also have cRb and bRa, so another use of transitivity gives cRa. Both directions hold, establishing aEc.

Thus E is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, hence an equivalence relation. Its classes group elements that are mutually related by R. In a directed-reachability interpretation, R says one vertex can reach another, and E groups vertices that can reach each other in both directions.

The proof does not claim that R itself is symmetric or antisymmetric. A reflexive, transitive relation is a preorder and may relate distinct elements in both directions. Passing to E-classes is precisely how the companion part removes that possible failure of antisymmetry.
derived_answer: E is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.

question_text: Let R be a reflexive and transitive relation on a set A. Define E={(a,b):aRb and bRa}. For E-classes C,D, define C≤D when there exist a∈C,b∈D with aRb. Prove that this gives a partial order on A/E.

First show that the existential definition is independent of representatives. Suppose aRb with a∈C,b∈D. If a′∈C and b′∈D, then a′Ea and bEb′, so a′Ra and bRb′. By transitivity, a′RaRbRb′ gives a′Rb′. Thus one pair of related representatives implies every pair is related; changing representatives cannot change the answer.

Reflexivity: choose a∈C. Since aRa, the defining witness gives C≤C.

Antisymmetry: suppose C≤D and D≤C. Choose any a∈C,b∈D. Representative independence gives aRb from the first relation and bRa from the second. Hence aEb, so a and b have the same E-class and C=D. Antisymmetry is equality of classes, not necessarily equality of their individual representatives.

Transitivity: suppose C≤D and D≤H. Choose a∈C,b∈D,c∈H. Representative independence supplies aRb and bRc; transitivity of R yields aRc. Therefore C≤H.

All partial-order axioms hold. The preliminary representative step is essential when starting from existential witnesses: the witness b from C≤D and the witness b′ from D≤H might be different elements of D. Their E-equivalence supplies bRb′, which connects the two chains. Omitting that link would leave a gap in a direct transitivity proof. No total-order claim follows: two equivalence classes can be incomparable when neither direction of R holds between them.
