subject: 05-algorithms
question_text: An undirected graph has vertices {a,b,e,f,g,h} and edges {ae,ab,af,eb,eg,bf,bh,fh,fg,gh}. Which listed sequences can be depth-first traversals starting at a, allowing arbitrary neighbor order? I. a,b,e,g,h,f; II. a,b,f,e,h,g; III. a,b,f,h,g,e; IV. a,f,g,h,b,e. A. I, II and IV only; B. I and IV only; C. II, III and IV only; D. I, III and IV only.
question_text_status: self-contained author paraphrase; visually checked against secondary reproductions; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. DFS must finish every reachable unexplored neighbor before returning from a vertex. The three accepted sequences can be realized without any backtrack until all six vertices are visited because each consecutive pair is an edge. In II the transition from f to e would require backtracking through b, but f still has unvisited neighbors g and h, so DFS cannot yet leave f. Hence e cannot be next.

2. I, III and IV each trace a simple path through all vertices using displayed edges, so a neighbor order realizes each. In II, f has no edge to e and still has unvisited neighbors g and h; DFS must visit one of these before backtracking. Thus II is impossible and the answer is D.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_text: Array insertion sort normally uses linear search to find where the next element belongs. If binary search replaces that search, what happens to worst-case total running time? A. It remains Θ(n²); B. It becomes Θ(n(log n)²); C. It becomes Θ(n log n); D. It becomes Θ(n).
question_text_status: self-contained author paraphrase; visually checked against secondary reproductions; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. During insertion into a sorted prefix of length i, search needs O(log i) comparisons but opening an array slot may move i elements. Summing these movements over all prefixes dominates the sum of logarithmic searches. Binary search improves comparisons, not the cost of physically maintaining the sorted array.

2. Binary search reduces comparisons needed to locate each insertion position, but array elements still must shift to make room. A reverse-sorted input needs 1+2+...+(n−1)=Θ(n²) moves. The worst-case runtime therefore remains Θ(n²), A, despite O(n log n) comparisons.

subject: 04-data-structures
question_title: Fixed-rank selection from a min heap
question_text: A min-heap has n elements, with its smallest at the root. For n≥7, what time is sufficient to find the seventh smallest element, as a function of n? A. Θ(n log n); B. Θ(n); C. Θ(log n); D. Θ(1).
question_text_status: self-contained author paraphrase; visually checked against secondary reproductions; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. The candidate frontier contains the roots of all unexplored subheaps. Heap order makes its minimum the smallest unseen element. Extract that node and add at most its two children, preserving the invariant. After seven iterations the frontier and work are bounded by constants independent of n.

2. Maintain a small candidate min-priority queue initially containing the root. Repeatedly remove its minimum and insert that node’s children; after seven removals the extracted value is seventh smallest. Only a constant number of nodes and candidate operations are used because rank 7 is fixed, hence Θ(1) with respect to n, D, assuming n≥7. Repeatedly deleting from the original n-element heap is unnecessarily expensive.

subject: excluded
question_text: Which typing statement is false? A. In statically typed languages each program variable has a fixed type; B. In untyped languages values do not have types; C. In dynamically typed languages variables have no types; D. In all statically typed languages each variable is associated with values of only a single type during execution.
question_text_status: self-contained author paraphrase; visually checked against secondary reproductions; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. Static type and runtime class are different concepts. A variable declared as a superclass reference retains that declared type while holding references to multiple subclasses. This gives a counterexample to D without implying that the compiler changes the declared type of the variable.

2. A variable in a statically typed language can have one declared static type while referring at different times to values of different compatible runtime subtypes. For example an Animal reference may refer to Dog and Cat objects. Thus D’s claim that values must have only a single runtime type in all statically typed languages is false. The other statements use the conventional distinction between declared variable types, dynamically typed values and untyped formalisms; that terminology is not uniform across every language theory.
derived_answer: D under the standard polymorphic-language distinction

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text: In the conventional comparison for a fixed-block-size file system, increasing block size leads to: A. Better disk throughput but poorer space utilization; B. Better throughput and better utilization; C. Poorer throughput but better utilization; D. Poorer throughput and poorer utilization.
question_text_status: self-contained author paraphrase; visually checked against secondary reproductions; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. Reading a larger contiguous block transfers more useful bytes per seek or setup cost for a sequential workload. But the last block of a file is allocated in full even when only partly used; increasing the allocation unit can increase this internal slack. These effects explain the conventional throughput/utilization tradeoff.

2. Larger blocks amortize per-I/O overhead across more bytes, often improving sequential disk throughput, but waste more unused space in partially occupied final blocks. Thus better throughput with poorer space utilization, A, under the conventional workload comparison. It is not a universal guarantee for every random-access workload.

question_title: Size of a flat page table
question_text: With 32-bit virtual addresses and 1 KB pages, why is a one-level page table impractical? A. Large internal fragmentation; B. Large external fragmentation; C. Large memory overhead for page tables; D. Large computation overhead in translation.
question_text_status: self-contained author paraphrase; visually checked against secondary reproductions; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. A 1 KB page means 2¹⁰ byte offsets, so a virtual address splits into 22 page-number bits and 10 offset bits. Even a sparsely used process address space requires all 2²² slots in a flat table. Four-byte entries are an illustration, not an additional given: they would occupy 16 MiB per table.

2. A 1 KiB page uses 10 offset bits, leaving 22 virtual-page bits in a 32-bit address. A flat table therefore needs 2^22 entries per address space; at 4 bytes each this is 16 MiB. The large memory overhead, C, motivates multilevel or other sparse organizations.

subject: 10-computer-networks
question_text: Which assertion about Internet Protocol is false? A. A computer can have several IP addresses; B. Packets from the same source to the same destination can take different routes; C. A packet is discarded if it cannot reach its destination within a bounded number of hops; D. A source cannot set an outgoing packet’s route, which is determined only by router routing tables.
question_text_status: self-contained author paraphrase; visually checked against secondary reproductions; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. A and B are compatible with multiple interfaces and datagram routing. For C, IPv4 routers decrement TTL and discard expired packets. To refute D it suffices to cite the historical source-route options; their rarity or filtering in current networks does not make the categorical protocol statement true.

2. Historical IPv 4 includes loose/strict source-route options that allow a sender to influence/specify a route. Therefore the categorical assertion that only router tables can determine the route is false, D. Multiple addresses and differing packet routes are possible, while TTL limits forwarding hops. Source routing is commonly filtered or disabled operationally, which does not erase the protocol capability considered by this historical question.

subject: 10-computer-networks
question_text: Which functionality must the transport protocol provide over and above network-layer service? A. Recovery from packet losses; B. Detection of duplicate packets; C. Correct-order packet delivery; D. End-to-end connectivity.
question_text_status: self-contained author paraphrase; visually checked against secondary reproductions; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. Network delivery addresses hosts; transport adds end-to-end communication between application endpoints, usually identified by ports. TCP implements the first three enhancements, whereas UDP provides transport service without promising any of them. Hence they cannot be universal requirements of the layer.

2. Transport supplies end-to-end process communication above network-layer host delivery, D. Reliability, duplicate suppression and in-order delivery are features of some transport protocols, notably TCP, but are not required of all: UDP does not guarantee them. End-to-end connectivity here means communication service, not necessarily a connection-oriented handshake.

subject: 09-database-management-systems
question_text: Which operation may lead to an irrecoverable database error? A. Writing an item after an uncommitted transaction reads it; B. Reading an item after an uncommitted transaction reads it; C. Reading an item written by a committed transaction; D. Reading an item written by an uncommitted transaction.
question_text_status: self-contained author paraphrase; visually checked against secondary reproductions; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. Use the concrete schedule W₁(X), R₂(X), C₂, A₁. Transaction 2 has already committed a result based on transaction 1’s value when transaction 1 aborts. Recovery would need to undo a committed dependency, which is why the schedule is nonrecoverable. The word “may” matters: a dirty read need not always lead to such a commit order.

2. If T 2 reads data written by uncommitted T 1, then T 2 commits before T 1 aborts, the schedule is nonrecoverable: a committed transaction depended on an aborted value. Thus D may lead to the stated error. A dirty read alone does not always force irrecoverability; delaying dependent commits can permit cascading rollback.

question_text: Translate SELECT DISTINCT a₁,a₂,...,aₙ FROM r₁,r₂,...,rₘ WHERE P into classical relational algebra. Every option first applies selection σ_P and then projection π_(a₁,...,aₙ). Their innermost operation is: A. r₁×r₂×...×rₘ; B. r₁⋈r₂⋈...⋈rₘ; C. r₁∪r₂∪...∪rₘ; D. r₁∩r₂∩...∩rₘ.

Finally SELECT chooses attributes, and DISTINCT removes repeated projected tuples. A natural join would additionally impose equality on common-named columns, which this arbitrary SQL query does not necessarily request.

2. The comma-separated FROM clause forms the Cartesian product of all relations, WHERE applies selection σ_P, and SELECT DISTINCT applies set projection onto the listed attributes. Thus π_attributes(σ_P(r 1×...×rm)), A, with attribute renaming/qualification as required and the classical relational-algebra interpretation.

question_title: Upward-closed truth in a partial order
question_text: A partially ordered set (S,≤) has two minimal elements a,b and a maximum c. A predicate P has P(a)=true, P(b)=false, and P(x)⇒P(y) whenever x≤y. Which cannot be true? A. subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_text: Let α(x), β(x) be first-order formulas whose only free variable is x. Which formula is logically valid? A. ((∀x α)⇒(∀x β))⇒∀x(α⇒β); B. (∀x α)⇒∃x(α∧β); C. ((∀x(α∨β))⇒(∃x α))⇒(∀x α); D. (∀x(α⇒β))⇒((∀x α)⇒(∀x β)).
question_text_status: self-contained author paraphrase; visually checked against secondary reproductions; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. For D, fix an arbitrary domain element a. Universal instantiation gives both α(a)⇒β(a) and α(a), hence β(a) by modus ponens. Since a was arbitrary, universal generalization proves ∀x β(x). To eliminate the other candidates, it is enough to exhibit one interpretation in which each is false, rather than attempting to prove their negations in every interpretation.

2. If every x satisfies α(x)→β(x), and every x satisfies α(x), then every x satisfies β(x). This is the valid formula in D. For A take a two-element domain with α true only at one point and β false everywhere: its premise is vacuously true but its conclusion fails. For B take α always true and β always false. For C take a two-element domain with α true at exactly one point. Then ∃xα is true, so the inner implication is true regardless of β, while ∀xα is false; the full implication fails. Thus the alternatives are not valid.

question_text: Consider α=[∀x(P(x)↔∀y(Q(x,y)↔¬Q(y,y)))]⇒[∀x ¬P(x)]. Interpretation I₁ has natural-number domain, P(x) meaning “x is prime”, and Q(x,y) meaning “y divides x”. I₂ is identical except P(x) means “x is composite”. Which satisfies α? A. I₁ only; B. I₂ only; C. Neither; D. Both.
question_text_status: self-contained author paraphrase; visually checked against secondary reproductions; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. First evaluate the inner universal formula for a fixed x. The condition at y=1 already fails: 1 divides x and also divides itself, so Q(x,1) is true while ¬Q(1,1) is false. Thus the proposed characterization is false for every natural x. The antecedent then asserts that P is empty, contrary to the existence of a prime in I₁ or a composite in I₂.

2. Q(y,y) is true because each positive natural number divides itself. Thus Q(x,y)↔¬Q(y,y) would require Q(x,y) false for every y. Taking y=x for positive x, or y=1, makes this impossible, so the universally quantified characterization on the right of the biconditional defining P is false. Both interpretations have some P-elements (primes in I 1, composites in I 2), making the antecedent ∀x[P(x)↔that characterization] false. Hence the full implication is true in both interpretations, D.

question_text: Distribute m identical balls among n distinct bags, each containing at least k balls, where k≥1 and m≥kn. How many distributions exist? subject: 05-algorithms
question_text: Given T(1)=1, find T(m²) for integer m≥1. GFG prints T(n+1)=T(n)+floor(sqrt(n−1)), n≥1; GateForum instead prints floor(sqrt(n+1)). Preserve both versions. Options: A. (m/6)(21m−39)+4; B. (m/6)(4m²−3m+5); C. (m/2)(3m^(2.5)−11m+20)−5; D. (m/6)(5m³−34m²+137m−104)+5/6.
question_text_status: self-contained author paraphrase; visually checked against secondary reproductions; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. For the alternate recurrence telescope from T(1)=1 to T(m²), so each integer j contributes floor(sqrt(j)). In the block k²≤j<(k+1)² the value is k and the block length is 2k+1. Use sum k=(m−1)m/2 and sum k²=(m−1)m(2m−1)/6 to simplify. For the literal GFG version the shifted range omits the final terms m and m−1 and adds the initial 1, explaining the difference −2m+2.

2. The reproductions differ: GFG visibly prints T(n+1)=T(n)+floor(sqrt(n−1)), while GateForum prints floor(sqrt(n+1)). For the latter, T(m²)=sum_(j=1)^(m²)floor(sqrt(j)). Group j from k² through(k+1)²−1: for k<m there are 2 k+1 copies of k, followed by the final m. Hence sum_(k=1)^(m−1)k(2 k+1)+m=m(4 m²−3 m+5)/6, option B. Literal GFG instead gives 1+sum_(j=0)^(m²−2)floor(sqrt(j))=m(4 m²−3 m+5)/6−2 m+2, including m=1. These are not silently equated; original wording/key are needed to resolve the source discrepancy.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_text: How many perfect matchings does the complete graph on six labeled vertices have? A. 15; B. 24; C. 30; D. 60.
question_text_status: self-contained author paraphrase; visually checked against secondary reproductions; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. A perfect matching partitions all six vertices into three disjoint unordered pairs. Choose the partner of one designated vertex, remove that pair, and repeat with a designated remaining vertex. This avoids counting the same matching in different pair orders. In the factorial calculation, division by 2³ removes within-pair order and division by 3! removes pair order.

2. Pair a fixed vertex with any of 5 others; pair the smallest remaining vertex with any of 3; the final pair is forced. Thus 5×3×1=15 perfect matchings, A. Equivalently 6!/(2³·3!)=15.

question_text: An injective map f:A→B induces g:2^A→2^B by g(C)={f(x):x∈C} and h:2^B→2^A by h(D)={x∈A:f(x)∈D}. Which holds for every D⊆B? A. g(h(D))⊆D; B. g(h(D))⊇D; C. g(h(D))∩D=∅; D. g(h(D))∩(B−D)≠∅.
question_text_status: self-contained author paraphrase; visually checked against secondary reproductions; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. An element b is in g(h(D)) exactly when b=f(a) for some a∈A whose image lies in D. This requires both b∈f(A) and b∈D, yielding D∩f(A). A value in D outside the image is never recovered, so injectivity does not justify the reverse containment.

2. h(D)=f^-1(D), so g(h(D))=f(f^-1(D))=D∩f(A), which is always a subset of D. Thus A. Equality need not hold because f is injective but not assumed onto B. This inclusion actually holds even without injectivity.

question_text: On {a,b,c}, binary operations + and × are specified by tables, with the left operand selecting the row and the right operand the column, columns a,b,c. question_text: Let Σ={a,b,c,d,e}, with g(a)=3,g(b)=5,g(c)=7,g(d)=9,g(e)=11, and let pᵢ be the ith prime (p₁=2). Encode a nonempty string s=a₁...aₙ by f(s)=product pᵢ^g(aᵢ), and a nonempty sequence of nonempty strings (s₁,...,sₘ) by h=product pᵢ^f(sᵢ). Which can be such an h? A. 2⁷3⁷5⁷; B. 2⁸3⁸5⁸; C. 2⁹3⁹5⁹; D. 2¹⁰5¹⁰7¹⁰.
question_text_status: self-contained author paraphrase; visually checked against secondary reproductions; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. Prime factorization makes the outer positions and exponents uniquely recoverable. Every inner nonempty string encoding begins with at least 2³, so it is divisible by 8. Thus exponents 7,9,10 cannot encode any inner string. Conversely exponent 8 is exactly f(a), and B uses consecutive outer primes with three such exponents.

2. A string encoding f(s) uses consecutive primes starting with 2, with exponents from{3,5,7,9,11}. In particular f(a)=2³=8. Therefore 2^8·3^8·5^8 is the sequence encoding of(a,a,a), so B. Exponents 7 and 9 are not valid nonempty string encodings because such encodings are divisible by 8. D skips prime 3 in the outer encoding and also uses exponent 10, which is invalid.

question_title: Minimum degree from an edge bound
question_text: An undirected graph G=(V,E) satisfies |E|≤3|V|−6. Its minimum degree is min over v∈V of degree(v). Which value cannot be the minimum degree? A. 3; B. 4; C. 5; D. 6.
question_text_status: self-contained author paraphrase; visually checked against secondary reproductions; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. Apply the handshake lemma: sum of vertex degrees equals twice the number of edges. If every vertex had degree at least 6, the sum would be at least 6|V|, contradicting the bound 6|V|−12. Therefore at least one vertex has degree below 6. No assumption that the graph is planar is needed.

2. The degree sum is 2|E|≤6|V|−12, so the average degree is strictly less than 6. At least one vertex therefore has degree≤5, and the minimum degree cannot equal 6, D. The argument needs an undirected graph and a nonempty vertex set satisfying the inequality, but does not require proving planarity from the edge bound.

question_title: Consistency condition for a rank-two linear system
question_text: The equations are 2x+y−4z=α, 4x+3y−12z=5, and x+2y−8z=7. The second and third coefficient columns are linearly dependent. For how many values of α are there infinitely many solutions? A. 0; B. 1; C. 2; D. Infinitely many.

solution:
1. The dependence of columns suggests combining y and z, not setting either to zero. Substitute u=y−4z; the last two equations have a nonsingular 2×2 coefficient matrix and determine x,u uniquely. The first then imposes one consistency condition on α. Once it holds, every real z gives a corresponding y, hence a one-parameter infinite solution set.

2. Put u=y−4 z. The last two equations become 4 x+3 u=5 and x+2 u=7, giving x=−11/5 and u=23/5. The first equation is then consistent only for α=2 x+u=1/5. At that value z is free and y=u+4 z, giving infinitely many solutions. Thus exactly one value of α works, option B.

question_title: Newton iteration on a piecewise-linear graph
question_text: A piecewise-linear f has drawn vertices (0,1), (0.5,0.5), approximately (0.8,−1), (1.55,0.5), and (2.05,1), with first and last straight segments extended. Marked roots are 0.6 and 1.3. Starting points x₀, x₁, x₂ lie respectively in the first descending segment, the steep descending segment, and the final rising segment. Newton–Raphson is started separately from each. Which roots result, in that order? A. (1.3,0.6,0.6); B. (0.6,0.6,1.3); C. (1.3,1.3,0.6); D. (1.3,0.6,1.3). Starting at x₀ on the leftmost segment gives x=1, which is on the rising middle segment and then gives the root 1.3. Starting at x₁ on the steep descending segment gives the root 0.6 immediately. Starting at x₂ on the rightmost segment gives 1.05, then 1.3 on the rising middle segment. Therefore the plotted-segment interpretation gives (1.3,0.6,1.3), D. subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_title: Largest spacing in a custom floating-point format
question_text: A 16-bit floating-point scheme has sign s at bit 15, six-bit exponent e at bits 14–9, and nine-bit mantissa integer m at bits 8–0. Its value is (−1)^s(1+m·2^(−9))2^(e−31) if e≠111111₂, and zero otherwise. What is the maximum difference between successive representable real numbers? A. 2^(−40); B. 2^(−9); C. 2^22; D. 2^31.
question_text_status: self-contained author paraphrase; visually checked against secondary reproductions; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. Within an exponent binade, incrementing the nine-bit mantissa integer by one increments the value by 2^(e−40). Maximizing this requires the largest nonreserved exponent, 62. The positive/negative sign duplicates gaps by symmetry; crossing zero and crossing adjacent exponent ranges cannot exceed the largest within-binade gap.

2. There are six exponent bits and nine fractional mantissa bits. Exponent 63 is reserved for zero, so the largest usable exponent is e=62. For fixed e, adjacent significands differ by 2⁻⁹, giving spacing 2^(e−31−9). This is largest at e=62, namely 2²², option C. Crossing a binade boundary has the smaller binade’s spacing, and the gaps adjacent to zero are only 2⁻³¹, so neither produces a larger gap.

subject: 01-digital-logic
question_title: Minimal states for a latched count-difference detector
question_text: A synchronous sequential circuit has one input and two output bits. Let zₖ,nₖ count zeros and ones in the first k input bits. Initially output is 00. When zₖ−nₖ first reaches 2, output becomes 10 forever. When nₖ−zₖ first reaches 2, output becomes 01 forever. What is the minimum number of states? A. 5; B. 6; C. 7; D. 8.
question_text_status: self-contained author paraphrase; visually checked against secondary reproductions; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. Before absorption retain only d=zₖ−nₖ. On input 0 increment d and on input 1 decrement it. Values −1,0,+1 are nonabsorbing and still output 00; reaching +2 or −2 selects different permanent outputs. Distinguish 0 from +1 by suffix 0, 0 from −1 by suffix 1, and −1 from +1 by suffix 0, proving the three transient states cannot merge.

2. Before a threshold is reached, it suffices to track d=(zeros seen)−(ones seen) in {−1,0,1}. Reaching +2 or −2 enters a separate absorbing state with output 10 or 01. Thus five states suffice. They are all distinguishable: the absorbing states have different outputs, and appropriate one-bit continuations separate each pair of the three pre-threshold states. Hence five states are necessary, option A.

question_title: Minimum literal counts for the reproduced Karnaugh map
question_text: Literal count counts every variable occurrence, complemented or not; for example xy+xz has four literals. Find minimum literal counts for a product-of-sums and a sum-of-products, respectively, for this four-variable Karnaugh map. Rows xy and columns zw both use Gray order 00,01,11,10. Rows are: 00:(X,1,0,1); 01:(0,1,X,0); 11:(1,X,X,0); 10:(X,0,0,X), with X a don’t-care. A. (11,9); B. (9,13); C. (9,10); D. (11,11). 1. For SOP, group 1 cells with optional X cells and never cover a specified 0; this yields ¬w¬y, w¬x¬z, x¬w¬z. For POS, group zeros with optional X cells, yielding factors (y∨¬x),(¬w∨¬z),(¬y∨¬z),(w∨x∨¬y). Count variable occurrences, not number of groups: SOP has 8 and POS has 9. subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_title: Controlled XOR inputs of an adder-subtractor
question_text:
An n-bit ripple-carry ALU has a full adder at each bit. At bit i its inputs are Ai, Bi XOR K, and carry Ci; the output is Si and the next carry. K is shared by all XOR gates and C0 is the least-significant carry input. For two's-complement operands, which operations can be performed by choosing only K and C0?
A. A+B and A−B, but not A+1
B. A+B and A+1, but not A−B
C. A+B, but neither A−B nor A+1
D. A+B, A−B and A+1
question_text_status: self-contained faithful paraphrase of visually reviewed third-party reproduction; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. A full-adder chain adds its two input words and the initial carry, so S=A+(B XOR K...K)+C0 modulo 2^n.
2. Enumerate the controls: (0,0) produces A+B; (0,1) produces A+B+1; (1,0) produces A+complement(B)=A−B−1; (1,1) produces A−B.
3. For arbitrary B none of these cancels B entirely. In particular the extra carry in (0,1) gives A+B+1, not A+1. Thus only addition and subtraction are generally available: A.

Baseline derivation and caveats (retained): The gates feeding the B inputs are XOR gates. For an n-bit word the circuit computes A+(B XOR K…K)+C₀ modulo 2ⁿ. Setting (K,C₀)=(0,0) gives A+B; setting (1,1) gives A+¬B+1=A−B. Neither setting can remove arbitrary B to give A+1 solely by changing those two control lines. Therefore A+B and A−B, but not general A+1, is option A.

subject: 01-digital-logic
question_title: Transitions through cascaded delayed XOR gates
question_text:
Two zero-delay XOR gates are cascaded. The first receives A directly and A through a non-inverting buffer delayed by 2 ns. Its output X feeds the second XOR directly and through a non-inverting buffer delayed by 4 ns. All wires/gates except those buffers have zero delay, and every signal is initially 0. A rises from 0 to 1 at t=1 ns and stays 1. How many transitions occur at the final output B from t=0 to 10 ns?
A. 1  B. 2  C. 3  D. 4
question_text_status: self-contained faithful paraphrase of visually reviewed third-party reproduction; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. Before 1 ns both first-XOR inputs are 0. At 1 ns its direct input rises, but its delayed input stays 0 until 3 ns. Therefore X is 1 exactly on [1,3).
2. The 4 ns delayed copy of X is 1 on [5,7). The second XOR is high when exactly one copy is high, so B is high on those two nonoverlapping intervals.
3. List the changes: 0→1 at 1 ns, 1→0 at 3 ns, 0→1 at 5 ns, and 1→0 at 7 ns. There are four, giving D.

Baseline derivation and caveats (retained): Let A(t) rise once at t=1 ns. The first XOR output is A(t) XOR A(t−2), a pulse on [1,3). The second output XORs this pulse with its copy delayed by 4 ns. The copies occupy [1,3) and [5,7), so they do not overlap and the output changes at 1,3,5,7 ns. There are four transitions in the stated interval, option D.

subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_title: Counting set bits with carry rotations
question_text:
A, B and C are 8-bit registers in a hypothetical processor. The program is:
MOV B,#0       ; B=0
MOV C,#8       ; C=8
Z: CMP C,#0    ; compare C with zero
JZ X          ; jump if zero flag is set
SUB C,#1      ; C=C-1
RRC A,#1      ; rotate A right through carry once
JC Y          ; jump if carry is set
JMP Z
Y: ADD B,#1   ; B=B+1
JMP Z
X:
RRC transforms A=a7...a0 and carry=c into A=ca7...a1 and carry=a0. Use the instruction effects listed for this hypothetical machine.
If A initially equals A0, what is B after execution?
A. Number of 0 bits in A0
B. Number of 1 bits in A0
C. A0
D. 8
question_text_status: self-contained faithful paraphrase of visually reviewed third-party reproduction; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. The C test is before the decrement: C=8,7,...,1 each enters the body, while C=0 exits. There are exactly eight rotations.
2. Write the original bits as a7...a0. The successive carry outputs are a0,a1,...,a7. Any incoming carry sits at the top and cannot emerge until a ninth rotation.
3. Only JC Y reaches ADD B,#1. Thus B increases once for every outgoing 1 and never for an outgoing 0. Starting from zero it ends at a0+...+a7, the population count: B.

Baseline derivation and caveats (retained): The counter C starts at eight and the loop performs exactly eight one-bit right rotations through carry. The carry tested immediately after the kth rotation is the kth original low-to-high bit of A. Newly inserted carry bits cannot reach the outgoing low position during these eight iterations. B starts at zero and is incremented exactly when the outgoing bit is one, so B is the population count of the original A, option B.

question_title: Restoring an eight-bit register after through-carry rotations
question_text:
A, B and C are 8-bit registers in a hypothetical processor. The program is:
MOV B,#0       ; B=0
MOV C,#8       ; C=8
Z: CMP C,#0    ; compare C with zero
JZ X          ; jump if zero flag is set
SUB C,#1      ; C=C-1
RRC A,#1      ; rotate A right through carry once
JC Y          ; jump if carry is set
JMP Z
Y: ADD B,#1   ; B=B+1
JMP Z
X:
RRC transforms A=a7...a0 and carry=c into A=ca7...a1 and carry=a0. Use the instruction effects listed for this hypothetical machine.
Which instruction inserted at X ensures that A ends with its original value?
A. RRC A,#1
B. NOP (no operation)
C. LRC A,#1 (rotate A left through carry once)
D. ADD A,#1
question_text_status: self-contained faithful paraphrase of visually reviewed third-party reproduction; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. Include carry in the state: (c,a7,a6,...,a0) is a nine-position ring. One RRC moves this ring one position right.
2. The loop performs eight rotations, so its accumulated permutation is R^8. Since R^9 is the identity, another RRC restores all nine bits.
3. NOP leaves R^8 unchanged; one left rotation gives R^7, not identity; adding 1 is not a bit-position inverse. Hence A works under the given instruction effects. This explicitly relies on other listed instructions not modifying carry.

Baseline derivation and caveats (retained): Treat carry and A together as a nine-bit circular register and use the instruction effects stated for this hypothetical processor. Eight right rotations leave one right rotation short of a full nine-bit cycle. Inserting RRC A,#1 at X therefore restores A, irrespective of the initial carry value, giving A. This reasoning uses carry preservation by instructions whose listed effects do not change carry; importing different flag side effects from a real ISA would require a new analysis.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_title: Counting constrained binary strings accepted by a DFA
question_text:
A DFA over {0,1} has states q0 (start), q1, q2 and q3 (the only accepting state). Transitions: q0 on 1→q0 and 0→q1; q1 on 1→q0 and 0→q2; q2 on 0→q2 and 1→q3; q3 on either symbol→q3. Let S contain seven-bit strings whose first, fourth and last bits are 1. How many strings of S are accepted?
A. 1  B. 5  C. 7  D. 8
question_text_status: self-contained faithful paraphrase of visually reviewed third-party reproduction; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. Reaching q2 requires two consecutive zeros; after reaching q2 a later 1 enters the absorbing accepting state q3.
2. Strings of S have form 1xy1zw1, leaving four free bits and 16 total strings. Adjacent zeros can occur only as xy=00 or zw=00, because fixed 1s separate the blocks.
3. Fixing xy=00 leaves four choices for zw; fixing zw=00 leaves four choices for xy. The string 1001001 is counted twice. Inclusion–exclusion yields 4+4−1=7, so C.

Baseline derivation and caveats (retained): The DFA accepts precisely strings that contain two consecutive zeros followed later by a one. With positions 1,4,7 fixed to one, a qualifying pair of zeros must occupy positions 2–3 or 5–6, and the following fixed one guarantees acceptance. Of the 16 assignments to the four free bits, four have the first zero pair, four have the second, and one has both. Inclusion–exclusion gives 4+4−1=7 accepted strings, option C.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text:
Let G=({S},{a,b},R,S), where R is S→aSb | SS | ε. Which statement is true?
A. G is not ambiguous.
B. There exist x,y in L(G) with xy not in L(G).
C. A deterministic pushdown automaton accepts L(G).
D. A deterministic finite-state automaton accepts L(G).
question_text_status: self-contained faithful paraphrase of visually reviewed third-party reproduction; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. Interpret a as an opening bracket and b as a closing bracket. aSb encloses a balanced string, SS concatenates two balanced strings, and ε is balanced. Conversely, split any nonempty balanced string at its first matching close to obtain these productions.
2. A deterministic stack machine pushes on a, pops on b, rejects a pop from an empty stack, and accepts exactly with empty stack at end. This establishes C.
3. A is false: ε has both the direct S→ε tree and S→SS→εε. B is false because S→SS supplies closure under concatenation. D is false because intersecting with regular a*b* leaves the nonregular language {a^n b^n:n≥0}.

Baseline derivation and caveats (retained): The grammar generates balanced strings with a as opening bracket and b as closing bracket, including concatenations and the empty word. A deterministic pushdown automaton pushes on a, pops on b, rejects an unmatched b, and accepts at the end exactly when its stack is empty. Thus C is true. The grammar itself is ambiguous, for example ε can be produced directly or through S→SS with two empty children. Its language is closed under concatenation by S→SS and is not regular, since intersection with a*b* gives {aⁿbⁿ:n≥0}.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_title: Decidability under a polynomial-time language isomorphism
question_text:
L1 and L2 are languages over Σ. A bijection f:Σ*→Σ* and its inverse are polynomial-time computable, and for every x, x∈L1 iff f(x)∈L2. Which cannot hold?
A. L1∈P and L2 is finite
B. L1∈NP and L2∈P
C. L1 is undecidable and L2 is decidable
D. L1 is recursively enumerable and L2 is recursive
Source caveat: GateForum drops the stars in the displayed domain/codomain; the GFG string-domain version is used here.
question_text_status: self-contained faithful paraphrase of visually reviewed third-party reproduction; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. Suppose L2 has a decider D2. An algorithm for L1 computes f(x), which always terminates, then returns D2(f(x)). The membership equivalence makes this algorithm correct and terminating.
2. Thus decidability of L2 forces decidability of L1, contradicting C. In fact the inverse supplies the converse reduction too.
3. The other combinations are not contradictions. Take f to be identity and L1=L2=∅: the language is finite, in P and NP, recursive and recursively enumerable. This single example witnesses the possibility of A, B and D.

Baseline derivation and caveats (retained): If L₂ is decidable, compute f(x) and run its decider; the membership equivalence decides L₁. Hence an undecidable L₁ and decidable L₂ cannot coexist, option C. The other alternatives are possible by choosing finite or otherwise polynomial-time decidable languages: P is contained in NP, and recursively enumerable does not mean nonrecursive. The GFG source specifies f:Σ*→Σ*, which is the interpretation used here; the GateForum retypesetting drops the stars in that displayed domain/codomain.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_title: Nonhalting behavior of a two-state Turing machine
question_text:
A single-tape Turing machine has states q0 (start), q1, tape symbols {0,1,B}, and input alphabet {0,1}; B is blank. A transition (q,s,D) means write s, move D, enter q. The table is:
q0 on 0: (q1,1,R); on 1: (q1,1,R); on B: Halt.
q1 on 0: (q1,1,R); on 1: (q0,1,L); on B: (q0,B,L).
Which is true?
A. M does not halt on any string in (0+1)+.
B. M does not halt on any string in (00+1)*.
C. M halts on all strings ending in 0.
D. M halts on all strings ending in 1.
Here + between symbols is union and superscript + means one or more repetitions.
question_text_status: self-contained faithful paraphrase of visually reviewed third-party reproduction; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. Empty input starts with a blank under q0 and halts immediately. Since ε belongs to (00+1)*, B cannot be true.
2. On any nonempty input q0 writes a 1 and moves right into q1. q1 passes over zeros, replacing each with 1, until reaching either a preexisting 1 or the right-hand blank.
3. At this boundary q1 moves left to q0. That left cell is now 1, so q0 moves right into q1 without changing it. q1 sees the same boundary symbol and moves left again. These two configurations repeat forever.
4. This applies to every nonempty binary input, regardless of its final symbol. Hence A, not C or D.

Baseline derivation and caveats (retained): On a nonempty input, q₀ writes 1 in the first cell and moves right in q₁. State q₁ changes any subsequent zeros to ones and moves right until it sees a 1 or the first blank. At either such boundary it moves left into q₀. The cell to its left is now 1, so q₀ moves right again to the boundary in q₁, producing a two-configuration loop. Thus every nonempty binary input diverges, option A. Empty input halts immediately, so option B, whose starred language includes ε, is false.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text:
Define L0={⟨M,w,0⟩: M halts on w} and L1={⟨M,w,1⟩: M does not halt on w}, where M is a Turing-machine encoding, w a string and the last component a bit. Let L=L0∪L1. Which is true?
A. L is recursively enumerable but its complement is not.
B. Its complement is recursively enumerable but L is not.
C. Both L and its complement are recursive.
D. Neither L nor its complement is recursively enumerable.
question_text_status: self-contained faithful paraphrase of visually reviewed third-party reproduction; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. The halting language H is recognizable, but its complement is not recognizable: recognizers for both would yield a decider by dovetailing them.
2. Map each halting-instance pair (M,w) to ⟨M,w,1⟩. It belongs to L exactly when M does not halt. Therefore a recognizer for L would recognize the complement of H, impossible.
3. Map the same pair to ⟨M,w,0⟩. It belongs to the complement of L exactly when M does not halt. A recognizer for that complement would give the same contradiction.
4. Neither tagged language is recognizable, so D. The different tags are essential; halting and nonhalting cases are not simply being unioned without a tag.

Baseline derivation and caveats (retained): Let H be the halting language. If L were recursively enumerable, mapping (M,w) to ⟨M,w,1⟩ would make the complement of H recursively enumerable, a contradiction. If the complement of L were recursively enumerable, mapping (M,w) to ⟨M,w,0⟩ would again recognize the complement of H. Therefore neither L nor its complement is recursively enumerable, option D. The tag prevents the union from simply being the universal set.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_title: Flipping final states in an NFA
question_text:
An NFA M over {0,1} has states p (start), q and r (only final). Transitions are p→q on 0 or 1; q→p on 0; q→q on 0 or 1; p→r on 1; q→r on 0; r→q on 0. There are no other transitions. Let L=L(M). M1 is obtained by making r nonfinal and p,q final, and L1=L(M1). Which statement is true?
A. L1={0,1}*−L
B. L1={0,1}*
C. L1⊆L
D. L1=L
question_text_status: self-contained faithful paraphrase of visually reviewed third-party reproduction; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. Since p is final in M1, ε is accepted.
2. For any nonempty word, choose p→q on its first symbol. Then choose the 0/1 loop at q for every remaining symbol. This accepting run exists for every word.
3. Therefore L1 is the universal binary language, B. In particular ε∈L1 but ε∉L, ruling out C and D. Since 1∈L as well as L1, they are not complements, ruling out A. NFA acceptance is existential over runs, which is why simply flipping finals fails as a complement construction.

Baseline derivation and caveats (retained): After the flip, the initial left state and the upper-right state are accepting. The empty string is accepted at the initial state. For every nonempty binary string, choose the transition from the initial state to the upper-right state on its first symbol and then use that state’s 0/1 loop for the suffix. Therefore the new language is all of {0,1}*, option B. Flipping final states complements a complete DFA, not a general NFA.

question_title: Predictive-table conflict for a dangling-else grammar
question_text_status: self-contained faithful paraphrase of visually reviewed third-party reproduction; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. FIRST(eS)={e}, so insert S′→eS in the e column.
2. S is the start symbol, so $∈FOLLOW(S). In S→iEtSS′, the first S is followed by nullable S′ whose nonempty FIRST is {e}; hence e∈FOLLOW(S) as well.
3. The final S′ inherits FOLLOW(S), giving FOLLOW(S′)={e,$}. For the ε production, put S′→ε in every FOLLOW column, therefore both e and $.
4. The resulting cells are {eS,ε} and {ε}, option D. The two entries in the e cell are the dangling-else conflict, so the grammar itself is not LL(1).

Baseline derivation and caveats (retained): FIRST(eS)={e}, so the rule S′→eS enters M[S′,e]. Because S′ can be empty and follows S in S→iEtSS′, e belongs to FOLLOW(S), while $ belongs to FOLLOW(S) because S is the start symbol. The trailing S′ inherits FOLLOW(S), giving FOLLOW(S′)={e,$}. Thus S′→ε also enters both cells. The e cell contains both alternatives and the $ cell contains only ε, option D; the conflict means this grammar is not LL(1).

subject: 07-compiler-design
question_title: LL(1) classification from disjoint FIRST sets
question_text:
Consider S→CC and C→cC | d. This grammar is:
A. LL(1)
B. SLR(1) but not LL(1)
C. LALR(1) but not SLR(1)
D. LR(1) but not LALR(1)
question_text_status: self-contained faithful paraphrase of visually reviewed third-party reproduction; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. C generates zero or more c symbols followed by d. Its alternatives begin with distinct terminal symbols: FIRST(cC)={c} and FIRST(d)={d}.
2. Neither C alternative is nullable, so no FIRST/FOLLOW overlap can create a second entry in its parsing-table cells. Put C→cC under c and C→d under d.
3. S has only one production; under either c or d use S→CC. No table cell has two choices. Thus one lookahead symbol always selects a production and the grammar is LL(1), A.

Baseline derivation and caveats (retained): For C→cC|d the alternatives have disjoint FIRST sets {c} and {d}, and neither can derive ε. S has only its single production S→CC. Therefore every predictive-table cell has at most one production and the grammar is LL(1), option A. No stronger bottom-up distinction is needed.

subject: 07-compiler-design
question_title: Output order of embedded translation actions
question_text:
A translation scheme is S→TR; R→+ T {print('+');} R | ε; T→num {print(num.val);}. Token num represents an integer, and num.val is its value. For input 9+5+2, what is printed?
A. 9+5+2
B. 95+2+
C. 952++
D. ++952
question_text_status: self-contained faithful paraphrase of visually reviewed third-party reproduction; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. Expand S→TR. The initial T consumes 9 and immediately prints 9.
2. The first R consumes + and invokes T on 5, printing 5. Its following action prints + before the recursive R begins.
3. That recursive R consumes +, invokes T on 2 and prints 2, then prints +. Its final R chooses ε and prints nothing.
4. Concatenating the actions yields 9,5,+,2,+, or 95+2+, B. Moving the plus action to after the recursive R would change the result, but that is not this scheme.

Baseline derivation and caveats (retained): The initial T prints 9. Each R expansion reads +, processes T (which prints the next number), prints +, and only then processes the remaining R. Hence the execution order is 9,5,+,2,+, yielding 95+2+, option B. The action is before the recursive R, so it does not postpone both plus signs to the end.

question_title: Three-address code from synthesized expression locations
question_text_status: self-contained faithful paraphrase of visually reviewed third-party reproduction; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. Reduce identifier Y using E→id: set its place to Y without generating an instruction. Reduce Z the same way, with place Z.
2. At the addition node, call newtemp once to obtain t1. Emit t1=Y+Z and make the addition expression's place t1.
3. At the assignment node, use X as the destination and the completed expression place as source. Emit X=t1.
4. The ordered output is precisely B. No identifier-copy actions occur in the definition, ruling out C and D; the addition action cannot be bypassed to get A.

subject: excluded
question_title: Distribution of the sum of module runtimes
question_text:
A program executes two modules sequentially. Their execution times have probability densities f1(t),f2(t). Which expression gives the density of total execution time?
A. f1(t)+f2(t)
B. ∫[0,t] f1(x)f2(x) dx
C. ∫[0,t] f1(x)f2(t−x) dx
D. max{f1(t),f2(t)} [GateForum; GFG instead prints max{f1(t)+f2(t)}.]
The statement does not explicitly assert independence.
question_text_status: self-contained faithful paraphrase of visually reviewed third-party reproduction; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. Let T=T1+T2. A contribution to density near t with T1=x must have T2 near t−x, not x. Nonnegative runtimes restrict x to [0,t].
2. If T1,T2 are independent, their joint density is f1(x)f2(y). Integrating along x+y=t yields ∫[0,t]f1(x)f2(t−x)dx, C.
3. Marginal densities alone do not supply that product. For example, if both times are uniform on [0,1], independent times give a triangular sum density, whereas T2=T1 gives a uniform sum on [0,2]. Sequential execution permits either dependency.
4. Therefore C is conditional on independence; the literal problem is underdetermined. One cannot infer independence merely because the modules run one after another.

Baseline derivation and caveats (retained): For independent nonnegative runtimes T₁,T₂, the density of T₁+T₂ is the convolution f(t)=∫₀ᵗ f₁(x)f₂(t−x) dx, option C. Sequential execution alone does not imply independence. In general the answer is ∫₀ᵗ f₁₂(x,t−x) dx using a joint density, when one exists, and marginal densities f₁,f₂ do not determine it. The same marginal distributions can give different sums under different dependencies, so C requires an extra independence assumption not stated in either reproduction.
derived_answer: C if the runtimes are independent; otherwise underdetermined

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_title: Expected inversion count in a uniform permutation
question_text:
For a permutation a1,...,an of n distinct integers, an inversion is an index pair i<j with ai>aj. All permutations of 1,...,n are equally likely. What is the expected inversion count?
A. n(n−1)/2
B. n(n−1)/4
C. n(n+1)/4
D. 2n floor(log2 n)
question_text_status: self-contained faithful paraphrase of visually reviewed third-party reproduction; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. There are choose(n,2)=n(n−1)/2 pairs of distinct positions i<j.
2. For any fixed pair, exchanging their two entries pairs every ordering ai>aj with an equally likely ordering ai<aj. Distinctness excludes equality, so the inversion probability is 1/2.
3. Let Iij be 1 for an inversion and 0 otherwise. Then E[Iij]=1/2 and total inversions I=Σi<j Iij.
4. Linearity gives E[I]=Σ E[Iij]=n(n−1)/4, B. Although different pairs' indicators may be dependent, linearity does not require independence.

Baseline derivation and caveats (retained): For each of the n(n−1)/2 index pairs i<j, define an indicator for aᵢ>aⱼ. Symmetry gives probability 1/2 for each pair. By linearity of expectation, the expected inversion count is [n(n−1)/2]×1/2=n(n−1)/4, option B. Independence among those indicators is unnecessary.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_title: Insertion sort on inputs with few inversions
question_text:
For a permutation a1,...,an of n distinct integers, an inversion is an index pair i<j with ai>aj. What is insertion sort's worst-case time if inputs are restricted to permutations of 1,...,n with at most n inversions?
A. Θ(n²)  B. Θ(n log n)  C. Θ(n^1.5)  D. Θ(n)
question_text_status: self-contained faithful paraphrase of visually reviewed third-party reproduction; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. In insertion sort, a larger element shifts right exactly when it is an inversion partner of the current key. Each original inversion causes one such shift and is then removed.
2. With I inversions, the inner loops therefore make I shifts. The n−1 outer iterations and their final failed/boundary tests add Θ(n) work, so total work is Θ(n+I).
3. The restriction I≤n gives O(n+n)=O(n). Reading and processing n entries still requires Ω(n), including an already sorted input.
4. Matching the upper and lower bounds gives Θ(n), D. The unrestricted reverse-order example has Θ(n²) inversions and is excluded here.

Baseline derivation and caveats (retained): In standard insertion sort, shifting an earlier larger element past the current key removes exactly one inversion. Total shifts equal the input inversion count I, and outer-loop work plus terminating comparisons contributes Θ(n). Hence running time is Θ(n+I). With I≤n this is O(n), while scanning the n elements requires Ω(n), so the restricted worst case is Θ(n), option D.

subject: 04-data-structures
question_title: Ordered set supporting minimum deletion and unique insertion
question_text:
A set of n integers must support (I) deleting its smallest element and (II) inserting an element only if it is not already present, each in O(log n) time. Which structure suffices?
A. A heap, but not a balanced binary search tree
B. A balanced binary search tree, but not a heap
C. Both a balanced binary search tree and a heap
D. Neither
question_text_status: self-contained faithful paraphrase of visually reviewed third-party reproduction; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. A balanced binary search tree has height O(log n). Follow left children to the minimum and delete/rebalance in O(log n). Search for a proposed key and, if absent, insert/rebalance along one root-to-leaf path in O(log n).
2. A min-heap can delete its root and sift down in O(log n), and can insert a known-new key in O(log n).
3. However, a heap is only partially ordered. Testing whether an arbitrary key already appears can require inspecting Θ(n) positions; insertion-if-absent includes that test.
4. Thus the balanced tree alone meets both requirements, B. A heap augmented with a separate search index is not the plain heap being compared.

Baseline derivation and caveats (retained): A balanced binary search tree supports membership search, insertion, and deletion of its minimum in O(log n) worst-case time. A plain heap supports minimum deletion and unrestricted insertion in O(log n), but checking whether an arbitrary proposed value is already present may require Θ(n) comparisons. Therefore the uniqueness requirement rules out the heap alone, leaving B. Augmenting a heap with a separate membership structure is outside the listed plain-structure comparison.

subject: 04-data-structures
question_title: Average residence time in a push-then-pop stack
question_text:
An initially empty stack of capacity n≥1 receives pushes of 1,...,n in order, followed by n pops. Each push/pop takes X seconds; a gap of Y seconds separates the end of each operation from the start of the next. The stack-life of m is the interval from the end of push(m) to the start of the pop removing m. What is the average stack-life?
A. n(X+Y)
B. 3Y+2X
C. n(X+Y)−X
D. Y+2X
question_text_status: self-contained faithful paraphrase of visually reviewed third-party reproduction; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. LIFO means m is removed after the n−m elements above it. Between the two specified endpoints lie n−m later pushes and n−m earlier pops, a total of 2(n−m) complete operations.
2. There is one more gap than intervening operations, so life(m)=2(n−m)X+[2(n−m)+1]Y. The push of m and its own pop are excluded by the endpoint definition.
3. Average n−m over m=1,...,n: [0+...+(n−1)]/n=(n−1)/2. Substitution gives (n−1)X+nY=n(X+Y)−X.
4. Hence C. For n=1, life is just Y, confirming the endpoint accounting.

Baseline derivation and caveats (retained): For item m, there are n−m later pushes and n−m earlier pops between the end of push(m) and the start of its pop. Those 2(n−m) complete intervening operations cost 2(n−m)X and the 2(n−m)+1 gaps cost [2(n−m)+1]Y. Average n−m over m=1,…,n is (n−1)/2, so the mean is (n−1)X+nY=n(X+Y)−X, option C. For n=1 it correctly reduces to the single gap Y.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_title: Bit complexity of integer cube root
question_text:
The integer cube root of a natural number n is the largest natural m with m³≤n. The input n is represented in binary. Which describes its computation complexity?
A. O(n), but not O(n^0.5)
B. O(n^0.5), but not O((log n)^k) for any constant k>0
C. O((log n)^k) for some constant k>0, but not O((log log n)^m) for any constant m>0
D. O((log log n)^k) for some constant k>0.5, but not O((log log n)^0.5)
question_text_status: self-contained faithful paraphrase of visually reviewed third-party reproduction; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. The input length is b=floor(log2 n)+1; complexity in n and in the bit length b must not be confused.
2. Binary search the integer interval [0,n], retaining the largest tested m with m³≤n. Halving the interval takes O(log n)=O(b) iterations.
3. Using schoolbook arithmetic, a multiplication of O(b)-bit numbers costs O(b²); two multiplications form m³. Hence this explicit algorithm costs O(b³), polynomial in log n.
4. The output cube root has about b/3 bits, so even writing it costs Ω(b), which dominates every fixed power of log b. Thus a polynomial in log log n cannot suffice in the bit model, and C follows.

Baseline derivation and caveats (retained): Let b be the number of input bits, so b=Theta(log n). Binary search for the largest m with m³≤n needs O(b) comparisons. Schoolbook multiplication computes a b-bit cube in O(b²) bit operations, giving an explicit O(b³) algorithm. The answer itself has Theta(b) bits for growing n, so writing it already requires Omega(b) bit operations. Thus the problem is polynomial in log n, but not polynomial in log log n, option C. This is a bit-complexity statement, not a unit-cost model for arbitrarily large integers.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_title: Detecting subgraph connectivity with zero-weight edges
question_text:
G=(V,E) is an undirected graph with subgraph G1=(V1,E1). Give an edge weight 0 if it is in E1, and 1 otherwise. Run single-source shortest paths from an arbitrary v1∈V1. Which property can always be inferred from the computed path costs?
A. Number of edges in shortest paths from v1 to every vertex of G
B. G1 is connected
C. V1 forms a clique in G
D. G1 is a tree
Interpret B as determining whether G1 is connected, not asserting connectivity on every input.
question_text_status: self-contained faithful paraphrase of visually reviewed third-party reproduction; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. With only weights 0 and 1, a finite path has total cost 0 precisely when all of its edges belong to E1.
2. Hence d(v1,v)=0 precisely for vertices in the G1 component of v1. Test this for every v∈V1: all distances zero means G1 is connected; any positive/infinite distance means it is not.
3. Cost does not count zero-weight edges. A zero-weight chain and a zero-weight clique on V1 can give identical distance-zero results but different edge counts and cycle structure.
4. Thus the distances determine connectivity (B), but neither clique/tree status nor shortest-path edge counts.

Baseline derivation and caveats (retained): An edge has weight zero exactly when it belongs to E1. Consequently, for a vertex v in V1, distance(v1,v)=0 exactly when v is connected to v1 using only edges of G1. Checking whether every vertex of V1 has zero distance therefore decides whether G1 is connected, B. Zero distances do not reveal edge counts, clique structure, or acyclicity: a tree and a triangle within the reachable zero-weight component can have identical distances. B must be read as determining connectivity, not asserting that every possible input G1 is connected.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_title: Minimum spanning tree of a weighted graph
question_text:
Find the weight of a minimum spanning tree of the undirected weighted graph with vertices a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h,i,j and edges:
ac:1; ad:2; cd:2; bg:2; ei:2; bd:3; fh:4; hi:4; ij:5; ab:6; ae:8; eh:8; gh:8; fi:9; ef:11; gi:14; dh:15; gj:19.
These edges describe the complete printed diagram; no other edges are present.
A. 29  B. 31  C. 38  D. 41
question_text_status: self-contained faithful paraphrase of visually reviewed third-party reproduction; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. Kruskal processes edges by nondecreasing weight, accepting an edge only when its endpoints lie in different components.
2. Accept ac(1), ad(2); reject cd(2), since a,c,d are already connected. Accept bg(2), ei(2), then bd(3), which joins {b,g} with {a,c,d}.
3. Accept fh(4), hi(4), connecting {f,h} to {e,i}; accept ij(5) to add j. Reject ab(6), whose endpoints are already in the first component.

5. Total=1+2+2+2+3+4+4+5+8=31, B. eh(8) is internal to the second component and is not needed.

question_title: Max-plus Floyd recurrence and simple-path bounds
question_text_status: self-contained faithful paraphrase of visually reviewed third-party reproduction; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. Initially every one-edge path has its length represented by A[j,k]≥1. Updates only increase entries, so established lower bounds persist.
2. For a simple path with internal vertices, take its highest-numbered internal vertex i. Splitting there gives two subpaths whose internal vertices have smaller indices. Inductively their lengths are bounded above by A[j,i] and A[i,k] before processing i.
3. The update therefore makes A[j,k] at least the sum of those lengths, the length of the original path. This proves D for every simple path.
4. This is not a correct longest-simple-path algorithm: it never checks that the joined paths are disjoint. Cycles can repeatedly inflate values, and zero is an unsafe unreachable marker for maximizing lengths. Therefore exactness, an n bound and Hamiltonian-cycle inference do not follow.

Baseline derivation and caveats (retained): The recurrence A[j,k]=max(A[j,k],A[j,i]+A[i,k]) gives option D. Induct on the largest-index internal vertex of a simple path: direct edges start at one; splitting a path at its largest-index internal vertex combines previously established lower bounds for the two pieces. Monotone updates cannot destroy them. Thus the final A[j,k] is at least the length of every simple j-to-k path. It need not equal a longest-path length: cycles and zero values used for nonexistent edges can inflate entries, so the other claims fail. For example, a directed two-vertex cycle with an isolated third vertex can produce values larger than n and large diagonal entries although there is no Hamiltonian cycle. Neither the claimed n bound nor the exact-longest-path interpretation is justified.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_title: Quantifying a Horn rule and an integrity constraint
question_text:
Logic program P has clauses A(x)←B(x,y),C(y) and ←B(x,x). Which first-order sentence is equivalent? All variables in clauses are universally quantified.
A. [∀x((∃y(B(x,y)∧C(y)))⇒A(x))] ∧ ¬∃x B(x,x)
B. [∀x((∀y(B(x,y)∧C(y)))⇒A(x))] ∧ ¬∃x B(x,x)
C. [∀x((∃y(B(x,y)∧C(y)))⇒A(x))] ∨ ¬∃x B(x,x)
D. [∀x((∀y(B(x,y)∧C(y)))⇒A(x))] ∧ ∃x B(x,x)
Option D above follows GateForum; GFG instead negates its final existential clause: ¬∃x B(x,x). Neither version changes the correct option A.
question_text_status: self-contained faithful paraphrase of visually reviewed third-party reproduction; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. The first clause means ∀x∀y((B(x,y)∧C(y))⇒A(x)). For each fixed x, a single witness y for the body is enough to force A(x).
2. Since y does not occur in A(x), move the body quantifier to obtain ∀x((∃y(B(x,y)∧C(y)))⇒A(x)). Using ∀y inside the antecedent would require every y to satisfy the body before forcing A, a weaker rule.
3. A headless clause is a constraint: B(x,x) must never hold. Thus the second clause means ∀x¬B(x,x), equivalently ¬∃x B(x,x).
4. Both clauses must hold together, requiring conjunction. These components match A exactly.

Baseline derivation and caveats (retained): The rule says that for every x,y, B(x,y) and C(y) together imply A(x). Since A(x) does not depend on y, this is equivalent to saying for every x that the existence of such a y implies A(x). The headless clause forbids every instance of B(x,x), hence contributes not-exists x B(x,x). A program containing both clauses requires their conjunction. This is option A. Moving a universal quantifier inside the antecedent would weaken the rule; joining the clauses with OR would not enforce both.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_text:
Resolution derives P∨Q from premises P∨R and Q∨¬R. Under the ordinary pivot-free residual-clause convention, which statement is false?
A. ((P∨R)∧(Q∨¬R))⇒(P∨Q) is logically valid.
B. (P∨Q)⇒((P∨R)∨(Q∨¬R)) is logically valid. [This is GFG; GateForum replaces the middle ∨ on the right by ∧.]
C. P∨Q is satisfiable iff (P∨R)∧(Q∨¬R) is satisfiable.
D. (P∨Q)⇒FALSE iff both P and Q are unsatisfiable.
Treat R as a pivot atom not occurring in residual P or Q.
question_text_status: self-contained faithful paraphrase of visually reviewed third-party reproduction; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. For A, if P and Q were both false, satisfying the first premise would require R=true and satisfying the second would require R=false. This contradiction proves soundness.
2. For C, soundness supplies one direction. Conversely, if P∨Q has a model, extend it with R=false when P is true, or R=true when Q is true. Both premises then hold. This extension uses the pivot-free assumption.
3. D follows because a disjunction has a model exactly when at least one disjunct has a model.
4. GFG B has R∨¬R on its right and is therefore always true. Thus none of its options is false. GateForum B instead has a conjunction: P=true,Q=false,R=true makes its antecedent true and consequent false, so that version has answer B.
5. If arbitrary residual formulas could contain R, C need not hold: P=R,Q=¬R makes the resolvent a tautology and the premises inconsistent. That is a different convention, not a silent repair of GFG.

Baseline derivation and caveats (retained): Under the ordinary resolution convention, R is the pivot atom and neither residual clause P nor Q contains it. The conjunction of the premises entails P∨Q, so A is sound. Conversely, any satisfying assignment of P∨Q can be extended by an appropriate value of R to satisfy both premises, which establishes the satisfiability equivalence in C without claiming logical equivalence. D expresses that P∨Q is unsatisfiable exactly when both disjuncts are unsatisfiable. GateForum B uses a conjunction on its right: choosing P=true,Q=false,R=true falsifies that implication, so B is its answer. GFG B instead uses a disjunction on its right, which contains R∨not-R and is a tautology; under the ordinary convention no GFG option is false. If P and Q may be arbitrary formulas involving R, C also fails: set P=R and Q=not-R. Then the resolvent is a tautology but the premises reduce to R∧not-R. That broader interpretation must not be silently substituted for the conventional pivot-free reading.

subject: 07-compiler-design
question_text_status: self-contained faithful paraphrase of visually reviewed third-party reproduction; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. Under static scope the actual expression i+j is bound to the globals visible at the call in main. P's local i does not replace that lexical binding.
2. Call-by-need postpones evaluation until first use and caches its result. At print(x+10), the actual is first demanded: global i+j=100+5=105. The first print is 105+10=115.
3. P then sets its own local i to 200 and global j to 20. Neither assignment changes the cached value 105.
4. The second print reuses that value, giving 105. Therefore D. Recomputing 100+20 would be call-by-name, not call-by-need.

Baseline derivation and caveats (retained): Under lexical scope the delayed actual expression i+j refers to main's enclosing global bindings, initially 100 and 5. Its first demand evaluates and memoizes 105, so print(x+10) emits 115. Assigning 200 to P's local i and 20 to global j cannot change the already cached actual value. The later print(x) emits 105. Thus D, 115 followed by 105. Call by need evaluates once on first demand; it is not repeated call-by-name evaluation.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_title: Startup cost of shared dynamic libraries
question_text:
Which is NOT an advantage of shared, dynamically linked libraries over statically linked libraries?
A. Smaller executable files
B. Lower overall page-fault rate in the system
C. Faster program startup
D. Existing programs need not be relinked to benefit from newer library versions
question_text_status: self-contained faithful paraphrase of visually reviewed third-party reproduction; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. Static linking copies required library code into each executable. Dynamic linking can leave that code in a separately loaded library, reducing executable size, so A is a conventional benefit.
2. Multiple processes can map the same read-only physical library pages. This reduces duplicated resident code and can reduce total memory pressure/page faults, the intended benefit in B.
3. A compatible replacement library may be used on the next load without rebuilding each application, explaining D; compatibility remains necessary.
4. Dynamic loading and symbol relocation/resolution add work at startup or first use. Faster startup is not a general advantage, so C is the requested exception. Actual cache and page-fault behavior still depends on workload.

Baseline derivation and caveats (retained): Dynamic linking can keep library code out of the executable, share physical library pages among processes, and permit compatible library updates without relinking each application. It also introduces runtime loading, relocation, or symbol-resolution work. Faster program startup is therefore not the characteristic advantage over static linking, option C. The other listed benefits are the conventional shared-library benefits; actual page-fault and startup measurements can depend on caching and workload.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_title: Scheduling alternating CPU and I/O bursts
question_text:
A uniprocessor runs only two processes, created nearly simultaneously. Each alternates a 10 ms CPU burst with a 90 ms I/O burst; their I/O can proceed in parallel. Which policy gives the least long-run CPU utilization?
A. First come, first served
B. Shortest remaining time first
C. Static priority with different priorities
D. Round robin with a 5 ms quantum
question_text_status: self-contained faithful paraphrase of visually reviewed third-party reproduction; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. Ignore switching overhead as the statement supplies none. Under FCFS one process runs 0–10 and the other 10–20. Their I/O ends at 100 and 110, and each finishes its next CPU burst just as the other becomes ready. Thus the CPU supplies 20 ms work per 100 ms: 20% utilization. SRTF and distinct priorities have the same sustained burst staggering here.
2. Under 5 ms round robin, the initial slices are P:0–5, Q:5–10, P:10–15, Q:15–20. Their I/O begins at 15 and 20, only 5 ms apart, and ends at 105 and 110.
3. With the usual ordering when I/O completion coincides with quantum expiry, Q gets the CPU at 110, so the next completed CPU bursts are at 120 and 125. This repeats the paired pattern after 105 ms.
4. Utilization is 20/105≈19.05%, less than 20%, making D the conventional answer. The smaller separation causes more simultaneous I/O and hence more CPU idle time.

Baseline derivation and caveats (retained): Ignoring context-switch cost, FCFS, shortest-remaining-time, and distinct static priorities run the two initial CPU bursts consecutively for 10 ms each. Their I/O completions stay offset by 10 ms, giving 20 ms of CPU work in a 100 ms steady-state period. With round robin at a 5 ms quantum, the initial bursts finish at 15 and 20 ms, so the processes enter I/O only 5 ms apart. Under the usual ready-queue ordering at simultaneous quantum expiry and I/O completion, this pattern repeats every 105 ms, giving utilization 20/105≈19.05%, below 20%. Thus D is the conventional answer: fine time slicing makes their long I/O intervals overlap more.

subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_title: Translation lookaside buffer and cache access time
question_text:
A byte-addressable processor has 32-bit virtual and physical addresses and two-level page tables stored in main memory. Address bits are split 10 bits for first-level index, 10 for second-level index, and 12 for page offset. All page-table entries are 4 bytes. TLB hit rate is 96%, physical-cache hit rate 90%; TLB and cache access each take 1 ns, and main memory takes 10 ns. With no page faults, what is mean virtual-address access time, approximately to the nearest 0.5 ns?
A. 1.5 ns  B. 2 ns  C. 3 ns  D. 4 ns
The statement does not specify whether page-table reads use the cache/hit rate.
question_text_status: self-contained faithful paraphrase of visually reviewed third-party reproduction; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. A cache-backed physical access costs 1 ns on a hit and 1+10=11 ns on a miss. Its mean is H=0.9×1+0.1×11=2 ns.
2. Every virtual access pays the 1 ns TLB lookup and one final data access. A TLB miss occurs with probability 0.04 and additionally reads two page-table entries.
3. If those reads also use this cache and hit rate, the conditional costs are 3 ns on a TLB hit and 7 ns on a miss. E=0.96×3+0.04×7=3.16 ns, rounding to 3.0 ns (C).
4. If page-table reads bypass the cache, a miss instead costs 1+20+2=23 ns. E=0.96×3+0.04×23=3.8 ns, rounding to 4.0 ns (D).
5. Both interpretations place page tables in main memory; this phrase alone does not resolve caching. Consequently retain the baseline underdetermination instead of asserting an unconditional option.

Baseline derivation and caveats (retained): If every physical memory reference, including page-table reads, uses the stated cache with 90% hit probability, its mean service time is H=1+0.10×10=2 ns, charging the cache probe before a miss fetch. A lookup always costs 1 ns for the TLB and one data reference; a TLB miss, probability 0.04, adds two page-table references. Thus E=1+(1+2×0.04)H=3.16 ns, which rounds to 3.0 ns, C. If the two page-table references instead bypass the cache and each costs 10 ns, E=1+0.04×20+H=3.8 ns, rounding to 4.0 ns, D. The statement that page tables reside in main memory does not itself specify whether their reads are cached or share the data-cache hit rate. C is the usual all-physical-accesses-cached interpretation, but an unconditional answer is withheld.

question_title: Memory used by sparse two-level page tables
question_text:
A byte-addressable processor has 32-bit virtual and physical addresses and two-level page tables stored in main memory. A process maps only two contiguous code pages starting at 0x00000000, two contiguous data pages starting at 0x00400000, and one stack page starting at 0xFFFFF000. How much storage is needed for its page tables?
A. 8 KB  B. 12 KB  C. 16 KB  D. 20 KB
question_text_status: self-contained faithful paraphrase of visually reviewed third-party reproduction; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. A 10-bit index selects 1024 entries. At four bytes per entry each full table occupies 4096 bytes, one 4 KiB page.
2. One second-level table covers 1024 virtual pages, or 1024×4096=4 MiB. The code pages fall in the first 4 MiB region, top-level index 0. The data begins exactly at 4 MiB, index 1. The stack address has index 1023.
3. The two contiguous code pages share one second-level table, as do the two data pages. The stack needs a third second-level table. Add one top-level table: four tables total.
4. Storage=4×4096=16384 bytes=16 KiB, option C. Mapped content pages are not additional page-table storage.

Baseline derivation and caveats (retained): Each page-table level has 2^10 entries of four bytes, so each allocated table uses 4096 bytes. The two code pages occupy top-level index 0; the two data pages starting at 0x00400000 occupy index 1; the stack page at 0xFFFFF000 occupies index 1023. Three second-level tables are therefore required, plus the first-level table. Total page-table storage is 4×4096=16384 bytes=16 KiB, option C. The five mapped code/data/stack pages are not themselves included in page-table storage.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text:
Two concurrent processes use binary semaphores S,T. Process P loops forever: W: [synchronization]; print '0'; print '0'; X: [synchronization]. Process Q loops forever: Y: [synchronization]; print '1'; print '1'; Z: [synchronization]. Synchronization can be placed only at W,X,Y,Z. P(S) means wait/decrement and V(S) means signal. Which always gives an output starting 001100110011...?
A. W=P(S), X=V(S), Y=P(T), Z=V(T); S=T=1 initially
B. W=P(S), X=V(T), Y=P(T), Z=V(S); S=1,T=0 initially
C. W=P(S), X=V(T), Y=P(T), Z=V(S); S=T=1 initially
D. W=P(S), X=V(S), Y=P(T), Z=V(T); S=1,T=0 initially
question_text_status: self-contained faithful paraphrase of visually reviewed third-party reproduction; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. The required output demands both pairwise exclusion and alternation starting with P's zeros. Initially only P should have permission: S=1 and T=0.
2. P passes wait(S), prints both zeros, then signals T. Q cannot print any one until this signal; once released it consumes T, prints both ones and signals S.
3. P's next wait(S) cannot pass before Q completes its pair. Inductively the execution consists of 00,11,00,11,..., so B works.
4. In A independent locks allow arbitrary interleaving. C initially lets both processes enter, so even the first pair need not be 00. In D Q waits forever on T because no other process signals T.

Baseline derivation and caveats (retained): Initially give P permission to run by setting S=1 and block Q with T=0. P waits on S at W, prints both zeroes, and signals T at X. Q waits on T at Y, prints both ones, and signals S at Z. Each process therefore hands permission to the other only after completing its pair, forcing 00,11,00,11,… starting with 00. This is B. Separate locks do not coordinate the processes, and initializing both cross-signalling semaphores to one would permit initial interleaving.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text:
Two concurrent processes use binary semaphores S,T. Process P loops forever: W: [synchronization]; print '0'; print '0'; X: [synchronization]. Process Q loops forever: Y: [synchronization]; print '1'; print '1'; Z: [synchronization]. Synchronization can be placed only at W,X,Y,Z. P(S) means wait/decrement and V(S) means signal. Which ensures the output never contains 0 1^n 0 or 1 0^n 1 with n odd?
A. W=P(S), X=V(S), Y=P(T), Z=V(T); S=T=1
B. W=P(S), X=V(T), Y=P(T), Z=V(S); S=T=1
C. W=P(S), X=V(S), Y=P(S), Z=V(S); S=1
D. W=V(S), X=V(T), Y=P(S), Z=P(T); S=T=1
question_text_status: self-contained faithful paraphrase of visually reviewed third-party reproduction; original official wording unverified
solution:
1. The forbidden patterns mean a run of ones between zeros, or zeros between ones, must have even length. It is sufficient for each process to print its identical pair atomically.
2. C uses the same initially available semaphore at both W and Y. Only one process can enter its two-print critical section, and it releases the mutex only after the pair.
3. Output is thus a concatenation of whole 00 and 11 blocks. Adjacent blocks of the same digit may merge, but their lengths remain multiples of two, proving the desired property.
4. A and B initially allow both processes inside, permitting P's first 0, Q's first 1, P's second 0: a forbidden 010. D does not make P acquire a common mutex and likewise does not ensure whole-pair exclusion. Therefore C.

Baseline derivation and caveats (retained): Use one common binary semaphore S, initially one, as a mutex around both print statements of either process: wait(S) at W and Y, signal(S) at X and Z. Each critical section then emits either 00 or 11 without interleaving, so any run between opposite digits is a concatenation of equal pairs and has even length. That is C. For example, when independent locks or two initially available cross-signalling permissions let P emit its first zero, Q one one, and P its second zero, the forbidden substring 010 occurs. Mutual exclusion of entire pairs is the needed property, not merely exclusion within each individual process.
