subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_title: Cache tag set and word bits
question_text:
A 4-way set-associative cache has 128 lines of 64 words each. Main-memory word addresses are 20 bits. What are the TAG, LINE and WORD field lengths, respectively?
Options:
(A) 9,6,5
(B) 7,7,6
(C) 7,5,8
(D) 9,5,6
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. First divide total lines by associativity to obtain sets. The address chooses a word inside a line, then a set; the remaining high bits form the tag.

2. Derivation and interpretation. There are 128/4=32 sets, needing 5 set-index bits. A 64-word line needs 6 word-offset bits. With 20-bit word addresses the tag uses 20−5−6=9 bits. Thus 9,5,6, option D; the stated LINE field is the set index in this associative organization.

question_title: Disk capacity and sector address bits
question_text:
A disk pack has 16 surfaces, 128 tracks per surface, 256 sectors per track and 512 bytes per sector, stored bit-serially. What are its capacity and the number of bits needed to address a sector?
Options:
(A) 256 Mbyte,19 bits
(B) 256 Mbyte,28 bits
(C) 512 Mbyte,20 bits
(D) 64 Gbyte,28 bits
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. Multiply surfaces, tracks and sectors for the number of addressable sectors. Multiply once more by bytes per sector for capacity; these two quantities require different address widths.

2. Derivation and interpretation. The number of sectors is 16×128×256=2^19. At 512=2^9 bytes each, capacity is 2^28 bytes=256 MiB. A sector address therefore needs 19 bits. Thus A, using the usual binary Mbyte convention; no byte/bit offset is needed when selecting a sector.

question_text:

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text:
Which statement about user-level and kernel-level threads is false?
Options:
(A) Context switches take longer for kernel-level than user-level threads
(B) User-level threads need no hardware support

question_title: Statement not equivalent to a disconnected graph existing
question_text:
Graph(x) means x is a graph and Connected(x) means x is connected. Which formula does NOT express “Not every graph is connected”?
Options:
(A) ¬∀x(Graph(x)⇒Connected(x))
(B) ∃x(Graph(x)∧¬Connected(x))
(C) ¬∀x(¬Graph(x)∨Connected(x))
(D) ∀x(Graph(x)⇒¬Connected(x))
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.

question_text:
Which graph is guaranteed to have an Eulerian circuit?

question_title: Minimal DFA for two modular counts
question_text:
What is the number of states in a minimum DFA for L={w∈{0,1}*: the number of 0s is divisible by 3 and the number of 1s is divisible by 5}?

(B) 11
(C) 10
(D) 9

2. Derivation and interpretation. Track the number of zeros modulo 3 and ones modulo 5, giving 3×5=15 states; accept residue (0,0). Every residue pair is reachable. Thus 15 states are necessary and sufficient, A.

question_title: Boolean forms not matching the minterms
question_text:
Let f(w,x,y,z)=Σm(0,4,5,7,8,9,13,15), with minterm bits in w,x,y,z order. Which listed expressions are NOT equivalent to f? Prime denotes complement. The source expressions are:
P = x′y′z′ + w′xy′ + wy′z + xz
Q = w′y′z′ + wx′y′ + xz
R = w′y′z′ + wx′y′ + xyz + xy′z
S = x′y′z′ + wx′y′ + w′y
Options:
(A) P only
(B) Q and S
(C) R and S
(D) S only
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. Read each complement mark carefully before testing equivalence. The source has Q=w′y′z′+wx′y′+xz. Expand product terms into minterms, or enumerate all sixteen inputs; a single extra or missing minterm disproves equivalence.

2. Derivation and interpretation. P, Q and R each produce minterms {0,4,5,7,8,9,13,15}, exactly the target set. For Q, w′y′z′ covers {0,4}, wx′y′ covers {8,9}, and xz covers {5,7,13,15}. For R, xyz+xy′z=xz, so R equals Q. S instead produces {0,2,3,6,7,8,9}: for instance input 0010 makes w′y true although minterm 2 is not in f. Thus only S is not equivalent, option D. The previous B answer resulted from dropping the prime on z in Q; the scanned original visibly contains that prime. This is a source-based independent correction, not an official-key match.

subject: 01-digital-logic
question_text:
Define X*Y=XY+X′Y′ for Boolean variables, and let Z=X*Y. Consider P: X=Y*Z; Q: Y=X*Z; R: X*Y*Z=1. Which statements hold?
Options:
(A) Only P and Q
(B) Only Q and R
(C) Only P and R
(D) All P,Q,R
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. The connective is equivalence/XNOR. Express it as 1⊕X⊕Y, then substitute the definition of Z; each variable appearing twice cancels under XOR.

2. Derivation and interpretation. The operation is XNOR, representable over modulo 2 arithmetic as X*Y=1⊕X⊕Y. With Z=1⊕X⊕Y, we get Y*Z=X and X*Z=Y. Moreover (X*Y)*Z=Z*Z=1; XNOR is associative here. Therefore all P,Q,R hold, D.

subject: 01-digital-logic
question_title: Universal function realization with one mux
question_text:
Only one multiplexer and one inverter may implement an arbitrary Boolean function of n variables. What is the minimum universal multiplexer size?
Options:
(A) 2^n-to-1
(B) 2^(n+1)-to-1
(C) 2^(n−1)-to-1
(D) 2^(n−2)-to-1
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. Shannon expansion fixes selector variables and leaves a cofactor at each data input. If one variable remains, its only four Boolean functions are 0,1,x,x′, all available with constants, a wire and one inverter.

2. Derivation and interpretation. Use n−1 variables as selector bits of a 2^(n−1)-to 1 multiplexer. For each selector assignment the remaining one-variable function is 0,1,x or x′, so a single shared inverter suffices. A smaller selector set leaves at least two variables; some cofactors, such as two-variable parity, cannot be supplied by a constant, a wire or one inversion. Thus the universal size under direct-variable selector wiring is 2^(n−1):1, C.

subject: 01-digital-logic
question_text:
For a 4-bit carry-lookahead adder, Pi=Ai⊕Bi, Gi=AiBi, Si=Pi⊕Ci and C_(i+1)=Gi+PiCi, where C0 is the input carry. All Pi and Gi are already available. With two-level AND–OR logic and unbounded gate fan-in, how many AND and OR gates are required for the carry generator used with outputs S3,S2,S1,S0,C4?
Options:
(A) 6 AND,3 OR
(B) 10 AND,4 OR
(C) 6 AND,4 OR
(D) 10 AND,5 OR
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. Expand every carry directly in terms of P,G,C0, avoiding a ripple chain. C1 has one product needing AND; C2 has two; C3 three; C4 four. The standalone Gi terms need no AND gates.

2. Derivation and interpretation. Expand C1=G0+P0C0; C2=G1+P1G0+P1P0C0; similarly C3 and C4 have 3 and 4 nontrivial product terms. With unbounded fan-in and all P,G supplied, the four carry outputs require 1+2+3+4=10 AND gates and one OR gate each, totaling 4 OR gates. Thus B. XOR sum generation is outside this AND/OR carry-generator count.

subject: 01-digital-logic
question_text:
A 4-bit up-counter has outputs A4,A3,A2,A1 from most to least significant. Control table: Clear=1 asynchronously clears to 0; Clear=0,Load=0,Count=0 holds; Clear=0 on a rising clock with Load=1 loads the parallel input; Clear=0 on a rising clock with Load=0,Count=1 counts up. The circuit fixes Count=1, Load=0 and parallel input=0011, and connects Clear=A3 AND A1. Starting at 0 and neglecting all gate/counter delays, which stable count cycle occurs?
Options:
(A) 0,3,4
(B) 0,3,4,5
(C) 0,1,2,3,4
(D) 0,1,2,3,4,5
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. First determine whether the parallel input is enabled. It is not, since Load=0. Then find the first binary count making the asynchronous clear condition true; that state immediately disappears.

2. Derivation and interpretation. The clear input is the AND of outputs A 3 and A 1. With Load=0 the displayed 0011 input is ignored and the device counts upward from 0. The first count having A 3=A 1=1 is 0101=5, which immediately asserts asynchronous clear. With negligible delays this transient 5 is not a stable count state; the stable cycle is 0,1,2,3,4 and back to 0, C.

subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_text:
A pipeline has IF, ID (decode/operand fetch), EX, WB. IF, ID and WB each take one cycle; EX takes one cycle for ADD/SUB and three for MUL. Operand forwarding is available. How many cycles complete this sequence?
ADD R2,R1,R0   (R2←R1+R0)
MUL R4,R3,R2   (R4←R3×R2)
SUB R6,R5,R4   (R6←R5−R4)
Options:
(A) 7
(B) 8
(C) 10
(D) 14
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. Draw one timeline per instruction. Forwarding removes waiting for register writeback, but it cannot make the three-cycle multiply result available before its EX stage finishes.

2. Derivation and interpretation. ADD uses IF1,ID2,EX3,WB4. Its result is forwarded to MUL, which uses IF2,ID3,EX4–6,WB7. SUB uses IF3,ID4 and waits for the EX unit/result, then executes EX7 and WB8. Therefore completion requires 8 cycles, B, assuming the stated forwarding permits consuming an EX result in the next cycle and no additional structural conflicts.

subject: 04-data-structures
question_text:
Evaluate the postfix expression 8 2 3 ^ / 2 3 * + 5 1 * − using a stack; ^ denotes exponentiation. What are the top two stack elements, top first, immediately after the first * is evaluated?
Options:
(A) 6,1
(B) 5,7
(C) 3,2
(D) 1,5
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. For each operand, push; for each binary operator, pop right operand then left operand, compute left op right, and push the result. Stop at the first multiplication rather than evaluating the whole expression.

2. Derivation and interpretation. Read 8,2,3, then exponentiation replaces 2,3 with 8; division replaces 8,8 with 1. Push 2 and 3; the first multiplication replaces them with 6. The stack is now [1,6] from bottom to top, so its top two elements are 6,1, A.

subject: 04-data-structures
question_text:
A binary tree has inorder traversal d,b,e,a,f,c,g and preorder traversal a,b,d,e,c,f,g. What is its postorder traversal?
Options:
(A) d,e,b,f,g,c,a
(B) e,d,b,g,f,c,a
(C) e,d,b,f,g,c,a
(D) d,e,f,g,b,c,a
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. The first preorder item is the root. Its position in inorder separates left and right subtrees; recursively repeat, then output left subtree, right subtree, root.

2. Derivation and interpretation. Preorder starts with root a. Inorder splits the left subtree as d,b,e and the right as f,c,g. The remaining preorder makes b the left root with children d,e, and c the right root with children f,g. Postorder is d,e,b,f,g,c,a, option A.

subject: 04-data-structures
question_title: Closed hashing with implicit linear probing
question_text:
An initially empty hash table has seven slots indexed 0–6 and h(x)=(3x+4) mod 7. Insert 1,3,8,10 in that order using “closed hashing” as stated in the source. Which final table is intended? A dash means an empty slot. The probing rule is not explicitly specified.
Options:
(A) [8,−,−,−,−,−,10]
(B) [1,8,10,−,−,−,3]
(C) [1,−,−,−,−,−,3]
(D) [1,10,8,−,−,−,3]
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. Under linear probing, collisions advance one slot at a time with wraparound modulo 7. Compute each home position before inserting and never overwrite an occupied slot.

2. Derivation and interpretation. The hash values for 1,3,8,10 are 0,6,0,6. With linear probing, place 1 at 0 and 3 at 6;8 probes from 0 to 1;10 probes 6,0,1 and lands at 2. The table is [1,8,10,empty,empty,empty,3], B. Closed hashing/open addressing does not alone specify the probing sequence; quadratic or double hashing could differ, so linear probing is an explicit assumption rather than a stated guarantee.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_title: Single-source shortest paths in an unweighted graph
question_text:
In an unweighted undirected connected graph, which method most efficiently finds shortest paths from a source S to every other vertex?
Options:
(A) Dijkstra from S
(B) Warshall
(C) DFS from S
(D) BFS from S
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. All edges have equal cost, so distance is the number of edges. A FIFO queue processes every distance-d vertex before any distance-(d+1) vertex.

2. Derivation and interpretation. BFS starts at S and discovers vertices in increasing number of edges from S. When a vertex is first discovered, its level is its shortest-path distance; parent pointers recover paths. With adjacency lists, every vertex and edge is processed O(1) times, giving O(V+E). DFS does not generally find shortest paths; generic Dijkstra adds priority-queue overhead, and Warshall solves a more expensive all-pairs/reachability problem. Thus D is the appropriate algorithm.

subject: 03-programming-in-c
question_title: Recursive function with shared static state
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. The static r is one persistent shared object, not a fresh zero-initialized local for each recursive call. Record the single assignment r=5 before unwinding the recursion.

2. Derivation and interpretation. The static variable r is shared by all activations. In f(5), r becomes 5, and the return expression is f(3)+2. Calls f(3), f(2), and f(1) each recurse with n−1 and add the unchanged r=5. The base f(0)=1. Hence f(1)=6, f(2)=11, f(3)=16, and f(5)=18 (D). No smaller activation changes r, so operand evaluation order does not affect this particular call.

subject: 04-data-structures
question_title: Leaves and branching factor of a full n-ary tree
question_text:
Here a complete n-ary tree means each node has exactly n children or none. It has I=10 internal nodes and L=41 leaves. Find n.
Options:
(A) 3
(B) 4
(C) 5
(D) 6
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. Count child edges once from the parent side and once using the identity edges=vertices−1 for a tree. Equating the counts eliminates the shape of the tree.

2. Derivation and interpretation. Count the edges in two ways. Each of the I internal nodes contributes exactly n child edges, while a tree with I+L vertices has I+L−1 edges. Thus nI=I+L−1 and n=(10+41−1)/10=5 (C). The question calls this complete, but explicitly defines the full n-ary property, which is all the calculation needs.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_title: Worst-case recursion depth of Euclid algorithm
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. This is Euclid’s algorithm. An upper bound comes from a constant-factor size reduction within two calls; a tight worst-case lower bound comes from consecutive Fibonacci arguments.

2. Derivation and interpretation. For positive integers n≥m>0, Euclid replaces (n,m) by (m,n mod m). Within two recursive steps the larger argument decreases by at least a factor of two, so there are O(log n) recursive calls. Consecutive Fibonacci inputs attain a matching lower bound: their quotients are one for most steps, and F_k grows exponentially in k, giving Θ(log n) calls in the worst case (A). The statement does not say worst case: when m divides n, there are zero recursive calls. Therefore Θ(log n) is not a pointwise bound for every input satisfying n≥m. Positive m is also necessary to avoid remainder by zero.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_title: Recursion repeatedly taking the square root
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. The function makes one recursive call, not n calls. Each square root halves the logarithm of the argument, so analyze the recursion in terms of log n.

2. Derivation and interpretation. Assuming unit-cost integer arithmetic and square root as intended, T(n)=T(floor(sqrt(n)))+Θ(1). After k reductions the argument is approximately n^(1/2^k), and reaches a constant when 2^k=Θ(log n). Thus k=Θ(log log n), giving D. Adding n to the returned value is one arithmetic operation, not n operations; floors change only constant-level stopping details.

subject: 04-data-structures
question_title: Binary search along the heap insertion path
question_text:
Insert an element into an array-represented max heap of n elements. Use binary search along the path from the new leaf to the root to locate its insertion position. What is the asymptotic worst-case number of key comparisons?
Options:
(A) Θ(log₂ n)
(B) Θ(log₂ log₂ n)
(C) Θ(n)
(D) Θ(n log₂ n)
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. The binary search is not across the entire array. It searches the sorted ancestor chain, whose length is logarithmic in n; take the logarithm of that length.

2. Derivation and interpretation. A complete binary heap has a root-to-new-leaf path containing Θ(log n) positions. Existing keys along this path are monotone because it is a max heap. Binary search among h=Θ(log n) positions uses Θ(log h)=Θ(log log n) key comparisons in the usual worst-case interpretation, so B. This is a bound on comparisons, not all insertion work: shifting keys along the path can still require Θ(log n) moves. Array indices allow an ancestor at a specified depth to be selected without doing key comparisons.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_title: Satisfying at least half the clauses of a CNF formula
question_text:
Which claim is true for formulas in conjunctive normal form under the usual nonempty-clause convention?
Options:
(A) Every formula has an assignment satisfying at least half its clauses
(B) Every formula has an assignment satisfying all its clauses
(C) Some formula has at most one quarter of its clauses satisfied under every assignment
(D) None of these
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. Pair any truth assignment with its complement. Each nonempty disjunctive clause has some literal, and that literal is true in exactly one of the two assignments.

2. Derivation and interpretation. For the conventional setting in which each clause contains at least one literal, consider any assignment and its bitwise complement. Every clause is satisfied by at least one of the two: choose any literal in it, which is true in one assignment. Hence the two assignments together satisfy at least m clause occurrences, and one satisfies at least m/2. This proves A. B fails for (x)∧(¬x), and the same half-clause guarantee rules out C. If empty clauses are permitted, the unstated nonempty-clause assumption matters: a formula consisting only of empty clauses is never satisfied at all, so A would fail and C could hold. The intended CNF convention excludes this degenerate case.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_title: A globally minimum-weight edge and minimum spanning trees
question_text:
In a connected undirected graph, w is the minimum edge weight and e is a particular edge of weight w. Which statement is false?
Options:
(A) Some minimum spanning tree contains e
(B) If an MST T omits e, every edge of the cycle in T+e has the same weight
(C) Every MST contains an edge of weight w
(D) Every MST contains e
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. Use the exchange argument: inserting a non-tree edge creates one cycle, and removing a cycle edge gives another spanning tree. Equal minimum-weight edges need not be individually mandatory.

2. Derivation and interpretation. Take any MST T. If e is absent, adding it creates a cycle. Every edge of that cycle has weight at least w by global minimality of w, and none can have weight greater than w: exchanging such an edge for e would make a strictly cheaper spanning tree. Thus all cycle edges have weight w, proving B; exchanging any one of them for e produces an MST containing e, proving A. Every MST contains an edge of weight w by the same argument (or contains e itself), proving C. However a triangle with all edges weight w has MSTs omitting any chosen edge, so e need not belong to every MST. D is false, assuming the usual loop-free graph convention.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_title: Comparison count to find both minimum and maximum
question_text:
Given an array of an even number n of values, both its minimum and maximum must be found. Which comparison-count claim is true?
Options:
(A) At least 2n−c comparisons are necessary for some constant c
(B) At most 1.5n−2 comparisons are sufficient
(C) At least n log₂ n comparisons are necessary
(D) None of these
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. A comparison within a pair simultaneously rules one element out as maximum and the other out as minimum. Exploit this dual use before separately reducing the two candidate sets.

2. Derivation and interpretation. Partition the even number n of values into n/2 pairs. Compare within each pair, putting its smaller member in a minimum-candidate set and larger member in a maximum-candidate set. Find the minimum of the n/2 smaller values and maximum of the n/2 larger values. The comparison count is n/2+(n/2−1)+(n/2−1)=3n/2−2, so B. This construction disproves the claimed asymptotically larger lower bounds in A and C.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_title: Bounds on the trial-division primality loop
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. A uniform lower bound must apply to easy inputs too. Even numbers terminate at i=2, whereas prime numbers make the loop test all candidate divisors through floor(√n).

2. Derivation and interpretation. Under the intended interpretation that n is the positive input integer, at most floor(sqrt(n))−1 candidate divisors are tested, so T(n)=O(sqrt(n)). For even n≥4, the first divisor i=2 causes immediate return, so T(n)=1 on an unbounded input family and no uniform Ω(sqrt(n)) lower bound is valid. For all sufficiently large n at least one iteration occurs, establishing Ω(1); B is therefore the intended answer. Prime n attain Θ(sqrt(n)). Source caveat: the printed function uses old-style IsPrime(n) and then declares int i,n inside its body, redeclaring its parameter n in the same scope. This is not valid C as printed; the algorithmic answer requires repairing the parameter declaration/removing the duplicate local n.

subject: 07-compiler-design
question_text:
A grammar has nonterminals S,C,S1, terminals a,b,i,t,e, start S, and productions S→iCtSS1 | a; S1→eS | ε; C→b. Why is this grammar not LL(1)?
Options:
(A) It is left recursive
(B) It is right recursive
(C) It is ambiguous
(D) It is not context-free
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. Read i,t,e as if, then, else. In nested conditionals, an else can attach to either the inner or the outer if. Exhibit two parses of the same string to prove ambiguity.

2. Derivation and interpretation. The grammar is S→iCtSS₁ | a, S₁→eS | ε, C→b. It is the dangling-else grammar. The string i b t i b t a e a has two parse trees: the e a can belong to the inner conditional (inner S₁→eS, outer S₁→ε) or the outer conditional (inner S₁→ε, outer S₁→eS). Therefore it is ambiguous and cannot be LL(1), giving C. Equivalently e belongs both to FIRST(eS) and FOLLOW(S₁), causing a prediction-table conflict with S₁→ε. Right recursion by itself is not an obstruction to LL(1), and these productions are context-free and not left recursive.

subject: 07-compiler-design
question_title: Regular grammars versus existence of LR(1) grammars
question_text:
Consider P: Every regular grammar is LL(1). Q: Every regular language has an LR(1) grammar. Which is true?
Options:
(A) Both P and Q true
(B) P true,Q false
(C) P false,Q true
(D) Both false
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. P concerns every presentation of a language, whereas Q asks whether a suitable presentation exists. A language can have a poorly factored grammar even though another grammar parses deterministically.

2. Derivation and interpretation. P is false: the right-linear regular grammar S→aA | aB, A→b, B→c has two alternatives whose FIRST sets both contain a, so this particular grammar is not LL(1). Q is true: construct a grammar from a DFA by using one nonterminal per state, production Q→aR for each transition on a, and Q→ε for each accepting state. Determinism gives at most one alternative per terminal; epsilon is selected at end of input. This yields an LL(1), hence LR(1), grammar for the regular language (or use the standard inclusion of regular languages in deterministic context-free languages). Thus P false and Q true, option C.

subject: 07-compiler-design
question_title: Register allocation and MOV count in a basic block
question_text:
A computer has only two registers. Instructions OP Rj,Ri store Rj OP Ri in Ri; OP m,Ri store M[m] OP Ri in Ri; OP is ADD or SUB. MOV m,Ri loads memory into a register and MOV Ri,m stores a register to memory. Generate code for t1=a+b; t2=c+d; t3=e−t2; t4=t1−t3. All operands start in memory and the final result must be in memory. What minimum MOV count is intended?
Options:
(A) 2
(B) 3
(C) 5
(D) 6
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. Track the unusual operand order: SUB e,R2 computes e−R2, not R2−e. Under expression-preserving generation, retain t1 in one register while computing t2 and t3 in the other. The scope of permitted algebraic rewrites affects the literal minimum.

2. Derivation and interpretation. For expression-preserving code generation, three MOVs suffice: MOV a,R1; ADD b,R1; MOV c,R2; ADD d,R2; SUB e,R2; SUB R1,R2; MOV R2,t4. The specified source-minus-destination semantics gives R1=t1, R2=t2 then t3=e−t2 then t4=t1−t3. There are two loads to initialize the two independently computed subexpressions and one store, yielding the intended option B (3). This minimum presumes the usual task of generating code for the given expression structure. If algebraic reassociation is allowed, two MOVs suffice: MOV c,R1; ADD d,R1; SUB e,R1; SUB a,R1; ADD b,R1; MOV R1,t4. This computes t4=a−(e−(c+d))+b. Furthermore, if arbitrary arithmetic instructions may initialize a register, SUB R1,R1 makes zero; replacing the initial MOV c,R1 by SUB R1,R1; ADD c,R1 leaves only the final MOV. Hence the literal unrestricted minimum is not 3, and the scope assumption must be disclosed; B is an intended, conditional answer rather than an unconditional theorem.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_title: Shortest remaining time scheduling and waiting time
question_text:
Shortest Remaining Time first schedules four processes: P1 arrives at 0 and requires 20 units; P2 at 15 requires 25; P3 at 30 requires 10; P4 at 45 requires 15. What is P2’s total waiting time?
Options:
(A) 5
(B) 15
(C) 40
(D) 55
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. At each arrival compare remaining service, not original burst lengths. Draw the execution intervals and count only the intervals after P2 arrives during which it is ready but not running.

2. Derivation and interpretation. P1 runs from 0 to 20: at P2's arrival at 15, P1 has only 5 units left versus P2's 25. P2 runs 20–30, leaving 15; P3 then arrives with 10 and runs 30–40. P2 resumes at 40. When P4 arrives at 45, P2 has 10 left versus P4's 15, so P2 continues until 55. Its waiting intervals are 15–20 and 30–40, totaling 5+10=15 (B). Equivalently completion−arrival−execution=55−15−25=15.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_title: FIFO anomaly and locality of reference
question_text:
A virtual-memory system uses FIFO replacement with a fixed allocation of frames. P: increasing a process’s frame allocation sometimes increases its page-fault rate. Q: some programs do not exhibit locality of reference. Which statement is true?
Options:
(A) Both true and Q explains P
(B) Both true but Q does not explain P
(C) P false,Q true
(D) Both false
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. Separate truth from causation. Belady’s anomaly is possible because FIFO does not retain a nested set of resident pages as frame count grows; locality is not the defining cause.

2. Derivation and interpretation. P is true: FIFO can exhibit Belady's anomaly. For example, reference string 1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5 incurs 9 faults with three initially empty frames but 10 with four. Q is also true: programs can make accesses without useful locality, for example broadly scattered independent random accesses. Q does not explain the anomaly; the issue is FIFO's failure of the stack-inclusion property, not simply the presence or absence of locality. Stack algorithms such as LRU do not exhibit this anomaly even on reference strings without locality. Thus B.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_title: Safe completion order from available resources
question_text:
Three processes share resource types X,Y,Z, with 5 units of each. Allocated and additionally requested vectors (X,Y,Z) are: P0 alloc=(1,2,1), request=(1,0,3); P1 alloc=(2,0,1), request=(0,1,2); P2 alloc=(2,2,1), request=(1,2,0). Each request is needed to finish, after which resources are released. Which process finishes last?
Options:
(A) P0
(B) P1
(C) P2
(D) None; the system is deadlocked
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. Subtract all allocations from the total vector to obtain current availability. Repeatedly choose a process whose remaining request fits componentwise, then add its old allocation back to availability.

2. Derivation and interpretation. Allocated totals are (1,2,1)+(2,0,1)+(2,2,1)=(5,4,3), so the initial available vector is (0,1,2). Only P1's remaining request (0,1,2) can be met. After P1 completes and returns all its resources, availability becomes (0,1,2)+(2,0,1)=(2,1,3). P0's request (1,0,3) can now be met, while P2 still needs two Y units but only one is available. P0 finishes next, leaving availability (2,1,3)+(1,2,1)=(3,3,4), which permits P2's request (1,2,0). The forced safe order is P1,P0,P2, so P2 finishes last (C), assuming each request is the additional resource vector needed for completion as stated.

question_title: Two intent flags give mutual exclusion but may deadlock
question_text:
Shared flags wants1,wants2 are initially false. P1 executes:
while(true) { wants1=true; while(wants2==true); /* critical section */ wants1=false; }
P2 executes:
while(true) { wants2=true; while(wants1==true); /* critical section */ wants2=false; }
The source places each remainder-section comment after its loop. Under atomic sequentially consistent flag operations, which statement is intended?
Options:
(A) Mutual exclusion is not ensured
(B) Bounded waiting is not ensured
(C) Critical sections must alternate strictly
(D) Deadlock is not prevented, but mutual exclusion is ensured
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. Test safety and progress separately. Two critical sections cannot overlap because each entrant advertises its intent. But if both advertise before either tests, neither can reach the instruction clearing its flag.

2. Derivation and interpretation. Under the standard sequentially consistent, atomic-read/write pseudocode model, each process sets its own wants flag before testing the other's flag and keeps it true throughout its critical section. Thus both cannot pass their tests and overlap in the critical section: whichever passes first prevents the other entering until it clears its flag. However, if both set their flags before either tests the other, each spins forever, giving deadlock. Thus D describes the decisive combination: mutual exclusion holds but deadlock prevention fails. Strict alternation is not required; one process can repeatedly enter while the other does not request entry. Option B needs care: under a broad interpretation that bounded waiting guarantees eventual entry, deadlock also violates it. In the usual bounded-overtaking formulation, distinguish this progress failure from another process overtaking a waiter indefinitely; the latter cannot occur here. D is the intended most specific answer, while the phrasing of B can be read more broadly.

subject: 09-database-management-systems
question_title: Relational difference detects missing female enrollments
question_text:
Relations are studInfo(studId,name,sex), keyed by studId, and enroll(studId,courseId), keyed by the pair. Every course has at least one male and one female enrollee. What does π_courseId(((π_studId(σ_sex="female"(studInfo))) × π_courseId(enroll)) − enroll) return?
Options:
(A) Courses taken by all female students
(B) Courses taken by a proper subset of female students
(C) Courses taken only by male students
(D) None of these
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. The Cartesian product enumerates required pairs for every female student to take every course. Subtraction identifies missing pairs, and projection asks which courses have at least one such missing pair.

2. Derivation and interpretation. Let F be the set of female student IDs and C the set of course IDs occurring in enroll. The Cartesian product F×C contains every possible female-student/course pair. Subtracting enroll leaves exactly pairs (f,c) for which female f is not enrolled in c. Projecting on courseId therefore returns courses missing at least one female student. Since the premise says every course has at least one female enrollee, these are courses whose female enrollee set is a nonempty proper subset of all female students. This is B, not courses taken by every female student.

question_text:
employee(name,sex,supervisorName) has key name. supervisorName names an employee’s supervisor. Interpret the tuple-calculus query {e.name | employee(e) ∧ ∀x[¬employee(x) ∨ x.supervisorName≠e.name ∨ x.sex="male"]}.

(B) Employees with no immediate male subordinates
(C) Employees with no immediate female subordinates
(D) Employees with a female supervisor
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:

2. Derivation and interpretation. The universal disjunction ¬employee(x) ∨ x.supervisorName≠e.name ∨ x.sex=male is the implication: if x is an employee supervised by e, then x is male. Consequently the result includes employees all of whose immediate subordinates are male, including employees with no subordinates by vacuous truth. Under the male/female domain convention used by the options, this is exactly employees with no immediate female subordinates (C). It says nothing about the sex of e's own supervisor.

question_title: Salary greater than every department employee
question_text:
employee(empId,name,department,salary) has more than one employee in department 5. We want employees paid more than every department-5 employee. Compare:
Q1: SELECT e.empId FROM employee e WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT * FROM employee s WHERE s.department="5" AND s.salary>=e.salary);
Q2: SELECT e.empId FROM employee e WHERE e.salary > ANY (SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employee s WHERE s.department="5");
Which statement is intended for an arbitrary table under non-NULL salary semantics?
Options:
(A) Q1 is correct
(B) Q2 is correct
(C) Both always produce the same answer
(D) Neither is correct
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. NOT EXISTS rejects the presence of a counterexample to “greater than everyone.” SQL ANY is existential: satisfying one comparison suffices. DISTINCT does not change that quantifier.

2. Derivation and interpretation. For each e, Q1 excludes e whenever any department-5 employee has salary >= e.salary. Thus it keeps exactly salaries strictly greater than the department maximum. Q2 uses > ANY, which means greater than at least one returned salary, not every salary. For department salaries 10 and 20, a salary 15 passes Q2 but not Q1. Hence A under the usual non-NULL salary interpretation. Strict SQL NULL semantics require qualification: NULL comparisons are UNKNOWN, so Q1 can admit NULL salaries or ignore unknown department salaries; no NOT NULL constraint is printed.

subject: 09-database-management-systems
question_text:
Which normalization statement is intended to be false? Interpret the textbook conventions discussed in the solution.
Options:
(A) Any two-attribute relation is in BCNF
(B) A relation whose every candidate key has one attribute is in 2NF
(C) A prime attribute can be transitively dependent on a key in a 3NF relation
(D) A prime attribute can be transitively dependent on a key in a BCNF relation
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. For a nontrivial dependency X→A, 3NF permits either X to be a superkey or A to be prime. BCNF removes the prime-attribute exception. Definitions of transitive dependence and empty determinants matter here.

2. Derivation and interpretation. Under standard textbook normalization conventions, a two-attribute relation is BCNF: a nontrivial dependency from one attribute to the other makes its determinant a key. Single-attribute candidate keys have no proper nonempty subset, so no partial dependency prevents 2NF. In 3NF a non-key determinant may determine a prime attribute, permitting the transitive dependency in C. BCNF instead requires every nontrivial determinant to be a superkey, so it excludes a transitive dependency through a non-key determinant. D is the intended false statement. Here transitive dependency means the normalization violation through a non-superkey, not merely any composable implication. The claims about two-attribute relations and singleton keys also assume the textbook convention excluding nontrivial empty-determinant dependencies. If such dependencies are allowed, R(A,B) with ∅ -> B and candidate key A violates both BCNF and 2NF: ∅ is not a superkey, and the nonprime B depends on a proper subset of key A. Consequently A and B are also false under that fully general interpretation, so D is the intended answer only with this convention.

question_text:
The order of a B+ tree leaf is the maximum number of (value,data-record-pointer) pairs it can hold. Block size is 1K bytes, value size 9 bytes, record-pointer size 7 bytes and block-pointer size 6 bytes. What is the leaf order?
Options:
(A) 63
(B) 64
(C) 67
(D) 68
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. Reserve space for the leaf’s next-block pointer before dividing the remaining bytes by entry size. Use 1K=1024 bytes and round the result down, because partial entries cannot be stored.

2. Derivation and interpretation. A leaf stores m pairs of 9-byte values and 7-byte record pointers, plus a 6-byte pointer to the next leaf. Therefore 16m+6 <= 1024, giving m <= floor(1018/16)=63. Answer A. Ignoring the leaf-link pointer would incorrectly give 64.

question_text:
For two transactions, consider schedules S1: r1(X);r1(Y);r2(X);r2(Y);w2(Y);w1(X) and S2: r1(X);r2(X);r2(Y);w2(Y);r1(Y);w1(X). Which are conflict serializable?
Options:
(A) Both
(B) S1 only
(C) S2 only
(D) Neither
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. Create a precedence edge only between different transactions on the same item when at least one access is a write. Read–read pairs do not conflict. A cycle is exactly the obstruction to conflict serializability.

2. Derivation and interpretation. In S1, r1(Y) precedes w2(Y), producing T1 -> T2, while r2(X) precedes w1(X), producing T2 -> T1. The cycle prevents conflict serializability. In S2, w2(Y) precedes r1(Y) and r2(X) precedes w1(X), both giving T2 -> T1; there is no reverse edge. S2 is equivalent to serial order T2,T1. Thus C.

question_text:
A slotted LAN has n stations. Each station independently attempts to transmit with probability p in a slot. What is the probability that exactly one station transmits?
Options:
(A) np(1−p)^(n−1)
(B) (1−p)^(n−1)
(C) p(1−p)^(n−1)
(D) 1−(1−p)^(n−1)
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. Choose which station is the sole sender, then require it to transmit and every other station to remain silent. The n resulting events are mutually exclusive, so add their probabilities.

2. Derivation and interpretation. Assuming independent station attempts, a fixed station transmits alone with probability p(1-p)^(n-1). There are n disjoint choices for the sole transmitter, giving np(1-p)^(n-1), option A.

A token-ring network transmits at 10^7 bits/s and signals propagate at 200 metres per microsecond. What cable length corresponds to a one-bit delay?

(B) 200 metres

question_title: Class B subnet and host counts
question_text:
A class B address is divided into subnets using a 6-bit subnet number. What maximum numbers of subnets and hosts per subnet are intended?
Options:
(A) 62 subnets,262142 hosts
(B) 64 subnets,262142 hosts
(C) 62 subnets,1022 hosts
(D) 64 subnets,1024 hosts
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. A class B prefix originally leaves 16 bits. Assigning six of those to subnet IDs leaves ten for hosts. Distinguish historical reserved subnet IDs from reserved host IDs and modern subnet conventions.

2. Derivation and interpretation. A class B network leaves 16 bits after its network prefix. Borrowing 6 subnet bits leaves 10 host bits, so usable ordinary unicast hosts per subnet are 2^10-2=1022. Under the historical convention excluding all-zero and all-one subnet numbers, the subnet count is 2^6-2=62, giving C. Modern subnetting permits those two subnet numbers and gives 64 subnets with 1022 hosts each; that pair is absent from the options. C is conditional on the obsolete convention, not a modern universal maximum.

question_title: CRC using polynomial x cubed plus one
question_text:
Protect message 11001001 using CRC generator x³+1. Which bit string should be transmitted?
Options:
(A) 11001001000
(B) 11001001011
(C) 11001010
(D) 110010010011
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. The generator degree is three, so append exactly three zero bits before polynomial division. Subtraction over GF(2) is XOR, with no borrowing. Replace the three zero placeholders by the remainder.

2. Derivation and interpretation. The generator x^3+1 is binary 1001. Append three zeroes to 11001001, obtaining 11001001000. Modulo-2 division by 1001 has remainder 011. Replace the trailing zeroes by this remainder to transmit 11001001011, option B. Dividing this codeword by 1001 gives zero remainder.

subject: 10-computer-networks
question_text:
Stations M,N are L kilometres apart. Frames have K bits; propagation delay is t seconds per kilometre; channel capacity is R bits/s; processing delay is negligible. What minimum sequence-number bit width is intended for maximum utilization with the stated “sliding window” protocol? ACK timing and protocol variant are not explicitly specified.
Options:
(A) ceil(log₂((2LtR+2K)/K))
(B) ceil(log₂(2LtR/K))
(C) ceil(log₂((2LtR+K)/K))
(D) ceil(log₂((2LtR+K)/(2K)))
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. A frame takes K/R seconds to serialize and an ACK takes a round trip of approximately 2Lt after the frame is sent. First find the necessary window in frames, then apply the Go-Back-N sequence-space constraint; do not confuse window size with number of labels.

2. Derivation and interpretation. Let transmission time T=K/R and one-way propagation time P=Lt. With negligible ACK serialization, full utilization needs an integer window W >= ceil(1+2P/T). For Go-Back-N with an m-bit sequence field, W <= 2^m-1, hence m >= ceil(log2(2+2LtR/K)); this is option A. The problem says only sliding window, not Go-Back-N, and does not state ACK timing: Selective Repeat instead needs sequence space at least 2W, while counting merely enough distinct labels without the Go-Back-N guard gives a different expression. Therefore A requires the standard Go-Back-N/negligible-ACK interpretation; the generic wording alone does not uniquely fix the answer.

question_title: Protocols matched to functional network layers
question_text:
Match P: SMTP, Q: BGP, R: TCP, S: PPP to 1: Application, 2: Transport, 3: Data link, 4: Network, 5: Physical layer.
Options:
(A) P-2,Q-1,R-3,S-5
(B) P-1,Q-4,R-2,S-3
(C) P-1,Q-4,R-2,S-5
(D) P-2,Q-4,R-1,S-3
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. SMTP transfers mail, TCP provides end-to-end transport, and PPP frames data on a link. The offered matching classifies BGP by its routing function; its TCP-based transport is a separate layering nuance.

2. Derivation and interpretation. SMTP provides application-layer mail transfer (1); BGP performs interdomain routing, conventionally classified here by its network-layer function (4); TCP is transport-layer (2); PPP is data-link-layer (3). Thus P-1,Q-4,R-2,S-3, option B. BGP actually exchanges control messages over TCP, so its implementation can also be described as an application-layer protocol; the offered matching uses routing function.

question_title: Data memory references in a loop
question_text:
R1,R2,R3 are general-purpose registers. The program, operation, and size in words are:
MOV R1,(3000): R1←M[3000], 2 words
LOOP: MOV R2,(R3): R2←M[R3], 1 word
ADD R2,R1: R2←R1+R2, 1 word
MOV (R3),R2: M[R3]←R2, 1 word
INC R3: R3←R3+1, 1 word
DEC R1: R1←R1−1, 1 word
BNZ LOOP: branch if the result is nonzero, 2 words
HALT: stop, 1 word.
Initially M[3000]=10, R3=2000 and each location 2000–2010 contains 100. The program begins at location 1000; all these numbers are decimal.
Assume word-addressable memory. How many data-memory references occur while running the whole program?
Options:
(A) 10
(B) 11
(C) 20
(D) 21
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. R1 is the countdown and starts at ten. Separate instruction fetches from data accesses: only the initial load and the two memory-operand MOVs inside each iteration count.

2. Derivation and interpretation. The initial MOV reads M[3000] once and sets R1=10. Each of 10 iterations reads M[R3] once and writes it once. All other operand operations are on registers; instruction fetches are not data references. Total data memory references = 1+10*2=21, option D.

question_title: Final value beyond loop write range
question_text:
R1,R2,R3 are general-purpose registers. The program, operation, and size in words are:
MOV R1,(3000): R1←M[3000], 2 words
LOOP: MOV R2,(R3): R2←M[R3], 1 word
ADD R2,R1: R2←R1+R2, 1 word
MOV (R3),R2: M[R3]←R2, 1 word
INC R3: R3←R3+1, 1 word
DEC R1: R1←R1−1, 1 word
BNZ LOOP: branch if the result is nonzero, 2 words
HALT: stop, 1 word.
Initially M[3000]=10, R3=2000 and each location 2000–2010 contains 100. The program begins at location 1000; all these numbers are decimal.
Assume word-addressable memory. What is the final content of location 2010?
Options:
(A) 100
(B) 101
(C) 102
(D) 110
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. Track the address used before INC R3, not after it. The first iteration uses 2000; after ten iterations R3 reaches 2010 only when the loop is about to terminate.

2. Derivation and interpretation. R3 starts at 2000. The 10 loop iterations access addresses 2000 through 2009, then R3 becomes 2010 and R1 becomes zero, ending the loop. Address 2010 is never written, so its initial content 100 remains. Answer A.

subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_text:
R1,R2,R3 are general-purpose registers. The program, operation, and size in words are:
MOV R1,(3000): R1←M[3000], 2 words
LOOP: MOV R2,(R3): R2←M[R3], 1 word
ADD R2,R1: R2←R1+R2, 1 word
MOV (R3),R2: M[R3]←R2, 1 word
INC R3: R3←R3+1, 1 word
DEC R1: R1←R1−1, 1 word
BNZ LOOP: branch if the result is nonzero, 2 words
HALT: stop, 1 word.
Initially M[3000]=10, R3=2000 and each location 2000–2010 contains 100. The program begins at location 1000; all these numbers are decimal.
Now assume byte-addressable memory and 32-bit words. If an ordinary interrupt occurs while INC R3 executes, what return address is pushed onto the stack?
Options:
(A) 1005
(B) 1020
(C) 1024
(D) 1040
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. Sum instruction lengths through the completed INC, multiply by four bytes per word, and add the program base. An ordinary interrupt resumes at the next instruction, not at the interrupted instruction’s starting address.

2. Derivation and interpretation. Instructions up through INC occupy 2+1+1+1+1=6 words. At 4 bytes per word, the next instruction DEC R1 is at byte address 1000+6*4=1024. An ordinary interrupt is serviced after the current instruction completes and saves the next instruction address, so C. The INC itself starts at 1020.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text:
A DFA over {a,b} has start state q0, accepting states q1,q2 and nonaccepting states q0,q3. Its complete transition table is: q0: a→q1,b→q0; q1: a→q2,b→q1; q2: a→q1,b→q2; q3: a→q1,b→q2.
Which regular expression denotes its language? Here + denotes union.
Options:
(A) b*ab*ab*ab*
(B) (a+b)*
(C) b*a(a+b)*
(D) b*ab*ab*
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. Before the first a the machine stays in nonaccepting q0. Once an a occurs, every later transition stays within the accepting pair q1,q2. q3 cannot affect strings read from the start state.

2. Derivation and interpretation. The start state q0 loops on b and is not accepting. Its first a enters accepting q1. Thereafter a alternates between q1 and q2 and b loops in either accepting state, so every suffix over {a,b} is accepted. q3 is unreachable from q0. Thus exactly the strings containing at least one a are accepted: b*a(a+b)*, option C.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text:
A DFA over {a,b} has start state q0, accepting states q1,q2 and nonaccepting states q0,q3. Its complete transition table is: q0: a→q1,b→q0; q1: a→q2,b→q1; q2: a→q1,b→q2; q3: a→q1,b→q2.
How many states does a minimum equivalent DFA have?
Options:
(A) 1
(B) 2
(C) 3
(D) 4
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. First remove unreachable states, then partition the remaining states by whether any suffix distinguishes their acceptance. q1 and q2 have identical future acceptance behavior even though their names differ.

2. Derivation and interpretation. Delete unreachable q3. States q1 and q2 are equivalent: both accept, b leaves each in the accepting class, and a switches within that class. Merge them. The remaining nonaccepting q0 and accepting merged state are distinguishable by the empty suffix, so two states are necessary and sufficient. Answer B.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_text:
Letters a,b,c,d,e,f occur with probabilities 1/2,1/4,1/8,1/16,1/32,1/32, respectively. Which list, in a,b,c,d,e,f order, is a Huffman code?
Options:
(A) 0,10,110,1110,11110,11111
(B) 11,10,011,010,001,000
(C) 11,10,01,001,0001,0000
(D) 110,100,010,000,001,111
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. Repeatedly merge the two lowest-probability nodes. Code length is leaf depth in the resulting binary tree; high-probability a should get a one-bit word. Prefix-free alone is not enough to guarantee optimality.

2. Derivation and interpretation. Huffman merging combines e and f (1/32 each) into 1/16, merges with d to 1/8, merges with c to 1/4, merges with b to 1/2, then merges with a. The resulting leaf depths for a,b,c,d,e,f are 1,2,3,4,5,5. Option A supplies a prefix code with these depths: 0,10,110,1110,11110,11111. Bit reversal at internal branches can give other equivalent codes, but A is the listed optimal code.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_text:
Letters a,b,c,d,e,f occur with probabilities 1/2,1/4,1/8,1/16,1/32,1/32, respectively. What is the average length of an optimal binary Huffman code (the linked Q76 code)? Derive the code lengths from these probabilities.
Options:
(A) 3
(B) 2.1875
(C) 2.25
(D) 1.9375
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. Average code length is probability-weighted, not the arithmetic mean of the six word lengths. Huffman merging gives lengths 1,2,3,4,5,5, with the shortest code assigned to the most frequent symbol.

2. Derivation and interpretation. Using the independently derived lengths 1,2,3,4,5,5, the weighted average is (1/2)*1+(1/4)*2+(1/8)*3+(1/16)*4+(1/32)*5+(1/32)*5 = 31/16 = 1.9375 bits per symbol. Answer D.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text:
A context-free grammar has nonterminals {S,A,B}, terminals {a,b}, start S, and productions S→aB | bA; B→b | bS | aBB; A→a | aS | bAA. Which string is generated?
Options:
(A) aaaabb
(B) aabbbb
(C) aabbab
(D) abbbba
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. Track the invariant #a−#b for strings derived from each nonterminal: it is 0 from S, +1 from A and −1 from B. Reject options violating the invariant, then construct a derivation for the survivor.

2. Derivation and interpretation. Every S-derived string has equal numbers of a and b; A-derived strings have one more a, and B-derived strings one more b. These invariants follow directly from all eight productions. Only aabbab among the four options has equal counts. It is generated by S => aB => aaBB => aabB => aabbS => aabbaB => aabbab. Thus C.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_title: Number of parse trees for aabbab
question_text:
A context-free grammar has nonterminals {S,A,B}, terminals {a,b}, start S, and productions S→aB | bA; B→b | bS | aBB; A→a | aS | bAA. For aabbab, the answer string to linked Q78, how many distinct derivation trees exist?
Options:
(A) 1
(B) 2
(C) 3
(D) 4
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. The first two a symbols force S→aB→aaBB. Enumerate how the remaining bbab splits between the two B subtrees. Count trees, not different orders of expanding the same tree.

2. Derivation and interpretation. The first two terminals aa force S -> aB and B -> aBB. The remaining bbab must split between the two B children. Each child has one more b than a. Exactly two splits work: b | bab and bba | b. For the first, the right child uniquely derives bab via B -> bS -> baB -> bab. For the second, the left child uniquely derives bba via B -> bS -> bbA -> bba. The single b children use B -> b. Thus there are 2 parse trees, option B; different orders of expanding a fixed tree do not count as additional trees.

subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_title: Cache misses across two array scans
question_text:
Main memory is byte-addressable with 2^16 bytes. A direct-mapped data cache has 32 lines, 64 bytes each, and starts empty. A 50×50 array of bytes is contiguous starting at hexadecimal address 1100H. The complete array is accessed twice, with no intervening changes to cache contents. The source does not specify traversal order; use increasing-address scans for the intended result. How many total data-cache misses occur?
Options:
(A) 48
(B) 50
(C) 56
(D) 59
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. Convert the starting address to a block number and count all touched blocks, including the partial final block. For the second scan, identify conflicts modulo the 32 cache lines instead of treating all 40 blocks as compulsory misses again.

2. Derivation and interpretation. Assuming each complete pass reads the array in increasing memory-address order, the 2500-byte array begins at 0x1100=4352, a 64-byte boundary. It spans ceil(2500/64)=40 blocks, numbered 68 through 107. The cold first pass misses 40 times. In the 32-line direct-mapped cache, blocks 68–75 and 100–107 compete for lines 4–11. In the second pass, loading 68–75 evicts 100–107, so both groups miss again, while the other 24 blocks hit. Total 40+8+8=56, option C. Merely saying the complete array is accessed does not specify traversal order; different orders can produce different miss counts.

question_title: Cache lines replaced on second scan
question_text:
Main memory is byte-addressable with 2^16 bytes. A direct-mapped data cache has 32 lines, 64 bytes each, and starts empty. A 50×50 array of bytes is contiguous starting at hexadecimal address 1100H. The complete array is accessed twice, with no intervening changes to cache contents. The source does not specify traversal order; use increasing-address scans for the intended result. Which cache lines are replaced by new blocks during the second access? Lines are numbered from zero.
Options:
(A) 4 through 11
(B) 4 through 12
(C) 0 through 7
(D) 0 through 8
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. Map each memory block to block_number mod 32. Forty sequential blocks exceed the cache by eight, so identify which eight line indices are used twice rather than assuming that replacements start at line zero.

2. Derivation and interpretation. With increasing-address scans as in Q80, the array occupies blocks 68–107. Modulo 32, the first eight blocks 68–75 and final eight 100–107 both map to cache lines 4–11. Only those lines are replaced in the second scan, first by 68–75 and later by 100–107. Answer A. Lines are numbered from zero; the result is conditional on the scan-order assumption omitted from the common statement.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text:
A process has three initially empty page frames and reference string 1,2,1,3,7,4,5,6,3,1. How many page faults occur with optimal replacement?
Options:
(A) 7
(B) 8
(C) 9
(D) 10
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. At a miss with full frames, evict the page whose next reference lies farthest in the future, treating never-used-again pages as farthest. Keeping pages 1 and 3 is valuable because both are referenced at the end.

2. Derivation and interpretation. For references 1,2,1,3,7,4,5,6,3,1 with three initially empty frames, first load 1,2,3 (the second reference to 1 hits). When 7 arrives, discard 2 because it is never needed again. Retain 1 and 3 while replacing the third frame successively by 7,4,5,6; each of these pages has no future use. The final 3 and 1 then hit. Faults are on 1,2,3,7,4,5,6, totaling 7, option A. Seven distinct pages also give a matching lower bound.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text:
A process has three initially empty page frames and reference string 1,2,1,3,7,4,5,6,3,1. How many more faults does LRU incur than optimal replacement?
Options:
(A) 0
(B) 1
(C) 2
(D) 3
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. LRU uses past recency rather than future references. Maintain a least-recent-to-most-recent list and move a page to the end even on a hit; then compare the full LRU count with the optimal count.

2. Derivation and interpretation. LRU faults on references 1,2,3,7,4,5,6,3,1; only the early repeated 1 hits. After loading 3, the least-recent order is 2,1,3; successive new pages evict 2, then 1, then 3, then 7. Therefore final references 3 and 1 also fault. LRU has 9 faults versus the optimal 7, an excess of 2, option C.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_title: Monotone lattice paths to ten ten
question_text:
A robot starts at (0,0). Each move increases either its x-coordinate or y-coordinate by one, so from (i,j) it can move to (i+1,j) or (i,j+1). How many paths reach (10,10)? C(n,k) denotes a binomial coefficient.
Options:
(A) C(20,10)
(B) 2^20
(C) 2^10
(D) None of these
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. Every valid path contains exactly ten right moves and ten up moves. Specify which ten of the twenty move positions are right moves; the rest are then fixed.

2. Derivation and interpretation. A path from (0,0) to (10,10) requires exactly ten right and ten up moves. Choose the positions of the ten right moves among the twenty total moves. The count is C(20,10)=184756, option A.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_title: Monotone paths avoiding a forbidden edge
question_text:
A robot moves one unit right or up at each step, starting at (0,0) and ending at (10,10). It may not traverse the edge (4,4)→(5,4). How many paths remain? C(n,k) denotes a binomial coefficient.
Options:
(A) 2^9
(B) 2^19
(C) C(8,4)×C(11,5)
(D) C(20,10)−C(8,4)×C(11,5)
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with all options and complete code or textual figure data; author visually checked all source pages. Independent expansion review completed; original fidelity remains separately qualified.
solution:
1. Approach. Count forbidden paths by splitting at the forbidden edge. Choose a path to (4,4), traverse the single forbidden step, then choose a path from (5,4) to the destination. Subtract this product from all paths.

2. Derivation and interpretation. Subtract paths using the forbidden edge (4,4)->(5,4) from all C(20,10) paths. A path using that edge has C(8,4) choices to reach (4,4), then the fixed forbidden step, then C(11,5) choices for five right and six up moves from (5,4) to (10,10). Thus the permitted count is C(20,10)-C(8,4)*C(11,5)=184756-70*462=152416, option D.

question_text:
Evaluate lim(x→∞) (x−sin x)/(x+cos x).

(A) 1
(B) −1
(C) ∞
(D) −∞
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. Divide both terms by x, obtaining (1−sin(x)/x)/(1+cos(x)/x).
2. Since |sin x|≤1 and |cos x|≤1, both divided trigonometric terms tend to zero by squeezing.
3. The denominator tends to 1, not zero, so the quotient limit is 1: A.

question_text:
For subsets P,Q,R of universe U, simplify (P∩Q∩R)∪(Pᶜ∩Q∩R)∪Qᶜ∪Rᶜ.

(A) Qᶜ∪Rᶜ
(B) P∪Qᶜ∪Rᶜ
(C) Pᶜ∪Qᶜ∪Rᶜ
(D) U
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. Distribute the common intersection: (P∩Q∩R)∪(Pᶜ∩Q∩R)=(P∪Pᶜ)∩Q∩R=Q∩R.
2. De Morgan gives Qᶜ∪Rᶜ=(Q∩R)ᶜ.
3. A set union its complement is U, giving D. The result is independent of P.

question_title: Parameter for a unique linear-system solution
question_text:
The equations x₁+x₂+2x₃=1, x₁+2x₂+3x₃=2, x₁+4x₂+αx₃=4 have a unique solution. The only possible value(s) of α is/are:

(A) 0
(B) Either 0 or 1
(C) One of 0,1,−1
(D) Any real number
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. Subtract the first equation from the second and third. The remaining coefficient rows are(0,1,1) and(0,3,α−2), so the determinant is α−5.
2. A unique solution exists exactly when α≠5. At α=5 the third reduced equation is three times the second, including its right side, so solutions are nonunique.
3. None of the printed choices gives the exhaustive set R minus{5}:0,1,−1 all work but are not the only possibilities, while any real number incorrectly includes5. No official key has been located; this is a source/options discrepancy, not a claimed official-key correction.
derived_answer: All real α except5; no exact listed option

subject: 01-digital-logic
question_text:
In IEEE floating-point representation, what does hexadecimal 0x00000000 represent?

(A) Normalized value 2^(−127)
(B) Normalized value 2^(−126)
(C) Normalized value +0
(D) Special value +0
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. Split binary32 into sign, exponent and fraction fields. Every field is zero here.
2. An all-zero exponent is reserved for zero/subnormal encodings, so the normalized-number formula with an implicit leading 1 does not apply.
3. The zero fraction makes the magnitude zero; sign bit 0 makes it +0. This is the special value in D.

subject: 01-digital-logic
question_text:
Minimize the Karnaugh map. Columns ab are 00,01,11,10; rows cd are 00,01,11,10. Rows of cell values are [1,1,0,1], [X,0,0,0], [X,0,0,0], [1,1,0,X]. X is a don’t-care; blank source cells are zero. Prime denotes complement.

(A) b′d′+a′d′
(B) a′b′+b′d′+a′bd′
(C) b′d′+a′bd′
(D) a′b′+b′d′+a′d′
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. Treat the map edges as adjacent. The four corners form a legal group by using the bottom-right don’t-care; b and d are zero throughout, giving b′d′.
2. Group the cells in the top and bottom rows of the left two columns. Here a=d=0, giving a′d′.
3. The union covers every specified 1 without any specified 0, so f=b′d′+a′d′, A. One implicant cannot cover both required ab=01 and ab=10 regions without including a forbidden ab=11 cell, so two terms are needed.

subject: 01-digital-logic
question_text:
For radix r, which r satisfy √(121ᵣ)=11ᵣ?

(A) Decimal 10
(B) Decimal 11
(C) Decimal 10 and 11
(D) Any valid radix greater than 2
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. Interpret the digits by place value: 121ᵣ=r²+2r+1=(r+1)², while 11ᵣ=r+1.
2. The positive square root is r+1 for every positive radix.
3. Digit 2 is valid only when the integer radix exceeds 2. Hence all valid r>2 satisfy the equation, D; there is nothing special about decimal 10 or 11.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_text:
What is the most efficient time complexity to count connected components in an undirected graph with n vertices and m edges?

(A) Θ(n)
(B) Θ(m)
(C) Θ(m+n)
(D) Θ(mn)
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. Maintain a visited flag for each vertex. Start a BFS/DFS at every vertex not yet visited and increment a component counter.
2. Each search visits precisely one previously unvisited component. Across all searches each vertex is processed once and each undirected edge twice.
3. With adjacency lists the total is Θ(n+m), C. The n term includes isolated vertices; an adjacency-matrix representation instead requires Θ(n²).

subject: 01-digital-logic
question_title: Compatible minterms of an internal signal
question_text:
An AND gate combines f₁ and f₂, and its output is ORed with f₃ to produce f. Given f₁=Σm(4,5,6,7,8), f₃=Σm(1,6,15), f=Σm(1,6,8,15), which offered f₂ works?

(A) Σm(4,6)
(B) Σm(4,8)
(C) Σm(6,8)
(D) Σm(4,6,8)
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. The circuit computes f=(f1∧f2)∨f3. Minterm8 must be supplied through f1f2, while4,5,7 must not be introduced.
2. Of the options, only f2=Σm(6,8) meets these conditions, giving final set{1,6,8,15}, C. The internal function is not uniquely determined over all possible minterms: values outside f1’s support are irrelevant and minterm6 is already covered by f3.
3. C is the unique compatible supplied choice.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text:
Which statement holds for {a^p | p is prime}?

(A) Not accepted by a Turing machine
(B) Regular but not context-free
(C) Context-free but not regular
(D) Neither regular nor context-free, but accepted by a Turing machine
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. Primality of the input length is decidable, so a Turing machine accepts the language. It is not regular: if a pumping length is p, choose prime q>p; a pumpable nonempty segment has length d≤p, and pumping it q+1 times changes length to q+qd=q(1+d), composite.
2. Every unary context-free language is regular (its length set is ultimately periodic/semilinear), so this language is not context-free either. Therefore D.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_title: Decidability questions about automata and grammar
question_text:
Which are decidable? I: whether the intersection of two regular languages is infinite. II: whether a given context-free language is regular. III: whether two pushdown automata accept the same language. IV: whether a given grammar is context-free.

(A) I and II
(B) I and IV
(C) II and III
(D) II and IV
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. For I, construct a product DFA for the intersection and test whether a reachable cycle can reach an accepting state; this decides infinitude. IV is a syntactic check of the grammar’s productions: every left side must be a single nonterminal.
2. Regularity of an arbitrary CFL and equivalence of arbitrary nondeterministic PDAs are undecidable. Thus I and IV, B.
3. IV asks whether the presented grammar is context-free in form, not whether an arbitrary grammar’s language happens to be a CFL.
