subject: 07-compiler-design
question_text:
Which describes a handle in LR parsing?

(A) A position in a sentential form for the next shift or reduce operation
(B) A nonterminal whose production is used for the next reduction
(C) A production possibly used for a future reduction and the position of the next shift or reduce operation
(D) The production used in the next reduction and the position of its right-hand side in the sentential form
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. Bottom-up LR parsing reverses a rightmost derivation: it replaces a production’s right-hand side by its left-hand-side nonterminal.
2. A handle must specify both which production to reduce and which occurrence of its right-hand side is the correct next one. Merely naming a position or a nonterminal is insufficient.
3. D gives exactly this production-and-position pair. A possible future reduction, as in C, is not necessarily the next handle.

subject: 07-compiler-design
question_text:
Why are some code optimizations performed on intermediate code?

(A) They enhance compiler portability to other target processors
(B) Program analysis is more accurate on intermediate code than machine code
(C) Dataflow-analysis information cannot otherwise be used for optimization
(D) Front-end information cannot otherwise be used for optimization
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. Intermediate code abstracts away many machine-specific details, allowing one optimization pass to serve several target back ends.
2. This reuse makes it easier to retarget the compiler, which is the portability benefit in A.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text:
If both L and its complement are recursively enumerable, L is necessarily:

(A) Regular
(B) Context-free
(C) Context-sensitive
(D) Recursive
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. Run recognizers for L and its complement in dovetailing fashion, alternating simulation steps so neither can prevent the other from progressing.
2. Every input lies in exactly one of the two languages, so exactly one recognizer eventually accepts. Accept if it is the L recognizer and reject otherwise.
3. This constructed decider halts on every input, making L recursive, D. Nothing here guarantees regularity, context-freeness or a linear-space bound.

question_title: Application data size passed to TCP
question_text:
What is the maximum size of data the application layer can pass to TCP?

(A) Any size
(B) 2^16 bytes minus TCP-header size
(C) 2^16 bytes
(D) 1500 bytes
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. TCP offers applications an ordered byte stream, rather than one application-message-per-packet service.
2. TCP divides that stream into segments; IP and link-layer limits constrain individual packets/frames, not the total stream length.
3. Thus neither 1500 nor 2^16 bytes is a maximum application stream size. A is intended. Real API calls may still impose implementation-specific buffer limits.

Which tuple-calculus expressions equal ∀t∈r P(t)? I: ¬∃t∈r P(t). II: ∃t∉r P(t). III: ¬∃t∈r ¬P(t). IV: ∃t∉r ¬P(t).

subject: 05-algorithms
question_text:
An undirected graph has vertices M,N,O,P,Q,R and edges MN,NO,OP,PQ,QM,QN,MR. Which is a possible queue-based breadth-first traversal?

(A) MNOPQR
(B) NQMPOR
(C) QMNPRO
(D) QMNPOR
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. BFS uses a FIFO queue, so all newly discovered neighbors enter behind previously queued vertices. Start at Q and discover M,N,P in that order.
2. Processing M next discovers R. Processing N then discovers O. Processing P adds nothing because O is already discovered.
3. The dequeue/visit order is Q,M,N,P,R,O, C. D puts O before R despite the specified first-layer order; the other offered orders violate BFS layers.

question_title: Trapezoidal error bound versus actual minimum
question_text:
What minimum number of equal subintervals is needed to approximate ∫₁² xe^x dx with error at most (1/3)×10^−6 using the trapezoidal rule?

(A) 1000e
(B) 1000
(C) 100e
(D) 100
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. For f(x)=xe^x on[1,2], f″(x)=(x+2)e^x is increasing, with maximum4e². The composite trapezoidal bound is |E_n|≤4e²/(12n²)=e²/(3n²). Requiring this upper bound≤10^−6/3 gives n≥1000e, corresponding to A; an integer subdivision count would be ceil(1000e)=2719.
2. This is a sufficient worst-derivative bound, not the exact minimum demanded by the wording. Direct high-precision evaluation gives error3.33057431918×10^−7 at n=2046, already within the tolerance and substantially below2719. At n=2045 the error is3.33383240096×10^−7.
3. Thus A describes the standard error-bound calculation, not a literal minimal integer answer. No official key is asserted.

question_title: Newton iteration for a square root
question_text:
The Newton–Raphson iteration xₙ₊₁=(xₙ+R/xₙ)/2 computes which quantity?

(A) Square of R
(B) Reciprocal of R
(C) Square root of R
(D) Logarithm of R
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. Newton iteration for f(x)=0 is x_next=x−f(x)/f′(x).
2. Set f(x)=x²−R; then f′(x)=2x and x_next=x−(x²−R)/(2x)=(x+R/x)/2.
3. Thus the fixed point satisfies x²=R. For R>0 and positive initial x, it computes the positive square root, C; zero starting values are invalid.

subject: 01-digital-logic
question_text:
Simplify (P+Q′)(PQ′+PR)(P′R′+Q′), where + is Boolean OR and juxtaposition is AND.

(A) PQ′
(B) PR′
(C) PQ′+R
(D) PR′+Q
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. Factor the middle term as P(Q′+R), so when P=0 the whole expression is 0.

question_text:
Aishwarya studies either CS or mathematics each day. After a CS day, the probability of mathematics next day is 0.6; after a mathematics day, the probability of CS next day is 0.4. Given CS on Monday, what is the probability of CS on Wednesday?

(A) 0.24
(B) 0.36
(C) 0.4
(D) 0.6
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. Interpret the given next-day probabilities as the transition probabilities of a two-state Markov chain. After CS, the chance of CS is 1−0.6=0.4.
2. Wednesday CS can arise through CS→CS→CS with probability 0.4×0.4=0.16 or CS→Math→CS with probability 0.6×0.4=0.24.
3. These cases are disjoint; add them to get 0.40, C. Without the usual Markov interpretation, unconditional pairwise information alone would not justify the two-step conditional calculation.

X is normal with mean +1 and variance 4. Y is normal with mean −1 and unknown variance. If P(X≤−1)=P(Y≥2), what is the standard deviation of Y?

(B) 2
(C) √2

question_text:
Which statements about auto-increment addressing are true? I: useful for self-relocating code. II: including it in an ISA requires an additional ALU for effective-address calculation. III: increment amount depends on the accessed data-item size.

question_text:
Which must be true of RFE (return from exception) on a general-purpose processor? I: it must be a trap instruction. II: it must be privileged. III: no exception can be allowed during its execution.

(B) II only
(C) I and II only

3. Architectures can instead permit restricted unprivileged returns that cannot escalate privilege, so the broad must wording is architecture-dependent.

subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_text:
Which are necessary for L1/L2 cache inclusion? I: L1 must be write-through. II: L2 must be write-through. III: L2 associativity must exceed L1 associativity. IV: L2 must be at least as large as L1.

(A) IV only
(B) I and IV only
(C) I,II,IV only
(D) I,II,III,IV
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. For every resident L1 block also to be represented in L2 while L1 can use its full capacity, L2 must be at least as large: IV. Write-back can be compatible with inclusion via appropriate dirty-state and invalidation handling, so I and II are not required.
2. Equal associativity can satisfy inclusion; it need not be strictly greater, so III is false. Hence A under the standard capacity convention.
3. A policy that deliberately underutilizes a larger L1 through back-invalidations could preserve resident-set inclusion with a smaller L2, so IV is not a purely set-theoretic necessity without the full-capacity convention.

Which are NOT true in a pipelined processor? I: bypassing handles all RAW hazards. II: register renaming eliminates all register-carried WAR hazards. III: dynamic branch prediction eliminates control-hazard penalties.

question_text:
Let f(n)=2^n, g(n)=n!, h(n)=n^(log n). Which asymptotic statement is true?

(A) f=O(g); g=O(h)
(B) f=Ω(g); g=O(h)
(C) g=O(f); h=O(f)
(D) h=O(f); g=Ω(f)
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. Compare logarithms, which preserve growth order for positive functions. log h=(log n)² up to base constants; log f=Θ(n). Since (log n)²=o(n), h grows slower than f.
2. Stirling gives log(n!)=n log n−n+O(log n), which grows faster than n. Thus f grows slower than g.
3. Therefore h=O(f) and g=Ω(f), D.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_title: Majority test in a sorted array
question_text:
What is the minimum worst-case number of comparisons needed to determine whether some integer appears more than n/2 times in a sorted array of n integers?

(A) Θ(n)
(B) Θ(log n)
(C) Θ(log* n)
(D) Θ(1)
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. If a value occurs more than n/2 times, it must occupy the middle array position. Take that value as candidate and use binary searches for its first and last occurrences; accept exactly when the count exceeds n/2.
2. This needs Θ(log n) comparisons in the worst case. A logarithmic lower bound follows by locating a candidate-block boundary among linearly many possible positions while distinguishing length floor(n/2) from floor(n/2)+1.
3. Sortedness is essential; without it a linear majority scan is needed. Thus B.

subject: 04-data-structures
question_title: Maximum splits in an order-four B-tree
question_text:
A B-tree of order 4 is built from empty by ten successive insertions. What is the maximum number of node-splitting operations?

(A) 3
(B) 4
(C) 5
(D) 6
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. An order-four B-tree has at most three keys per node. The maximum is five splits. For ordinary overflow-triggered insertion, inserting 1 through 10 in ascending order and promoting the lower middle key splits a leaf on insertions 4, 6, 8 and 10; the fourth leaf split also overflows and splits the root. For a timing-independent bound, after L leaf splits there are L+1 nonempty leaves. A B-tree with L+1 leaves has exactly L separator keys in all internal nodes combined: each internal node has one fewer key than children, and summing over the tree gives leaves minus one.
2. Consequently n≥(L+1)+L=2L+1. With n=10, L≤4. Under overflow-triggered insertion, the first internal split needs the root to receive four separators from four leaf splits. With no further leaf split possible, no second internal split can occur. Thus there is at most one internal/root split and the total is at most 4+1=5.
3. Under preemptive splitting, the full root may instead split after three leaf splits, distributing its three separators into a new root with one key and two internal children with one key each. At most one further leaf split is possible, which can increase only one such child to two keys; no internal node can become full again. The same upper bound therefore holds, and increasing-key insertion attains five splits under this convention too.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_title: Two edge-disjoint spanning trees and connectivity
question_text:
A graph G has n vertices and 2n−2 edges partitionable into two edge-disjoint spanning trees. Which statement is NOT true?

(A) Every induced subgraph on k vertices has at most 2k−2 edges
(B) The minimum cut has at least two edges
(C) Every pair of vertices has two edge-disjoint paths
(D) Every pair of vertices has two internally vertex-disjoint paths
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. The claim about two internally vertex-disjoint paths is not guaranteed. Take two copies of K4 sharing exactly one vertex: n=7 and m=12=2n−2. Each K4 decomposes into two spanning trees (for example a path on its four vertices and its complementary path); joining corresponding trees at the shared vertex gives two edge-disjoint spanning trees of the whole graph.
2. The common vertex is nevertheless an articulation vertex, so paths between the two sides must share it. A is true because each tree induces a forest with at most k−1 edges on a nonempty k-vertex set. B is true since each spanning tree contributes a distinct edge across every nontrivial cut.
3. C follows by taking the unique path in each of the two edge-disjoint trees.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_title: Quicksort recurrence from bounded partition sizes
question_text:
A quicksort pivot procedure splits the list into two sublists each containing at least n/5 elements. If T(n) counts sorting comparisons, which offered upper recurrence follows?

(A) T(n)≤2T(n/5)+n
(B) T(n)≤T(n/5)+T(4n/5)+n
(C) T(n)≤2T(4n/5)+n
(D) T(n)≤2T(n/2)+n
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. Each recursive subproblem has size at most 4n/5, because each side has at least n/5 elements. With the usual monotone worst-case upper-bound interpretation of T and linear partitioning cost, both recursive costs are bounded individually by T(4n/5), so T(n)≤2T(4n/5)+n, option C.
2. This loose recurrence follows immediately from the given size bounds. The tempting expression T(n/5)+T(4n/5)+n assumes that the most unequal permitted split maximizes the sum of recursive costs; monotonicity alone does not establish that.
3. More precisely the general recurrence is T(n)≤max_{n/5≤k≤4n/5}{T(k)+T(n−k)}+O(n), ignoring pivot/rounding constants. The standard comparison model includes linear partition/pivot overhead; the statement does not specify the cost of an arbitrary extra pivot-selection procedure.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_text:
Subset sum asks whether a subset of n positive integers sums to a positive integer W. Algorithm Q takes O(nW) time. Which statement is false?

(A) Q is polynomial-time for unary input encoding
(B) Q is polynomial-time for binary input encoding
(C) Subset sum belongs to NP
(D) Subset sum is NP-hard
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. B is false. The dynamic program takes O(nW), polynomial in the numerical value W, not in its binary encoding length Θ(log W).
2. For binary input W can be exponential in the input length, so this is a pseudo-polynomial algorithm. With unary encoding the input has length at least W and at least n, hence nW is polynomial in that length.
3. A subset is a polynomial-size certificate whose sum can be checked in polynomial time, so subset sum is in NP; its standard decision form is NP-complete and therefore NP-hard. Thus A, C and D are true.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_title: Dijkstra on the given negative-edge graph
question_text:
Run Dijkstra from a in this directed weighted graph: a→b:1, b→c:2, c→d:3, d→a:2, b→e:−3, c→h:−5, d→g:2, h→e:1, g→h:2, g→e:1, e→f:2, f→g:3. To which vertices does it compute correct shortest-path distances?

(A) Only a
(B) Only a,e,f,g,h
(C) Only a,b,c,d
(D) All vertices
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. All vertices receive the correct distance despite the negative edges. From a, settle b at 1, which sets c=3 and e=−2. Settle e at −2, then f at 0, setting g=3. Vertices c and g tie at 3.
2. Whichever is handled first, c sets h=3−5=−2 before h is settled (if g was handled first it only proposes h=5). Vertex h proposes e=−1, not an improvement over −2. Vertex d gets 6 from c and offers no improvement to a or g. Final distances (a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h)=(0,1,3,6,−2,0,3,−2).
3. They also satisfy every edge relaxation inequality, with each value attained by a path, proving optimality. Negative edges invalidate Dijkstra’s general guarantee, but do not force failure on every particular input.

subject: 04-data-structures
question_text:
Given the postorder traversal P of a BST on distinct elements 1,…,n, what is the most efficient time to construct the unique BST having traversal P?

(A) Θ(log n)
(B) Θ(n)
(C) Θ(n log n)
(D) None: the tree cannot be uniquely determined
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. Θ(n) time is sufficient and necessary. Read the postorder sequence backward: the next element is the root, followed by the right subtree in reverse postorder and then the left.
2. A recursive builder with allowed key interval (low,high) consumes a value only if it belongs in that interval; after creating a node with key r, build the right interval (r,high), then the left (low,r). Each key is consumed once and there are O(n) calls, so the time is O(n).
3. Distinct BST keys and their ordering make the construction unique. Reading and outputting n nodes requires Ω(n), yielding Θ(n).

subject: 04-data-structures
question_title: Batch insertion into a binary heap
question_text:
A binary heap contains n elements. Insert another n elements, not necessarily one at a time. What is the optimum total time?

(A) Θ(log n)
(B) Θ(n)
(C) Θ(n log n)
(D) Θ(n²)
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. Append all n new elements to the existing n-element heap array, then run bottom-up BUILD-HEAP on the resulting 2n elements. Its total sift-down work is O(n), since the number of nodes of height h decreases geometrically and Σh/2^h is constant.
2. Reading/storing n new elements requires Ω(n), so the optimum total is Θ(n), option B. The permission to insert them in a batch is crucial: n separate ordinary heap insertions can require Θ(n log n).

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_title: False claim about recursively enumerable subsets
question_text:
Which statement is false?

(A) Every NFA has an equivalent DFA
(B) Every nondeterministic TM has an equivalent deterministic TM
(C) Every regular language is context-free
(D) Every subset of a recursively enumerable set is recursive
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. D is false. The set Σ* is recursive and hence recursively enumerable, but it contains nonrecursive subsets, including an encoding of the halting language.
2. Even a recursively enumerable set itself need not be recursive. A holds by the subset construction for NFAs.
3. B holds because a deterministic Turing machine can dovetail the finitely branching computation tree of a nondeterministic machine, accepting exactly when an accepting branch is found. C holds because a finite automaton can be converted to a right-linear context-free grammar.

question_text:
DFA Y has start 1, final 2, and transitions on (a,b): 1→(1,2), 2→(2,1). DFA Z has start 1, final 2: 1→(2,2), 2→(1,1). Which printed table is their intersection product Z×Y? In every offered table P is initial, R is the only final state, and each row below lists its (a,b) destinations.

(A) P:(S,R), Q:(R,S), R:(Q,P), S:(Q,P)
(B) P:(S,Q), Q:(R,S), R:(Q,P), S:(P,Q)
(C) P:(Q,S), Q:(R,S), R:(Q,P), S:(Q,P)
(D) P:(S,Q), Q:(S,R), R:(Q,P), S:(Q,P)

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text:
Which statements are true? I: every left-recursive grammar can be converted to a right-recursive grammar and vice versa. II: all ε-productions can be removed from any CFG by suitable transformations. III: a CFG with only X→w or X→wY, where w is a terminal string and Y a nonterminal, always generates a regular language. IV: derivation trees for a CFG in Chomsky normal form are always binary trees.

(A) I,II,III,IV
(B) II,III,IV only
(C) I,III,IV only
(D) I,II,IV only
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. Under the conventional grammar-transformation interpretation, I, III and IV are true, giving C. I refers to eliminating left recursion using right-recursive auxiliaries and the symmetric transformation for right recursion; it does not mean every context-free grammar becomes a right-linear regular grammar.
2. II is false as stated: if ε belongs to the language, removing every ε-production cannot preserve that language, since no nonempty sentential form can derive the empty string without one. III is a right-linear grammar, possibly with multi-terminal labels; expanding labels into paths yields a finite automaton, so its language is regular.
3. IV is true in the at-most-two-children sense of binary tree: CNF uses A→BC or A→a (and possibly the special start ε-rule), so no derivation-tree node has more than two children.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_title: Matching language patterns to compiler requirements
question_text:
Match E: checking identifiers are declared before use; F: agreement of numbers of formal and actual function parameters; G: arithmetic expressions with matched parentheses; H: palindromes. Models: P={a^n b^m c^n d^m | n,m≥1}; Q: X→XbX|XcX|dXf|g; R={wcw | w∈{a,b}*}; S: X→bXb|cXc|ε.

(A) E–P,F–R,G–Q,H–S
(B) E–R,F–P,G–S,H–Q
(C) E–R,F–P,G–Q,H–S
(D) E–P,F–R,G–S,H–Q
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. The matching is E–R, F–P, G–Q, H–S, option C. E requires the same identifier string in declaration and use, modeled by the copy language wcw.
2. F matches counts of formal and actual parameters; a^n b^m c^n d^m models the two cross-referenced counts. G is modeled by X→XbX | XcX | dXf | g: b and c act as binary operators, d/f as matched opening/closing parentheses, and g as an operand.
3. H is modeled by X→bXb | cXc | ε, which generates even-length palindromes. These are structural analogies, not claims that the small grammars capture every feature of a programming language or all odd-length palindromes.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_title: Matching four NFAs to regular expressions
question_text:
Match four NFAs to regular expressions. Each NFA has lower state L (initial and accepting), upper-left A and upper-right B. Unlisted transitions are absent. P: L−0→A, A−0→L and B, B−1→A and B; B is also accepting. Q: L−0→A, A−0→L, A−1→B, B−1→A, B−0→B; only L accepts. R: L−0→A, A−1→L and B, B−1→A, B−0→B; only L accepts. S has R’s transitions with both L and B accepting. Expressions: 1: ε+0(01*1+00)*01*; 2: ε+0(10*1+00)*0; 3: ε+0(10*1+10)*1; 4: ε+0(10*1+10)*10*.

(A) P–2,Q–1,R–3,S–4
(B) P–1,Q–3,R–2,S–4
(C) P–1,Q–2,R–3,S–4
(D) P–3,Q–2,R–1,S–4
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. Name the lower start state L, upper-left state A and upper-right state B. Every automaton accepts ε at L; every nonempty accepted path begins with 0 from L to A. In P, cycles from A back to A are 00 via L or 01*1 via B, and a finishing path to either accepting state is represented by 01*.
2. Hence P matches expression 1: ε+0(01*1+00)*01*. In Q, the A-cycles are 00 or 10*1, with final 0 to L, giving expression 2. In R, the A-cycles are 10 or 10*1, with final 1 to L, giving expression 3.
3. In S, the same cycles apply but B is also accepting, so a final 10* covers both possible accepting destinations, giving expression 4. Thus P–1,Q–2,R–3,S–4, option C.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text:
Which sets are regular? I: {a^n b^(2m) | n,m≥0}. II: {a^n b^m | n=2m}. III: {a^n b^m | n≠m}. IV: {xcy | x,y∈{a,b}*}.

(A) I and IV only
(B) I and III only
(C) I only
(D) IV only
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. I and IV are regular, giving A. I has expression a*(bb)*: n and m are independent and only the parity of the b-count is restricted.
2. IV has expression (a|b)*c(a|b)* because x and y need not be equal. II is {a^(2m)b^m}; applying the pumping lemma to a^(2p)b^p pumps only a symbols and destroys the required 2:1 relation.
3. III is not regular: if it were, subtracting it from the regular language a*b* would make {a^n b^n} regular by closure under difference, a contradiction.

subject: 07-compiler-design
question_title: Activation records, recursion and escaping closures
question_text:
Which are true? I: a language without globals or nested procedures, but with recursion, can use static storage allocation. II: multilevel access links/displays are needed only for languages with nested procedures. III: recursion cannot use dynamic storage allocation. IV: nesting and recursion require heap allocation and cannot use stack activation records. V: languages allowing a function to return a function cannot use only stack allocation for activation records.

(A) II and V only
(B) I,III,IV only
(C) I,II,V only
(D) II,III,V only
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. Under the standard language-runtime assumptions, II and V are true, giving A. I is false: recursive calls can have arbitrarily many simultaneously live instances of local variables, so one statically allocated activation record per procedure is insufficient even without globals or nested procedures.
2. II is true: multilevel static access links/displays serve access to lexically enclosing procedures; without lexical nesting no multilevel environment chain is needed. III is false because dynamic stack allocation supports ordinary recursion.
3. IV is false because nested procedures and recursion alone can use stack activation records with static/dynamic links. V describes a returned nested function that can retain its defining environment after the creator returns: pure stack allocation cannot preserve that environment, so escaping environments need extended lifetime, normally heap allocation or copying.
4. The literal statement V is too broad without that escaping-closure assumption: a function may return a pointer to a global function, or a function with no captured environment, while ordinary activation records remain stack allocated. Thus A is the intended answer under the nested escaping-function interpretation, not a universal consequence of merely returning any function.

subject: 07-compiler-design
question_text:
An LALR(1) parser for G has shift-reduce conflicts if and only if:

(A) Its SLR(1) parser has shift-reduce conflicts
(B) Its LR(1) parser has shift-reduce conflicts
(C) Its LR(0) parser has shift-reduce conflicts
(D) Its LALR(1) parser has reduce-reduce conflicts
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. The equivalence is with canonical LR(1), option B. An LALR state merges LR(1) states having the same LR(0) core and unions lookaheads. Suppose a merged state has a reduction A→α on lookahead a and a shift on a.
2. The reduction/lookahead pair came from some original LR(1) state. The shift item is in the shared LR(0) core, so it also occurred in that very original state. Thus the shift-reduce conflict already existed before merging.
3. Conversely a conflict in an original LR(1) state survives the merge. Merging can introduce reduce-reduce conflicts, but cannot create a new shift-reduce conflict. SLR/LR(0) may report conflicts avoided by finer LR(1) lookaheads.

subject: 10-computer-networks
question_text:
During TCP slow start, how does the congestion-window size grow over successive round trips?

(A) Does not increase
(B) Linearly
(C) Quadratically
(D) Exponentially
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. The congestion window grows exponentially over successive round-trip times in slow start, option D. In the simplified textbook model each acknowledged segment increases the window by one MSS; a window of W segments produces about W acknowledgments in one RTT, so the window becomes approximately 2W.
2. After k such rounds it is approximately 2^k times its initial value, until reaching a threshold or encountering loss. Growth is per ACK rather than continuous time; delayed ACKs and practical implementations affect the precise factor but not the intended exponential-versus-linear distinction.

subject: 10-computer-networks
question_title: Usable hosts under a /21 IPv4 mask
question_text:
A Class B network uses subnet mask 255.255.248.0. What is the maximum number of hosts per subnet?

(A) 1022
(B) 1023
(C) 2046
(D) 2047
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
Step 1: 255.255.248.0 has 8+8+5=21 leading one bits because 248=11111000₂. Thus 32−21=11 host bits remain.
Step 2: A subnet has 2^11=2048 addresses; reserving the all-zero host part for the subnet address and the all-one host part for broadcast leaves 2046 usable host addresses, option C. The original Class B label does not change the host count once the subnet mask is supplied.

subject: 10-computer-networks
question_text:
A computer transmits on a 10-Mbit/s network through a token bucket replenished at 2 Mbit/s. Initially it holds its full capacity of 16 Mbits. How long can transmission continue at the full 10 Mbit/s?

(A) 1.6 seconds
(B) 2 seconds
(C) 5 seconds
(D) 8 seconds
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. At full output rate 10 Mbit/s, tokens are consumed at 10 Mbit/s while replenishment continues at 2 Mbit/s. The initially full 16-Mbit bucket therefore drains at a net rate of 8 Mbit/s.
2. Its maximum full-rate burst lasts 16/(10−2)=2 seconds, option B. Equivalently 10t≤16+2t gives t≤2.
3. Ignoring concurrent refill would incorrectly produce 1.6 seconds.

subject: 10-computer-networks
question_title: TCP connect before the server calls accept
question_text:
A TCP server executes socket(), bind(), listen(), then is preempted before any accept(). A client executes socket() and connect() to it. Which event can occur in the intended normal setting?

(A) connect() returns successfully
(B) connect() blocks
(C) connect() returns an error
(D) connect() causes a core dump
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. The client connect() can return successfully, option A. After socket(), bind() and listen(), the server kernel has a listening TCP endpoint and can complete the three-way handshake while the server process is descheduled.
2. The resulting established connection waits in the listener’s accept queue; accept() subsequently removes an entry and returns a connected socket to the server process. Hence user-space accept() is not required for the client handshake to complete.
3. The intended setting assumes an available backlog slot and normal network operation; incidental loss, queue exhaustion or unrelated errors can of course affect real calls.

subject: 03-programming-in-c
question_title: Aliased pointer updates and a value parameter
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. The scan prints **ppz += 1; z = *ppz; with only one dereference in the assignment to z. Since ppz has type int **, *ppz is an int * rather than the integer value of c. Assigning that pointer to int z violates the standard C simple-assignment constraints and requires a diagnostic. Consequently the printed program has no portable numeric answer among the options; accepting it as an extension does not make z equal to 5.
2. If the apparent typo is explicitly repaired to z = **ppz, the intended alias trace is: x starts as a separate copy 4; **ppz += 1 makes c=5 and z=5; *py += 2 makes c=7 and y=7; x += 3 makes x=7. The sum is then 7+7+5=19, option B only for that repaired program.
3. The source also uses historical void main() and omits the stdio declaration. Those conventions do not remove the single-dereference defect. The derived answer is therefore conditional: B applies only after the stated repair, and no listed portable answer is justified for the printed code. No official key is available.
derived_answer: B only if z=*ppz is repaired to z=**ppz; no portable numeric answer as printed

subject: 04-data-structures
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. p starts at the first node and q at the second. The temporary variable exchanges their value fields; no next pointer is modified.
2. p=q->next advances to the next pair’s first node, and q becomes its successor when it exists. Thus pairs (1,2), (3,4), (5,6) swap.
3. The final node 7 has no partner, so q becomes null and the loop stops. The sequence is 2,1,4,3,6,5,7, B.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text:
Counting-semaphore operations are P(s): decrement s and wait if s<0; V(s): increment s and wake one waiter if s≤0. Given binary-semaphore wait/signal Pb,Vb, consider:
P(s): Pb(xb); s=s−1; if(s<0){Vb(xb); Pb(yb);} else Vb(xb);
V(s): Pb(xb); s=s+1; if(s≤0) Vb(yb); Vb(xb);
What initial values should xb,yb have respectively?

(A) 0,0
(B) 0,1

Which statement about synchronous/asynchronous I/O is NOT true in the interrupt-driven model?

(A) An ISR is invoked on synchronous completion but not asynchronous completion

question_text:
Which is NOT true of deadlock prevention and avoidance?

(A) Prevention always grants a request if the resulting state is safe
(B) Avoidance always grants a request if the resulting state is safe
(C) Avoidance is less restrictive than prevention
(D) Avoidance needs resource requirements known in advance
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. Prevention breaks a necessary condition for deadlock, for example by requiring a fixed acquisition order or all-at-once requests. It may deny a request even though granting it would leave a safe state.
2. Avoidance explicitly tests safety using declared maximum needs and grants an otherwise valid request if safety is preserved.
3. Thus A incorrectly attributes avoidance’s rule to prevention. The conventional comparison makes B,C,D true: avoidance is less structurally restrictive but needs advance resource information.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text:
A process executes for(i=0;i<n;i++) fork();. How many child processes are created in total, assuming all forks succeed?

(A) n
(B) 2^n−1
(C) 2^n
(D) 2^(n+1)−1
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. Both parent and new child continue the loop after each successful fork. Hence each iteration doubles the number of processes still executing.
2. From one process, n iterations yield 2^n total processes. Equivalently the iterations create 1+2+⋯+2^(n−1) children.
3. Subtract the one original process: 2^n−1, B. Counting only n forks by the original parent misses descendants’ forks.

question_title: Pointer bits in a three-level page table
question_text:
A processor has 36-bit physical and 32-bit virtual addresses, 4-KiB page frames, and 4-byte page-table entries. Its three-level translation indexes level 1 with VA bits 30–31, level 2 with bits 21–29, level 3 with bits 12–20; bits 0–11 are page offset. How many address bits in entries at levels 1,2,3 identify the next table or final frame, respectively?

(A) 20,20,20
(B) 24,24,24
(C) 24,24,20
(D) 25,25,24
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. Each second- and third-level table has 2^9 entries of 4 bytes, so it occupies 2^11 bytes. With compact 2-KiB-aligned tables in a 36-bit physical address space, a pointer to either table needs 36−11=25 bits.
2. A data page frame occupies 2^12 bytes and its frame number needs 36−12=24 bits. The result is (25,25,24), option D.
3. This uses the intended natural table-size alignment; forcing every table to a separate 4-KiB frame would instead produce 24-bit table-frame pointers.

question_text:
R(P,Q,R1,R2,R3) and S(P,Q,S1,S2) each have key {P,Q}. Which relational-algebra queries are equivalent? ⋈ denotes natural join. I: πP(R⋈S). II: πP(R)⋈πP(S). III: πP(πP,Q(R)∩πP,Q(S)). IV: πP(πP,Q(R)−(πP,Q(R)−πP,Q(S))).

(B) I and III only
(C) I,II,III only
(D) I,III,IV only
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships

3. Thus only I, III and IV are equivalent, option D.

question_title: Normal forms of Book and Collection
question_text:
Book(Title,Author,Catalog_no,Publisher,Year,Price) and Collection(Title,Author,Catalog_no) have key {Author,Title}. Dependencies: Title Author→Catalog_no; Catalog_no→Title Author Publisher Year; Publisher Title Year→Price. Which statement is true?

(A) Both are in BCNF
(B) Both are in 3NF only
(C) Book is in 2NF and Collection is in 3NF
(D) Both are in 2NF only
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. In Book, both {Title,Author} and {Catalog_no} are candidate keys. No given dependency makes a nonprime attribute depend on a proper subset of a candidate key, so Book is in 2NF.
2. Publisher,Title,Year→Price violates 3NF because its determinant is not a superkey and Price is nonprime. Collection has only Title, Author and Catalog_no; its nontrivial determinants are candidate keys, so it is BCNF and hence also 3NF.
3. Therefore C is true. The wording of C does not say Collection is only in 3NF.

question_text:
A file has 16384 records of 32 bytes each, with a 6-byte key. It is ordered on a non-key field and uses unspanned organization. Block size is 1024 bytes and block pointers occupy 10 bytes. A multilevel secondary index is built on the key. How many first- and second-level index blocks are needed?

(B) 128 and 6
(C) 256 and 4
(D) 512 and 5

question_text:
A machine has a 64-KiB, two-way set-associative data cache with 16-byte blocks, managed using 32-bit virtual addresses; pages are 4 KiB. A row-major double ARR[1024][1024] starts at the beginning of virtual page 0xFF000. A double occupies 8 bytes. The cache is initially empty, there is no prefetching, and only ARR causes data-memory references. The code is:
for(i=0;i<1024;i++)
 for(j=0;j<1024;j++) ARR[i][j]=0.0;
What is the total tag storage in the cache directory?

(A) 32 Kibits
(B) 34 Kibits
(C) 64 Kibits
(D) 68 Kibits
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. The 64-KiB cache with 16-byte blocks contains 4096 lines. Two ways give 2048 sets, requiring 11 index bits; the byte offset needs 4 bits.
2. The 32-bit virtual address therefore leaves 32−11−4=17 tag bits per line. Total tag storage is 4096×17=69632 bits=68 Kibits, option D.
3. Valid, dirty and replacement bits are not tags and are excluded.

for(i=0;i<1024;i++)

1. Sequential row-major stores touch two adjacent 8-byte doubles in each 16-byte cache line. With the intended write-allocate policy and an initially empty cache, the first store misses and allocates the line, and the second store hits.

3. No line is reused after the traversal moves beyond it, so capacity misses do not change this pairing. A no-write-allocate cache would leave every store a miss and yield 0% (A).

subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_title: Semantics of an unconditional delay slot
question_text:
Delayed branching handles control hazards. For a delayed conditional branch, regardless of whether the condition is true or false, which statement holds?

(A) The instruction immediately following the branch in memory is executed
(B) The first instruction in the fall-through path is executed
(C) The first instruction in the taken path is executed
(D) The branch takes longer than any other instruction
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. In the ordinary non-annulling delayed-branch model, the instruction immediately following the branch in memory executes before control transfers, regardless of whether the branch is taken. That is the delay-slot instruction, option A.
2. Instructions beyond the delay slot on the fall-through or target paths are not both guaranteed to execute. Some ISAs offer annulled slots, but those are outside the simple delayed-branch model used by this linked pair.

subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_title: Safe instruction for a branch delay slot
question_text:
A processor has one branch delay slot. Which instruction can be moved into it without other program changes?
I1: ADD R2←R7+R8
I2: SUB R4←R5−R6
I3: ADD R1←R2+R3
I4: STORE Memory[R4]←R1
BRANCH to Label if R1==0

(A) I1
(B) I2
(C) I3
(D) I4
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. I4 stores R1 through address R4 but changes neither register used by the branch condition. Moving it from immediately before the branch to the single delay slot preserves its unconditional execution and lets the branch still test the R1 computed by I3.
2. I1 cannot move because I3 needs R2; I2 cannot move because I4 needs R4; I3 cannot move because I4 and the branch need R1. Thus I4, option D, is the legal choice in the stated dependency model.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_title: Counting strings with no consecutive zeros
question_text:
Let xₙ count binary strings of length n containing no consecutive zeros. Which recurrence does it satisfy?

(A) xₙ=2xₙ₋₁
(B) xₙ=x⌊ₙ/₂⌋+1
(C) xₙ=x⌊ₙ/₂⌋+n
(D) xₙ=xₙ₋₁+xₙ₋₂
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. Divide valid strings of length n≥2 by their first bit. A leading 1 can be followed by any valid length-(n−1) string.
2. A leading 0 must be followed by 1, leaving any valid length-(n−2) suffix. These two groups cannot overlap and cover every valid string.
3. Add their counts: xₙ=xₙ₋₁+xₙ₋₂, D. Initial values are x₀=1 and x₁=2, which are essential for numerical evaluation.

question_title: Length-five strings with no consecutive zeros
question_text:
Let xₙ count binary strings of length n containing no consecutive zeros. What is x₅?

(A) 5
(B) 7
(C) 8

subject: 05-algorithms
question_text:
Given positive integers S={a₁,…,aₙ} and target W>0, a subset-sum dynamic program uses Boolean X with n rows and W+1 columns. X[i,j] is true iff some subset of {a₁,…,aᵢ} sums to j, for 1≤i≤n and 0≤j≤W. Which recurrence is valid for 2≤i≤n and aᵢ≤j≤W?

(A) X[i,j]=X[i−1,j]∨X[i,j−aᵢ]
(B) X[i,j]=X[i−1,j]∨X[i−1,j−aᵢ]
(C) X[i,j]=X[i−1,j]∧X[i,j−aᵢ]
(D) X[i,j]=X[i−1,j]∧X[i−1,j−aᵢ]
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. Consider whether the chosen subset contains aᵢ. If not, the first i−1 elements alone must sum to j, represented by X[i−1,j].
2. If aᵢ is included, remove it once; the remaining subset of the first i−1 elements must sum to j−aᵢ, represented by X[i−1,j−aᵢ].
3. Either alternative suffices, so combine with OR, giving B. Using row i in the second term allows repeated copies of aᵢ; AND incorrectly requires both choices.

question_text:
Given positive integers S={a₁,…,aₙ} and target W>0, a subset-sum dynamic program uses Boolean X with n rows and W+1 columns. X[i,j] is true iff some subset of {a₁,…,aᵢ} sums to j, for 1≤i≤n and 0≤j≤W. Which entry, if TRUE, implies there is a subset summing to W? (This preserves the printed one-way wording.)

(B) X[n,0]
(C) X[n,W]
(D) X[n−1,n]

3. B is always true via the empty subset and D concerns sum n rather than W. Thus A and C both satisfy the literal one-way implication; C alone is necessary and sufficient for the full problem.

subject: 09-database-management-systems
question_title: Minimum relations for an ER diagram
question_text:
An ER diagram has strong entities M with attributes M1 (key), M2,M3, and P with attributes P1 (key),P2. Relationship R1 is many-to-one from M to P, with total participation of M. N is a weak entity with partial key N1 and attribute N2. Its identifying relationship R2 is many-to-one from N to owner P, with total participation of N. Neither relationship has attributes. What is the minimum number of tables in the standard relational mapping?

(A) 2
(B) 3
(C) 4
(D) 5
question_text_status: essential wording and all options transcribed; diagrams encoded as complete tables/edges/relationships
solution:
1. Use three relations: P(P1,P2), M(M1,M2,M3,P1), and N(P1,N1,N2). R1 is many-to-one from M to P with total participation of M, so a P1 foreign key in M represents it without a separate relationship table.
2. N is weak, R2 is its identifying many-to-one relationship with P, and N1 is the partial key; include P1 in N, whose primary key is (P1,N1). Thus the standard ER-to-relational mapping needs three tables, option B.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_text: Which property is not required of a group? A commutativity; B associativity; C an inverse for each element; D an identity element.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
Associativity, an identity and inverses are group axioms. Commutativity is an additional property of abelian groups, not all groups; for example permutations of three objects need not commute. Thus A.

Teaching detail:
A group requires closure, associativity, an identity and an inverse for every element. Commutativity is an extra condition defining an abelian group. For a counterexample to its necessity, permutations of three objects form a group under composition, but swapping 1/2 then 2/3 differs from doing those swaps in reverse order. Thus A is not a required axiom; B, C, D are.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_text: A simple connected graph on n≥2 vertices has no odd cycle. Find its chromatic number: A 2; B 3; C n−1; D n.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
An undirected graph with no odd cycle is bipartite, so two colors suffice. Connectedness and n≥2 ensure at least one edge, so one color cannot suffice. The chromatic number is exactly 2, A.

Teaching detail:
A graph has a two-colouring exactly when it has no odd cycle. One construction assigns colours by even or odd distance from a chosen root. If an edge joined equal-parity vertices, the corresponding paths would create an odd closed walk and hence an odd cycle. The given connected graph with at least two vertices has an edge, so one colour is insufficient. Therefore its chromatic number is exactly 2, not merely at most 2.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_title: Repeated degree in a connected graph
question_text: Which statement holds for every simple connected undirected graph with more than two vertices? A all degrees distinct; B at least two equal degrees; C at least three equal degrees; D all degrees equal.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
For n vertices in a simple connected graph with n>2, each degree lies in{1, ..., n−1}. There are n vertices but only n−1 possible degrees. By the pigeonhole principle at least two share a degree, B. Three equal degrees are not necessary, as a path on four vertices shows.

Teaching detail:
Connectivity excludes degree 0, and simplicity excludes degree above n−1. Thus n vertices must be assigned one of only n−1 possible degree values. The pigeonhole principle forces a repeated degree, proving B. A three-vertex path has degrees 1, 2, 1, so neither three equal degrees nor all equal degrees is necessary. This example also makes clear why the claim is about at least two, not a particular pair.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_title: Symmetry and antisymmetry of a relation
question_text: On {x, y, z}, R={(x, y), (x, z), (z, x), (z, y)}. Classify R: A symmetric but not antisymmetric; B antisymmetric but not symmetric; C both; D neither.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
The pair(x, y) is present but(y, x) is absent, so the relation is not symmetric. Both(x, z) and(z, x) are present with x≠z, so it is not antisymmetric either. Therefore D.

Teaching detail:
Symmetry would require (y, x) whenever (x, y) belongs, but (y, x) is missing. Antisymmetry would forbid distinct elements relating both ways; here (x, z) and (z, x) are both present with x≠z. Hence each property fails by a concrete witness, giving D. Antisymmetry does not mean the logical negation of symmetry; it is a separate condition.

subject: 01-digital-logic
question_text: Convert octal 1217 to the equivalent choice: A hexadecimal 1217; B hexadecimal 028F; C decimal 2297; D hexadecimal 0B17.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
Octal 1217 expands to binary 001 010 001 111. Grouping in fours gives 0010 1000 1111, hexadecimal 28F, or 028F with a leading zero. Hence B. Its decimal value is 512+128+8+7=655.

Teaching detail:
Using place values, octal 1217 equals 1·8³+2·8²+1·8+7=512+128+8+7=655. Divide into hexadecimal place values:655=2·256+8·16+15, so it is 028F hexadecimal. The same conversion follows by octal digit triples 001010001111, regrouped into binary quartets 0010 1000 1111.

subject: 01-digital-logic
question_text: Implement F=AB+C using only two-input NOR gates. Find the minimum gate count: A 2; B 3; C 4; D 5.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
Factor AB+C=(A+C)(B+C). Compute u=NOR(A, C), v=NOR(B, C), then NOR(u, v)=(A+C)(B+C), using three gates. Two do not suffice: with at most two gates, the final NOR receives only primary inputs and the output of one preceding NOR; exhaustive truth-table enumeration of all such input choices finds no realization. Thus 3, B. The accompanying check script verifies the lower bound without assuming complementary inputs are supplied.

Teaching detail:
Use the product-of-sums identity AB+C=(A+C)(B+C). Gate 1 gives ¬(A+C); gate 2 gives ¬(B+C); their NOR yields ¬[¬(A+C)+¬(B+C)]=(A+C)(B+C). Thus three gates suffice. With only two NOR gates, the last gate can take raw inputs and at most one derived NOR signal; checking these structural possibilities cannot produce this three-variable function. The accompanying exhaustive small-circuit checker supplies the lower-bound check, so three is minimal.

subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_text: How many 32K×1 RAM chips are needed for 256K bytes of memory? A 8; B 32; C 64; D 128.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
Each 32K×1 chip stores 32K bits. The required 256K bytes equal 2048K bits. Therefore 2048K/32K=64 chips, C.

Teaching detail:
A 32K×1 chip stores 32K bits, not 32K bytes. The requested capacity is 256K·8 bits. Dividing gives(256·8)/32=64 chips. Equivalently, eight chips in parallel provide a byte-wide 32K bank, and eight banks provide 256K byte addresses. Confusing width in bits with bytes would undercount by a factor of eight.

subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_text: When does a CPU normally begin interrupt service? A immediately when raised; B after checking at the end of fetch; C after checking when the current instruction finishes; D at fixed time intervals.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
In the conventional instruction-cycle model, an enabled pending interrupt is checked after the current instruction completes, then control transfers to its service routine. This preserves an instruction boundary rather than interrupting immediately at an arbitrary internal step. Thus C.

Teaching detail:
The usual instruction-cycle model completes an instruction before recognizing a pending interrupt and saving a consistent next-instruction state. This gives C. An asynchronous request can arrive earlier, but arrival is not the same as immediate transfer of control. Fetch completion is too early in that simple model, and periodic checking is not the general interrupt mechanism. Architecture-specific restartable instructions and precise-exception implementations are finer details outside this convention.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text: For which listed page replacement policy may Belady’s anomaly occur? A FIFO; B optimal; C LRU; D MRU.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
FIFO can incur more faults with more frames: the standard reference string 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 has 9 faults with 3 frames and 10 with 4. LRU and optimal replacement have the stack-inclusion property; ordinary MRU also preserves inclusion for nested initially empty caches. Thus FIFO is the supplied policy exhibiting the anomaly, A.

Teaching detail:
FIFO can evict a page because it arrived long ago even if it will be reused immediately; adding frames changes that queue order and can increase faults. The classic reference string 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 produces 9 FIFO faults with three frames and 10 with four. LRU and optimal have the inclusion/stack property that prevents this anomaly. The intended listed answer is FIFO; the baseline qualification concerning the exact MRU model remains important.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text: What is essential in each conventional page-table entry? A virtual page number; B physical page-frame number; C both numbers; D access-right information.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
A conventional page table is indexed by the virtual page number, so that number need not be stored again in each entry. Its essential mapping result is the physical page-frame number, B. Permission and status bits may also be included; inverted/hashed organizations have different entry layouts and are not the conventional indexed table assumed here.

Teaching detail:
A conventional page table is indexed by virtual page number, so that number is implicit in the entry’s position rather than necessarily stored again. The essential translation payload identifies the physical frame. Protection, valid and dirty information may also be stored, but access rights alone cannot perform address translation. Thus B is the expected minimum translation information; hashed or inverted page-table organizations can require additional explicit tags.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_text: What is the worst-case number of swaps in selection sort on n elements? A Θ(n); B Θ(n log n); C Θ(n²); D Θ(n² log n).
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
Each pass places one selected minimum using at most one swap, and there are n−1 passes. Inputs exist requiring a linear number of those swaps, so the worst-case swap count is Θ(n), A, despite Θ(n²) comparisons.

Teaching detail:
Selection sort scans the remaining suffix to find its minimum and moves that minimum into the next position. There are n−1 such placements and at most one swap per placement. Some inputs require a swap in a linear number of passes, giving a tight Θ(n) worst-case swap count. This differs from its Θ(n²) comparison count, since each pass may examine many elements before performing only one exchange.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text: For grammar S→aSa|bSb|a|b over {a, b}, identify the language: A all palindromes; B odd-length palindromes; C all strings beginning and ending with the same symbol; D even-length palindromes.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
The base productions produce a single a or b. Every recursive production adds the same symbol at both ends, preserving the palindrome property and odd length. Conversely strip matching outer pairs from any odd palindrome until one central symbol remains, yielding a derivation. Thus exactly all odd-length palindromes, B.

Teaching detail:
Every derivation starts from a one-symbol base a or b and adds matching symbols around the outside. Length therefore remains odd and the string remains a palindrome. Conversely, removing the equal end symbols from any odd palindrome repeatedly reaches its one-symbol centre, giving a reverse derivation. Even palindromes are excluded because no ε base exists; a string such as aabba begins/ends alike but is not generated.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_text: For single-source Bellman–Ford, assess P: always detects a negative cycle if any exists; Q: detects whether a negative cycle is reachable from the source. A P only; B Q only; C both; D neither.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
Single-source Bellman-Ford detects a negative cycle reachable from that source by checking for a further relaxable edge after n−1 passes. A negative cycle in an unreachable component remains at infinite distance and need not be found. Therefore Q is true but P is not, giving B.

Teaching detail:
Bellman–Ford initializes only the source distance as finite. Vertices unreachable from it remain at infinity, so a disconnected negative cycle does not cause a finite relaxation. After |V|−1 passes, an additional successful relaxation among reachable vertices detects a reachable negative cycle. Therefore Q is true and P, which omits reachability, is false. Connecting a new super-source to every vertex would change the setup and allow global detection.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_text: Problem π belongs to NP. Which assertion follows? A no polynomial algorithm exists; B a deterministic polynomial algorithm for π would imply P=NP; C if π is NP-hard then it is NP-complete; D π may be undecidable.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
A problem already in NP is NP-complete exactly when it is also NP-hard, so C. Membership in NP does not exclude membership in P, and solving an arbitrary NP problem efficiently would not by itself prove P=NP. Every NP decision problem is decidable.

Teaching detail:
NP-complete means both membership in NP and NP-hardness. Since membership is given, adding NP-hardness proves C directly. NP also contains easy problems in P, so a polynomial algorithm for an arbitrary member does not settle P versus NP. All NP languages are decidable by finite exhaustive certificate search, ruling out D, and A is not generally true.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_title: Regular expression with two distinguished zeros
question_text: Describe (0+1)*0(0+1)*0(0+1)*: A strings containing 00; B at most two zeros; C at least two zeros; D strings beginning and ending with either 0 or 1.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
Each starred(0+1) factor permits any binary string, but the two explicit 0 symbols must occur in order. Hence the expression accepts exactly strings with at least two zeros, not necessarily adjacent, C.

Teaching detail:
Each explicit 0 in the expression must consume a separate symbol, so every generated string contains at least two zeros. The three starred factors can contain arbitrary binary strings, including more zeros, and may be empty. Conversely, choose any two zeros in a string and assign the prefix, intervening segment and suffix to the three starred factors. The zeros need not be adjacent, so 010 is accepted despite lacking substring 00. Hence C.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text: Which is false? A each regular language has a unique minimal DFA (up to renaming); B each NFA has an equivalent PDA; C the complement of every CFL is recursive; D every NPDA has an equivalent DPDA.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
Minimal DFAs are unique up to state renaming; an NFA can be simulated by a PDA that ignores its stack. Every CFL is decidable, so its complement is recursive. But deterministic PDAs recognize a proper subclass of the CFLs recognized by NPDAs. Thus the universal conversion in D is false.

Teaching detail:
A PDA can simulate an NFA without using its stack. Context-free membership is decidable, so complementing that decision gives a decider for the complement. Minimal DFAs are unique up to state renaming. Deterministic PDAs, however, recognize a proper subset of context-free languages; nondeterminism cannot always be eliminated. For instance, unmarked palindromes need a nondeterministic guess of the midpoint. Thus D is the false universal claim.

question_text: Match P regular expressions, Q pushdown automata, R dataflow analysis, S register allocation to 1 syntax analysis, 2 code generation, 3 lexical analysis, 4 code optimization. A P4Q1R2S3; B P3Q1R4S2; C P3Q4R1S2; D P2Q1R4S3.

Teaching detail:
Regular expressions specify lexical tokens, giving P3. A pushdown store models nested grammatical structure in syntax analysis, giving Q1. Dataflow facts support optimizations such as dead-code elimination and constant propagation, giving R4. Register allocation assigns machine storage during code generation, giving S2. All four pairings are needed: option B is the unique complete match.

subject: 03-programming-in-c
question_text: C function fun(n, f_p) sets *f_p=1 and returns 1 if n≤1; otherwise t=fun(n−1, f_p), f=t+*f_p, *f_p=t, then returns f. main initializes x=15 and prints fun(5, &x). Choices A 6; B 8; C 14; D 15.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
At n=1 the function returns 1 and stores 1 through the pointer, overwriting the initial 15. For n=2, 3, 4, 5 the pairs(returned value, stored value) are(2, 1), (3, 2), (5, 3), (8, 5). The printed return value is 8, B.

Teaching detail:
The pointer is shared through all recursive calls, so its value must be tracked alongside the returned integer. The deepest call overwrites 15 with 1; thus 15 contributes nothing to the result. Each unwinding step returns the sum of the previous two Fibonacci-like values and stores the former return value for the next step. A trace gives n1:(1, 1), n2:(2, 1), n3:(3, 2), n4:(5, 3), n5:(8, 5). printf uses the returned 8, not the final stored 5.

subject: excluded
question_text: Rank coupling strongest to weakest: I content, II common, III control, IV stamp, V data. A I-II-III-IV-V; B V-IV-III-II-I; C I-III-V-II-IV; D IV-II-V-III-I.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
From strongest to weakest, content coupling reaches into another module’s internals; common coupling shares global state; control coupling passes control flags; stamp coupling passes a larger composite record; data coupling passes only needed data values. Thus I, II, III, IV, V, option A.

Teaching detail:
The ordering measures how much one module relies on another’s implementation. Content coupling directly accesses internals and is most intrusive. Common coupling shares globals; control coupling tells another module which action to take; stamp coupling passes a composite structure with more fields than needed; data coupling passes only the required values. Thus I-II-III-IV-V is the conventional ranking, A. This software-engineering topic is retained as supplemental coverage.

question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
The logical 3×3 grid is [ab, cd, cd], [ab, ef, gh], [ik, ik, gh]. Counting distinct vertically separated cells in each column gives 2, 3, 2. Counting distinct horizontally separated cells in each row likewise gives 2, 3, 2. Thus C. These counts refer to the visible cell regions after spans, not the number of underlying grid coordinates.

Teaching detail:
Expand the spans onto a three-by-three logical grid: row 1 ab, cd, cd; row 2 ab, ef, gh; row 3 ik, ik, gh. In column 1 the first two slots form one ab cell and the last is ik, giving 2 regions. Column 2 has cd, ef, ik, giving 3. Column 3 has cd then a two-row gh, giving 2. The same horizontal counting gives 2, 3, 2 by row. The question counts distinct drawn regions, not the three underlying grid positions in each direction.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_text: For a biased six-faced die, P(odd)=0.9P(even), the three even faces are equally likely, and P(even | value>3)=0.75. Which is closest to P(value>3)? A 0.453; B 0.468; C 0.485; D 0.492.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
Let E=P(even). Since P(odd)=.9E and probabilities sum to 1, E=10/19. Each even face has probability 10/57. Therefore P(even and >3)=P(4)+P(6)=20/57. Dividing by the given conditional probability 3/4 gives P(>3)=80/171≈.46784, closest to.468, B.

Teaching detail:
Let total even probability be e. Then 1=e+0.9e=1.9e, so e=10/19. Equal even faces each have probability e/3=10/57. Event even and greater than 3 consists precisely of 4 and 6, giving 20/57. Conditional probability equals intersection divided by P(value>3); hence 0.75=(20/57)/p and p=80/171≈0.46784. Choose the nearest offered value 0.468. No equality assumption for the three odd faces was needed.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_text: A cyclic group has rows/columns a, b, c, d and multiplication rows [a, b, c, d], [b, a, d, c], [c, d, b, a], [d, c, a, b]. Which pair generates the group? A a, b; B b, c; C c, d; D d, a.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
The identity is a. The powers of c are c, b, d, a, and those of d are d, b, c, a, so each generates all four elements. The element b has order 2 and a order 1. Thus the generators are c, d, option C.

Teaching detail:
The first row/column shows a acts as identity. The element b squares to a, so it generates only{a, b}. From the table c²=b, c³=d, c⁴=a, which visits all elements. Similarly d²=b, d³=c, d⁴=a. Therefore exactly c and d have order 4 and generate the cyclic group, option C. Being nonidentity alone does not guarantee being a generator.

question_text: G(x), S(x), P(x) mean x is a gold ornament, silver ornament, precious. Formalize “Gold and silver ornaments are precious.” A ∀x(P→(G∧S)); B ∀x((G∧S)→P); C ∃x((G∧S)→P); D ∀x((G∨S)→P).

question_text: Evaluate ∫₀^(π/4)(1−tan x)/(1+tan x) dx. A 0; B 1; C ln2; D(1/2)ln2.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
The integrand equals tan(π/4−x). Substitute u=π/4−x to obtain the integral of tan u from 0 toπ/4. Its antiderivative is−ln(cos u), giving−ln(1/√2)=½ln2, D.

Teaching detail:
Use tan(α−β)=(tanα−tanβ)/(1+tanαtanβ) with α=π/4. The integrand becomes tan(π/4−x). Set u=π/4−x; reversing the bounds cancels the minus from dx, leaving ∫₀^(π/4)tan u du. The antiderivative −ln(cos u) evaluates to−ln(1/√2)+ln1=(1/2)ln2. The interval contains no pole, so the substitution is valid throughout.

question_text: Which pair is equivalent? I ¬∀xP(x); II ¬∃xP(x); III ¬∃x¬P(x); IV ∃x¬P(x). A I, III; B I, IV; C II, III; D II, IV.

solution:
By quantifier negation, ¬∀xP(x) is equivalent to∃x¬P(x). These are I and IV, option B. II means every object fails P, while III means every object satisfies P; neither is generally equivalent to I.

Teaching detail:
Negating “every object satisfies P” means “some object does not satisfy P.” Thus I and IV express precisely the same proposition. In contrast, II says no object satisfies P, while III says no object fails P. On a domain with one P-object and one non-P-object, I/IV are true but II/III are false; this separates the alternatives directly. Answer B.

subject: 01-digital-logic
question_title: Shortest input to a specified FSM output
question_text: A two-bit state AB starts 00. For input 0, states 00, 01, 10, 11 transition respectively to 00, 10, 01, 10 with outputs 1, 0, 0, 0. For input 1 they transition to 01, 00, 01, 00 with outputs 0, 1, 1, 1. Minimum input length that arrives in 01 while emitting 1? A 3; B 4; C 5; D 6.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
The only transition ending in state 01 with output 1 is from state 10 on input 1. From 00, reaching 10 requires at least two inputs:00 --1/0-->01 --0/0-->10. Appending 1 reaches 01 and emits 1. Thus input 101 achieves the target in 3 steps, and the predecessor argument rules out shorter inputs. Answer A.

Teaching detail:
Work backward from the desired transition: among rows ending in 01, output 1 occurs only from 10 on input 1. From initial 00, a single input reaches only 00 or 01, never 10, so at least two inputs are needed before the final 1. Input 1 reaches 01 with output 0, then 0 reaches 10 with output 0, then 1 reaches 01 with output 1. This witness 101 has length 3 and matches the lower bound.

subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_text: Four pipeline stages S1–S4 require cycles per instruction: I1=(2, 1, 1, 1), I2=(1, 3, 2, 2), I3=(2, 1, 1, 3), I4=(1, 2, 2, 2). Execute two iterations of I1, I2, I3, I4. Find total cycles under overlapping buffered-stage execution, ignoring loop-control overhead: A 16; B 23; C 28; D 30.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
Ignoring loop-control overhead and allowing the eight instructions from two iterations to overlap, each stage starts after both its instruction’s previous stage and the previous instruction’s same stage finish. The four stage-completion times are(2, 3, 4, 5), (3, 6, 8, 10), (5, 7, 9, 13), (6, 9, 11, 15), (8, 10, 12, 16), (9, 13, 15, 18), (11, 14, 16, 21), (12, 16, 18, 23). Thus completion is at cycle 23, B. This recurrence uses buffered stage outputs; it does not charge an additional loop branch or force a pipeline drain between iterations. Such implementation choices are not explicitly specified by the prompt.

Teaching detail:
Construct a completion-time grid. A cell cannot start until the same instruction finishes its prior stage and the previous instruction releases this stage. Thus completion(i, j)=max(completion(i−1, j), completion(i, j−1))+duration(i, j). Applying it to the eight instruction rows yields final completion 23; the full row table is given above. Simply summing durations would ignore overlap, while assuming every stage takes one cycle ignores the supplied table. Pipeline draining or stage blocking without buffers changes the model, so those assumptions remain explicit.

question_text: An initially empty four-way cache has 16 blocks and memory 256 blocks. Reference sequence:0, 255, 1, 4, 3, 8, 133, 159, 216, 129, 63, 8, 48, 32, 73, 92, 155. With LRU within each set, which block is absent at the end? A 3; B 8; C 129; D 216.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
There are 16/4=4 sets, selected by block number modulo 4. Simulating LRU gives oldest-to-newest final sets: set 0=[8, 48, 32, 92], set 1=[1, 133, 129, 73], set 2=[], set 3=[3, 159, 63, 155]. Thus 3, 8, 129 remain but 216 has been evicted, D. In set 0, insertion 32 removes 4 and insertion 92 removes 216 after 8 was refreshed.

Teaching detail:
There are 16/4=4 sets; choose set number by block modulo 4. Only blocks mapping to the same set compete for four ways. In set 0, references are 0, 4, 8, 216, 8, 48, 32, 92. The second 8 refreshes its recency; inserting 48 removes 0, 32 removes 4, and 92 removes 216. The final set is 8, 48, 32, 92. Other sets retain 3 and 129. Hence 216, option D, is the absent listed block.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text: Resources R1, R2, R3, R4 have totals 3, 2, 3, 2. Requests are nonpreemptive and all-or-nothing. Independent progress timelines: P1 t0 requests 2R2, t1 requests 1R3, t3 requests 2R1, t5 releases 1R2+1R1, t7 releases 1R3, t8 requests 2R4, t10 finishes. P2 t0 requests 2R3, t2 requests 1R4, t4 requests 1R1, t6 releases 1R3, t8 finishes. P3 t0 requests 1R4, t2 requests 2R1, t5 releases 2R1, t7 requests 1R2, t8 requests 1R3, t9 finishes. Starting together, choose A all finish; B only P1/P2 deadlock; C only P1/P3 deadlock; D all deadlock.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
Initially P1 holds both R2 units, P2 two R3 units, and P3 one R4. P1 obtains its R3 at 1; P2 obtains its R4 and P3 two R1 at 2. P1 then waits for two R1 at 3 because only one is free. P2 can take that last R1 at 4. At 5 P3 releases its two R1, allowing P1 to resume. Its local-time 5 releases now occur at wall time 7, providing the R2 requested by P3. P2 releases R3 at 6 and finishes at 8, so P3 can obtain R3 at 8 and finish at 9. P1’s later two-R4 request can be satisfied after those completions, and it finishes. No circular wait persists; A. The timeline treats each listed time as progress time in an independently running process, with blocked execution delayed.

Teaching detail:
A temporary wait is not sufficient evidence of deadlock: check whether another process can still progress and release the needed resource. At time 3, P1 lacks its two R1 units, but P3 will release two at time 5 without needing anything from P1 first. That release allows P1 to resume. P1’s later release of R2 lets P3 progress; P2 independently releases R3 and finishes. The dependency chain therefore has an escape. Using progress times delayed during blocking gives the timeline above and all processes eventually finish, A. Treating delayed operations as occurring retroactively at their original wall times would be inconsistent.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text: A disk has 100 cylinders, head initially 50, all requests pending in listed order 4, 34, 10, 7, 19, 73, 2, 15, 6, 20. SSTF costs 1 ms per cylinder moved. Total seek time? A 95; B 119; C 233; D 276 ms.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
With all listed requests pending, SSTF visits 50→34→20→19→15→10→7→6→4→2→73. The decreasing leg costs 48 cylinders and the final increasing leg 71, totaling 119. At 1 ms per adjacent cylinder the seek time is 119 ms, B, excluding unspecified transfer/rotation costs.

Teaching detail:
At 50, the nearest pending request is 34 (distance 16), not 73 (distance 23). From 34 choose 20, then 19, 15, 10, 7, 6, 4, 2, always the nearest remaining cylinder. This monotone descent costs 50−2=48 in total. Only 73 then remains, costing 73−2=71. Total movement 119 times 1 ms gives 119 ms. Initial request order is irrelevant after all are pending under SSTF; FCFS would follow that order and produce a different answer.
