subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text: Process transitions: A Start→Ready; B Ready→Running; C Running→Ready; D Running→Terminated; E Blocked→Ready; F Running→Blocked. A uniprocessor always has some ready processes. Assess I D immediately causes another A; II E may occur while another process runs; III preemptive scheduling; IV nonpreemptive scheduling. A I/II; B I/III; C II/III; D II/IV.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
D terminates a running process; another ready process is dispatched through B, not newly admitted through A, so I is false. A blocked process can become ready by E while another runs, so II is true. The running-to-ready edge C represents preemption in the conventional diagram, making III true and IV false. Thus II and III, C. If C were instead explicitly defined as voluntary yield, the drawing alone would not establish preemption; the usual state-diagram convention is used.

Teaching detail:
Termination frees the CPU, so the scheduler dispatches an already ready process along B. It need not create or admit a process along A, making I false. An I/O completion can move a different process from blocked to ready while the CPU is busy, making II true. Under the conventional interpretation, C is preemption and distinguishes the diagram from a purely nonpreemptive scheduler. Thus III is selected with II; if C instead explicitly meant voluntary yield, that additional meaning would need a separate analysis.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text: Shared lock X starts 0. enter_CS spins while atomic test-and-set(X) returns true; leave_CS writes X=0. Assess I deadlock-free; II starvation-free; III FIFO entry; IV multiple simultaneous entrants. A I only; B I/II; C II/III; D IV only.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
Atomic test-and-set allows exactly one contender to observe 0 and enter, preserving mutual exclusion. When the current holder eventually leaves and resets X, some contender can acquire it, so the lock is deadlock-free under ordinary progress assumptions. There is no FIFO order or bounded-wait guarantee: the same process can repeatedly win and starve another. Only I holds, A. X denotes shared lock storage in this pseudocode, not an ordinary pass-by-value C local.

Teaching detail:
The atomic operation returns the old flag and sets it to 1 as one indivisible action. Only one contender can see old 0, so IV is false. Once the holder releases, some waiting process can succeed, assuming the holder and scheduler make ordinary progress; this supplies deadlock freedom. But no queue orders contenders. A newly arriving or repeatedly scheduled process can keep winning before another waiter, defeating both FIFO and starvation freedom. Therefore only I is justified.

question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
A sparse virtual address space need not allocate lower-level page tables for unused regions. This can reduce the resident page-table storage compared with a full flat table, B. Extra levels do not inherently shorten a page walk, eliminate page faults or become mandatory merely because a TLB exists.

Teaching detail:
A flat table allocates an entry for every possible virtual page even when most virtual regions are unused. A multilevel table can omit entire lower-level tables for absent regions, saving storage. This is the purpose captured by B. The price may be additional memory references on a TLB miss, not a guaranteed speedup. Neither a TLB nor the page-replacement policy logically requires a multilevel representation.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_text: T(n)=n for n≤3, otherwise T(n)=T(n/3)+cn with fixed c>0. Which growth rate? A Θ(n); B Θ(n log n); C Θ(n²); D Θ(n² log n).
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
Expanding T(n)=T(n/3)+cn gives cn+cn/3+cn/9+... plus a constant-size base case. For fixed positive c this is bounded above by(3c/2)n+O(1) and below by cn. Hence Θ(n), A, with routine integer rounding not changing the asymptotic result.

Teaching detail:
The recursion tree has only one child, whose size shrinks by 3. Work by level is cn, cn/3, cn/9, … . The geometric sum is below cn/(1−1/3)=1.5cn, while the root alone contributes cn. These upper and lower linear bounds establish Θ(n). The depth is logarithmic, but multiplying n by that depth overcounts because work per level decreases rather than remaining n.

subject: 04-data-structures
question_text: Insert 12, 18, 13, 2, 3, 23, 5, 15 in an empty 10-slot table using h(k)=k mod 10 and linear probing. Candidate A stores 2:2, 3:23, 5:15, 8:18; B stores 2:12, 3:13, 5:5, 8:18; C stores slots 2–9 as 12, 13, 2, 3, 23, 5, 18, 15; D chains 2:[12, 2], 3:[13, 3, 23], 5:[5, 15], 8:[18]. Other slots empty. Which is correct?
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
Insertions place 12 at 2, 18 at 8, 13 at 3, 2 at 4, 3 at 5, 23 at 6, 5 at 7 and 15 at 9 after probing past occupied slots 5 through 8. The final slots 2–9 are 12, 13, 2, 3, 23, 5, 18, 15, exactly option C.

Teaching detail:
Probe consecutive slots until empty. First 12→2 and 18→8; 13→3. Key 2 collides at 2 and 3, so goes 4. Key 3 goes 5; 23 goes 6; 5 goes 7. Finally 15 probes 5, 6, 7, 8 before reaching 9. This yields candidate C. D instead uses chaining, which is explicitly not the requested collision strategy; A/B discard keys rather than preserving them in later empty slots.

subject: 04-data-structures
question_title: Maximum AVL height with seven nodes
question_text: Maximum edge-height of an AVL tree with 7 nodes, with singleton height 0? A 2; B 3; C 4; D 5.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
The minimum-node recurrence for edge height h is N(h)=1+N(h−1)+N(h−2), with N(−1)=0, N(0)=1. Hence N(1)=2, N(2)=4, N(3)=7, N(4)=12. Seven nodes attain height 3 but cannot reach 4, so B.

Teaching detail:
To make an AVL tree as tall as possible with few nodes, give its two subtrees heights h−1 and h−2. Thus the minimum nodes at height h obey N(h)=1+N(h−1)+N(h−2). Starting with empty height−1 and singleton 0 gives 0, 1, 2, 4, 7, 12. Seven nodes suffice exactly for height 3, but any height 4 tree needs at least 12. This proves both attainability and impossibility, so B.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_text: Weighted undirected graph edges ab 5, ac 3, bc 4, be 2, bd 6, cd 5, de 6, df 6, cf 6, ef 3, eg 5, fg 4. Which accepted-edge sequence cannot be Kruskal? A be, ef, ac, bc, fg, cd; B be, ef, ac, fg, bc, cd; C be, ac, ef, bc, fg, cd; D be, ef, bc, ac, fg, cd.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
Kruskal considers accepted edges in nondecreasing weight. The relevant weights are be 2, ef 3, ac 3, bc 4, fg 4, cd 5. Equal-weight 3 or 4 edges may be interchanged in the valid choices. D instead accepts bc of weight 4 before ac of weight 3, even though ac can be safely accepted at that point. Thus D is not a possible Kruskal acceptance order.

Teaching detail:
Kruskal sorts by edge weight and accepts an edge whenever it connects two different components. The unique weight 2 edge be comes first. Both weight 3 edges ef and ac can be accepted, in either order, before any weight 4 edge. The weight 4 pair bc, fg can also be exchanged. D violates this by putting bc before ac. At that point ac is not cyclic, so it cannot have been skipped. The other orders respect both sorted weights and cycle avoidance.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_title: Quicksort with a fixed-rank fractional pivot
question_text: Quicksort selects the n/4-th smallest key as pivot using a linear-time selection algorithm. What is its worst-case time? A Θ(n); B Θ(n log n); C Θ(n²); D Θ(n² log n).
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
Selecting the one-quarter order statistic in linear time gives recurrence T(n)=T(n/4)+T(3n/4−1)+Θ(n). Each recursion level has linear total work, and the longest/shortest nontrivial paths are logarithmic up to constants. Equivalently the Akra–Bazzi exponent is 1 because 1/4+3/4=1. Thus Θ(n log n), B, assuming rank partitioning is implemented appropriately for distinct keys or duplicates.

Teaching detail:
At each partition, linear-time selection plus partitioning costs Θ(n), and subproblems have sizes approximately n/4 and 3n/4. Both are fixed fractions, so recursion depth is Θ(log n); total size across a complete level remains proportional to n until leaves. Consequently total cost is Θ(n log n). Choosing the quarter-rank pivot is not perfectly balanced, but still prevents the n−1 versus 0 split responsible for quadratic quicksort.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text: L1={a^m b^m c a^n b^n:m, n≥0}; L2={a^i b^j c^k:i, j, k≥0}; L=L1∩L2. Classify: A not recursive; B regular; C context-free but nonregular; D RE but not context-free.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
L1 contains exactly one c between a^m b^m and a^n b^n. For membership in L2=a*b*c*, no a or b may follow that c, so n=0. Thus the intersection is{a^m b^m c:m≥0}. A grammar for it is S→Tc, T→aTb|ε. The language is context-free and nonregular: removing its fixed final c by regular right quotient would otherwise make{a^m b^m} regular. Therefore C.

Teaching detail:
L2 permits only a block of a’s, then b’s, then c’s. A word of L1 has one central c, so its trailing a^n b^n must be empty to fit L2. Thus L={a^m b^m c:m≥0}. The grammar S→Tc and T→aTb|ε proves context-freeness. For nonregularity, removing the final fixed c from a hypothetical finite automaton would recognize the classic nonregular language a^m b^m. Hence C, not the much stronger undecidability alternatives.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text: A DFA starts q0, accepts only q2. On 0, q0→q1→q2→q2; on 1, all states go q0. What does it accept? A strings beginning 0 or 1; B ending 0; C ending 00; D containing 00.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
The states record zero, one, or at least two consecutive zeros at the end. Every 1 returns to the start state; 0 advances to the accepting state after the second consecutive zero, where further zeros loop. Hence exactly strings ending 00 are accepted, C, rather than all strings that merely contain 00 somewhere.

Teaching detail:
The state records the length of the current suffix of consecutive zeros, capped at 2. Reading 1 resets that suffix to length 0. Reading a second consecutive 0 reaches q2; additional zeros stay accepting. A string such as 001 contains 00 but ends in 1 and is rejected, separating C from D. A single 0 reaches q1 and is rejected, separating C from B.

subject: 07-compiler-design
question_text: Assess I some programming-language parsers have complexity below Θ(n³); II recursion can be implemented with static storage allocation; III no L-attributed definition can be evaluated bottom-up; IV optimization can occur at source and intermediate-code levels. A I/II; B I/IV; C III/IV; D I/III/IV.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
I is true: LL/LR parsing for suitable grammars runs in linear time, below the general cubic CFL bound. II is false for unrestricted recursion under static allocation of activation records, since simultaneous recursive calls need distinct storage. III is false because S-attributed definitions are also L-attributed and can be evaluated bottom-up. IV is true: optimizations may occur at source and intermediate-code levels. Thus I and IV, B. Tail-recursive/bounded special cases do not justify the unrestricted static-allocation claim.

Teaching detail:
LL/LR parsers for suitable grammars run in linear time, establishing I without claiming every CFG can be parsed that way. Unbounded recursive activation records cannot all be assigned one fixed static location, so II is false in the intended general model. S-attributed definitions are a subclass of L-attributed ones and can be evaluated bottom-up, disproving III’s universal negative. Algebraic source rewrites and intermediate-code optimizations illustrate IV. Therefore I and IV are true.

subject: 09-database-management-systems
question_text: T1=R1x, W1x, W1y; T2=R2x, R2y, W2y. S1=R1x, R2x, R2y, W1x, W1y, W2y; S2=R1x, R2x, R2y, W1x, W2y, W1y; S3=R1x, W1x, R2x, W1y, R2y, W2y; S4=R2x, R2y, R1x, W1x, W1y, W2y. Which are conflict-serializable? A S1/S2; B S2/S3; C S3 only; D S4 only.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
S1 has T2→T1 from r2(x) before w1(x), but T1→T2 from w1(y) before w2(y), so it cycles. S2 has only T2→T1: both its reads and final write of y precede T1’s conflicting writes. S3 has only T1→T2, as w1(x) and w1(y) precede T2’s accesses. S4 cycles for the same opposing x and y directions as S1. Therefore S2 and S3 are conflict-serializable, B.

Teaching detail:
Build one vertex per transaction and add an edge when an earlier operation conflicts with a later operation of the other transaction on the same item, with at least one write. Reads of different items or two reads do not conflict. S2 has only 2→1, so it is equivalent to serial T2, T1; S3 has only 1→2. S1/S4 each contain both directions and therefore a directed cycle. Acyclicity, not whether operations are interleaved, determines conflict serializability.

subject: 04-data-structures
question_text: Insert 10, 3, 6, 8, 4, 2, 1 into an empty B+ tree. Internal nodes allow at most 3 child pointers; leaves at most 2 data items. What is the maximum number of leaf splits, allowing valid choices of how 3 overflow items split? A 2; B 3; C 4; D 5.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
There can be at most one leaf split per insertion; the first two keys fit in the initial two-item leaf, so at most five splits occur. This bound is attained by leaving two smaller keys in the left leaf and one larger key in the right leaf at each overflow. Starting[3, 10], insertion 6 gives[3, 6]|[10]; 8 gives[3, 6]|[8]|[10]; 4 gives[3, 4]|[6]|[8]|[10]; 2 gives[2, 3]|[4]|[6]|[8]|[10]; 1 gives[1, 2]|[3]|[4]|[6]|[8]|[10]. Thus all five later insertions split a leaf, D. Internal-node splits are not counted. Exhaustive permitted split-choice enumeration confirms the maximum 5.

Teaching detail:
The first two insertions cannot split a capacity-two leaf. There are only five insertions left and each can overflow at most one leaf, so five is an upper bound. The explicit sequence of valid 1/2 splits in the baseline attains one split on each remaining insertion. That witness proves the maximum, not merely an observed count under one fixed implementation. Promoted separator changes and internal-node splits do not add to the requested leaf-split count.

subject: 09-database-management-systems
question_text: Relations r on R={a, b, c}, s on S={c}. I=π_ab(r)−π_ab((π_ab(r)×s)−r). II={t∈π_ab(r):∀u∈s ∃v∈r(u=v[c]∧t=v[ab])}. III replaces that quantification by∀v∈r ∃u∈s with the same equality predicates. IV SELECT R.a, R.b FROM R, S WHERE R.c=S.c. Which pair is equivalent? A I/II; B I/III; C II/IV; D III/IV.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
I begins with candidate(a, b) pairs from r and removes those for which some c in s is missing from r, exactly relational division r÷s. II expresses the same condition: for every tuple u in s there exists a tuple v in r matching both u’s c and the candidate(a, b). Thus I and II are equivalent, A, including empty s because both restrict candidates to the projection of r. III reverses the quantifiers and requires all r tuples to share the candidate pair; IV is only an existential matching join, not universal division.

Teaching detail:
Division asks for candidates paired with every c in s. Expression I constructs all required candidate/c combinations, subtracts actual tuples to find missing combinations, then removes the candidates with any missing one. II directly quantifies the same every-c requirement. A join only requires at least one matching c, so IV cannot replace division. Empty s is handled consistently because both I and II retain candidates only fromπ_ab(r), rather than introducing an infinite domain.

subject: 10-computer-networks
question_text: RSA has n=pq and φ(n)=(p−1)(q−1), message 0<M<n. The source calls(e, n) private and(d, n) public. Assess I M′=M^e mod n and M=(M′)^d mod n; II ed≡1 mod n; III ed≡1 mod φ(n); IV both message exponentiations use modulusφ(n). A I/II; B I/III; C II/IV; D III/IV.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
RSA exponentiation is modulo n=pq, and the chosen exponents obey ed≡1 (mod φ(n)), with φ(n)=(p−1)(q−1). Thus statements I and III are correct, option B. Writing ed=1+kφ(n), Euler’s theorem proves M^(ed)≡M modulo n when M is coprime to n; reduction separately modulo p and q, followed by the Chinese remainder theorem, also proves it for non-coprime messages. Statement II incorrectly uses modulus n for the exponent-inverse condition; IV incorrectly performs message arithmetic modulo φ(n). The question reverses the usual names of e and d (calling e private and d public), but RSA’s mathematical inversion works either way and the answer is unchanged.

Teaching detail:
Two different moduli serve different roles. Messages live modulo n, while the inverse relationship between exponents is taken moduloφ(n) (or a suitable Carmichael modulus in other formulations). Combining the message exponentiations gives M^(ed); choosing ed=1+kφ(n) returns M. This explains I and III and rejects the distractors that interchange these moduli. The source’s naming of e and d is reversed from many textbooks but does not alter the algebra.

subject: 10-computer-networks
question_text: TCP initial sequence numbers use the low 32 bits of a persistent time-of-day counter incremented once per millisecond. Maximum packet lifetime 64 s. The source asks the minimum permissible rate of sequence-number increase in a connection. Choices A 0.015/s; B 0.064/s; C 0.135/s; D 0.327/s. Connection duration is not specified; the listed-result derivation requires an explicit extra model.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
Let S=2^32, clock rate C=1000/s, packet lifetime M=64 s, and a constant-rate connection start at time 0 with initial sequence number 0, so its sequence trajectory is q(t)=rt. For r<C, the next occurrence of this sequence value on the returning clock trajectory is at time (S+rt)/C. To let a packet sent at t expire before that clock reuse, require (S+rt)/C−t≥M, equivalently (C−r)t≤S−CM. Requiring this throughout a connection of duration D therefore gives r≥C−(S−CM)/D (with nonnegative rates understood). If the intended duration is one clock cycle, D=S/C, this becomes r≥C²M/S=1000²×64/2^32=0.0149011612/s, closest to A, 0.015/s. This is an exact conditional derivation under the stated constant-rate, returning-clock model. The question does not actually specify D: the tiny minimum is therefore conditional on the one-clock-cycle interpretation, not a universal minimum. In particular, every r<C eventually reaches the returning forbidden strip if the connection continues indefinitely. The original 1/M shortcut is unjustified and is not used. Conceptual reference: Tanenbaum, Computer Networks, 5th edition, Figure 6-10 (clock-based forbidden regions); https://csc-knu.github.io/sys-prog/books/Andrew%20S.%20Tanenbaum%20-%20Computer%20Networks.pdf .

Teaching detail:
Do not infer a universal rate from 64 seconds alone:1/64 is not derived from the supplied 32-bit clock. Under a constant-rate trajectory and a connection lasting exactly one clock wrap, substitution yields r≥1000²·64/2³²≈0.014901/s, nearest A. The baseline derives the time-to-reuse inequality and shows where that extra duration enters. For an indefinitely long connection, any rate below the clock slope eventually meets the returning forbidden region. subject: 10-computer-networks
question_text: What condition on CRC generator G(x) detects all odd-weight bit errors? A more than two terms; B G does not divide 1+x^k for any k within frame length; C 1+x divides G; D an odd number of terms.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
Over GF(2), an error polynomial E(x) with an odd number of nonzero coefficients satisfies E(1)=1. If x+1 divides G(x), every multiple of G(x) evaluates to zero at x=1. Therefore no odd-weight E(x) is divisible by G(x), and every such error has a nonzero CRC syndrome. Hence C. Option B instead addresses two-bit errors of the form x^i(1+x^k); merely having more than two terms is insufficient, and an odd number of terms makes G(1)=1 rather than giving the needed x+1 factor.

Teaching detail:
A polynomial has factor x+1 over GF(2) exactly when its value at 1 is 0, meaning an even number of nonzero coefficients. An odd-weight error has E(1)=1, so it cannot be a multiple of a generator that vanishes at 1. Therefore its division remainder cannot be zero, and the CRC detects it. This parity argument establishes C without enumerating error positions. The condition about 1+x^k is associated with two-bit errors, not all odd-weight errors.

question_text: DFD assertions: I context diagram represents system as one bubble; II external entities must be identified at every level; III control information should not appear; IV stores may connect directly to another store or external entity. A II/III; B I/II/IV; C I/III; D I/II/III.

solution:

II is false: external entities need not be repeated at every decomposition level; lower-level DFDs elaborate relevant processes and flows. III is true in conventional DFD notation: a DFD models data transformation and movement, not execution-control information. IV is false: a data store cannot directly exchange data with another store or an external entity; a process must intervene. Therefore I and III, option C. A context diagram deliberately hides internal decomposition behind one process, so I describes its purpose. Lower-level diagrams refine relevant flows and need not duplicate every external entity, refuting II. Ordinary DFD arrows describe data rather than the temporal order or branching control of execution, supporting III. Data must pass through a transforming process between a store and another store/entity, refuting IV. These conventions select C; real-time DFD extensions require additional notation.

subject: excluded
question_text: Cyclomatic complexity assertions: I equals maximum independent circuits; II equals decisions+1; III gives independent paths for basis-path tests. A I/II; B II/III; C I/III; D all. Interpret circuit augmentation and binary-decision conventions explicitly.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
Under the standard software-testing convention all three statements are true, option D. For a connected module with E control-flow edges and N nodes, V(G)=E−N+2. Adding a virtual exit-to-entry edge gives a strongly connected/closed flow graph whose cycle-space dimension is (E+1)−N+1=E−N+2, explaining statement I’s independent-circuit interpretation. For binary predicates V(G)=number of decisions+1 (II), and V(G) gives the number of independent paths in a basis-path test set (III). The circuit wording presupposes this conventional augmentation; the raw unaugmented graph has ordinary undirected cycle rank E−N+1. Likewise a multiway branch contributes outdegree−1 rather than one unless reduced to binary decisions. Supplemental topic: software engineering / testing, outside the twelve core subject buckets.

Teaching detail:
For a connected single-entry/single-exit module, V=E−N+2. The independent-cycle interpretation uses a virtual edge from exit back to entry; omitting that augmentation gives cycle rank E−N+1 instead. Each binary predicate adds one independent alternative, yielding decisions+1, and those alternatives form a basis of test paths. Thus all three hold under the intended testing convention. Multiway decisions contribute more than one unless decomposed into binary predicates, so the wording is not an unrestricted graph theorem.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text: Disk has 63 sectors/track, 10 platters with 2 surfaces each, 1000 cylinders. Zero-based address(c, h, s) orders sectors then surfaces then cylinders. Convert(400, 16, 29) to linear sector index: A 505035; B 505036; C 505037; D 505038.

Convert to sector index 8016·63+29=505037. Every multiplication moves one level down the address hierarchy. The explicit zero-based convention means no extra 1 is added at the end.

question_title: Convert sector number to disk address
question_text: For the same disk with 20 surfaces/cylinder and 63 sectors/track, convert zero-based linear sector 1039 to(c, h, s): A(0, 15, 31); B(0, 16, 30); C(0, 16, 31); D(0, 17, 31).

solution:

subject: 05-algorithms
question_text: Let l(i, j) be LCS length of prefixes of lengths i, j of zero-indexed X, Y. Boundary l=0 if either prefix empty; expr1 applies if last symbols match, expr2 otherwise. Which proposal is correct? A expr1=l(i−1, j)+1; B expr1=l(i, j−1); C expr2=max(l(i−1, j), l(i, j−1)); D expr2=max(l(i−1, j−1), l(i, j)).
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
Let l(i, j) be the LCS length of the first i elements of X and first j elements of Y. If either prefix is empty, l(i, j)=0. When X[i−1]=Y[j−1], the matching final elements extend an optimal LCS of both shortened prefixes, so expr1=l(i−1, j−1)+1. If they differ, an LCS omits at least one of the two final elements, yielding expr2=max(l(i−1, j), l(i, j−1)). Only option C gives a correct proposed expression. A omits shortening Y in the matching case, B omits both the match increment and shortening X, and D is circular.

Teaching detail:
If the last symbols match, use that matched pair and extend the best solution for both shorter prefixes: l(i−1, j−1)+1. If they differ, a common subsequence must omit at least one of them, so take the larger of the two one-prefix-shortened values. Only C states a valid supplied formula. Option D references l(i, j) on its own right side and cannot define a bottom-up recurrence.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_text: Store the LCS recurrence in L[m+1, n+1]. Which is true? A every cell must first be zero; B increasing row-major or column-major computation works; C neither works; D L[p, q] must precede L[r, s] whenever p<r OR q<s.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
Initialize only the empty-prefix boundary L[0, j]=L[i, 0]=0. Every other L[i, j] depends on L[i−1, j−1] in the matching case, or on L[i−1, j] and L[i, j−1] in the nonmatching case. Increasing-index row-major order computes all predecessors first; increasing-index column-major order also does so. Therefore B. Initializing every cell to zero is not necessary (A), and C contradicts these valid orders. D overstates the dependency: p<r alone does not require an arbitrarily far-right cell L[p, q] before L[r, s]; its OR condition can even demand opposite orders for incomparable cells such as (1, 2) and (2, 1).

Teaching detail:
The dependency arrows point left, up or diagonally up-left. Both increasing row order and increasing column order place all those predecessor cells before the current cell. Only row 0 and column 0 require initialization; every interior cell can be assigned when reached. The proposed OR ordering in D is too strong: cells(1, 2) and(2, 1) would each be required before the other. Therefore B.

subject: 09-database-management-systems
question_text: Schema Suppliers(sid key, sname, city, street), Parts(pid key, pname, color), Catalog(sid, pid composite key, cost). Query SELECT S.sname FROM Suppliers S WHERE S.sid NOT IN(SELECT C.sid FROM Catalog C WHERE C.pid NOT IN(SELECT P.pid FROM Parts P WHERE P.color<>blue)). Relations nonempty. Options suppliers who A supplied a non-blue part; B have not supplied a non-blue part; C supplied only blue parts; D have not supplied only blue parts. Preserve SQL-null/referential-integrity and wording qualifications.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
The innermost query finds non-blue part IDs. The middle query finds supplier IDs for catalog rows whose part is not in that set, i.e. suppliers of a blue part under the intended referential-integrity and non-NULL color assumptions. The outer NOT IN therefore returns names of suppliers who supply no blue parts, including suppliers with no catalog rows. The intended option is D, but its printed wording is imprecise: “have not supplied only blue parts” logically also includes mixed-color suppliers, whereas the SQL excludes them. A asks for any non-blue supply and also includes mixed suppliers; B and C concern suppliers with no non-blue supply / only blue supply, the opposite condition. Thus no option states the exact result under a literal reading. Do not present D as an officially verified or exact semantic equivalence.

Teaching detail:
Read the nested NOT IN clauses from inside out. First collect non-blue part IDs; next collect suppliers with a catalog part outside that set, meaning a blue part under non-null referential-integrity assumptions; finally exclude those suppliers. The result is suppliers with no blue supply, including suppliers with no catalog row. A supplier of both blue and red is excluded. That mixed-supply example demonstrates why printed D is not literally equivalent to the SQL despite being the intended choice. The discrepancy is semantic, not a reason to invent an official key.

subject: 10-computer-networks
question_title: Sequence bits for frames in flight
question_text: Frames 1000 bits traverse a 10^6 bps duplex link with one-way propagation 25 ms, packed back-to-back in transit. Minimum bits l to distinguish frames physically in the link? A 2; B 3; C 4; D 5.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
Frame transmission time is 1000/10^6=0.001 s=1 ms. One-way propagation time is 25 ms, so the link can hold (10^6×0.025)/1000=25 frames in transit. Distinguishing these requires l=ceil(log2 25)=5 bits, option D. This question asks about frames physically within the one-way link, not the sender window needed to cover a complete data-plus-ACK round trip; that latter calculation is not the quantity requested here.

Teaching detail:
Transmission consumes 1 ms per frame. During the 25 ms one-way propagation delay, 25 complete frame-lengths can occupy the channel, so at least 25 distinct labels are needed. Four bits give only 16 labels; five give 32 and suffice. The quantity is one-way in-flight frames, not the round-trip bandwidth-delay product for a continuously busy sender. That distinction prevents mistakenly demanding six bits here.

subject: 10-computer-networks
question_title: Waiting after a full sliding window
question_text: Using the preceding l, sender window is 2^l frames and ACKs always piggyback on return frames. After the initial full window, minimum wait before next transmission, ignoring processing? A 16; B 18; C 20; D 22 ms. Immediate equal-size return frame is the timing convention.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
From Q57 l=5, so the stated sender window is 2^5=32 frames. Sending those frames takes 32×1=32 ms. The first frame is fully received after 1+25=26 ms. With an immediately sent equal-sized return frame carrying the piggybacked acknowledgment, its serialization takes 1 ms and propagation another 25 ms, so the ACK is fully received at 52 ms. The sender thus waits 52−32=20 ms after its initial burst, option C. This is the minimum: any delay waiting for a return data frame would increase it. The question stipulates the window size; do not replace it with protocol-specific Go-Back-N or Selective-Repeat sequence-space restrictions.

Teaching detail:
The first outgoing frame finishes transmission at 1 ms and arrives fully at 26 ms. An immediately transmitted 1000-bit return frame finishes its own serialization at 27 ms and arrives fully back at 52 ms. The initial 32-frame window completes sending at 32 ms. Thus the minimum additional wait is 20 ms. Waiting for return application data would increase it, so immediate piggybacking is the minimum-time assumption, not a guaranteed real traffic pattern.

solution:
In a zero-based heap each parent at i must be at least as large as children at 2i+1 and 2i+2. In C, [25, 14, 16, 13, 10, 8, 12], the checks are 25≥14, 16; 14≥13, 10; and 16≥8, 12, so every edge satisfies max-heap order. A fails because parent 12 has child 13; B fails because parent 14 has child 16; D fails because parent 12 has child 16. Thus C alone is a max-heap.

Teaching detail:
A max-heap needs parent≥child along every edge, not a globally descending array. In C, root 25 exceeds 14/16; 14 exceeds 13/10; 16 exceeds 8/12. A fails at 12<13; B at 14<16; D at 12<16. Checking only the root would wrongly admit the distractors; every internal node must satisfy the local condition.

question_text: Perform two delete-max operations on the valid heap from Q59. Result? A[14, 13, 12, 10, 8]; B[14, 12, 13, 8, 10]; C[14, 13, 8, 12, 10]; D[14, 13, 12, 8, 10].

solution:
Start from Q59’s heap [25, 14, 16, 13, 10, 8, 12]. Delete 25, move final element 12 to the root, and sift down by swapping with the larger child 16. The six-element heap is [16, 14, 12, 13, 10, 8]. Delete 16 and move final element 8 to the root: [8, 14, 12, 13, 10]. Swap 8 with larger child 14, then with larger child 13, giving [14, 13, 12, 8, 10]. This is option D. Each deletion removes the maximum and reduces the active heap length by one.

Delete-max replaces the root by the last active element, shrinks the heap and repeatedly swaps downward with the larger child. First deletion moves 12 to the root and swaps it with 16, yielding[16, 14, 12, 13, 10, 8]. Second deletion moves 8 to the root, then swaps with 14 and 13, yielding[14, 13, 12, 8, 10]. Choosing the smaller child would not restore heap order, which explains several plausible-looking alternatives.

question_text:
Choose the most appropriate completion: “His rather casual remarks on politics ______ his lack of seriousness about the subject.”
Options: (A) masked; (B) belied; (C) betrayed; (D) suppressed.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
The remarks reveal, rather than hide or contradict, the lack of seriousness. In this context betrayed means inadvertently revealed. Hence C; masked, belied and suppressed have the wrong relationship to the evidence.

Teaching detail: The sentence treats the casual remarks as evidence of a lack of seriousness. “Betray” can mean reveal something unintentionally, as a nervous voice betrays anxiety. “Masked” and “suppressed” would hide the lack, while “belied” would contradict it. The contextual sense is revelation, not the separate sense of disloyalty.

question_text:
Choose the word closest in meaning to “circuitous.”
Options: (A) cyclic; (B) indirect; (C) confusing; (D) crooked.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
Circuitous means taking a roundabout rather than direct route, literally or figuratively. Indirect is therefore the closest synonym, B. Cyclic means repeating in a cycle, which is not required.

Teaching detail: A circuitous explanation reaches its point by a roundabout route; a circuitous road reaches its destination indirectly. “Cyclic” instead means recurring in cycles, “confusing” describes difficulty understanding, and “crooked” can mean physically bent or dishonest. These may sometimes accompany a circuitous route, but indirect is the closest direct synonym.

question_text:
Choose the most appropriate completion: “If we manage to ______ our natural resources, we would leave a better planet for our children.”
Options: (A) uphold; (B) restrain; (C) cherish; (D) conserve.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
Conserve means protect resources from waste or depletion, fitting the consequence of leaving a better planet for children. Uphold ordinarily takes a principle or decision, restrain means hold back, and cherish means value emotionally. D is the appropriate verb.

Teaching detail: The consequence about future children points to protecting resources for later use. “Conserve” directly expresses reducing waste and preserving availability. “Cherish” conveys affection but not necessarily preservation; “uphold” normally applies to principles or decisions; “restrain” means hold back a person, force or action. Only conserve supplies the intended environmental action.

subject: 11-general-aptitude
question_text:
Of 25 people in a room, 15 play hockey, 17 play football and 10 play both. How many play neither sport?
Options: (A) 2; (B) 17; (C) 13; (D) 3.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
Inclusion–exclusion gives 15+17−10=22 people playing at least one of the two sports. The complement in the 25-person room has size 25−22=3, option D. Subtracting the intersection once avoids double counting.

Teaching detail: A disjoint-region check gives hockey only 15−10=5, football only 17−10=7 and both=10. Together these account for 22 people, leaving three outside both circles. The tempting 15+17=32 double-counts the ten people in the overlap and cannot be subtracted directly from 25.

question_text:
Choose the pair with the same relationship as “Unemployed : Worker.”
Options: (A) fallow : land; (B) unaware : sleeper; (C) wit : jester; (D) renovated : house.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
An unemployed worker is available for work but not currently employed. Fallow land is land left uncultivated rather than actively used for crops. This shared relation of productive capacity temporarily unused makes A the closest analogy.

Teaching detail: Preserve both the order and the nature of the relation: an adjective describes a noun whose normal productive use is temporarily absent. Fallow land is not currently cultivated, just as an unemployed worker is not currently employed. The other pairs describe awareness, a characteristic associated with a performer, or a completed improvement rather than unused productive capacity.

subject: 11-general-aptitude
question_text:
If 137+276=435, how much is 731+672? Use the intended interpretation that all numerals are written in a common positional base.
Options: (A) 534; (B) 1403; (C) 1623; (D) 1513.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
Assume the numerals use one positional integer base b. Expanding 137_b+276_b=435_b gives 3b²+10b+13=4b²+3b+5, so (b−8)(b+1)=0. The valid base is 8. Then 731_8+672_8 has units 3, tens 3+7=10 decimal giving digit 2 and carry 1, and hundreds 7+6+1=14 decimal giving digit 6 and carry 1. The result is 1623_8, option C. This uses the intended common-base interpretation; an arbitrary invented operation would not be uniquely determined.

Teaching detail: A base must exceed every digit used, so b>7 rules out the negative root −1 of the quadratic. Carrying is then in base eight: the tens-column sum 10 in decimal is 12 in octal, and the hundreds-column sum 14 in decimal is 16 in octal. As a check, the addends are 473 and 442 in decimal, totaling 915, whose octal representation is 1623.

question_text:
Hari (H), Gita (G), Irfan (I), and Saira (S) are siblings, all born on January 1, with no twins. Successive siblings differ in age by less than three years. H’s age+G’s age>I’s age+S’s age. G and S differ by one year; G is not oldest and S is not youngest. Find their order, oldest first.
Options: (A) HSIG; (B) SGHI; (C) IGSH; (D) IHSG.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
Since all birthdays are January 1 and there are no twins, adjacent age gaps are positive integers 1 or 2. Gita and Saira differ by one year, so they are adjacent in birth order. A places Irfan between them. In C, the order Irfan–Gita–Saira–Hari gives I>G and S>H, hence I+S>G+H, contradicting condition (i). D gives Irfan oldest and Hari second, also forcing H+G<I+S. Only B, Saira–Gita–Hari–Irfan, can satisfy the inequalities: ages 5,4,3,1 give H+G=7>I+S=6 and all adjacent gaps are below 3. Thus B.

Teaching detail: For option D, I>H>S>G and the difference I−H is positive while S−G=1, so (I+S)−(H+G)>0, contradicting the required inequality. Option A already violates the one-year G–S gap because another sibling lies between them. The ages used for B are only a feasibility witness; adding the same constant to all four ages preserves every condition.

subject: 11-general-aptitude
question_text:
A passage says modern warfare has shifted from large army clashes to suppression of civilians. Silent chemical agents appear suited to this warfare, and “regretfully” some military personnel consider them useful tools. Which statement best sums up the passage?
Options: (A) Modern warfare has resulted in civil strife; (B) Chemical agents are useful in modern warfare; (C) Use of chemical agents in warfare would be undesirable; (D) People in military establishments like to use chemical agents in war.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
The writer describes chemical warfare against civilians and explicitly says regretfully when noting support for it. The best summary must preserve that disapproval: use of chemical agents in warfare would be undesirable, C. B and D omit the author’s evaluative point, and A substitutes civil strife for suppression of civilians.

Teaching detail: A main-point answer should capture both subject matter and the author’s stance. The word “regretfully” signals disapproval of using chemical agents against civilians. Option B turns an attributed military belief into the author’s endorsement, while D reports that belief without the evaluative point. C preserves the central negative judgment.

subject: 11-general-aptitude
question_text:
Five skilled workers build a wall in 20 days; eight semi-skilled workers build it in 25 days; ten unskilled workers build it in 30 days. How long will two skilled, six semi-skilled and five unskilled workers together take?
Options: (A) 20 days; (B) 18 days; (C) 16 days; (D) 15 days.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
One skilled worker builds 1/(5·20)=1/100 wall per day; one semi-skilled worker builds 1/(8·25)=1/200; one unskilled worker builds 1/(10·30)=1/300. The team rate is 2/100+6/200+5/300=1/15 wall per day. Therefore completion takes 15 days, D, assuming additive constant productivity as in the question.

Teaching detail: Convert each class to per-worker productivity before combining headcounts. Two skilled workers contribute 2/100=6/300 walls/day; six semi-skilled contribute 6/200=9/300; five unskilled contribute 5/300. Their sum is 20/300=1/15 wall/day, so the reciprocal is 15 days. Adding or averaging the three completion times would ignore team size and differing productivity.

subject: 11-general-aptitude
question_text:
Using digits from the multiset {2,2,3,3,3,4,4,4,4}, how many distinct four-digit numbers greater than 3000 can be formed? A digit cannot be used more often than it occurs.
Options: (A) 50; (B) 51; (C) 52; (D) 54.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
The available digits are two 2s, three 3s and four 4s. A number above 3000 starts with 3 or 4. After a leading 3, the remaining three positions have 3³ possibilities except 222 and 333, giving 25. After a leading 4, only 222 is forbidden, giving 26; 444 is allowed because four 4s are available overall. Total 25+26=51, B. Equal copies are not distinguished.

Teaching detail: Count arrangements of digit values, not permutations of distinguishable physical copies. There are initially 27 suffixes for either allowed leading digit. With leading 3, suffix 333 would require four 3s and 222 would require three 2s; with leading 4, only 222 exceeds supply. No leading 2 can produce a number above 3000, so the two cases are exhaustive.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_text:
For a graph G=(V,E), define ξ(G)=Σ_d i_d·d, where i_d is the number of vertices of degree d. S and T are two different trees satisfying ξ(S)=ξ(T). Which relation holds between their numbers of vertices |S| and |T|?
Options: (A) |S|=2|T|; (B) |S|=|T|−1; (C) |S|=|T|; (D) |S|=|T|+1.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
The defined sum counts every vertex degree and hence equals 2|E| by the handshake lemma. A tree with v vertices has v−1 edges, so ξ=2(v−1). Equal ξ for S and T implies equal vertex counts |S|=|T|, C; the trees need not be isomorphic.

Teaching detail: Why the degree sum works: each edge has two endpoints, so contributes exactly two to Σ_d i_d d. Writing s=|S| and t=|T| gives 2(s−1)=2(t−1), hence s=t. “Different” need not mean different sizes: two nonisomorphic trees can have the same vertex count and therefore the same degree sum.

question_text:
Apply one Newton–Raphson iteration to x²−13=0, starting from x₀=3.5. What is the resulting approximation?
Options: (A) 3.575; (B) 3.677; (C) 3.667; (D) 3.607.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
For f(x)=x²−13, Newton’s update is x₁=x₀−(x₀²−13)/(2x₀). With x₀=3.5, x₁=3.5−(12.25−13)/7=3.607142857…, which rounds to 3.607, D. This is one iteration, not the exact square root.

Teaching detail: Newton’s method replaces the curve locally by its tangent: f(x₀)+f′(x₀)(x₁−x₀)=0. Here f′(x)=2x and the negative residual f(3.5)=−0.75 makes the update increase x by 0.75/7. As a reasonableness check, 3.6²=12.96<13 and 3.61²=13.0321>13, so 3.607 lies in the expected interval.

question_text:
How many reflexive relations exist on a set with five elements?
Options: (A) 2^10; (B) 2^15; (C) 2^20; (D) 2^25.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
A relation on five elements is a subset of 25 ordered pairs. Reflexivity forces the five diagonal pairs to be present. Each of the other 20 pairs can independently be present or absent, giving 2²⁰ relations, C.

Teaching detail: Label the elements 1,…,5 and draw a 5×5 Boolean relation matrix. All diagonal entries must be 1; the 20 off-diagonal entries are free binary choices. The answer is not 2^25 because that counts all relations, including nonreflexive ones. Reflexivity does not impose symmetry, so (i,j) and (j,i) remain independent choices.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_title: Cube roots of unity under multiplication
question_text:
Let S={1,ω,ω²}, where ω and ω² are the nonreal cube roots of unity. With * denoting multiplication, which algebraic structure does (S,*) form?
Options: (A) A group; (B) A ring; (C) An integral domain; (D) A field.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
The set {1,ω,ω²} is closed under multiplication because exponents reduce modulo 3. Multiplication is associative, 1 is the identity, and ω and ω² are inverses of each other. Hence it forms a cyclic group of order 3, A. A ring, integral domain or field additionally requires an additive operation and its associated axioms, not just this multiplicative structure.

Teaching detail: A generator is ω: its powers are 1,ω,ω²,ω³=1. The multiplication table therefore cycles through these three elements. In particular, ω·ω²=1 and (ω²)²=ω. A field would require closure under an addition making an abelian group, including an additive identity; the specified single operation supplies no such structure.

subject: excluded
question_text:
Evaluate lim as n→∞ of (1−1/n)^(2n).
Options: (A) 0; (B) e^(−2); (C) e^(−1/2); (D) 1.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
Let L_n=(1−1/n)^(2n). Its logarithm is 2n log(1−1/n), which tends to −2 since log(1−x)/x tends to −1 as x tends to zero. Exponentiating yields e^(−2), option B.

Teaching detail: A shorter route is the standard limit (1−1/n)^n→e^(−1); squaring it gives e^(−2). It is incorrect to replace the base by its limit 1 first and conclude 1: the exponent also tends to infinity, producing the indeterminate form 1^∞. Taking logarithms resolves that interaction.

subject: 01-digital-logic
question_text:
Find the minterm expansion of f(P,Q,R)=PQ+Q¬R+P¬R. Use P,Q,R as the most-significant to least-significant bits of each minterm index.
Options: (A) m₂+m₄+m₆+m₇; (B) m₀+m₁+m₃+m₅; (C) m₀+m₁+m₆+m₇; (D) m₂+m₃+m₄+m₅.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
The expression is PQ+Q R̄+P R̄, with variable order P,Q,R. PQ covers minterms 6 and 7; Q R̄ covers 2 and 6; P R̄ covers 4 and 6. Taking their union gives m₂+m₄+m₆+m₇, option A. Repeated minterm 6 is included only once.

Teaching detail: To convert products to minterms, include missing variables: PQ=PQ¬R+PQR, Q¬R=¬PQ¬R+PQ¬R, and P¬R=P¬Q¬R+PQ¬R. Their binary assignments are 110,111; 010,110; and 100,110. OR is idempotent, so duplicate 110 is not counted again. The resulting truth vector in index order 0 through 7 is 00101011.

subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_title: Refreshing a bank of DRAM chips
question_text:
A 4-megabyte main memory is built from 1M×1-bit DRAM chips. Each chip has 1K rows with 1K cells in each row. One refresh operation takes 100 ns. How long does one complete refresh of all memory cells take?
Options: (A) 100 ns; (B) 100×2^10 ns; (C) 100×2^20 ns; (D) 3200×2^20 ns.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
A refresh operation refreshes one row in each chip in parallel. Each chip has 1K=2¹⁰ rows, requiring 2¹⁰ refresh operations to cover all its cells. At 100 ns each, the total is 100·2¹⁰ ns, B. The memory needs 32 chips for 4 MiB, but the standard parallel-bank refresh model does not multiply the refresh time by 32.

Teaching detail: The row count, rather than the total cell count, determines the number of refresh commands: all 1024 cells on the selected row are refreshed together. Memory capacity determines how many chips are needed, but chips sharing refresh control perform that command concurrently in the model used here. Multiplying by 2^20 would incorrectly refresh individual cells separately.

subject: 01-digital-logic
question_text:
A signed 16-bit integer P has two’s-complement hexadecimal representation F87B. What is the 16-bit two’s-complement representation of 8P?
Options: (A) C3D8; (B) 187B; (C) F878; (D) 987B.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
The 16-bit pattern F87B represents 0xF87B−0x10000=−1925. Multiplication by 8 gives −15400, which is within the signed 16-bit range. Its two’s-complement encoding is 65536−15400=50136=0xC3D8, A; equivalently shift F87B left three positions and retain 16 bits.

Teaching detail: The top hexadecimal digit F sets the sign bit, so interpreting F87B as an unsigned positive number without subtracting 2^16 gives the wrong signed value. The range check −32768≤−15400≤32767 confirms that multiplying by eight does not overflow here. Hexadecimal shifting also gives F87B×8=7C3D8, whose low four digits are C3D8.

subject: 01-digital-logic
question_text:
A 4-to-1 multiplexer has data inputs I₀=R, I₁=¬R, I₂=¬R, I₃=R. The select inputs are S₁=P and S₀=Q (S₁ is the more significant selection bit). Find its output f.
Options: (A) ¬(P⊕Q⊕R); (B) P⊕Q⊕R; (C) P+Q+R; (D) ¬(P+Q+R).
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
The select bits are S₁=P and S₀=Q. Inputs 0 and 3 equal R, while inputs 1 and 2 equal R̄. Thus f=R when P=Q and f=R̄ when P≠Q, exactly f=P⊕Q⊕R, option B.

Teaching detail: The four select combinations are PQ=00→R, 01→¬R, 10→¬R, 11→R. XOR with P⊕Q flips R exactly in the middle two cases, establishing the answer for both possible R values. For example P=Q=R=0 yields f=0, immediately excluding the complemented-XOR and complemented-OR choices.

subject: 04-data-structures
question_title: Odd subtree sizes in a binary tree
question_text:
A binary tree has n nodes. Every node has an odd number of descendants, counting the node itself as its own descendant. How many nodes have exactly one child?
Options: (A) 0; (B) 1; (C) (n−1)/2; (D) n−1.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
The descendants of a node, including itself, form its subtree. If a node had exactly one child, its subtree size would be 1 plus the child’s odd subtree size, hence even. This contradicts the condition at that node. Therefore no node has exactly one child: 0, A.

Teaching detail: The parity condition applies to every child subtree as well as the root. A leaf has subtree size 1, which is allowed. A node with two children has size 1+odd+odd, also odd. Exactly one child gives 1+odd, even, which is impossible; thus the hypothesis forces a full binary tree, although it need not be balanced or perfect.

question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
Initially i=0 and j=1. The local parameter assignment p=q redirects p to j, without altering i or the caller’s pointer arguments. Then *p=2 writes j=2. The printed values are 0 2, option D.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_text:
A database contains 10^k records. To process n records, package A takes 0.0001n² time units and B takes 10n log₁₀n time units. What is the smallest offered value of k for which B is preferred to A?
Options: (A) 12; (B) 10; (C) 6; (D) 5.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
Put n=10^k. Package B is faster when 10·10^k·k < 0.0001·10^(2k), equivalently 10^(k−5)>k. At k=5 this is 1>5, false; at k=6 it is 10>6, true. For positive integer k≤5, 10^(k−5)≤1≤k, so 6 is the smallest positive integer exponent, C. The meaningful growing-database interpretation excludes the degenerate n=1 case k=0.

Teaching detail: The inequality compares actual running-time formulas, not only asymptotic orders. At k=5, A=10^6 and B=5×10^6 time units, so A wins. At k=6, A=10^8 and B=6×10^7, so B wins. This illustrates why the smaller-growth algorithm need not be faster at small inputs when its constant factor is much larger.

subject: 07-compiler-design
question_text:
Which compiler data structure manages information about variables and their attributes?
Options: (A) Abstract syntax tree; (B) Symbol table; (C) Semantic stack; (D) Parse table.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
A symbol table stores identifier entries and attributes such as type, scope, storage location and parameter information. An abstract syntax tree represents program structure, a parse table guides parsing, and a semantic stack supports intermediate parser actions. Therefore the data structure asked for is the symbol table, B.

Teaching detail: For example, a declaration “int count” can create a symbol-table entry recording the name count, integer type and scope. Later uses look up that entry for type checking and storage access. The syntax tree may refer to the entry but is not itself the lookup structure; a parse table instead maps parser states/lookahead to parsing actions.

subject: 07-compiler-design
question_text:
Which class of programming languages necessarily needs heap allocation in its runtime environment?
Options: (A) Languages supporting recursion; (B) Languages using dynamic scoping; (C) Languages allowing dynamic data structures; (D) Languages using global variables.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
Dynamically created data structures can have sizes and lifetimes unrelated to the last-in-first-out nesting of procedure activations, so their runtime storage requires heap-style allocation in the standard implementation model. Recursion and dynamic scope can be supported with activation stacks; global variables can use static storage. C is the intended distinction. A language implementation may realize the allocator through a preallocated arena, but that is still heap-style management rather than a counterexample to the storage-lifetime distinction.

Teaching detail: A recursive call creates a new activation record that can be popped when the call returns, so recursion alone needs a stack, not a heap. A linked node returned to a caller may have to survive its creator’s return and be freed in an arbitrary order. That non-LIFO lifetime is the key distinction tested by dynamic data structures.

subject: 10-computer-networks
question_text:
Which statement best explains why an IP datagram has a Time-to-Live (TTL) header field?
Options: (A) To prioritize packets; (B) To reduce delays; (C) To optimize throughput; (D) To prevent packet looping.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
Routers decrement TTL as a datagram is forwarded and discard it when the limit is exhausted. A packet caught in a routing loop therefore cannot circulate indefinitely. This bounds packet lifetime rather than prioritizing traffic, directly reducing delay or optimizing throughput: D.

Teaching detail: If routers A and B mistakenly route a destination through each other, the same packet can alternate indefinitely without a hop/lifetime bound. TTL makes each traversal consume part of a finite budget. It does not repair the routing error itself; it limits the damage by eventually dropping the circulating datagram.

subject: 10-computer-networks
question_text:
Which is not a client–server application in the conventional networking classification?
Options: (A) Internet chat; (B) Web browsing; (C) E-mail; (D) Ping.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
Ping uses ICMP echo requests and replies handled by the network protocol stack, rather than a conventional application-layer client talking to an application server. Web browsing, ordinary email and server-based Internet chat use client-server application models. Thus D is the intended classification; request–reply alone does not make a utility an application-layer client-server service.

Teaching detail: The relevant distinction is the protocol layer and service model, not merely whether one machine sends and another responds. A web server, mail server or chat server implements an application service. Ping normally asks the remote IP/ICMP stack to generate an echo reply, without a separately running user-level application server.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_title: Differences of recursive and enumerable languages
question_text:
L₁ is recursive. L₂ and L₃ are recursively enumerable but not recursive. Which statement is not necessarily true?
Options: (A) L₂−L₁ is recursively enumerable; (B) L₁−L₃ is recursively enumerable; (C) L₂∩L₃ is recursively enumerable; (D) L₂∪L₃ is recursively enumerable.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
L₂−L₁=L₂∩complement(L₁) is recursively enumerable because L₁ is decidable and its complement is decidable. Recursively enumerable languages are also closed under union and intersection, proving C and D. But take L₁=Σ* and L₃ an undecidable recursively enumerable language: L₁−L₃ is its complement and cannot be recursively enumerable, or L₃ would be decidable by dovetailing both recognizers. Therefore B is not necessarily true.

Teaching detail: To recognize an intersection of two recursively enumerable languages, simulate both recognizers in parallel and accept only after both accept; for a union accept after either does. For L₂−L₁, first decide nonmembership in L₁, then run the L₂ recognizer. This construction fails for L₁−L₃ because nonmembership in undecidable L₃ cannot generally be recognized.

subject: 09-database-management-systems
question_text:
In a B+ tree, the maximum number of keys in a node is five. What is the minimum number of keys in any nonroot node?
Options: (A) 1; (B) 2; (C) 3; (D) 4.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
With at most five keys, an internal node has at most six child pointers. A nonroot internal node must have at least ceil(6/2)=3 children and therefore at least two separator keys. Such an internal node attains the minimum, giving 2, B. Under the usual leaf convention a leaf with capacity five has at least three data keys; the requested minimum over nonroot nodes is still two, not a claim that every leaf may have two.

Teaching detail: An internal search node with c child pointers has c−1 separator keys. The maximum of five keys therefore corresponds to order six, whose half-full lower bound is three children, not three keys. The root is exempt from the ordinary minimum occupancy rule. Keeping child counts distinct from key counts avoids the common off-by-one error.

question_text:
Schemas: Passenger(pid,pname,age) and Reservation(pid,class,tid).
Passenger rows: (0,Sachin,65), (1,Rahul,66), (2,Sourav,67), (3,Anil,69).
Reservation rows: (0,AC,8200), (1,AC,8201), (2,SC,8201), (5,AC,8203), (1,SC,8204), (3,AC,8202).
Which pids does this query return?
SELECT pid FROM Reservation
WHERE class='AC' AND EXISTS
 (SELECT * FROM Passenger WHERE age>65 AND Passenger.pid=Reservation.pid);
Options: (A) 1,0; (B) 1,2; (C) 1,3; (D) 1,5.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
The outer query first keeps AC reservation rows, whose passenger IDs are 0,1,5,3. The correlated EXISTS requires a Passenger row with the same pid and age greater than 65. ID 0 has age exactly 65 and fails; ID 5 has no Passenger row and fails. IDs 1 and 3 have ages 66 and 69 and pass, giving 1,3, option C.

Teaching detail: EXISTS tests whether at least one matching subquery row exists; it does not require every Passenger row to meet the age condition. Passenger 2 is old enough but its only reservation is SC, so the outer AC filter removes it. Passenger 1’s additional SC reservation also does not add another output row. No ORDER BY is present, so 1,3 describes the result members rather than a guaranteed row order.

subject: 09-database-management-systems
question_text:
Which concurrency-control protocols ensure both conflict serializability and freedom from deadlock? I: two-phase locking. II: timestamp ordering.
Options: (A) I only; (B) II only; (C) Both I and II; (D) Neither I nor II.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
Two-phase locking guarantees conflict serializability but can create a cycle of transactions waiting for locks, so I does not guarantee deadlock freedom. Basic timestamp ordering enforces conflicts in timestamp order and rejects/aborts violating operations rather than making transactions wait on locks. It is conflict serializable and deadlock-free, although retries can still starve a transaction. Thus II only, B.

Teaching detail: A simple 2PL deadlock is T1 holding lock X while requesting Y and T2 holding Y while requesting X; neither needs to violate the two-phase rule. Timestamp ordering instead disallows an operation inconsistent with the fixed transaction order. Deadlock freedom does not imply starvation freedom: repeated abort/restart of one transaction is still possible.

question_text:
Modules A and B each have cyclomatic complexity 10. The combined flow executes A and then B in sequence, with no additional branch between them. What is the cyclomatic complexity of this sequential integration?
Options: (A) 19; (B) 21; (C) 20; (D) 10.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
For a connected single-entry/single-exit flow graph, cyclomatic complexity is the number of decision points plus one. Complexity 10 in each component means nine independent decisions each. Sequentially composing them adds their decision counts but introduces only one overall baseline path: 9+9+1=19. Equivalently V(A;B)=V(A)+V(B)−1, so A.

Teaching detail: The flow-graph formula gives the same result. Connecting A’s exit to B’s entry adds one edge while leaving N_A+N_B vertices. Thus E−N+2=(E_A−N_A+2)+(E_B−N_B+2)−1=19. Simply adding 10+10 counts the straight-through baseline path twice.

Teaching detail: The pairing follows what each phase produces: requirements establish the domain problem; design models the proposed system; implementation creates and combines executable modules; maintenance improves or repairs an existing system. subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
P1 passes its guard only when S1≠S2; P2 passes only when S1=S2. Neither changes the shared state until leaving its critical section, so while one is inside the other’s guard stays blocking: mutual exclusion holds. Progress fails: if S1=S2 and only P1 wants to enter, P1 spins forever unless P2 participates and changes S2. The symmetric case also occurs. This is strict alternation, so A, assuming atomic sequentially consistent accesses as the pseudocode model does.

Teaching detail: After P1 exits it sets S1=S2, making P2 eligible and itself ineligible; after P2 exits it makes S2 the opposite of S1, restoring P1’s turn. Consequently the processes alternate even if one no longer wants the critical section. Mutual exclusion is a safety property; progress additionally requires that an uninterested process not prevent an interested one from entering.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_title: FIFO forward and reverse page scan
question_text:
A FIFO page-replacement system has four frames, initially empty. It accesses 100 distinct pages in some order, then accesses those same 100 pages in the reverse order. How many page faults occur?
Options: (A) 196; (B) 192; (C) 197; (D) 195.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
The first 100 distinct references all fault. The four resident pages are then the last four in forward order, and the reverse scan hits these four first. Every one of the other 96 reverse references is to a page not yet resident; those faults evict only pages already visited in the reverse scan. Therefore faults total 100+96=196, option A. Hits do not refresh FIFO order.

Teaching detail: Name the forward sequence p₁,…,p₁₀₀. The reverse sequence starts p₁₀₀,p₉₉,p₉₈,p₉₇, all already resident. Then p₉₆,…,p₁ must each fault because none remains from the forward scan. There are 200 total references and exactly four hits, giving 200−4=196 independently of the original ordering.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text:
Which statements about CPU scheduling are true? I: shortest-remaining-time-first may cause starvation. II: preemptive scheduling may cause starvation. III: round robin is better than FCFS in response time.
Options: (A) I only; (B) I and III only; (C) II and III only; (D) I,II and III.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
SRTF may indefinitely postpone a long job when shorter jobs keep arriving, so I is true. SRTF is itself preemptive, establishing that preemptive scheduling may cause starvation, so II is true. Round robin’s time slices let waiting jobs receive CPU service without waiting for a long earlier job to finish, which is the conventional interactive response-time advantage asserted by III. The intended answer is all three, D. III is a qualitative textbook comparison, not a strict improvement for every workload and quantum; for a quantum exceeding all bursts, RR reduces to FCFS.

Teaching detail: Starvation means unbounded waiting, not merely a long finite delay. Under SRTF, a long job can be repeatedly preempted by a stream of shorter jobs. Round robin uses a bounded quantum to distribute service opportunities among ready jobs, which improves typical interactive first-response behavior, while potentially increasing context-switch cost. The word “may” in I and II is essential.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_title: Fault declarations with an imperfect test
question_text:
A computer assembly is faulty with probability p. A test gives the correct result for any computer with probability q. What is the probability that a computer is declared faulty?
Options: (A) pq+(1−p)(1−q); (B) (1−q)p; (C) (1−p)q; (D) pq.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
Partition computers into faulty with probability p and nonfaulty with probability 1−p. The test declares a faulty computer faulty with conditional probability q, while it incorrectly declares a nonfaulty computer faulty with probability 1−q. Total probability gives pq+(1−p)(1−q), option A. The phrase correct result for any computer supplies the same conditional accuracy q in each class.

Teaching detail: A probability tree has two paths ending in “declared faulty”: truly faulty then correctly identified, probability pq; or truly sound then incorrectly classified, probability (1−p)(1−q). These events are disjoint, so add them. Checks: if q=1 the result is p; if q=0 the result is 1−p; if q=1/2 it is 1/2 regardless of p.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_title: Random divisor divisible by a large power
question_text:
A positive divisor of 10^99 is selected uniformly at random. What is the probability that it is a multiple of 10^96?
Options: (A) 1/625; (B) 4/625; (C) 12/625; (D) 16/625.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
Since 10⁹⁹=2⁹⁹5⁹⁹, every positive divisor is uniquely 2^a5^b with 0≤a,b≤99, giving 100² equally likely divisors. Being a multiple of 10⁹⁶ requires a,b≥96, leaving four choices for each exponent. Probability=16/10000=1/625, option A. Uniform choice is over divisors, not over integers up to 10⁹⁹.

Teaching detail: The admissible exponents for each prime are 96,97,98,99, so the favorable divisors number 4×4=16. Divisibility requires both prime exponents to be large enough; satisfying only the exponent of 2 or only the exponent of 5 is insufficient. Reducing 16/10000 gives the offered 1/625.

question_text:
Which sequences cannot be degree sequences of any simple graph? I: (7,6,5,4,4,3,2,1); II: (6,6,6,6,3,3,2,2); III: (7,6,6,4,4,3,2,2); IV: (8,7,7,6,4,2,1,1).
Options: (A) I and II; (B) III and IV; (C) IV only; (D) II and IV.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
IV has eight vertices but a degree of 8, impossible in a simple graph. For II, the four highest degrees sum to 24; their vertices can contribute at most 4·3=12 internally and at most 3+3+2+2=10 from the other vertices, totaling only 22. Thus II also fails. Havel–Hakimi reduces I via (5,4,3,3,2,1,0) to (3,2,2,1,0,0), then (1,1,0,0,0), then zeros. III reduces via (5,5,3,3,2,1,1) to (4,2,2,1,1,0), then (1,1,0,0,0), then zeros. Hence I and III are graphical and exactly II and IV fail: D.

Teaching detail: The even degree-sum condition alone cannot settle this question: all four sums are even. Sequence II fails an Erdős–Gallai bound on its four degree-six vertices: a vertex inside that set has only three possible neighbors inside it, while vertices outside cannot supply more incidences than their own degrees. Sequence IV already violates the individual maximum n−1=7.

question_text:
The matrix A=[[2,3],[x,y]] has eigenvalues 4 and 8. Find x,y.
Options: (A) x=4,y=10; (B) x=5,y=8; (C) x=−3,y=9; (D) x=−4,y=10.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
The trace equals the eigenvalue sum: 2+y=4+8=12, giving y=10. The determinant equals the eigenvalue product: 2y−3x=4·8=32. Substituting y=10 gives x=−4. Thus x=−4,y=10, option D.

Teaching detail: Trace and determinant avoid solving the characteristic polynomial from scratch. Equivalently det(λI−A)=λ²−(2+y)λ+(2y−3x), and the desired polynomial is (λ−4)(λ−8)=λ²−12λ+32. Matching coefficients gives the same two linear equations. Substituting x=−4,y=10 verifies both invariants.

question_text:
F(x,y,t) means person x can fool person y at time t. Which sentence best expresses ∀x∃y∃t ¬F(x,y,t)?
Options: (A) Everyone can fool some person at some time; (B) No one can fool everyone all the time; (C) Everyone cannot fool some person all the time; (D) No one can fool some person at some time.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential paraphrase with options and complete code or textual figure data; visually checked against original scan.
solution:
The formula ∀x∃y∃t ¬F(x,y,t) says that for each person x there is at least one person y and time t when x cannot fool y. Equivalently, ∀x ¬∀y∀t F(x,y,t): no one can fool everyone all the time. That is B. It does not prohibit fooling some people at some times.

Teaching detail: Negating “x can fool everyone all the time” moves the negation across two universal quantifiers: ¬∀y∀t F becomes ∃y∃t ¬F. The outer ∀x then says this failure occurs for every would-be deceiver. The witnesses y and t may depend on x; the formula does not assert a single universally unfoolable person or a single common time.
