subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text: Q1≤p3-SAT≤pQ2. Which is “consistent” with this? A Q1 in NP, Q2 NP-hard; B Q2 in NP, Q1 NP-hard; C both in NP; D both NP-hard. Official choice interprets the question as what is necessarily implied.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
A polynomial reduction Q1≤p3-SAT implies Q1∈NP, by composing the reduction with a 3-SAT verifier. The reduction 3-SAT≤pQ2 makes Q2 NP-hard. Thus A is necessarily implied. The literal word consistent is weaker: taking Q1=Q2=3-SAT satisfies all four options simultaneously. The key A requires reading the question as asking what is guaranteed, not merely possible.

Teaching detail:
A reduction from Q1 to 3-SAT converts a Q1 instance in polynomial time and lets an NP verifier check the resulting formula certificate, so Q1 belongs to NP. A reduction in the other direction from an NP-complete problem to Q2 shows Q2 is at least as hard as every NP problem, so it is NP-hard; it need not belong to NP. These are directional implications, not equivalence. Literal consistency is weaker than logical entailment: choosing both problems equal to 3-SAT makes every listed classification possible, which is why the source wording is explicitly qualified.
derived_answer: A is guaranteed; all choices can be consistent

subject: 07-compiler-design
question_text: Match P lexical analysis, Q parsing, R register allocation, S expression evaluation with 1 graph colouring, 2 DFA minimization, 3 postorder traversal, 4 production tree. A P2Q3R1S4; B P2Q1R4S3; C P2Q4R1S3; D P2Q3R4S1.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
Lexical analysis uses minimized DFAs; parsing constructs production/parse trees; register allocation uses interference-graph coloring; expression evaluation visits operands before operators in postorder. Therefore P-2, Q-4, R-1, S-3, C.

Teaching detail:
Lexical patterns are recognized by finite automata, which can be minimized without changing recognized tokens. Parsing uses grammar productions organized into a parse tree. Register-allocation interference graphs put simultaneously live variables at adjacent vertices, so colouring assigns nonconflicting registers. To evaluate an expression tree, children must be evaluated before their operator parent, which is postorder. Combining all four gives the single complete matching C.

subject: 07-compiler-design
question_text: About AST and CFG, which is true? A successors always correspond to later source code; B neither can contain a cycle; C maximum successors can depend on input program; D each node corresponds to at most one statement.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
AST node arity can vary with program constructs, and CFG successor counts can vary with multiway branches such as switch. Thus C under the general AST/basic-block CFG representation. CFGs can contain loop cycles, successors need not follow source order, and a basic block can contain several statements.

Teaching detail:
An AST can represent a construct with a variable number of operands or children, while a CFG can give a multiway branch many successor blocks. Thus a fixed universal successor count does not follow from the general names. CFG loop back-edges directly disprove B, and also disprove A’s assumption that all successors appear later in source. A basic-block CFG node can contain several sequential statements, disproving D. Different fixed-arity normalized intermediate representations are possible, but are not specified here.

The printed exp notation must be read as the intended exponent placement; the conventional exponential function e^x would yield different equations.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text: A system has 6 identical resources, N processes, each claiming at most 2 resources. Which N could deadlock? A1, B2, C3, D4. Published answer D conflicts with literal total-claim premises.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
With maximum claim 2, a blocked process can hold at most 1 resource. If all N≤4 processes are blocked, at most 4 of the 6 resources are held, leaving enough to satisfy at least one pending request. Hence deadlock is impossible for every listed N. Six processes each holding 1 and requesting 1 provide the first possible deadlock. Official D (N=4) conflicts with the stated 6 resources/max 2 total claim; do not silently change either premise.

Teaching detail:
If a process has obtained both resources it needs, it can finish and release them. A blocked unfinished process therefore holds at most one unit. With N≤4, even if every process holds one, at most 4 of 6 units are occupied, leaving spare units to let a process finish. In general, R≥N(maxclaim−1)+1 guarantees this progress for identical reusable units. For maxclaim 2, the first deadlock configuration is 6 processes each holding 1 and waiting for 1. None of the four offered counts realizes it; preserve the published D only as a conflicting score, not the mathematical conclusion.
derived_answer: None under maximum-total-claim reading; official D

subject: 09-database-management-systems
question_text: Transaction transfers 50 from x to y: read(x); x:=x−50; write(x); read(y); y:=y+50; write(y). Preserving x+y is which ACID property? A atomicity; B consistency; C isolation; D durability.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
Preserving the invariant x+y across the transaction is consistency, B. Atomicity is all-or-nothing execution, isolation concerns concurrent visibility, and durability concerns persistence after commit.

Teaching detail:
The declared invariant defines which database states are valid. Subtracting 50 from one account and adding 50 to the other preserves the invariant x+y, so this is consistency. Atomicity would ensure both changes occur or neither does. Isolation concerns interference between concurrent transactions, and durability concerns survival after commit. The invariant is not itself a claim about failure recovery or scheduling.

subject: 10-computer-networks
question_text: Order UNIX listening-server calls: A listen, accept, bind, recv; B bind, listen, accept, recv; C bind, accept, listen, recv; D accept, listen, bind, recv.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
A listening server binds its local address, listens for connections, accepts one, then receives on the accepted connected socket. Thus bind, listen, accept, recv, B.

Teaching detail:
Binding associates the socket with its local address/port. Listening converts it into a passive connection endpoint. Accept waits for and returns a connected socket for one client. Receive then reads data on that connected socket. Calling accept before listen or before binding a specified listening address does not implement the requested server sequence. The original listening socket and the accepted connection socket have different roles.

subject: 10-computer-networks
question_text: Stop-and-wait link rate 10^6 bits/s, 1000-byte data packets, negligible ACK transmission/processing, and equal forward/back propagation. Efficiency 25%. Find one-way propagation delay in ms.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
Transmission time is 8000/10^6=8 ms. Efficiency 8/(8+2Tp)=1/4 gives 8+2Tp=32, hence Tp=12 ms.

Teaching detail:
Data transmission time is 1000×8/10^6=.008 seconds=8 ms. One complete stop-and-wait cycle is 8+2t_pms when ACK transmission and processing are negligible. Efficiency is useful transmission time divided by cycle time, so 8/(8+2t_p)=.25. Multiply through to get 8+2t_p=32 and t_p=12 ms. The two propagation traversals explain why the leftover 24 msmust be halved.

subject: 10-computer-networks
question_text: Which cookie claim is NOT correct? A a cookie is executable code capable of compromising user security; B cookies arrive via HTTP headers; C a cookie has expiry date/time; D cookies can track browsing at a site.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
A cookie is stored data, not executable code, so A is false. Servers set cookies through HTTP headers and they can support tracking. Persistent cookies have expiration metadata; session cookies can instead omit an explicit expiration and expire with the session, qualifying the blanket wording of C.

Teaching detail:
A cookie is an HTTP state value stored and resent by the user agent, not a script executed as a program. It can still carry sensitive identifiers or enable tracking, so “not code” does not imply “no privacy/security risk.” Set-Cookie is an HTTP response header, and subsequent Cookie headers return applicable values. The expiry statement needs a distinction: persistent cookies have an expiry/max-age, whereas session cookies may omit that field. The intended false definition is A, but C is not universal as literally worded.

Longest-prefix matching sends 171.92 through 170.0/23 to interface 0; 167.151 matches 166.0/23 and 164.0/22, choosing the longer/23 to R2; 163.151 matches only default R4; 165.121 matches 164.0/22 to R3. Thus i-a, ii-c, iii-e, iv-d, A.

Never stop at the first matching broad prefix without checking whether a more specific one exists.

question_text: UDP user data 8880 bytes, UDP header 8 bytes, IPv4 header 20 bytes, no options, Ethernet MTU1500. Find number of IPv4 fragments and final fragment offset: A6, 925; B6, 7400; C7, 1110; D7, 8880.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
IP payload includes the 8-byte UDP header, totaling 8888 bytes. Each full fragment holds 1500−20=1480 bytes, a multiple of 8. Six hold 8880 bytes, leaving 8 bytes for a seventh. Its offset is 8880/8=1110. Thus 7 fragments and 1110, C.

Teaching detail:
Fragmentation splits the IP payload, which already includes the entire UDP header:8880+8=8888 bytes. Each fragment gets its own 20-byte IP header, leaving 1480 payload bytes within the 1500MTU.1480 is divisible by 8, so six full payloads consume 8880 bytes and an 8-byte remainder requires a seventh fragment. The final fragment begins after 8880 original-IP-payload bytes; divide by the 8-byte offset unit to get 1110. Omitting the UDP header incorrectly gives only six fragments.

subject: 10-computer-networks
question_text: At TCP bandwidth 1048560 bits/s, find RTT threshold α(in nearest integer ms)above which the unscaled receive window limits full use, and largest scaled window β. Options combine α63 or 500 ms with β65535×2^14 or 65535×2^16 bytes; correct-labelled C pairs 500 with 2^14.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
An unscaled window holds 65535 bytes=524280 bits. At1048560 bits/s this spans 0.5s=500 ms. The maximum scale shift is 14, giving 65535·2^14 bytes. Therefore C, for sustaining the stated bandwidth without receive-window limitation.

Teaching detail:
The 16-bit unscaled advertised receive window represents at most 65535 bytes. To sustain rate R over round-trip time T, the flight capacity must be at leastRT. Express the window as 524280 bits, then T=524280/1048560=.5 seconds. Larger RTT requires scaling for full bandwidth use. TCP’s maximum permitted scale shift is 14, not 16; therefore maximum represented window is 65535×2^14 bytes. The threshold is a receive-window capacity calculation, not a claim that congestion control always sends at that rate.

subject: 09-database-management-systems
question_text: Simple checkpoint log: startT4; writeT4 y2→3; startT1; commitT4; writeT1 z5→7; checkpoint; startT2; writeT2 x1→9; commitT2; startT3; writeT3 z7→2; crash. Choose undo/redo lists: A undoT3, T1/redoT2; B same undo/redoT2, T4; C no undo/redo all four; D undoT3, T1, T4/redoT2.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
T4 committed before the completed checkpoint and needs no redo. T2 committed after it and must be redone. T1 and T3 are incomplete at crash and must be undone, including T1 begun before the checkpoint. Hence Undo{T3, T1}, Redo{T2}, A, under the stated simple checkpoint model.

Teaching detail:
Classify transactions by completion relative to the checkpoint and crash. T4 committed before the completed checkpoint, so the simple model treats its effects as safely checkpointed. T2 committed later and needs redo to ensure its updates appear. T1 and T3 have no commit record, so their changes must be undone, even though T1 started before the checkpoint. Starting before a checkpoint does not automatically make an unfinished transaction safe. More elaborate recovery protocols may scan different worklists, but this is the stated simple model.

subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_text: Disk 15000 RPM, transfer 50×10^6 bytes/s. Average seek is twice average rotational delay; controller transfer time is 10 times disk transfer time. Find total average read/write time for 512 bytes in ms.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
A revolution takes 60000/15000=4 ms, hence average rotational delay 2 ms and seek 4 ms. Disk transfer is 512/(50·10^6)s=0.01024 ms. Controller transfer adds ten times that, 0.1024 ms. Total 4+2+0.01024+0.1024=6.11264 ms, within 6.1 to 6.2.

Teaching detail:
One revolution takes 60/15000=.004 seconds=4 ms. A uniformly random angular position gives mean rotational waiting of half a revolution, 2 ms, and the stated seek is 4 ms. Transferring 512 bytes at 50 million bytes/s takes.01024 ms; controller work adds.1024 ms. Sum 4+2+.01024+.1024=6.11264 ms. Keep units consistent: confusing seconds with milliseconds or using a full revolution instead of an average half revolution changes the result drastically.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text: Physical addresses 32 bits, pages 8 KB. PTE has valid bit, dirty bit, 3 permission bits, and frame translation. Maximum page table 24 MB. Under packed entries, find virtual address width.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
An8 KiB page uses 13 offset bits. A physical frame number needs 32−13=19 bits, and the five status/permission bits make a 24-bit (3-byte) packed PTE. A24 MiB table then holds 2^23 entries, giving 23+13=36 virtual address bits. This assumes the entries are packed into 3 bytes rather than padded and the maximum table maps the full virtual page space.

Teaching detail:
An8KiB page needs 13 offset bits. From 32 physical bits, 19 remain for the physical frame number. Add 1 valid+1 dirty+3 permission bits to obtain 24 bits=3 bytes per packed entry. A24MiB table holds 24×2^20/3=8×2^20=2^23 entries, one per virtual page. Therefore the virtual address has 23 page-number bits plus 13 offset bits=36. Alignment that padded entries to 4 bytes would define a different organization, so packing is an explicit assumption.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text: How many states does the minimal DFA for(0+1)*(10)have?
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
The language consists of binary strings ending 10. Track no matching suffix, suffix 1, and suffix 10 (accepting). On0 the transitions are q0, q2, q0; on 1 all go to q1. These three states are distinguishable: q2 accepts empty suffix, and suffix 0 distinguishes q1 from q0. Thus 3.

Teaching detail:
Track the longest suffix that is also a prefix of target 10: empty, 1, and 10. Reading 1 always leaves suffix 1. Reading 0 moves from suffix 1 to accepting 10, and otherwise to empty. These three states suffice. They are also necessary: accepting 10 differs from both nonaccepting states on ε, and suffix 1 differs from empty on continuation 0. This distinguishability proof prevents merely guessing the count from the pattern length.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text: Which languages are regular? L1={wxw^R:w, x∈{a, b}*, |w|, |x|>0}; L2={a^n b^m:m≠n, m, n≥0}; L3={a^p b^q c^r:p, q, r≥0}. A L1, L3; B L2 only; C L2, L3; D L3 only.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
L1 consists exactly of length≥3 strings with equal first/last symbols: choose the one-symbol w and nonempty interior x. Its regex is a(a+b)(a+b)*a + b(a+b)(a+b)*b, so regular. If L2 were regular, subtracting it from a*b* would make{a^n b^n} regular, contradiction. L3=a*b*c* is regular. Thus L1, L3, A.

Teaching detail:
In L1, the first and last symbols must agree because w and its reversal surround x. Conversely, any length≥3 string with equal ends can choose a one-symbol w and the nonempty middle as x, so that simple description is exact and regular. L2 is the unequal-count complement within a*b*. If it were regular, subtracting it from regular a*b* would make the equal-count language regular, contradicting its pumping argument. L3 has the direct regular expression a*b*c*. Thus A contains exactly the regular choices.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_text: Match algorithms 1Dijkstra, 2Floyd–Warshall, 3 binary search, 4 backtracking with i divide/conquer, ii dynamic programming, iii greedy, iv DFS, v BFS. A1i2 iii 3i4v; B1 iii 2 iii 3i4v; C1 iii 2 ii 3i4 iv; D1 iii 2 ii 3i4v.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
Dijkstra uses greedy finalization; Floyd–Warshall uses dynamic programming; binary search divides the search interval; backtracking explores depth first. Hence 1-iii, 2-ii, 3-i, 4-iv, C.

Teaching detail:
Dijkstra commits the currently smallest tentative distance using a greedy safe-choice argument. Floyd–Warshall improves paths by allowing successively larger sets of intermediate vertices, which is dynamic programming. Binary search reduces the search interval to one half, matching divide-and-conquer here. Backtracking explores one partial-choice path before undoing it and trying another, so its traversal is depth-first rather than breadth-first. The complete matching is 1 iii, 2 ii, 3i, 4 iv.

subject: 04-data-structures
question_text: Young tableau rows[1, 2, 5, 14], [3, 4, 6, 23], [10, 12, 18, 25], [31, ∞, ∞, ∞], increasing rows/columns. Remove 1 and move other entries so that the result remains a Young tableau, allowing unfilled entries to be marked ∞. What is the minimum number of other entries shifted? The solution below uses the conventional adjacent-hole deletion algorithm.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
Standard Young-tableau deletion moves the smaller right/down neighbor into the hole. Removing 1 successively shifts 2, 4, 6, 18, 25, then places infinity at(3, 4), giving five moved entries. At each step selecting a larger adjacent neighbor would violate the row/column inequality with the smaller one, so this is the forced minimum adjacent-shift deletion path.

Teaching detail:
In conventional adjacent-hole deletion, after removing 1 the hole at the top-left must receive the smaller of its right/down neighbors to preserve both monotonic directions. The forced choices are 2, then 4, then 6, then 18, then 25; the hole finally reaches a position that may become∞. Moving the larger neighbor at an earlier step would leave a smaller value below or to the right of the moved entry, violating order. This proves minimality for the conventional adjacent-hole sliding model, not by itself for arbitrary whole-table rearrangement; the source does not explicitly restrict movements to adjacent cells.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_text: partition(a, n)moves first-element pivot to end of left part and prose says it returns left part COUNT. Skeleton sets p=partition(a, n); if(p+1==k)return a[p]; if(p+1>k)return kth_smallest(…); else return kth_smallest(…). Missing calls: A(a, p, k), (a+p+1, n−p−1, k−p−1); B(a, p, k), (a, n−p−1, k−p−1); C reverse A calls; D(a, n−p−1, k−p−1), (a, p, k). The fixed code instead requires pivot INDEX.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
With pivot index p, its rank is p+1. The left recursive call uses(a, p, k); the right uses(a+p+1, n−p−1, k−p−1), giving A. However the prose explicitly says partition returns the left-part COUNT, which is p+1. The fixed skeleton then compares the wrong rank and accesses the wrong element; no option repairs that. Correct by assigning left_end=partition(a, n)−1 or changing the function contract to return the pivot index. Official A retains this index interpretation.

Teaching detail:
If p were the zero-based pivot index, its rank would be p+1. Recursing left keeps the same base pointer and k but changes length to p. Recursing right advances past the pivot byp+1 and subtracts that many elements from both length and rank. These are A’s arguments. But the prose-returned count is p+1 already; assigning it to p makes the fixed equality and a[p] off by one before either missing call runs. Thus no choice repairs the literal contract. A applies only after changing the contract or subtracting 1 on assignment.
derived_answer: A only if partition returns zero-based pivot index

subject: 04-data-structures
question_text: Which hash best distributes integers i=0…2020 over buckets 0…9? A i²mod 10; B i³mod 10; C11i²mod 10; D12 imod 10.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
Cubing permutes decimal residues: 0, 1, 8, 7, 4, 5, 6, 3, 2, 9. Therefore each block of 10 consecutive keys places one in each bucket. Among 2021 keys bucket 0 gets 203 and every other bucket 202, optimally balanced. Squares use only six residues, 11i² is identical modulo 10, and 12i only reaches even buckets. Thus B.

Teaching detail:
Only the last decimal digit matters modulo 10. Cubes of residues 0 through 9 give 0, 1, 8, 7, 4, 5, 6, 3, 2, 9, which is a permutation. Each full ten-key block therefore hits every bucket once. The 2021 keys consist of 202 full blocks plus one extra key 0 mod 10, giving counts 203, 202, …, 202, as balanced as possible. Squaring collapses residues, 11i²has the same residues as i², and 12i≡2i can only reach even buckets.

subject: excluded
question_text: A root-finding procedure stores successive estimates xa, xb and fb=f(xb). Each iteration computes xt, then sets xa=xb, xb=xt, fb=f(xb). Identify the secant update among the displayed alternatives. The correct candidate C is xb−(xb−xa)fb/[fb−f(xa)]. Options: A xb−(fb−f(xa))fb/(xb−xa); B xa−(fa−f(xa))fa/(xb−xa); C xb−(xb−xa)fb/(fb−f(xa)); D xa−(xb−xa)fa/(fb−f(xa)). The procedure does not define fa.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
The secant through(xa, f(xa)) and(xb, fb) has slope(fb−f(xa))/(xb−xa). Setting its linear approximation to zero gives xt=xb−(xb−xa)*fb/(fb−f(xa)), option C. This uses quantities defined by the procedure and requires a nonzero denominator. An equivalent formula anchored at xa would require fa=f(xa), but fa is not initialized in the displayed procedure.

Teaching detail:
The secant line through (xa, f(xa)) and (xb, fb) has slope (fb−f(xa))/(xb−xa). Its x-intercept solves 0=fb+slope·(xt−xb). Rearranging gives xt=xb−fb(xb−xa)/(fb−f(xa)), exactly C. The stored fb is the current endpoint value, so replacing its numerator by an unrelated function value would not describe this line. The denominator must be nonzero; as with ordinary secant iteration, convergence is not guaranteed for arbitrary starting points.

subject: 03-programming-in-c
question_text: A global int pointer A and global stkTop coexist with stkFunc’s static int size=0, stkTop=0. Opcode −1 sets size=val; opcode 0 pushes A[stkTop++]=val when stkTop<size; the default returns A[--stkTop] if nonempty, otherwise −1. main points A at B[20], sets global stkTop=−1, sets capacity 10, pushes 5 then 10, and prints stkFunc(1, 0)+stkFunc(1, 0). Find the output.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
The function-local static stkTop starts at 0 and shadows the global stkTop, so assigning the global variable−1 does not affect the stack. After configuring size 10 and pushing 5 then 10, the two pops return 10 and 5 in whichever operand-evaluation order is chosen. Their sum is 15. Although the + operands have unspecified order, the two function executions are indeterminately sequenced rather than interleaving their bodies; this is not the direct unsequenced-increment case.

Teaching detail:
Track the function-local static top, not the global of the same name. Capacity initialization leaves the local top at 0. Pushing 5 writes B[0] and changes it to 1; pushing 10 writes B[1] and changes it to 2. The two calls then return 10 and 5, in whichever operand-call order is chosen. Their sum is 15. A function’s static local persists between calls, and lexical scope makes it hide the global stkTop, so setting that global to −1 does not underflow this stack.

subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_text: Instructions are MUL R5, R0, R1; DIV R6, R2, R3; ADD R7, R5, R6; SUB R8, R7, R4. Pipeline stages IF, OF and WB take one cycle; PO takes 3 for MUL, 5 for DIV and 1 for ADD/SUB. PO output can forward to OF. Find total cycles under the stated single occupied PO-stage interpretation.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
With a single occupied PO stage and the stated forwarding, MUL uses IF1, OF2, PO3–5, WB6. DIV uses PO6–10, ADD uses PO11 and SUB uses PO12; SUB writes back in cycle 13. The dependent ADD/SUB operand fetches use the forwarded results at the end of the preceding producer PO cycle. Thus total 13 cycles. This is the conventional in-order, non-internally-pipelined PO-stage model; independent or internally pipelined functional units would require more scheduling details.

Teaching detail:
Count occupied execution cycles rather than adding all independent instruction latencies. MUL starts PO in cycle 3 and occupies cycles 3–5. DIV cannot use the same PO stage until cycle 6, then occupies 6–10. ADD depends on both results and uses PO in cycle 11 after forwarding; SUB follows in cycle 12. Its WB is cycle 13. The explicit resource model matters: a separately pipelined multiplier/divider would permit a different schedule, and a non-forwarding design would add dependency stalls.

subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_text: A byte-addressed machine has two-byte registers and an upward-growing stack. SP is 016E hexadecimal and PC is 5FA0 immediately before a two-word CALL that pushes PC and PSW. What is the resulting SP? A 016A; B 016C; C 0170; D 0172.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
CALL pushes the two-byte PC and two-byte PSW onto an upward-growing stack, adding 4 to SP. Thus hexadecimal 016E+4=0172, D. Instruction length affects the return-address value pushed, not the number of bytes added to this stack.

Teaching detail:
Each pushed register consumes two bytes. Two pushes therefore add four to the stack pointer: 0x016E+0x0004=0x0172. The two-word length of the CALL affects the saved return PC, not how many registers are pushed. Similarly, the current PC value is not an address increment to add to SP. A downward-growing stack would subtract four, but the question explicitly gives upward growth, ruling out 016A.

subject: 01-digital-logic
question_text: How many minterms remain in the minimized function [¬D + A¬B + ¬AC + A¬CD + ¬A¬CD] complemented as a whole? Here juxtaposition is AND and + is OR.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
For the outer complement to be 1, every inner OR term must be 0. D′=0 requires D=1. With D=1 and C=0, AC′D+A′C′D=A+A′=1, impossible; hence C=1. Then A′C=0 requires A=1, and AB′=0 requires B=1. Conversely A=B=C=D=1 makes all inner terms zero. The function is exactly ABCD, one minterm.

Teaching detail:
Complementing a sum means that every product inside must be zero. The ¬D term first forces D=1. Then A¬CD and ¬A¬CD combine to ¬C, so C must be 1. With C=1, the term ¬AC forces A=1; with A=1, A¬B forces B=1. Thus exactly A=B=C=D=1 survives. Conversely that assignment makes every original summand zero, verifying the result ABCD and exactly one minterm.

subject: excluded
question_text: For f(x)=x^(−1/3) on −1≤x≤1, assess I continuity throughout the interval, II unboundedness, and III nonzero finite area between the curve and x-axis. Options: A II only; B III only; C II and III only; D I, II and III.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
For real x, x^(−1/3)=1/cuberoot(x) is undefined at 0 and unbounded near it, so I is false and II true. The geometric area is the improper integral 2*integral(0..1)x^(−1/3)dx=2*(3/2)=3, positive and finite. Thus II and III, C; signed cancellation across zero would not be the geometric area.

Teaching detail:
At x=0 the function is undefined and its magnitude grows without bound as x approaches zero, so I is false and II is true. Geometric area uses absolute value, not cancellation of the odd function’s signed integral. On the positive half, ∫₀¹ x^(−1/3)dx=[(3/2)x^(2/3)]₀¹=3/2, finite despite the singularity. The negative half contributes the same area, for total 3. Therefore III is true. A divergent function value at one endpoint does not automatically make an improper integral diverge.

question_text: Start with matrix [[3, 4, 45], [7, 9, 105], [13, 2, 195]]. Add row 3 to row 2, then subtract column 3 from column 1. Find the determinant of the resulting matrix.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
The third column is 15 times the first: 45=15*3, 105=15*7, 195=15*13. The original determinant is therefore 0. Adding one row to another and subtracting one column from another preserve determinant, so the resulting determinant remains 0.

Teaching detail:
Before doing arithmetic, observe that the third column is exactly 15 times the first: 45=15·3, 105=15·7 and 195=15·13. Hence the original determinant is zero. Adding one row to another does not change a determinant; subtracting one column from another also preserves it. After the specified column operation, column 1 is −14 times its former value and remains proportional to column 3, so dependence remains directly visible. The requested determinant is therefore 0 without expanding nine cofactors.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_text: How many onto functions exist from a four-element set to a three-element set?
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
There are 3^4 total functions. Exclude functions omitting at least one codomain value by inclusion-exclusion: 3^4−C(3, 1)2^4+C(3, 2)1^4=81−48+3=36. Equivalently choose the repeated pair of domain elements in 6 ways, its image in 3 ways and assign the other two images in 2 ways.

Teaching detail:
There are 3⁴=81 functions in total. For each of the three codomain elements, 2⁴=16 functions omit it. Subtract 3·16, then restore the three intersections where only one codomain element is used. The result is 81−48+3=36. Equivalently, an onto function must have fiber sizes 2, 1, 1: choose the repeated pair in C(4, 2)=6 ways, its image in 3 ways and assign the remaining two images in 2 ways. Both counts give 36.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_text: Choose uniformly from all functions from a two-element set to a twenty-element set. Find the probability that the function is one-to-one.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
The first domain element has 20 possible images and the second must choose one of the remaining 19 for injectivity. Among 20² equally likely functions, 20*19 are injective, giving 19/20=0.95.

Teaching detail:
The first domain element may map to any of 20 values. Of the 20 choices for the second, exactly 19 differ from the first. Uniform independent choices among all 20² functions therefore give 20·19/20²=19/20=0.95. The number 20·19 is a count of injective functions, not the requested probability. The uniformity over all functions is essential to this simple ratio.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text: Solve language equations X0=1X1, X1=0X1+1X2, X2=0X1+{ε}, where concatenation and union have their regular-expression meanings. Determine X0; option C is 1(0+10)*1. Options: A 10(0*+(10)*)1; B 10(0*+(10)*)*1; C 1(0+10)*1; D 10(0+10)*1+110(0+10)*1.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_text: For which residue classes of n modulo 4 can a simple self-complementary graph have n vertices? Options: A multiple of 4; B even; C odd; D n≡0 or 1 (mod 4).
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
A simple self-complementary graph has the same number m of edges as its complement, so 2m=C(n, 2), or m=n(n−1)/4. This must be an integer, forcing n congruent 0 or 1 modulo 4. Thus D. The statement is a necessary condition; it does not assert every graph of those orders is self-complementary.

Teaching detail:
If a graph has m edges, its complement has n(n−1)/2−m. An isomorphism between them requires equal edge counts, so m=n(n−1)/4 must be an integer. Among four consecutive residue possibilities, n(n−1) is divisible by 4 exactly when n≡0 or 1 modulo 4. This establishes the necessary arithmetic restriction; the standard existence theorem for self-complementary graphs establishes these classes are attainable, rather than claiming edge integrality alone constructs a graph.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_text: A bridge is an edge whose removal disconnects a connected graph. Which assertion is true? A a tree has no bridges; B a bridge cannot lie on a simple cycle; C every edge of a clique of size at least 3 is a bridge; D a graph with bridges cannot contain a cycle.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
If an edge lies on a simple cycle, the rest of that cycle still connects its endpoints after removal, so it cannot disconnect a connected graph. Therefore a bridge cannot lie on a simple cycle, B. Every edge of a nontrivial tree is a bridge, and attaching a leaf to a triangle gives a graph with both a bridge and a cycle.

Teaching detail:
If an edge lies on a cycle, removing it leaves the rest of that cycle as an alternate path between its endpoints. It therefore cannot disconnect the graph, proving B. Every edge of a nontrivial tree is a bridge, refuting A. Clique edges with at least three vertices lie in triangles, refuting C. A triangle with a single pendant edge has both a cycle and a bridge, refuting D. These examples separate a property of one edge from a property of the entire graph.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_text: Which displayed first-order formula is a tautology? A (∀x∃y R(x, y))↔(∃y∀x R(x, y)); B (∀x[∃y R(x, y)→S(x, y)])→∀x∃y S(x, y), with the printed quantifier scope retained; C [∀x∃y(P(x, y)→R(x, y))]↔[∀x∃y(¬P(x, y)∨R(x, y))]; D (∀x∀y P(x, y))→∀x∀y P(y, x). The published key selects C alone.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
C follows pointwise from P→R being equivalent to NOT P OR R, preserved under the same quantifiers. But D is also valid as literally printed: from forall x forall y P(x, y), every ordered pair satisfies P, including the pair(y, x), hence forall x forall y P(y, x). Universal quantifiers commute and bound-variable names can be renamed. Thus the single-choice question has at least two valid options, C and D, although the embedded official answer marks only C. A fails for equality on a two-element domain; B can have a false existential antecedent with S everywhere false.

Teaching detail:
Material implication P→R is equivalent pointwise to ¬P∨R. Applying identical quantifiers to equivalent predicates preserves equivalence, so C is valid. D is also valid: if P holds on every ordered pair, it holds on every swapped pair; exchanging the dummy variable names changes nothing. A fails on a two-element domain with R equality: each x has a matching y but no single y matches both. For B, take R and S both always false on a nonempty domain; the implication in its premise is true while the conclusion is false, regardless of the scope ambiguity in the displayed y. Thus the single-choice key omits another valid answer D.
derived_answer: C and D are valid; official C only

subject: 01-digital-logic
question_text: Construct a full adder from two half adders and an OR gate, and a four-bit ripple-carry adder from four such full adders. Each AND/OR gate delay is 1.2 microseconds; each XOR gate delay is 2.4 microseconds. Determine propagation delay, distinguishing a lumped full-adder timing model from gate-level overlapping propagation.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential question context with source links; not a certified verbatim original. Source-specific wording and figure qualifications remain explicit.
solution:
Each XOR delay is 2.4 microseconds and each AND/OR delay 1.2. A full adder made from two half adders has P=A XOR B, sum=P XOR Cin and Cout=AB+P*Cin. Its worst input-to-output delay is 4.8. Multiplying this black-box delay by four gives the published 19.2. However in a gate-aware ripple circuit all four P signals are computed in parallel. The first carry settles by 4.8, and each later carry needs only AND+OR=2.4 more, giving carry delays 4.8, 7.2, 9.6, 12; the last sum also settles by 9.6+2.4=12. Thus 19.2 is a conservative lumped-stage estimate, not the tight standard gate-level propagation bound under simultaneous operand arrival. A fixed zero initial carry or different arrival assumptions can further change sensitized timing. The intended timing model is not explicit.

Teaching detail:
At gate level all bit propagate signals P=A XOR B become ready after 2.4 microseconds, and generates G=AB after 1.2. The first carry using P·Cin followed by OR is ready after 4.8. Later carries traverse only an AND and OR using already-ready P, adding 2.4 each: 7.2, 9.6 and 12.0. The last sum is also ready at 9.6+2.4=12.0. By contrast, treating each full adder as a black box with worst-case delay 4.8 and multiplying by four gives the published 19.2. These calculations use different overlap assumptions; the source/key discrepancy must remain visible rather than silently selecting a timing model.
derived_answer: Official19.2 uses lumped full-adder delays; gate-aware model gives12

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_text: Let S={1,2,3,4,5,6}, U be its power set, |T| denote cardinality, T′ denote complement relative to S, and T\R denote set difference. Which statement is true? (A) For every X∈U, |X|=|X′|. (B) There exist X,Y∈U with |X|=|Y|=5 and X∩Y=∅. (C) For every X,Y∈U, |X|=2, |Y|=3 and X\Y=∅. (D) For every X,Y∈U, X\Y=Y′\X′.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential context, options and figure/code givens transcribed or paraphrased from visually inspected source; not a verbatim reproduction.
solution:
1. For A, take X=∅: its size is 0 while its complement has size 6. For B, inclusion-exclusion gives |X∩Y|≥5+5−6=4, so disjointness is impossible. For C, its universal cardinality claims already fail at X=∅; even restricting to sizes 2 and 3 does not force containment, e.g. X={1,2}, Y={3,4,5}.

2. For any element t, t∈X\Y iff t∈X and t∉Y iff t∈Y′ and t∉X′, hence X\Y=Y′\X′. Thus D. Equal complement sizes need not hold, two5-subsets of a 6-set cannot be disjoint, and arbitrary2/3-subsets need not satisfy the proposed containment.

subject: 09-database-management-systems
question_text: Relation X(P,Q,R,S,T,U) has functional dependencies F={ {P,R}→{S,T}, {P,S,U}→{Q,R} }. F⁺ is the closure of F. Which listed dependency is trivial? (A) {P,R}→{S,T}; (B) {P,R}→{R,T}; (C) {P,S}→{S}; (D) {P,S,U}→{Q}.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential context, options and figure/code givens transcribed or paraphrased from visually inspected source; not a verbatim reproduction.
solution:
1. The closure notation does not make a nontrivial dependency trivial. In A the right side introduces S,T; in B it introduces T; in D it introduces Q. Only C has no right-side attribute outside the left side.

2. A functional dependency X→Y is trivial precisely when Y⊆X. Here{P, S}→{S} meets this condition, C, independently of the other dependencies.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text: For a computer system with n CPUs, what is the maximum number of processes that can be in the Ready state? Options: (A) n; (B) n²; (C) 2ⁿ; (D) independent of n.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential context, options and figure/code givens transcribed or paraphrased from visually inspected source; not a verbatim reproduction.
solution:
1. At most n processes can execute simultaneously on n single-threaded CPUs, but that bound applies to Running, not Ready. A ready queue may contain many more processes while the CPUs execute others.

2. Ready processes are waiting to be scheduled, not currently executing. Their possible count is not bounded by the CPU count n; it depends on system/process resources. Thus independent of n, D.

subject: 07-compiler-design
question_text: Among simple LR (SLR), canonical LR and look-ahead LR (LALR), identify, in order, the easiest method to implement and the most powerful method. Options: (A) SLR, LALR; (B) canonical LR, LALR; (C) SLR, canonical LR; (D) LALR, canonical LR.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential context, options and figure/code givens transcribed or paraphrased from visually inspected source; not a verbatim reproduction.
solution:
1. SLR uses one FOLLOW set for all reductions of a nonterminal, whereas canonical LR keeps the lookahead specific to each item/context. LALR merges compatible LR states for smaller tables but may introduce conflicts that canonical LR avoids.

2. SLR uses LR(0) states plus FOLLOW sets and is the simplest of the three. Canonical LR(1) retains item-specific lookaheads and recognizes the broadest grammar class. Thus SLR, canonical LR, C.

subject: 01-digital-logic
question_text: For Boolean variables define X#Y=X′+Y′, where prime means NOT and + means OR. Consider S1: (P#Q)#R=P#(Q#R); S2: Q#R=R#Q. Which holds for all Boolean P,Q,R? (A) only S1; (B) only S2; (C) both; (D) neither.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential context, options and figure/code givens transcribed or paraphrased from visually inspected source; not a verbatim reproduction.
solution:
1. By De Morgan, X′+Y′=NOT(XY). For the counterexample, 0#1=1 and 1#1=0, so the left grouping is 1#1=0 while the right grouping is 0#0=1.

2. X#Y=¬X+¬Y is NAND and is commutative. It is not associative: P=0, Q=1, R=1 gives(P#Q)#R=0 while P#(Q#R)=1. Thus only S2, B.

question_text: Calculate the function point metric for a software project with external inputs I=30, external outputs O=60, external inquiries E=23, files F=8, and external interfaces N=2. Their respective complexity weights are 4,5,4,10,7. Of fourteen value-adjustment factors, four are not applicable (value 0), four have value 3, and the remaining six have value 4. Use the standard adjusted function-point formula.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential context, options and figure/code givens transcribed or paraphrased from visually inspected source; not a verbatim reproduction.
solution:
1. The method first multiplies each information-domain count by its complexity weight and sums to obtain unadjusted function points. It then multiplies that total by 0.65+0.01 times the sum of the fourteen adjustment ratings. Four plus four factors account for eight ratings, leaving six ratings of value 4.

2. Unadjusted points=30·4+60·5+23·4+8·10+2·7=606. Adjustment sum=4·0+4·3+6·4=36. The factor is 0.65+0.01·36=1.01, giving606·1.01=612.06, within the official612 to 613 range.

subject: 10-computer-networks
question_text: Consider: I. TCP connections are full duplex. II. TCP has no option for selective acknowledgment. III. TCP connections are message streams. Which are correct? (A) I only; (B) I and III; (C) II and III; (D) all three.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential context, options and figure/code givens transcribed or paraphrased from visually inspected source; not a verbatim reproduction.
solution:
1. Full duplex means each endpoint can send while also receiving on the same connection. The TCP selective-acknowledgment option reports received data blocks beyond a gap, so statement II is false. Applications see an ordered byte stream: one send need not correspond to one receive, so statement III is false.

2. TCP is full-duplex, has a selective-acknowledgment option, and exposes a byte stream rather than preserving application-message boundaries. Therefore only I is correct, A.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_text: Let X=Σ(i³), i=0,...,n. Which asymptotic descriptions of X are valid? I: Θ(n⁴); II: Θ(n⁵); III: O(n⁵); IV: Ω(n³). Options: (A) only I; (B) only II; (C) I or III or IV, but not II; (D) II or III or IV, but not I.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential context, options and figure/code givens transcribed or paraphrased from visually inspected source; not a verbatim reproduction.
solution:
1. The exact polynomial is n⁴/4+n³/2+n²/4. Its leading term supplies a two-sided Θ(n⁴) bound; a looser upper bound n⁵ and looser lower bound n³ remain valid, whereas a two-sided n⁵ bound does not.

2. Sum(i³, i=0..n)=[n(n+1)/2]²=Θ(n⁴). It is consequently O(n⁵) and Ω(n³), but not Θ(n⁵). Thus I, III, IV, C; equality to an asymptotic class is conventional membership notation.

subject: 04-data-structures
question_text: A binary tree T has 200 leaf nodes. How many nodes in T have exactly two children? Nodes with exactly one child are allowed.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential context, options and figure/code givens transcribed or paraphrased from visually inspected source; not a verbatim reproduction.
solution:
1. Let n0,n1,n2 count nodes with zero, one and two children. Every non-root node contributes one incoming edge, so E=n0+n1+n2−1. Counting edges from parents instead gives E=n1+2n2; subtracting cancels n1 and yields the result without assuming a full binary tree.

2. Counting tree edges gives n1+2n2=n0+n1+n2−1. Hence the number with two children is n2=n0−1=200−1=199.

subject: 04-data-structures
question_text: A hash table T has 25 slots and stores 2000 elements. Find its load factor α.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential context, options and figure/code givens transcribed or paraphrased from visually inspected source; not a verbatim reproduction.
solution:
1. Load factor measures the average number of elements per table slot, rather than the fraction of slots that are nonempty. With separate chaining, several elements may share a slot, so a load factor greater than one is meaningful.

2. Load factor is number of stored elements divided by number of slots: 2000/25=80. This is possible with chaining rather than a one-element-per-slot open-addressed table.

question_text: The matrix A has rows (1,−1,2), (0,1,0), (1,2,1). One eigenvalue is 1. Which set gives all eigenvectors for that eigenvalue? Each option uses nonzero real α: (A) {α(4,2,1)}; (B) {α(−4,2,1)}; (C) {α(√2,0,1)}; (D) {α(−√2,0,1)}.

solution:

2. Solving(A−I)v=0 gives−y+2z=0 and x+2y=0. Therefore y=2z, x=−4z, so the nonzero eigenvectors are scalar multiples of(−4, 2, 1), B.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_text: A room contains only Type 1 people, who always tell the truth, and Type 2 people, who always lie. You give a fair coin to someone of unknown type, ask them to toss it and hide the result, then ask the result. They reply: “The result of the toss is head if and only if I am telling the truth.” Which option is correct? (A) The result is head. (B) The result is tail. (C) If the person is Type 2, the result is tail. (D) If the person is Type 1, the result is tail.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential context, options and figure/code givens transcribed or paraphrased from visually inspected source; not a verbatim reproduction.
solution:
1. Let T indicate that the speaker tells the truth and H that the coin is heads.

2. The assertion is H↔T, whose truth value must equal T. If T is true, H must be true; if T is false, H↔false must be false, again requiring H true. Thus the coin is heads, A.

question_text: Evaluate the postfix expression whose tokens are: 10 5 + 60 6 / * 8 −. Options: (A) 284; (B) 213; (C) 142; (D) 71.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential context, options and figure/code givens transcribed or paraphrased from visually inspected source; not a verbatim reproduction.
solution:
1. A stack evaluator pops the right operand first and left operand second. After + the stack contains 15; after / it contains 15,10; after * it contains 150; the final subtraction is 150−8, not 8−150.

2. Postfix evaluation gives 10+5=15, 60/6=10, then15·10=150, and 150−8=142. Thus C.

subject: 04-data-structures
question_text: An array in level-order heap representation is (89,19,50,17,12,15,2,5,7,11,6,9,100). What is the minimum number of interchanges needed to convert it into a max-heap? An interchange swaps two elements. Options: (A) 4; (B) 5; (C) 2; (D) 3.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential context, options and figure/code givens transcribed or paraphrased from visually inspected source; not a verbatim reproduction.
solution:
1. With 1-based indices, swaps (13,6), (6,3), (3,1) yield (100,19,89,17,12,50,2,5,7,11,6,9,15). Check each parent against its children: every parent is at least as large. This gives a concrete three-swap witness, not merely the count performed by an unspecified heapify routine.

2. Three swaps along the ancestor chain move100 through indices 13→6→3→1, producing a valid max-heap. Fewer cannot suffice: 100 must reach the root. If swapped directly with 89, the resulting89 at 13 exceeds both ancestors15 at 6 and 50 at 3; one additional swap cannot repair both (swapping with 3 leaves50 below15; swapping with 6 leaves89 below50). If100 reaches the root in two swaps, at least one of the remaining displaced chain values is still out of heap order. Thus the minimum is 3, D.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text_status: Self-contained essential context, options and figure/code givens transcribed or paraphrased from visually inspected source; not a verbatim reproduction.
solution:
1. If both flags become true before either loop test, both processes can enter their critical sections, so mutual exclusion fails.

2. The inner loops are not waiting loops: their bodies execute the critical section when the other flag is true. Under fair execution and terminating critical sections, a false test returns to the outer loop and reasserts the flag; there is no state where both wait permanently for an action the other cannot perform. Thus A. Literal unsynchronized C threads would instead require a memory-model analysis; the source is treated as synchronization pseudocode.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text: Let Σ={0,1} and L be the language of the regular expression Σ*0011Σ*. What is the minimum number of states in a DFA recognizing the complement of L? Options: (A) 4; (B) 5; (C) 6; (D) 8.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential context, options and figure/code givens transcribed or paraphrased from visually inspected source; not a verbatim reproduction.
solution:
1. Writing states as matched-prefix lengths 0..4, transitions on (0,1) are 0→(1,0), 1→(2,0), 2→(2,3), 3→(1,4), 4→(4,4). For pattern containment only state 4 accepts; for its complement states 0..3 accept. For any i<j, the suffix completing prefix length j reaches state 4 from j but not from i, proving distinguishability.

2. A DFA tracks the longest suffix matching a prefix of 0011: lengths0, 1, 2, 3, 4, with 4 an absorbing found-pattern state. These five states are pairwise distinguishable by completing the pattern; flipping accepting states recognizes avoidance of 0011 without changing minimal state count. Thus5, B.

question_text: A program is deliberately seeded with 100 artificial faults. Testing detects 159 faults in total, including 75 seeded faults. Assuming real and seeded faults have the same nature and distribution, estimate the number of undetected real faults.

solution:

subject: 10-computer-networks
question_text: A CSMA/CD network transmits at 100 Mbps (10⁸ bits/s) over a 1 km cable without repeaters. Its required minimum frame size is 1250 bytes. Find signal speed in km/s, using the collision-detection minimum-frame condition. Options: (A) 8000; (B) 10000; (C) 16000; (D) 20000.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential context, options and figure/code givens transcribed or paraphrased from visually inspected source; not a verbatim reproduction.
solution:
1. A transmitting station must still be transmitting when a worst-case collision indication returns from the far end of the cable. Therefore frame serialization time must cover two one-way propagation delays. Convert bytes to bits before comparing the frame size with the bit rate.

2. Minimum frame serialization time is 1250·8/10^8=10^−4s, which must equal the cable’s round-trip propagation time at the minimum. One-way delay=5·10^−5s, so speed1km/(5·10^−5s)=20000km/s, D.

subject: 09-database-management-systems
question_text: A B+ tree has search keys of 12 bytes, blocks of 1024 bytes, record pointers of 10 bytes, and block pointers of 8 bytes. What is the maximum number of keys that fit in each non-leaf node? Use the usual internal-node layout with one more child pointer than keys and no additional stated overhead.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential context, options and figure/code givens transcribed or paraphrased from visually inspected source; not a verbatim reproduction.
solution:
1. For k=50 the node uses 50·12+51·8=1008 bytes, which fits. For k=51 it needs 51·12+52·8=1028 bytes, exceeding the block. These adjacent checks establish the maximum, not just a rounded estimate.

2. An internal node with k keys has k+1 child pointers, so 12k+8(k+1)≤1024. Thus20k≤1016 and k≤50. Record pointers belong in leaves and are not counted here.

question_text: Suppose L1 is polynomial-time reducible to L2, L3 is polynomial-time reducible to L2, and L2 is polynomial-time reducible to L4. Which statements follow? I: If L4∈P, then L2∈P. subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text: Which languages are context-free? L1={a^m b^n a^n b^m | m,n≥1}; L2={a^m b^n a^m b^n | m,n≥1}; L3={a^m b^n | m=2n+1}. Exponents denote nonnegative integer counts unless constrained otherwise. Options: (A) L1 and L2 only; (B) L1 and L3 only; (C) L2 and L3 only; (D) L3 only.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential context, options and figure/code givens transcribed or paraphrased from visually inspected source; not a verbatim reproduction.
solution:
1. L1=a^m b^n a^n b^m has nested dependencies: S→aSb|aTb and T→bTa|ba generates m, n≥1, so it is CFL.

2. L3 is generated by U→aaUb|a for n≥0. L2=a^m b^n a^m b^n is not CFL: for pumping length p, choose a^p b^p a^p b^p. The pumping window of length≤p touches at most two adjacent blocks, so pumping changes at least one block but cannot change its corresponding nonadjacent equal block; if a pumped piece crosses a boundary, pumping can also destroy the four-block form. Thus pumping fails. L1, L3 only, B.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text: For mutually exclusive resources, which policies can prevent deadlock? I: A process acquires all resources at the start; if any is unavailable, it releases those acquired so far. II: Resources have unique numbers and requests occur only in increasing number order. III: Resources have unique numbers and requests occur only in decreasing number order. IV: Resources have unique numbers and a process may request only a resource numbered higher than all resources it currently holds. Options: (A) any one of I and III, but not II or IV; (B) any one of I,III,IV, but not II; (C) any one of II and III, but not I or IV; (D) any one of I,II,III,IV.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential context, options and figure/code givens transcribed or paraphrased from visually inspected source; not a verbatim reproduction.
solution:
1. I removes hold-and-wait by releasing partial acquisitions if all cannot be obtained.

2. II and III each impose a strict global resource order, excluding circular wait. IV likewise permits only requests larger than every held resource, so any wait cycle would require strictly increasing numbers around a loop, impossible. Each policy individually prevents deadlock, D; this does not promise starvation freedom.

subject: 10-computer-networks
question_text: Two systems are separated by 8000 km. The link rate is 500×10⁶ bits/s, propagation speed is 4×10⁶ m/s, and average packet size is 10⁷ bits. Design a Go-Back-N sliding-window protocol that fully utilizes the link, neglecting processing delays and using the standard negligible-ACK-transmission model. What minimum number of sequence-number bits is required?
question_text_status: Self-contained essential context, options and figure/code givens transcribed or paraphrased from visually inspected source; not a verbatim reproduction.
solution:
1. Full utilization requires enough outstanding packets to bridge a packet’s serialization plus the round-trip propagation before its ACK permits reuse. A 201-packet window meets this bound; the Go-Back-N sequence space must contain at least 202 distinct sequence numbers to avoid old/new ambiguity.

2. One-way propagation=8·10^6/(4·10^6)=2s. Packet serialization=10^7/(500·10^6)=0.02s. To stay busy with negligible ACK time, window≥1+2·2/0.02=201 packets. Go-Back-N requires W≤2^k−1; 2^7−1=127 is insufficient and 2^8−1=255 suffices. Thus8 bits.

subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_text: A three-stage pipeline has a five-column reservation table. Stage S1 is used at time slots 1 and 5, S2 at slots 2 and 4, and S3 only at slot 3; all other cells are blank. Determine the minimum average initiation latency (MAL). Initiation times may vary, but no two active operations may use the same stage simultaneously.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential context, options and figure/code givens transcribed or paraphrased from visually inspected source; not a verbatim reproduction.
solution:
1. The forbidden separations come from differences between occupied columns in the same row, not from differences across different stages. Thus the initial forbidden-latency set is exactly {2,4}. To attain average 3, start operations at times 0,3,6,9,...; every pairwise separation is a positive multiple of 3 and therefore safe.

2. Repeated use in S1 forbids initiation separation4; S2 forbids2. Therefore allowed positive gaps include1, 3, 5. Constant gap3 is collision-free because no multiple of 3 is 2 or4, achieving average3. If any gap is 1, its next gap cannot1 or3 (the two-gap total would be2 or4) and must be at least5. Pair each such1 with its following≥5 gap; every pair averages≥3, while unpaired gaps are≥3. Thus no lower long-run average is possible.

question_text: A partial schedule lists these operations in time order: 1 T1:read(A); 2 T1:write(A); 3 T2:read(C); 4 T2:write(C); 5 T2:read(B); 6 T2:write(B); 7 T2:read(A); 8 T2:commit; 9 T1:read(B). T1 fails immediately after time 9. Which statement is correct? (A) Abort T2, then restart both T1 and T2 to ensure atomicity. (B) The schedule is non-recoverable and cannot ensure transaction atomicity. (C) Abort and restart only T2 to ensure atomicity. (D) The schedule is recoverable and ensures atomicity without doing anything else.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential context, options and figure/code givens transcribed or paraphrased from visually inspected source; not a verbatim reproduction.
solution:
1. T2 reads A at time7 after T1 writes it at time2, before T1 commits.

2. T2 then commits at 8. When T1 fails after 9, its uncommitted value has already influenced a committed transaction. This violates recoverability: a reader must not commit before the transaction whose value it read. T2 cannot simply be treated as an uncommitted transaction to roll back. Thus B.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_text: A connected undirected graph G has 100 vertices and 300 edges. The weight of a minimum spanning tree is 500. If the weight of every edge in G is increased by 5, what is the new minimum spanning-tree weight?
question_text_status: Self-contained essential context, options and figure/code givens transcribed or paraphrased from visually inspected source; not a verbatim reproduction.
solution:
1. The 300 graph edges do not all belong to the spanning tree. Connectedness makes every spanning tree have exactly |V|−1=99 edges, so the increment is 99·5 rather than 300·5. Because all candidate trees receive the same increment, a previously minimum tree remains minimum.

2. Every spanning tree on100 vertices has 99 edges. Adding5 to every edge increases every spanning-tree weight by exactly495, preserving their ordering and the set of minimum spanning trees. The new minimum weight is 500+495=995.

question_text: In positional notation, (43) base x equals (y3) base 8, where x is a valid integer base and y is a valid octal digit. How many (x,y) solutions are possible?

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_text: R is a relation on ordered pairs of positive integers, with ((p,q),(r,s))∈R iff p−s=q−r. Which description is correct? (A) reflexive and symmetric; (B) reflexive but not symmetric; (C) not reflexive but symmetric; (D) neither reflexive nor symmetric.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential context, options and figure/code givens transcribed or paraphrased from visually inspected source; not a verbatim reproduction.
solution:
1. The condition p−s=q−r is equivalent to p+r=q+s, unchanged by swapping the two ordered pairs; the relation is symmetric.

2. Reflexivity at(p, q) would require2p=2q, which fails for example at(1, 2). Thus it is not reflexive but is symmetric, C.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_text: X1,X2,X3 are independent, identically distributed bits with P(Xi=0)=P(Xi=1)=1/2. Let Y=(X1X2) XOR X3, where juxtaposition denotes ordinary multiplication of bits. Find P(Y=0 | X3=0).
question_text_status: Self-contained essential context, options and figure/code givens transcribed or paraphrased from visually inspected source; not a verbatim reproduction.
solution:
1. The four conditional equally likely (X1,X2) pairs are 00,01,10,11. With X3=0, XOR changes nothing, so the first three give Y=0 and only 11 gives Y=1.

2. Conditioning on X3=0 makes Y=X1X2. Independence leaves X1 and X2 independent fair bits. Their product is 1 only when both are1, with probability1/4. Therefore Pr(Y=0|X3=0)=3/4=0.75.

subject: 01-digital-logic
question_text: For Boolean f(w,x,y,z)=Σ(0,2,4,5,6,10), with minterm indexing in variable order w,x,y,z, find the total number of prime implicants. There are no don't-care minterms.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential context, options and figure/code givens transcribed or paraphrased from visually inspected source; not a verbatim reproduction.
solution:
1. The four-cell group {0,2,4,6} fixes w=0,z=0; pair {4,5} fixes w=0,x=1,y=0; pair {2,10} fixes x=0,y=1,z=0. All singleton minterms and remaining valid pairs expand into one of these maximal groups. Count prime implicants, not just a selected minimum cover.

2. The maximal all-one cubes are0--0 covering0, 2, 4, 6; 010- covering4, 5; and-010 covering2, 10. They correspond to w′z′, w′xy′ and x′yz′. No cube can expand without including a zero minterm, and every other valid cube is contained in one of these three. Thus there are3 prime implicants.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_text: DOSOMETHING(c,a,n) receives a bit array c[0..k−1] and positive integers a,n. It sets z=1; then for i=0,...,k−1 sets z=z² mod n, and, if c[i]=1, sets z=(z×a) mod n; finally it returns z. For k=4, c=(1,0,1,1), a=2, n=8, what is returned?
question_text_status: Self-contained essential context, options and figure/code givens transcribed or paraphrased from visually inspected source; not a verbatim reproduction.
solution:
1. Iteration details: bit 1 gives 1²·2 mod 8=2; bit 0 gives 2² mod 8=4; bit 1 gives (4² mod 8)·2 mod 8=0; the last bit 1 keeps the value 0. Each iteration squares before the optional multiplication.

2. The loop processes the binary exponent1011 from most significant bit to least. The successive z values modulo8 are2, 4, 0, 0: square and multiply by 2 when the current bit is 1. Equivalently it computes2^11 mod8=0.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_text: Let f(n)=n and g(n)=n^(1+sin n), for positive integers n, with sine measured in radians. Which asymptotic statements hold? I: f(n)=O(g(n)); II: f(n)=Ω(g(n)). Options: (A) I only; (B) II only; (C) both; (D) neither.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential context, options and figure/code givens transcribed or paraphrased from visually inspected source; not a verbatim reproduction.
solution:
1. The ratio g(n)/f(n)=n^(sin n).

2. Since1/(2π) is irrational, integer n modulo2π is dense, and every tail is dense. There are therefore arbitrarily large n with sin n≥1/2 and arbitrarily large n with sin n≤−1/2. Along the former subsequence g/f≥sqrt(n) is unbounded, ruling out f=Ω(g); along the latter f/g≥sqrt(n) is unbounded, ruling out f=O(g). Thus neither statement holds, D, with sine in radians.

subject: 07-compiler-design
question_text: Grammar G has productions S→F|H, F→p|c, H→d|c. S,F,H are nonterminals; p,d,c are terminals. Assess S1: LL(1) can parse all strings generated using grammar G; S2: LR(1) can parse all strings generated using grammar G. Options: (A) S1 only; (B) S2 only; (C) both; (D) neither. The question concerns this grammar, not whether its language has a different LL(1) or LR(1) grammar.
question_text_status: Self-contained essential context, options and figure/code givens transcribed or paraphrased from visually inspected source; not a verbatim reproduction.
solution:
1. The string c has two parse trees: S→F→c and S→H→c.

2. Thus the displayed grammar is ambiguous and is neither LL(1) nor LR(1). Concretely FIRST(F) and FIRST(H) both contain c, causing an LL conflict; after shifting c, completed F→c and H→c items both reduce on end-of-input, causing an LR reduce/reduce conflict. Therefore D for parsing with this grammar. Its finite language can of course be represented by a different unambiguous grammar S→p|d|c.

subject: 11-general-aptitude
question_text: Choose the grammatically and idiomatically correct sentence. A: I will not leave the place until the minister does not meet me. B: I will not leave the place until the minister doesn't meet me. C: I will not leave the place until the minister meet me. D: I will not leave the place until the minister meets me.
question_text_status: Self-contained source-grounded paraphrase with all essential givens, choices, code and textual figure reconstructions; not a verbatim facsimile.
solution:
Until introduces the positive event that ends the refusal: I will not leave until the minister meets me. Singular minister requires meets, and a second negation reverses the intended condition. Thus D.

The word until marks the event that ends the waiting period. The intended meaning is that leaving becomes possible after a meeting occurs, not after a refusal to meet. In a future time clause, English normally uses present tense: “until he meets,” even though the main clause says “will.” A and B have the same unnecessary negation; C lacks the third-person singular ending. These are separate meaning and agreement checks, both satisfied by D.

question_text: A rewording of something written or spoken is a _____. A: paraphrase. B: paradox. C: paradigm. D: paraffin.
question_text_status: Self-contained source-grounded paraphrase with all essential givens, choices, code and textual figure reconstructions; not a verbatim facsimile.
solution:
A paraphrase restates written or spoken material in different words while preserving its meaning. Thus A.

The defining feature is preservation of meaning while changing wording. For example, “She departed early” paraphrases “She left ahead of time.” A paradox is an apparently contradictory statement, a paradigm is a model or pattern, and paraffin is a substance. Matching the definition to the word is more reliable than choosing solely by the shared prefix para-.

subject: 11-general-aptitude
question_text: Archimedes said, “Give me a lever long enough and a fulcrum on which to place it, and I will move the world.” What kind of statement is this? A: figurative. B: collateral. C: literal. D: figurine.
question_text_status: Self-contained source-grounded paraphrase with all essential givens, choices, code and textual figure reconstructions; not a verbatim facsimile.
solution:
Moving the world with a lever is an exaggerated illustration of leverage, not a literal proposal. This is figurative language, A.

The image dramatizes the mechanical advantage of a lever by using an impossible scale. Figurative language includes this kind of hyperbole. Literal would mean the statement describes an actual practical undertaking without exaggeration; figurine means a small statue and is not the adjective for figurative speech. Collateral means accompanying or secondary and does not classify this rhetorical use.

subject: 11-general-aptitude
question_text: In a code, relftaga means carefree, otaga means careful, and fertaga means careless. Which could mean aftercare? A: zentaga. B: tagafer. C: tagazen. D: relffer.
question_text_status: Self-contained source-grounded paraphrase with all essential givens, choices, code and textual figure reconstructions; not a verbatim facsimile.
solution:
The shared element taga corresponds to care. In all three examples the other English component follows care but its coded component precedes taga, so the component order is reversed. Aftercare therefore puts taga first, followed by a new component for after: tagazen, C.

Compare repeated parts rather than guessing whole words. Care is common to all three meanings, and taga is common to all three codes. The fragments relf, o, and fer therefore stand for free, ful, and less. In the examples these fragments precede taga even though they follow care in English. Maintaining that reversal makes aftercare become care-code followed by after-code. B would use the already assigned fragment for less, so it cannot introduce after.

subject: 11-general-aptitude
question_text: A large cube is assembled from 64 unit-side cubes. One unit cube is removed from each of its eight corners. Find the surface area of the remaining solid in square units. A: 56. B: 64. C: 72. D: 96.
question_text_status: Self-contained source-grounded paraphrase with all essential givens, choices, code and textual figure reconstructions; not a verbatim facsimile.
solution:
The original cube has side 4 and surface area 6·4²=96. Removing a corner unit cube removes three exposed unit faces but reveals three previously internal unit faces. The eight corner removals do not overlap, so net area change is zero. Thus 96, D.

A useful distinction is between surface area and volume. The volume falls from 64 to 56, but 56 is not the surface area. At each removed corner, the lost faces are the three exterior faces meeting at that corner; its other three faces were touching neighboring cubes and become newly exposed. Counting all newly exposed faces, including the inward-facing recess surfaces, leaves the total unchanged. Since the side length is 4, different corner cuts do not remove adjacent cubes or overlap one another's exposed faces.

subject: 11-general-aptitude
question_text: A company sells four razors at unit prices in rupees: Elegance 48, Smooth 63, Soft 78, Executive 173. Quarterly quantities, in that product order, are Q1:(27300,20009,17602,9999), Q2:(25222,19392,18445,8942), Q3:(28976,22429,19544,10234), Q4:(21012,18229,16595,10109). Which product contributes the greatest fraction of annual revenue? A: Elegance. B: Executive. C: Smooth. D: Soft.
question_text_status: Self-contained source-grounded paraphrase with all essential givens, choices, code and textual figure reconstructions; not a verbatim facsimile.
solution:
Sum the quarterly quantities and multiply by unit prices. Annual revenues are Elegance 4,920,480; Smooth 5,043,717; Soft 5,630,508; Executive 6,796,132 rupees. The common total-revenue denominator does not affect ordering, so Executive contributes the greatest fraction, B.

The annual quantities are 102510,80059,72186,39284 in the given product order. Revenue is price times quantity, not quantity alone: the cheapest product sells the most units but is not the revenue leader. To compare revenue fractions R_i/(sum R_j), cancel the common positive denominator and compare the four numerators. This avoids unnecessary percentage calculations and explains why Executive's higher price outweighs its smaller sales volume.

subject: 11-general-aptitude
question_text: Indian currency notes display denominations in at least seventeen languages. The passage says, “If this is not an indication of the nation's diversity, nothing else is.” What follows? A: India has exactly seventeen languages. B: Linguistic pluralism is the only indicator of national diversity. C: The notes have enough space for all Indian languages. D: Linguistic pluralism is strong evidence of India's diversity.
question_text_status: Self-contained source-grounded paraphrase with all essential givens, choices, code and textual figure reconstructions; not a verbatim facsimile.
solution:
At least 17 displayed languages is offered as strong evidence of diversity. It does not say exactly 17 languages exist, that language is the sole possible evidence, or that all languages fit. Thus D.

“At least” supplies a lower bound, not an exact count, eliminating A. The second sentence is emphatic praise of this particular evidence; it does not quantify over all possible indicators of diversity, so B is too strong. Nothing in the passage concerns available printing space, which excludes C. D preserves the actual evidential claim without adding uniqueness, completeness or an unsupported number of languages.

subject: 11-general-aptitude
question_text: Four poker players satisfy: P always beats Q; R always beats S; S loses to P only sometimes; R always loses to Q. Which conclusions follow? (i) P is likely to beat all three others. (ii) S is the absolute worst player. A: i only. B: ii only. C: both. D: neither.
question_text_status: Self-contained source-grounded paraphrase with all essential givens, choices, code and textual figure reconstructions; not a verbatim facsimile.
solution:
The premises give pairwise outcomes, not a transitive total skill ranking or numerical winning probabilities. P sometimes loses to S, and no P-versus-R outcome is supplied, so i is not entailed. S sometimes beats P, which rules out the asserted absolute-worst conclusion ii. Therefore neither follows, D.

Do not silently make “beats” a transitive relation: a beats b and b beats c do not logically entail a beats c in a game. Nor does “sometimes” provide a numerical win probability. Thus the given individual matchup statements cannot establish that P is likely to defeat everyone. S has victories against P, so an absolute bottom ranking is not established either. The test is what the premises entail, not a plausible informal ranking from selected outcomes.

question_text: For f(x)=2x^7+3x−5, which is a polynomial factor? A: x^3+8. B: x−1. C: 2x−5. D: x+1.

The factor theorem says x−r divides a polynomial exactly when substituting r gives zero. Testing the simple candidate root 1 is enough to identify B.
