subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text: Running process P encounters one of these events. Which always move P to a non-running state in the intended model? A an actually blocking disk-read system call; B a page fault for a page in swap; C a disk interrupt delivering another process’s data; D a timer interrupt.
question_text_status: Author-written essential paraphrase with choices and textual diagram/code descriptions; exact original wording and artwork remain at the linked official source.
solution:
Approach: Ask whether P must wait for something unavailable, rather than merely whether control enters the kernel.

1. Derivation. A genuinely blocking disk read puts P into a waiting state while I/O completes. A fault on a page currently in swap also requires storage I/O, so P is blocked pending page-in. An interrupt for another process need not deschedule P, and a timer interrupt may return to P if no switch is needed. Thus A, B. A mere user-to-kernel mode switch is not necessarily a switch to a different process; blocking in A is taken as actual blocking, as stipulated.

2. Explanation and checks. For A, the CPU cannot complete P’s read until the requested I/O finishes; for B, execution cannot retry the memory access until the swapped page is brought into memory. Both create a reason to block P and run another process or idle. In C, handling an interrupt can make a different process ready without forcing immediate preemption. In D, the scheduler may choose P again. Kernel entry and saving a trap frame alone are not the requested process context switch.

subject: 09-database-management-systems
question_text: Which file organizations are I/O-efficient for scanning all records? A sorted file; B heap file; C unclustered tree index; D unclustered hash index.
question_text_status: Author-written essential paraphrase with choices and textual diagram/code descriptions; exact original wording and artwork remain at the linked official source.
solution:
Approach: Optimize for reading the entire data set, not for retrieving a few qualifying records.

1. Derivation. A full scan of a sorted file or a heap file reads the data pages sequentially, usually once each. Scanning through an unclustered index can chase record pointers to many scattered data pages, causing repeated/random I/O. Thus the I/O-efficient file organizations for the full scan are A, B; a selective index lookup is a different workload.

2. Explanation and checks. For a data file occupying B pages, scanning the file in its physical order takes about B page reads whether the records have a sorted order or an arbitrary heap order. An unclustered index does not group the data records in index traversal order, so neighboring index entries may point to different pages and cause random accesses or rereads. The index also has its own pages to read. Selectivity can make an index attractive for lookup, but that is absent in a full scan.

subject: 09-database-management-systems
question_text: Which statements about two-phase locking are true? A it permits only serializable schedules; B every operation locks just before and releases immediately after; C after the first lock release a transaction can acquire no new lock; D deadlock can occur.
question_text_status: Author-written essential paraphrase with choices and textual diagram/code descriptions; exact original wording and artwork remain at the linked official source.
solution:
Approach: Apply the no-new-locks-after-release rule and distinguish serializability from progress.

1. Derivation. Two-phase locking first acquires locks and then, after the first release, only releases locks. The no-new-locks shrinking-phase rule proves C. Ordering transactions by their lock points proves conflict serializability, hence A. It does not release every lock immediately after each operation, and deadlock is possible: T1 holds X and waits for Y while T2 holds Y and waits for X. Thus A, C, D.

2. Explanation and checks. The growing phase permits acquisition but no release; the shrinking phase permits release but no acquisition. The instant at which a transaction acquires its final lock is its lock point; ordering transactions by such points is consistent with every conflicting dependency, giving a serial order. Holding X while waiting for Y and holding Y while waiting for X obey the growing-phase rule, so 2PL can still deadlock. Releasing each lock immediately, as B claims, would prevent later acquisitions and is not the general protocol.

subject: 10-computer-networks
question_text: Which IPv4 statements are intended to be true? A only the source fragments; B any router fragments a datagram exceeding its outgoing MTU; C reassembly occurs only at the destination; D every intermediate router reassembles. The printed B does not mention the Don’t Fragment bit.
question_text_status: Author-written essential paraphrase with choices and textual diagram/code descriptions; exact original wording and artwork remain at the linked official source.
solution:
Approach: State the fragmentation-permitted model separately from the literal unrestricted assertion.

1. Derivation. In ordinary IPv4 with fragmentation permitted, an intermediate router can fragment a datagram larger than its outgoing MTU, and reassembly occurs only at the final IP destination. This gives the official B, C. However B is overbroad without the DF-bit condition: when Don’t Fragment is set, the router drops an oversized datagram and normally sends an ICMP fragmentation-needed message instead of fragmenting it. Thus B is not an unconditional statement about every IPv4 datagram. A and D are false; C remains true. Preserve official B, C, and distinguish the intended DF=0 model from the literal unrestricted claim.

2. Explanation and checks. A fragment is itself an IP packet and can follow routing decisions independently, so intermediate reassembly would both require storage and assume all fragments meet at the same router. Destination-only reassembly avoids that assumption. When DF=0 an oversized fragment or datagram may be fragmented further. When DF=1, B’s asserted behavior cannot occur: the router must not fragment. This is a wording/model discrepancy, not a reason to silently replace the published B;C answer with a different scoring value.
derived_answer: B;C when DF=0; C without that qualification

subject: 07-compiler-design
question_text: Select FALSE statements. A an attribute grammar is an SDD whose semantic functions have no side effects; B L-attributed definitions cannot always be evaluated depth first; C synthesized attributes can be evaluated during bottom-up parsing; D every L-attributed definition on an LR(1) grammar can be evaluated by bottom-up parsing.
question_text_status: Author-written essential paraphrase with choices and textual diagram/code descriptions; exact original wording and artwork remain at the linked official source.
solution:
Approach: Check the allowed dependency direction and distinguish a completed-tree traversal from evaluation during parsing.

1. Derivation. The question asks for false statements. A is the usual side-effect-free definition of an attribute grammar. L-attributed definitions admit a left-to-right depth-first evaluation, assigning inherited attributes on entry and synthesized ones on return, so B is false. Synthesized attributes can be computed at reductions, making C true. Arbitrary inherited dependencies in an L-attributed definition need not be available at the relevant point in an LR parse, so D’s universal claim about evaluation during bottom-up parsing is false. Thus B, D. Constructing a full parse tree and doing a separate attribute-evaluation traversal is distinct from the intended parsing-time claim.

2. Explanation and checks. An L-attributed production restricts an inherited attribute of a child to information available from the parent and earlier siblings. A left-to-right depth-first traversal can therefore compute it before entering that child and compute synthesized values after returning. A bottom-up reduction naturally has child synthesized values available, but arbitrary inherited context may be required earlier than that reduction. Hence an LR(1) grammar alone does not ensure the claimed parsing-time attribute evaluation. The question asks for the false choices, not the true ones.

subject: 01-digital-logic
question_text: For Boolean x select the FALSE identities. A x·1=x; B x+1=x; C x·x=0; D x+¬x=1. Here · means AND and + means OR.
question_text_status: Author-written essential paraphrase with choices and textual diagram/code descriptions; exact original wording and artwork remain at the linked official source.
solution:
Approach: Use Boolean truth tables, not ordinary arithmetic addition.

1. Derivation. Boolean identities give x·1=x and x+NOT x=1, so A, D are true. In contrast x+1=1, not x when x=0; and x·x=x, not0 when x=1. The false identities are B, C. Complement bars were visually checked.

2. Explanation and checks. For x=0 the left sides of A,B,C,D are 0,1,0,1, while the asserted right sides are 0,0,0,1; B already fails. For x=1 the left sides are 1,1,1,1 and the right sides are 1,1,0,1; C fails. Thus an identity must hold for both input values to be true. A is the AND identity law, C misstates idempotence, and D is the complement law.

subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_text: Instructions have destination first: I1 DIV R3,R1,R2; I2 SUB R5,R3,R4; I3 ADD R3,R5,R6; I4 MUL R7,R3,R8. Which are true? A I1→I2 RAW on R3; B I1→I3 WAR on R3; C I2→I3 RAW on R3; D I3→I4 WAW on R3.
question_text_status: Author-written essential paraphrase with choices and textual diagram/code descriptions; exact original wording and artwork remain at the linked official source.
solution:
Approach: Write down which instruction produces a register and which consumes it; retain the stated register name.

1. Derivation. I1 writes R3 and I2 reads R3, a read-after-write dependency, so A is true. I1 and I3 both write R3, making their relation WAW rather than WAR. I2 reads R3 and I3 writes it, giving WAR on R3 (they also have RAW on R5). I3 writes R3 and I4 reads it, giving RAW rather than WAW. Only A.

2. Explanation and checks. On R3 the four operations are write, read, write, read. A later read after an earlier write is RAW, two writes give WAW, and a write after an earlier read gives WAR. This sequence directly classifies each proposed pair. Although I2→I3 does have a RAW dependency on R5, option C explicitly says R3 and is therefore false. A dependency is a program-order relationship; whether it produces an actual stall depends on the implementation.

subject: 10-computer-networks
question_text: Which IP-header fields are always updated by an ordinary forwarding router in the IPv4 model? A source IP; B protocol; C TTL; D header checksum.
question_text_status: Author-written essential paraphrase with choices and textual diagram/code descriptions; exact original wording and artwork remain at the linked official source.
solution:
Approach: Find the field representing the remaining hop lifetime, then account for header integrity.

1. Derivation. An IPv4 router decrements TTL before forwarding. TTL is covered by the IPv4 header checksum, which must therefore be updated. Ordinary routing need not alter the source IP address or the upper-layer protocol field. Thus C, D. The header-checksum option makes the IPv4 model implicit.

2. Explanation and checks. TTL decreases as a packet is forwarded; if it expires the packet is discarded rather than forwarded. Changing TTL changes the header over which the IPv4 checksum is defined, so the checksum must be recomputed or incrementally adjusted. The protocol value still indicates the same encapsulated transport protocol. Source address changes can occur under NAT, but NAT is not a necessary operation of every router. IPv6 is a different header format and has no IPv4-style header checksum.

subject: 03-programming-in-c
question_text: In C, fX(char *a) sets char *b=a, executes while(*b) b++, then returns b−a as int. Which claims are true? A fX("abcd") returns; B with char c[]="abcd", fX(c) returns; C the function does not compile; D with char *c="abcd", fX(c) returns.
question_text_status: Author-written essential paraphrase with choices and textual diagram/code descriptions; exact original wording and artwork remain at the linked official source.
solution:
Approach: Trace the pointer until the null terminator and distinguish reading a literal from modifying it.

1. Derivation. The pointer b advances until it reaches the terminating null byte and returns the element difference b−a, the string length. Each stated argument is a valid null-terminated four-character string, so each call returns 4. The function only reads characters; it does not modify string literals. Therefore A, B, D are true and the code is valid C. Pointer subtraction here is within the same array and the small result fits int.

2. Explanation and checks. The bytes at offsets 0,1,2,3 are a,b,c,d and are nonzero, so the loop advances four times. At offset 4 the terminating zero makes the condition false. Both pointers remain associated with the same character array, so subtraction gives four elements. The function never assigns through either pointer, and the supplied arguments are terminated, avoiding two common string errors. These are C examples; a stricter C++ string-literal type rule is not the language specified.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_text: On {1,2,3,4}, a partial order contains every reflexive pair and (1,2),(3,2),(3,4). How many total orders extend it?
question_text_status: Author-written essential paraphrase with choices and textual diagram/code descriptions; exact original wording and artwork remain at the linked official source.
solution:
Approach: Choose only minimal elements first and branch on those choices.

1. Derivation. The restrictions are1 before 2, 3 before 2, and 3 before 4. If1 is first, 3 must be second and 2, 4 may be ordered either way, giving1324 and 1342. If3 is first, the remaining order only requires1 before 2, giving3124, 3142, 3412. These exhaust the choices, so there are5 linear extensions.

2. Explanation and checks. Initially 1 and 3 are eligible: 2 requires both to precede it, while 4 requires 3. In the branch starting with 1, only 3 is eligible next, leaving two orders of 2 and 4. In the branch starting with 3, the remaining three elements need only respect 1 before 2, which holds in half of their 3!=6 permutations. The reflexive pairs impose no extra restriction on the sequence of distinct elements.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_text: The distance of an integer array is the least number of entries replaced by arbitrary integers to make it nondecreasing. Find the distance of [2,5,3,1,4,2,6].
question_text_status: Author-written essential paraphrase with choices and textual diagram/code descriptions; exact original wording and artwork remain at the linked official source.
solution:
Approach: Any entries kept in place must already form a nondecreasing subsequence; combine that lower bound with an explicit repair.

1. Derivation. Any unchanged elements must form a nondecreasing subsequence. Longest nondecreasing subsequence lengths ending at the seven positions are1, 2, 2, 1, 3, 2, 4, so at most4 elements can remain unchanged and at least7−4=3 replacements are needed. Keep the subsequence2, 3, 4, 6 at positions1, 3, 5, 7; replace positions2, 4, 6 by 2, 3, 4 respectively to obtain[2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 6]. Thus3 is achievable and minimal.

2. Explanation and checks. For each position i define L[i]=1+max L[j] over j<i with A[j]≤A[i], or 1 if there is no such j. This yields [1,2,2,1,3,2,4], with maximum 4. Therefore keeping five entries is impossible. The displayed repair keeps four original entries and changes exactly three, establishing the matching upper bound. It is a replacement problem, not a sorting-by-swaps problem, and equality is allowed in the final array.

subject: 03-programming-in-c
question_text: C code declares double a[2]={20.0,25.0}; sets p=a and q=p+1; and prints "%d,%d" with (int)(q−p), (int)(*q−*p). Which output? A 4,8; B 1,5; C 8,5; D 1,8.
question_text_status: Author-written essential paraphrase with choices and textual diagram/code descriptions; exact original wording and artwork remain at the linked official source.
solution:
Approach: Evaluate the pointer expression and the dereferenced arithmetic expression separately.

1. Derivation. p points to a[0] and q=p+1 points to a[1]. Pointer subtraction counts array elements, not bytes, so q−p=1. The values differ by 25.0−20.0=5.0, cast to 5. The output is 1, 5, option B, independent of sizeof(double).

2. Explanation and checks. Adding one to a double pointer moves by the storage occupied by one double, but subtracting two double pointers converts the byte displacement back into an element count. Thus it is one regardless of the implementation’s double size. Dereferencing yields the numeric values 25.0 and 20.0, whose difference is exactly 5.0 here. The integer casts produce 1 and 5 for the two %d arguments; they do not turn the pointer difference into a byte distance.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text: Four processes have (arrival,burst): A(0,10), B(2,6), C(4,3), D(6,7). Find average waiting times for SRTF and nonpreemptive SJF. A 6,7; B 6,7.5; C 7,7.5; D 7,8.5.
question_text_status: Author-written essential paraphrase with choices and textual diagram/code descriptions; exact original wording and artwork remain at the linked official source.
solution:
Approach: Draw a separate timeline for each policy, then use waiting=completion−arrival−burst.

1. Derivation. SRTF runs A0–2, B2–4, C4–7, B7–11, D11–18, A18–26. Completion times A26, B11, C7, D18 give waiting times16, 3, 0, 5 after subtracting arrival and burst, average24/4=6. Nonpreemptive SJF runs A0–10, C10–13, B13–19, D19–26, giving waiting times0, 11, 6, 13 and average30/4=7.5. Answer B. D’s arrival at 6 does not preempt C, whose remaining time is 1.

2. Explanation and checks. For SRTF, at time 2 A has 8 left and B needs 6, so B preempts A. At time 4 B has 4 left and C needs 3, so C preempts B. At time 6 C needs only 1 more, so D does not preempt it. In nonpreemptive SJF, A cannot be displaced after starting at time 0; when it finishes at 10 all others are ready and C is shortest. These decisions explain the difference in the two timelines.

solution:
Approach: Find the common binary prefix and verify both size and alignment.

1. Derivation. The range contains two consecutive /24 blocks, third octets2 and 3. Their common prefix fixes the first 7 bits of that octet, yielding16+7=23 network bits and 9 host bits. The aligned base is 10.12.2.0, so the exact512-address range is 10.12.2.0/23, option A.

2. Explanation and checks. The third octets are 00000010 and 00000011: their first seven bits agree and their final bit varies. Together with the entire final octet, that leaves nine variable bits and 2^9=512 addresses. A /24 contains only 256 addresses. A /22 leaves ten host bits and spans four third-octet values, too many; moreover 10.12.2.0 is not an aligned /22 network base. Both endpoints of A agree exactly with the requested range.

subject: 04-data-structures
question_text: A BST is built by inserting distinct integers from a known set V into an empty tree, with smaller keys in each left subtree. The insertion order and tree are unknown. What can always be determined from V? A inorder traversal; B root; C preorder; D postorder.
question_text_status: Author-written essential paraphrase with choices and textual diagram/code descriptions; exact original wording and artwork remain at the linked official source.
solution:
Approach: Use the BST order invariant and test the other traversals on two possible insertion sequences.

1. Derivation. An inorder traversal of a BST with distinct keys and smaller keys to the left always visits exactly the sorted set V, regardless of insertion order. The first inserted key becomes the root, and different insertion orders can change the root, preorder, and postorder. Hence only inorder is determined in general, option A. Trivial sets can coincidentally determine more, but do not establish those claims for arbitrary V.

2. Explanation and checks. For V={1,2,3}, inserting 2,1,3 gives root 2, preorder 2,1,3 and postorder 1,3,2. Inserting 1,2,3 gives root 1, preorder 1,2,3 and postorder 3,2,1. Both have inorder 1,2,3. Recursively, inorder visits smaller values, then the node, then larger values; thus it is the sorted list for every valid shape. The examples demonstrate why knowledge of the set alone cannot recover the shape-sensitive alternatives.

subject: 07-compiler-design
question_text: Grammar: S→AaAb | BbBa, A→cS | ε, B→dS | ε. Missing table cells are (1) M[S,c], (2) M[S,d], (3) M[A,b], (4) M[B,a]. Options: A AaAb,BbBa,ε,ε; B BbBa,AaAb,ε,ε; C AaAb,BbBa,blank,blank; D BbBa,AaAb,blank,blank (right sides for the relevant row nonterminal).
question_text_status: Author-written essential paraphrase with choices and textual diagram/code descriptions; exact original wording and artwork remain at the linked official source.
solution:
Approach: Use FIRST for nonempty alternatives and FOLLOW for epsilon alternatives.

1. Derivation. FIRST(AaAb)={c, a}, while FIRST(BbBa)={d, b}. Thus the S-row c cell chooses S→AaAb and the d cell S→BbBa. A occurs before a and b in the first production, so FOLLOW(A)={a, b}; its epsilon production is entered for both lookaheads. Similarly FOLLOW(B)={b, a}, so B→epsilon goes in both a, b cells. Hence cells(1)–(4) are S→AaAb, S→BbBa, A→epsilon, B→epsilon, option A. The table columns and productions were visually checked.

2. Explanation and checks. A can disappear, so AaAb can start with a; if A does not disappear it begins with c. The same reasoning yields b or d for BbBa. Each occurrence of A in the S production is followed immediately by a terminal, once a and once b, so both terminals enter FOLLOW(A). The two B occurrences similarly supply b and a. There is no need to put an epsilon production under every lookahead: only FOLLOW lookaheads receive it.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text: NFA states are 1(start),2,3,4,5, with 2 and 5 accepting. Epsilon edges: 1→2,1→4,3→5. Edges labeled 0: 2→3 and 3→2. Edges labeled 1: 4→5 and 5→4. All other transitions absent. Choose regex: A (00)*+1(11)*; B 0*+(1+0(00)*)(11)*; C (00)*+(1+(00)*)(11)*; D 0+ +1(11)*+0(11)*. Here outer + denotes union; 0+ in D means one or more zeros.
question_text_status: Author-written essential paraphrase with choices and textual diagram/code descriptions; exact original wording and artwork remain at the linked official source.
solution:
Approach: Enumerate paths ending in each accepting state and track the parity before and after the epsilon jump.

1. Derivation. The initial epsilon choice reaches state2 or4. State2 accepts an even number of 0s; after an odd number of 0s the machine is in 3 and can take epsilon to accepting5, after which an even number of 1s returns to 5. The direct state4 branch accepts an odd number of 1s. Thus the language is(00)* + 0(00)*(11)* + 1(11)*. The pure even/odd zero cases together equal0*, so it can be written0*+(1+0(00)*)(11)*, option B. Diagram directions and accepting states 2, 5 were visually checked.

2. Explanation and checks. Staying in the upper component accepts an even zero count; reaching 3 requires an odd zero count and jumping to 5 then permits an even one count. Starting at 4 instead requires an odd one count. A misses the accepted word 0. C wrongly accepts 11 (take ε from (00)* and one pair of ones), whereas the NFA cannot accept pure even-positive ones. D misses ε, which is accepted via 1→2. These witnesses isolate B beyond merely manipulating algebraic expressions.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_text: For positive X[0..n−1], initialize first=second=len1=len2=maxlen=0. For each v=X[i]: if v==first increment both len1,len2; else if v==second increment len2, set len1=P, second=first; else set len2=Q, len1=1, second=first. Update maxlen=max(maxlen,len2), then first=v. len1 is the equal-value suffix length; len2 is the suffix length with at most two distinct values. Choose P,Q: A len1+1,len2+1; B 1,len1+1; C 1,len2+1; D len2+1,len1+1.
question_text_status: Author-written essential paraphrase with choices and textual diagram/code descriptions; exact original wording and artwork remain at the linked official source.
solution:
Approach: Interpret the saved values before the current iteration updates them.

1. Derivation. first is the previous element and len1 is its final equal-value run length. If the next item equals second but differs from first, the final equal run starts anew, so P=1, while the valid two-value suffix extends by one. If a third distinct value arrives, only the previous final run can accompany it; therefore the new two-value suffix has length len1+1, giving Q=len1+1. The assignments update second to the old first. Thus B; positive input values ensure initial zero sentinels are not actual array values.

2. Explanation and checks. For the prefix [1,2,2], len1=2 and len2=3. If the next value is 1, it is the other known value: the two-value suffix grows to 4, but the same-value suffix has length 1. If instead the next value is 3, keeping all three old elements would create three distinct values; only [2,2,3] is legal, of length old len1+1=3. Updating first last preserves the old run value while second is assigned.

question_text: Expression x[i]=(p+r)*−s[i]+u/w has triples (0) + p r; (1) missing; (2) uminus (1); (3) missing; (4) / u w; (5) + (3) (4); (6) missing; (7) = (6) (5). Approach: Follow the expression tree from input values to the final indexed assignment.

1. Derivation. Triple1 must read s[i], denoted =[] s i. Triple2 negates that value. Triple3 multiplies results(0) and(2), forming(p+r)×−s[i]. Triple6 identifies the destination x[i], denoted []= x i, and triple7 stores the accumulated result(5) there. Only A has all three operations and the correct index i. A triple refers to the result of an earlier triple by its parenthesized index; (5), for example, denotes the computed right-hand-side value, not the source-language subscript i. Loading s[i] must precede negation. Multiplication then combines p+r with that negative value, followed by addition of u/w. The final destination must still be element i of x. question_text: Random variables x,y lie in [0,1], may be dependent, and z=xy. Which always holds? A E[z]=E[x]E[y]; B E[z]≤E[x]E[y]; C E[z]≥E[x]E[y]; D E[z]≤E[x].

1. Derivation. Since0≤y≤1 and x≥0, pointwise xy≤x. Taking expectations preserves the inequality, giving E[xy]≤E[x], option D. No independence is assumed. To test the other answers take x equal to 0 or 1 with probability one half each. Choosing y=x makes the variables positively associated, while y=1−x makes them mutually exclusive. Their means remain one half in both examples, yet their product means differ, ruling out any universal product-of-means comparison.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text: Threads share s1=1,s2=0,x=0. T1: wait(s1); x++; print(x); wait(s2); signal(s1). T2: wait(s1); x++; print(x); signal(s2); signal(s1). Possible outcomes? A T1 prints 1 then T2 prints 2; B T2 prints 1 then T1 prints 2; C T1 prints 1 then deadlock without T2 printing; D T2 prints 1 then deadlock without T1 printing.
question_text_status: Author-written essential paraphrase with choices and textual diagram/code descriptions; exact original wording and artwork remain at the linked official source.
solution:
Approach: Branch on which thread acquires s1 first, since this excludes the other thread from its increment.

1. Derivation. The first successful wait(s1) excludes the other thread. If T1 acquires it first, T1 increments and prints 1, then blocks on initially zero s2 while still holding s1; T2 cannot reach its signal(s2), so this deadlocks, giving C. If T2 acquires first, it prints 1 and signals s2 and s1. T1 can then acquire s1, print2, consume s2, and finish, giving B. Thus B, C.

2. Explanation and checks. In the T1-first branch the wait-for chain is T1 waiting for s2, which only T2 signals; T2 waits for s1, which T1 will not signal until its s2 wait finishes. In the T2-first branch signal(s2) either stores a permit or satisfies a waiting thread, so T1’s later wait(s2) cannot deadlock. The mutual exclusion around x prevents a lost increment, but it does not prevent the circular wait caused by the semaphore ordering.

question_text: B is obtained by swapping two rows of a real n×n matrix A. Select true statements: A det(B)=−det(A); B invertibility of A implies invertibility of B; C symmetry of A implies symmetry of B; D zero trace of A implies zero trace of B.
question_text_status: Author-written essential paraphrase with choices and textual diagram/code descriptions; exact original wording and artwork remain at the linked official source.
solution:
Approach: Use the determinant rule for the positive claims and small explicit matrices to refute universal claims.

1. Derivation. A single row swap negates the determinant, proving A. If det(A) is nonzero then det(B)=−det(A) is nonzero as well, proving B. Symmetry is not preserved: swapping rows of diag(1, 2) gives[[0, 2],[1, 0]], which is not symmetric. Zero trace is not preserved: A=[[1, 2],[3,−1]] has trace0, but its row-swapped matrix has trace5. Answer A, B.

2. Explanation and checks. A row swap is multiplication on the left by an invertible permutation matrix P, so B=PA and B^−1=A^−1 P^−1 whenever A is invertible. This supplies another proof of B. In contrast symmetry would naturally be preserved by applying the same permutation to rows and columns, PAP^T, not by a row permutation alone. Trace invariance also applies to similarity transformations, not arbitrary independent row operations. The two counterexamples in the derivation make these distinctions concrete.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_text: A connected undirected graph has positive integer edge weights and every spanning tree has even total weight. What must hold? A all edges even; B all edges share one parity; C every cycle has only even edges; D within each cycle all its edges share one parity.
question_text_status: Author-written essential paraphrase with choices and textual diagram/code descriptions; exact original wording and artwork remain at the linked official source.
solution:
Approach: Exchange one cycle edge in a spanning tree and compare the two total weights modulo two.

1. Derivation. Fix a cycle C and an edge e on it. The path C minus e is acyclic and can be extended to a spanning tree T. For any other cycle edge f, T−f+e is another spanning tree. Both tree weights are even, so w(e)−w(f) is even. Thus every pair of cycle edges has the same parity, proving D. A and B fail for a graph that is itself a tree with edge weights1, 1, 2: its only spanning tree has even total 4 but mixed parity. C fails for a triangle with all three weights1, whose spanning trees all weigh2 although its cycle edges are odd.

2. Explanation and checks. The extension step is justified because any acyclic edge set in a connected graph can be extended to a spanning tree by repeatedly joining components. Adding e to the tree containing C−e creates exactly the cycle C, so removing any f in that cycle returns a tree. Equal parity of tree sums forces equal parity of e and f. Bridges do not belong to cycles, explaining why D places no restriction on their individual parity and why global uniform parity need not follow.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text: Grammar S→aS | aSbS | c generates w. Let na,nb,nc count the respective terminals in w. Which always hold? A na>nb; B na>nc−2; C nc=nb+1; D nc=2nb.
question_text_status: Author-written essential paraphrase with choices and textual diagram/code descriptions; exact original wording and artwork remain at the linked official source.
solution:
Approach: Count how each production changes both the terminal totals and the outstanding nonterminals.

1. Derivation. Let u count applications of S→aS and v count applications of S→aSbS. Then n_a=u+v and n_b=v. A derivation starts with one S; unary rules leave the number of outstanding S unchanged, binary rules increase it by one, and S→c decreases it by one. Thus n_c=v+1, proving C. Also n_a≥v=n_c−1>n_c−2, proving B. A fails for w=c, where both a and b counts are0; D also fails for c, whose c count is 1 and b count 0.

2. Explanation and checks. Each binary rule contributes one b and creates one additional S requiring eventual termination by a c-rule. Starting with one S therefore requires exactly one more terminating c-rule than binary rules. Unary aS rules can add any extra a’s without changing b or c counts. Consequently na−nb equals their nonnegative number; it may be zero, so A’s strict inequality is too strong. In B the weaker strict bound still holds because na≥nc−1 is an integer stronger than na>nc−2.

subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_text: A disk rotates at 6000 RPM, has average seek time 5 ms, 500 sectors/track, and 512 bytes/sector. A file occupies 3000 randomly located sectors. Using average rotational latency, estimate total read time in seconds to two decimals.
question_text_status: Author-written essential paraphrase with choices and textual diagram/code descriptions; exact original wording and artwork remain at the linked official source.
solution:
Approach: For each random sector add average seek, half a revolution, and one-sector transfer time.

1. Derivation. At6000RPM one revolution takes 60/6000=0.01s=10ms. Mean rotational latency is 5ms; one of 500 sectors transfers in 10/500=0.02ms. Using a separate average seek and rotational wait for each randomly placed sector gives 3000×(5+5+0.02)ms=30060ms=30.06s. This is an average random-read estimate, not a guaranteed realized time; cache, scheduling and correlated sector positions are not modeled.

2. Explanation and checks. At 100 revolutions/s the entire track passes in 0.01 seconds. A sector is 1/500 of that track, so its transfer time is 0.00002 seconds. The sector byte count cancels if transfer speed is computed as 500×512 bytes per revolution and divided into a 512-byte request. Because locations are random, the intended model charges seek and rotation for every sector rather than only once for a contiguous file. The derived 30.06 lies inside the preserved official acceptance range 29.50–30.50.

subject: 10-computer-networks
question_text: A TCP connection has congestion window 12 MSS when a timeout occurs. All segments in the next two RTTs are acknowledged successfully. Under textbook timeout slow start, what is the congestion window during the third RTT, in MSS?
question_text_status: Author-written essential paraphrase with choices and textual diagram/code descriptions; exact original wording and artwork remain at the linked official source.
solution:
Approach: Distinguish the window used during an RTT from its value after that RTT’s acknowledgements.

1. Derivation. Under the standard timeout slow-start model, a timeout sets ssthresh to half the old congestion window, 6MSS, and resets cwnd to 1MSS. The first subsequent RTT uses1 and its successful ACKs grow cwnd to 2; the second uses2 and grows it to 4. Thus during the third RTT cwnd is 4MSS, still below the threshold. This assumes the textbook one-MSS post-timeout reset and per-round doubling.

2. Explanation and checks. The timeout halves the threshold, not the new sending window: ssthresh becomes 6 while cwnd restarts at 1. Thus the three rounds begin with windows 1,2,4 respectively. Doubling the third round’s window to 8 would describe a later update, and would also require handling the threshold transition. The requested third round begins below ssthresh, so that boundary detail does not affect the answer. This is the stipulated textbook congestion-control model, not a universal statement about every modern TCP implementation.

subject: 10-computer-networks
question_text: An Ethernet segment transmits at 10^8 bits/s, has maximum length 500 m and signal propagation speed 2×10^8 m/s. What theoretical minimum frame length in bits permits collision detection?
question_text_status: Author-written essential paraphrase with choices and textual diagram/code descriptions; exact original wording and artwork remain at the linked official source.
solution:
Approach: Ensure that the sender is still transmitting when a worst-case collision indication returns.

1. Derivation. The one-way propagation delay is 500/(2×10⁸)=2.5μs. To detect a collision originating at the far end, transmission must continue for at least the round-trip delay5μs. At10⁸bits/s this requires10⁸×5×10⁻⁶=500 bits. This is the theoretical collision-detection minimum from the supplied parameters, not the separate standardized512-bit Ethernet minimum.

2. Explanation and checks. A distant node may begin transmitting just before the first signal reaches it. Evidence of that collision must then travel back to the original sender, making the worst-case duration approximately twice the one-way propagation delay. Frame transmission time L/R must therefore satisfy L/R≥2d/v, or L≥2dR/v. Substituting gives 500 bits. Using only the one-way delay yields 250 bits and can let the sender finish too early to detect the collision.

question_text: On a schema of four attributes, call X→Y useful when X and Y are both nonempty and X∩Y=∅. How many different such dependencies are possible?
question_text_status: Author-written essential paraphrase with choices and textual diagram/code descriptions; exact original wording and artwork remain at the linked official source.

Exclude assignments with X empty (2⁴) and Y empty (2⁴), then restore the all-neither assignment counted twice. The number is 3⁴−2⁴−2⁴+1=81−16−16+1=50. This counts possible syntactic dependencies, not dependencies that necessarily hold on a particular instance.

2. Explanation and checks. An alternative count chooses the size k of X: sum from k=1 to 3 of C(4,k)(2^(4−k)−1). For k=1 there are 4×7=28 choices; k=2 gives 6×3=18; k=3 gives 4×1=4, totaling 50. X→Y and Y→X are different dependencies because direction matters. Multiattribute right sides are allowed by the definition; restricting Y to a single attribute would answer a different question.

question_text: A nonpipelined 2 GHz unit averages 6 cycles/instruction. A 5-stage redesign at the same frequency ideally achieves 1 instruction/cycle. question_text: Undirected graph vertices a,b,c,d,e,f,g have weight-1 edges ab,af,cd,de; weight-2 edges ag,bg,fg,cg,dg,eg; weight-3 edges bc,fe; and no others. How many distinct minimum-weight spanning trees exist?

solution:
Approach: Force uniquely lightest cut edges, contract them, then count independent minimum connections.

1. Derivation. Each weight1 edge (ab, af, cd, de) is uniquely lightest across the cut isolating its noncentral endpoint b, f, c, e, respectively, so all four occur in every MST. Contracting them gives components L={a, b, f}, R={c, d, e}, and{g}. There are three weight2 choices linking L to g and three linking R to g. A minimum tree uses one of each, giving3×3=9 distinct MSTs, each weight4+2+2=8. Weight3 links L–R cannot improve that value. All edge labels were visually checked.

2. Explanation and checks. After contraction only three supervertices remain, requiring exactly two additional edges. Connecting g to the left component has three distinct original choices; connecting g to the right has another three. Each pair is acyclic and connects all seven original vertices once the four forced edges are restored. Choosing a weight-3 left–right link instead would require at least one further weight-2 edge and yield total at least nine rather than eight. Therefore it cannot contribute an alternative minimum tree.

subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_text: A 32-bit ISA has 150 instructions, 75 each of R-type and I-type, and 50 registers. OPCODE includes a 1-bit type tag plus operation bits. R-type fields: OPCODE, UNUSED, DST, SRC1, SRC2. solution:
Approach: Count the operation bits within each type, add the type bit, then subtract register fields from each format.

1. Derivation. There are75 operations per instruction type, requiring7 operation bits plus the 1-bit type tag, so Y=8. Each of 50 architectural registers requires6 bits. The R-type unused field has X=32−8−3×6=6 bits; the I-type immediate field has Z=32−8−2×6=12 bits. Hence X+2Y+Z=6+16+12=34.

2. Explanation and checks. Six bits encode only 64 operations, insufficient for 75, so seven operation bits are necessary. The one-bit type discriminator brings the full opcode width to eight. Similarly five register bits encode only 32 names, while six accommodate 50. The R-type equation is X+Y+18=32 and the I-type equation is Y+12+Z=32. Adding those equations directly gives X+2Y+Z=64−30=34, which independently checks the field-by-field calculation.

question_text: L1 is described by b*ab*(ab*ab*)*. L2 contains all strings over {a,b} of length at most four. How many strings belong to both?
question_text_status: Author-written essential paraphrase with choices and textual diagram/code descriptions; exact original wording and artwork remain at the linked official source.

It therefore accepts exactly the strings with an odd positive number of a’s. For any positive length ℓ exactly half of the 2^ℓ binary strings have odd a-parity, by flipping one fixed position. Lengths1 through4 contribute1+2+4+8=15; ε has even parity and is excluded.

2. Explanation and checks. The one initial a plus any number of pairs makes the a-count odd; the b* runs admit arbitrary b’s before, between and after those a’s. The empty string has no a and cannot match the mandatory initial a.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_text: Zn is the additive group modulo n. How many elements of Z2×Z3×Z4 are their own inverse?
question_text_status: Author-written essential paraphrase with choices and textual diagram/code descriptions; exact original wording and artwork remain at the linked official source.
solution:
Approach: Solve 2x=0 modulo the corresponding modulus independently in each coordinate.

1. Derivation. An element is its own inverse exactly when twice it is 0 in each coordinate. Z2 contributes0, 1 (two choices); Z3 contributes only 0; Z4 contributes0, 2 (two choices). The product group therefore has 2×1×2=4 such elements.

2. Explanation and checks. The identity element counts: it is always its own inverse. In Z2 both residues satisfy 2x≡0; in Z3 only zero does, because two is invertible modulo three; in Z4 the solutions are zero and two. Explicitly the four product elements are (0,0,0), (0,0,2), (1,0,0), (1,0,2). The coordinate choices multiply because the group operation is coordinatewise, so there is no additional compatibility condition between them.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text: A 32-bit byte-addressed system uses 4 KiB pages and 4-byte PTEs. Each process receives one outer directory page. Inner table pages are allocated only when they hold a valid mapping. A process accesses 2000 distinct pages and none is swapped out. Let X and Y be minimum and maximum total page-table pages over both levels. Find X+Y; do not count data pages.
question_text_status: Author-written essential paraphrase with choices and textual diagram/code descriptions; exact original wording and artwork remain at the linked official source.
solution:
Approach: Compute how many data-page mappings each inner table can hold and how many inner tables the directory can address.

1. Derivation. A4KB table page holds4096/4=1024 entries. The32-bit address divides into 10 outer-index bits, 10 inner-index bits and 12 offset bits, allowing1024 inner table pages. Minimum table storage for2000 mapped pages packs them into ceil(2000/1024)=2 inner pages plus the allocated outer page: X=3. Maximum spreads mappings across all1024 distinct outer entries, possible with 2000 pages, giving Y=1024+1=1025. Thus X+Y=1028. Data pages themselves are not counted.

2. Explanation and checks. To achieve the minimum, map 1024 data pages through one outer entry and the remaining 976 through a second. To achieve the maximum, use at least one data page in each of the 1024 outer regions; the remaining 976 accesses can fall in regions already used. This construction shows the upper bound is attainable, not just theoretical. An outer entry does not itself map one data page: it selects an entire inner table, so counting 2000 table pages would be incorrect.

subject: 07-compiler-design
question_text: Augmented grammar: S′→S; S→SS | Aa | bAc | Bc | bBa; A→d#; B→@. Terminals are a,b,c,d,#,@. I0=CLOSURE({S′→·S}). For an SLR parser, how many items are in GOTO(I0,S)?

solution:
Approach: Move dots over S only where S immediately follows the dot, then close the resulting item set.

1. Derivation. The initial closure contains S′→·S and S→·SS, plus the other four S-start items and A→·d#, B→·@. GOTO on S shifts the first two into S′→S· and S→S·S. The latter requires closure under S, adding all five S-start items: ·SS, ·Aa, ·bAc, ·Bc, ·bBa. Closure of their leading A/B adds A→·d# and B→·@. The total is 2+5+2=9 distinct LR(0) items; SLR FOLLOW sets do not change this item-set construction.

2. Explanation and checks. The full resulting set is S′→S·; S→S·S; S→·SS; S→·Aa; S→·bAc; S→·Bc; S→·bBa; A→·d#; B→·@. The item S→·SS does not generate endlessly many items: closure is a set and revisiting the same production adds no duplicate. Terminals b,d,@ do not cause further closure expansion. Both # and @ are explicitly terminals here, so neither denotes epsilon or the end marker. FOLLOW sets govern SLR reduction entries, not this GOTO construction.

question_text: Fill the three blanks in this sentence: Ravi had ___ younger brother who taught at ___ university and was regarded as ___ honorable man. Options: A a; a; an. B the; an; a. C a; an; a. D an; an; a.

solution:

3. In “honorable”, h is silent and the first pronounced sound is a vowel. Thus the final phrase is “an honorable man”.
The required sequence is a; a; an, option A. Each of B, C and D uses “an university” and “a honorable”, which fail the sound-based rule.

subject: 11-general-aptitude
question_text: A class average was recorded as 30.8. One mark had been entered as 24 instead of 42. Correcting that single mark changes the mean to 31.4. Find the number of students. A 25; B 28; C 30; D 32.
question_text_status: Author paraphrase with essential givens, options and text descriptions of diagrams; exact original wording/artwork remains at the anchored official source.
solution:
Approach: Compare the change in total marks with the change in the average; the number of observations stays fixed.
Let n be the class size and S the originally recorded total. Then S/n=30.8. Replacing 24 by 42 increases the total by 42−24=18, so (S+18)/n=31.4.
Subtract the first equation from the second: 18/n=31.4−30.8=0.6. Consequently n=18/0.6=30, option C.
As a check, the original total would be 30×30.8=924 and the corrected total 942. Dividing 942 by 30 indeed gives 31.4. The correction is positive, so an increased rather than decreased mean is consistent. The other proposed sizes would not make an 18-mark correction produce a 0.6-mark mean increase.

question_text: P is Q’s brother; S is Q’s daughter; T is S’s sister; R is Q’s mother. Assess: (1) R is S’s grandmother; (2) P is uncle to S and T; (3) R has only one son; (4) Q has only one daughter. Choices: A both 1 and 2; B both 1 and 3; C only 3; D only 4.

P is Q’s male sibling, so under the ordinary family-tree convention he is uncle to Q’s children S and T. Statement 2 is true. That convention treats the stated sisters as sharing the indicated parent.
Statement 3 does not follow. Q’s gender is unspecified, and the statements do not rule out further children of R. Statement 4 is false under the intended family relationships because S and T are two daughters of Q.

subject: 11-general-aptitude
question_text: In triangle PQR, S lies on PQ and T on PR, with ST parallel to QR. The perpendicular separation of ST and QR is half the perpendicular distance from P to QR. Find area(PST)/area(SQRT), where SQRT is the remaining trapezium. A 1/3; B 1/4; C 2/5; D 1/2.
question_text_status: Author paraphrase with essential givens, options and text descriptions of diagrams; exact original wording/artwork remains at the anchored official source.
solution:
Approach: Use similarity to obtain the small triangle’s fraction of the whole, then subtract to obtain the trapezium’s fraction.
Let P’s altitude above QR be h. Since ST is h/2 above QR, P’s altitude above ST is h−h/2=h/2. Parallelism gives equal corresponding angles, so triangles PST and PQR are similar with linear scale factor (h/2)/h=1/2.
Areas scale as the square of a linear factor. If the large triangle has area A, then area(PST)=A/4. The trapezium occupies the remainder, A−A/4=3A/4. Their ratio is (A/4)/(3A/4)=1/3, option A.
Option B, 1/4, is the small triangle’s ratio to the entire triangle, not the requested trapezium. Option D incorrectly treats area as scaling linearly with height. No right angle or symmetry of the sloping sides is required.

subject: 11-general-aptitude
question_text: A fair six-sided die is rolled independently three times. Find the probability of exactly one result equal to 6. Options: A 75/216; B 1/6; C 1/18; D 25/216.
question_text_status: Author paraphrase with essential givens, options and text descriptions of diagrams; exact original wording/artwork remains at the anchored official source.
solution:
Approach: Count the mutually exclusive possible positions of the sole six.
If the first roll is the only six, the pattern is six, non-six, non-six. Its probability is (1/6)(5/6)(5/6)=25/216. The same probability applies when the unique six is second or third.
These three events cannot occur together, so their probabilities add: 3×25/216=75/216, option A. Equivalently, among the 6³=216 equally likely ordered outcomes, choose the position of the six in 3 ways and the other two faces in 5 ways each, giving 3×5²=75 favorable outcomes.
D counts just one fixed placement. B is the probability of a six on one specified roll, not exactly one across three rolls. Independence is what permits multiplication within each three-roll pattern.

subject: 11-general-aptitude
question_text: A square is folded first along its top-left–bottom-right diagonal, leaving the upper-right triangular half, and then along the line from the upper-right corner to the midpoint of the first diagonal, producing a downward-pointing triangle. The final folded triangle has three black cut shapes: a small upward-pointing triangular notch at the midpoint of its horizontal top edge, a filled right-triangular cut against its left sloping edge, and a thin rectangular notch against its right sloping edge. Choose the unfolded pattern. A has four outward-pointing triangular edge notches, axis-aligned square holes near upper-left/lower-right and right-angle notches near upper-right/lower-left. B replaces the square holes by diamonds. C reverses the top/bottom triangular orientations. D places a square hole at the centre instead of the two opposite near-corner squares. Exact cut geometry and the four artwork options are on the linked original page.
question_text_status: Author paraphrase with essential givens, options and text descriptions of diagrams; exact original wording/artwork remains at the anchored official source.
solution:
Approach: Reverse the last fold first. Every cut in a folded stack appears at its reflected position when that fold is opened; repeat for the first fold.
The horizontal edge of the final triangle represents outer edges of the original square. Its triangular cut produces four edge notches on unfolding. Reflection preserves which side of each outer edge is removed, so their apices face outward; it does not turn the top and bottom triangles inward.
The cut touching one diagonal is mirrored across that diagonal into a square. The square’s sides remain horizontal/vertical in the original square, not diagonal. Opening the other fold gives its companion near the opposite corner. The rectangular cut meeting the other folded edge produces paired right-angle shapes at the other two near-corner positions.
These features together match A. B incorrectly rotates the square holes, C reverses the vertical triangles, and D introduces a central square unsupported by any cut at the fold intersection. Both folding arrows and all choices were visually inspected; the linked artwork remains necessary for exact shape-by-shape visual reproduction.

subject: 11-general-aptitude
question_text: There are four distinct ice-cream flavours. Buy exactly three scoops, allowing repeats, and regard purchases differing only in scoop order as identical. How many purchases are possible? A 4; B 20; C 24; D 48.
question_text_status: Author paraphrase with essential givens, options and text descriptions of diagrams; exact original wording/artwork remains at the anchored official source.
solution:
Approach: Represent a purchase by the number of scoops of each flavour, not by an ordered sequence.
Let x1,x2,x3,x4 be the non-negative integer counts. Every purchase corresponds uniquely to x1+x2+x3+x4=3. With three stars for scoops and three separators for the four flavours, stars and bars gives C(3+4−1,4−1)=C(6,3)=20, option B.
An independent case count checks this: three identical scoops give 4 choices; a pair of one flavour plus a different flavour gives 4×3=12 choices; three different flavours give C(4,3)=4 choices. Total 4+12+4=20.
Using 4³ would count ordered selections and overcount many purchases. Using only C(4,3) would forbid repeated flavours, contrary to the question.

subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_text: A non-pipelined single processor receives an asynchronous device interrupt while running a program. Order these steps: (i) save the program counter, (ii) load the ISR start address into the program counter, (iii) finish the current instruction. A iii,i,ii; B i,iii,ii; C i,ii,iii; D iii,ii,i. Options C and D continue on source page 11.
question_text_status: Author paraphrase with essential givens, options and text descriptions of diagrams; exact original wording/artwork remains at the anchored official source.
solution:
Approach: Preserve a consistent return point before redirecting instruction execution.
First finish the instruction already in progress: step iii. In the usual instruction-boundary interrupt model, this leaves the program’s architectural state consistent and determines the address at which it must resume. Interrupts are asynchronous arrivals, but service is begun at an instruction boundary.
Next save the program counter containing that resume address: step i. Finally load the ISR entry address into the program counter: step ii. Fetching now begins in the interrupt routine, and the saved address remains available for return.
The sequence is iii,i,ii, option A. B and C save before the current instruction has completed; D overwrites the return address with the ISR address before saving it. This ordering describes the stipulated simple processor, not an attempt to interrupt halfway through a partially completed instruction.

subject: 07-compiler-design
question_text: Which claim about a compiler symbol table is false? A It tracks variable scope. B It can use a binary search tree. C It is no longer needed after parsing. D It is created during lexical analysis.
question_text_status: Author paraphrase with essential givens, options and text descriptions of diagrams; exact original wording/artwork remains at the anchored official source.
solution:
Approach: Follow identifier information through the compiler rather than treating parsing as the last compilation phase.
A symbol table maps names to attributes such as type, declaration scope and storage location. Scope checking needs those associations, so A describes a normal role. A binary search tree can support lookup and insertion by identifier name, so B is a valid implementation possibility even though hash tables are also common.
After parsing, semantic analysis still needs symbol information for declaration and type checks; later code generation may need storage and addressing attributes. Therefore C’s claim that the table is unnecessary after parsing is false, and C is the keyed answer.
D reflects the conventional introductory pipeline in which lexical analysis begins identifier entries. Real implementations may create or enrich tables at other stages, so D should not be read as a universal requirement on every compiler architecture. The decisive false claim in the intended model is C.

subject: 07-compiler-design
question_text: Which compiler activity uses live-variable analysis? A runtime function-call management; B assigning registers to variables; C strength reduction; D constant folding.
question_text_status: Author paraphrase with essential givens, options and text descriptions of diagrams; exact original wording/artwork remains at the anchored official source.
solution:
Approach: Ask which optimization needs to know whether an existing variable value can be used again.
A variable is live at a program point if some execution path may read its current value before assigning a new value to that variable. Registers hold only a limited number of such values. If two values must remain available at the same time, allocating the same physical register to both can destroy a value that will be needed.
Register allocation therefore uses live ranges, commonly creating an interference edge between values that are simultaneously live. Values whose live ranges do not overlap can reuse a register. This selects B.
Strength reduction, C, replaces an expensive operation with an equivalent cheaper one, while constant folding, D, evaluates expressions with known constants. Neither is identified by the need for liveness in this question. Runtime call management concerns the calling convention and activation records rather than this particular analysis.

subject: 08-operating-systems
question_text: A byte-addressable demand-paged machine has 32-bit logical addresses, 20-bit physical addresses, and 2048-byte pages. What is the maximum number of entries in a conventional page table? A 2^21; B 2^20; C 2^22; D 2^24.
question_text_status: Author paraphrase with essential givens, options and text descriptions of diagrams; exact original wording/artwork remains at the anchored official source.
solution:
Approach: Count virtual pages, because a conventional page table has one possible entry per virtual page.
The page size is 2048=2^11 bytes, so the low 11 bits of a logical address identify a byte within its page. The remaining 32−11=21 bits identify the virtual page. There are therefore 2^21 possible virtual-page numbers, selecting A.
Equivalently, the virtual address space has 2^32 bytes and dividing by 2^11 bytes per page gives 2^21 pages. Physical-address width is not the numerator in this calculation. It determines that physical memory can contain 2^(20−11)=2^9 frames and that a frame number needs 9 bits.
Demand paging may leave many entries invalid or pages absent from physical memory, but that does not reduce the maximum number of distinct virtual pages the table must represent.

subject: 09-database-management-systems
question_text: A database schedule is R1(X), W1(Y), R2(X), R2(Y), R3(Y), followed by ABORT(T1). No intervening commit or write is shown. Which other transactions must roll back? A only T2; B only T3; C both T2 and T3; D neither.
question_text_status: Author paraphrase with essential givens, options and text descriptions of diagrams; exact original wording/artwork remains at the anchored official source.
solution:
Approach: Track reads of a value produced by an uncommitted transaction; read-read overlap alone is not a rollback dependency.
W1(Y) installs T1’s new value of Y. R2(Y) occurs after that write and before T1 commits, so T2 reads an uncommitted value from T1. R3(Y) sees the same value because no intervening write to Y is shown; T3 also depends on T1.
When T1 aborts, its write to Y must be undone. Both dependent transactions have computed using a value that cannot be retained, so both must roll back. This is a cascading rollback and gives C.
The reads R1(X) and R2(X) do not establish a dirty-read dependency because neither transaction writes X in this schedule. The important issue is which transaction produced the value read, not simply whether two transactions access the same data item.

subject: 10-computer-networks
question_text: Match layers (a) network, (b) transport, (c) data link to functions (I) packet routing, (II) framing and error handling, (III) host-to-host communication. A a-I,b-II,c-III; B a-I,b-III,c-II; C a-II,b-I,c-III; D a-III,b-II,c-I.
question_text_status: Author paraphrase with essential givens, options and text descriptions of diagrams; exact original wording/artwork remains at the anchored official source.
solution:
Approach: Identify the most specific layer functions before assigning the less precise phrase.
The network layer handles packet routing across networks, so a must match I. The data-link layer groups bits into frames for a link and handles link-level error detection or control, so c matches II. Those two matches already identify B among the choices.
The remaining b-III match is the question’s intended description of transport-layer end-to-end communication. More precisely, transport protocols provide process-to-process service using endpoint identifiers such as ports; “host-to-host” is broader wording than the usual precise definition.
A misassigns framing to transport; C assigns framing to network; D assigns routing to data link. Thus B is correct in the supplied matching scheme. Error handling can also exist at other layers, but “framing and error handling” together points to the data-link layer here.

subject: 12-discrete-mathematics
question_text: Let g:A→B and f:B→C. Both f and f∘g are surjective. Which property must g have? A surjective; B injective; C bijective; D neither injectivity nor surjectivity is required.
question_text_status: Author paraphrase with essential givens, options and text descriptions of diagrams; exact original wording/artwork remains at the anchored official source.
solution:
Approach: Determine whether hitting every point of C requires hitting every point of B. Different points of B can share the same image under f, so it need not.
Construct a counterexample: A={1,2}, B={u,v}, C={w}. Define g(1)=g(2)=u and f(u)=f(v)=w. The function f is onto C because w has a preimage. The composition sends both elements of A to w, so it is also onto C.
However g is not injective, because its two inputs share the output u, and is not onto B, because v is missed. This single example refutes the necessary-property claims in A, B and C and establishes D.
Conceptually, g only needs to hit enough points of B to cover all f-fibres over C. The conclusion would differ if extra assumptions, such as injectivity of f, were supplied; none is supplied here.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_text: G is an undirected graph with positive edge weights and T is a minimum spanning tree. Let d1(u,v) be the shortest-path distance in G and d2(u,v) that in T. Which holds for all vertices and all such graphs? A d1=d2; B d1≤d2; C d1≥d2; D d1≠d2.
question_text_status: Author paraphrase with essential givens, options and text descriptions of diagrams; exact original wording/artwork remains at the anchored official source.
solution:
Approach: Compare the sets of paths available in the graph and its spanning-tree subgraph.
The unique u-to-v path in T uses only edges of G. Thus it is one candidate among the paths minimized over when defining d1. Minimizing over a set containing that candidate cannot give a larger value than its length: d1(u,v)≤d2(u,v). Therefore B always holds.
Equality is possible, for example if G itself is a tree. Strict inequality is also possible: take a triangle with all edge weights 1 and a spanning tree consisting of two edges. Between the endpoints of the omitted edge, the graph distance is 1 but the tree distance is 2. These examples reject A and D as universal claims and reject C.
An MST minimizes total chosen-edge weight, not every pairwise path distance. Indeed the inequality holds for any spanning tree; minimum total weight is unnecessary for this particular proof.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text: A grammar has start symbol S and productions S→aaB | Abb, A→a | aA, B→b | bB. Choose its language: A {a²b^n:n≥1}∪{a^nb²:n≥1}; B {a^nb^(2n):n≥1}∪{a^(2n)b^n:n≥1}; C {a^nb^n:n≥1}; D {a^(2n)b^(2n):n≥1}.
question_text_status: Author paraphrase with essential givens, options and text descriptions of diagrams; exact original wording/artwork remains at the anchored official source.
solution:
Approach: First identify what each helper nonterminal can generate, then substitute into each start production.
A→a is the base case. Each application of A→aA adds one a before eventually taking the base case, so A generates exactly a^n for n≥1. Similarly B generates exactly b^n for n≥1. Neither can generate the empty string.
Taking S→aaB fixes the number of a’s at two and allows any positive number of b’s. Taking S→Abb allows any positive number of a’s and fixes the number of b’s at two. The language is the union of these alternatives, which is A.
For example aabbb is generated by the first branch, and ab b (the word abb) by the second. The grammar does not synchronize the two counts, so the equality and ratio conditions in B–D are unjustified. The common word aabb belongs to both branches but is counted just once in the language.

subject: 05-algorithms
question_text: T(0)=1 and T(n)=2T(n−1)+n·2^n for n>0. Which asymptotic order is correct? A Θ(n²2^n); B Θ(n2^n); C Θ((log n)²2^n); D Θ(4^n).
question_text_status: Author paraphrase with essential givens, options and text descriptions of diagrams; exact original wording/artwork remains at the anchored official source.
solution:
Approach: Divide out the homogeneous growth factor 2^n so that the remaining recurrence becomes a simple cumulative sum.
Define U(n)=T(n)/2^n. Dividing the recurrence by 2^n gives U(n)=T(n−1)/2^(n−1)+n=U(n−1)+n, with U(0)=1. Repeated substitution yields U(n)=1+1+2+⋯+n=1+n(n+1)/2.
Therefore T(n)=2^n[1+n(n+1)/2]. The bracket is a quadratic polynomial with positive leading coefficient, so it is Θ(n²). Multiplication by 2^n gives Θ(n²2^n), option A.
B overlooks the accumulation of n successive normalized contributions. C grows too slowly by replacing that quadratic sum with logarithms, and D is exponentially larger than the exact solution. A master theorem for T(n/b) is not the natural tool because this recurrence decreases n by one, rather than dividing it.

subject: 09-database-management-systems
question_text: A pictured B+ tree has a root with keys [6,12,19] and four leaf children, shown left to right as [1,4,3], [7,9,10], [13,15,17], [20,21,22]. Each node holds at most three keys, and there are five nodes initially. Insert 23 using ordinary B+ tree insertion. Which statements hold? A no node splits; B at least one node splits and redistributes; C node count stays unchanged; D height increases. The unsorted first leaf [1,4,3] is reproduced literally, not silently repaired.
question_text_status: Author paraphrase with essential givens, options and text descriptions of diagrams; exact original wording/artwork remains at the anchored official source.
solution:
Approach: Follow the insertion path and propagate any overflow upward.
Because 23 exceeds the largest root separator, it routes to the rightmost leaf [20,21,22]. Adding it produces four keys in a node whose capacity is three. This leaf must split into two leaves under the ordinary insertion algorithm; for example its data can be distributed as [20,21] and [22,23]. A separator for the new leaf is inserted into the parent.
The parent is the root and is already full with three keys. Its overflow requires an internal-node split and a new root above the split pieces. Thus the height increases by one. B and D are true, while A and C are false. The usual allocation adds one leaf, one internal node and one new root, raising five nodes to eight.
Source qualification: the printed first leaf is unsorted, so the figure is not literally a valid B+ tree. Separator conventions also are not fully specified. The intended overflow argument uses the unaffected rightmost branch and assumes a valid initial tree apart from the diagram defect. The official B;D answer is preserved, with that limitation explicit.

subject: 10-computer-networks
question_text: Let P1,P2,P3 be the three successive packets of the ordinary TCP connection-establishment handshake. Select true claims: A P3 has SYN=1,ACK=1; B P2 has SYN=1,ACK=1; C P2 has SYN=0,ACK=1; D P1 has SYN=1.
question_text_status: Author paraphrase with essential givens, options and text descriptions of diagrams; exact original wording/artwork remains at the anchored official source.
solution:
Approach: Separate the request to synchronize sequence numbers from the acknowledgment of the peer’s request.
P1 is the initiating SYN: it starts synchronization with SYN=1 and, in the ordinary initial handshake, ACK=0. Hence D is true.
P2 both acknowledges the first SYN and announces the responding endpoint’s own initial sequence number. Its flags are SYN=1 and ACK=1. This makes B true and C false.
P3 acknowledges the responder’s SYN. It is an ACK with SYN=0,ACK=1, so A is false. The correct selection is B and D.
The ACK flag indicates that the acknowledgment-number field is valid; it is not merely a generic statement that a packet arrived. This question is about the standard three-way establishment sequence, not simultaneous open or later connection teardown.

subject: excluded
question_text: For real k, consider x+ky=1 and kx+y=−1. Select true claims: A exactly one k gives no solution; B infinitely many k give no solution; C exactly one k gives a unique solution; D exactly one k gives infinitely many solutions.
question_text_status: Author paraphrase with essential givens, options and text descriptions of diagrams; exact original wording/artwork remains at the anchored official source.
solution:
Approach: Use the determinant to locate exceptional parameter values, then test consistency at those values.
The coefficient matrix is [[1,k],[k,1]], with determinant 1−k². For every k other than 1 or −1, this determinant is nonzero, so the system has a unique solution. There are infinitely many such k, which disproves C.
At k=1, the equations become x+y=1 and x+y=−1. Their left sides agree but their right sides do not, so no solution exists.
At k=−1, the equations become x−y=1 and −x+y=−1. The second is the first multiplied by −1, leaving one equation in two variables. All pairs (x,y)=(1+t,t) solve it, so there are infinitely many solutions.
There is exactly one inconsistent value and exactly one infinitely-solvable value, giving A and D. The record remains in its existing supplemental/excluded subject classification; the mathematics is included for paper completeness.

subject: 01-digital-logic
question_text: X(a,b,c)=1 precisely when at least two of a,b,c equal 1. Select identities valid for every Boolean input: A X(a,b,X(c,d,e))=X(X(a,b,c),d,e); B X(a,b,X(a,b,c))=X(a,b,c); C X(a,b,X(a,c,d))=X(a,b,a) AND X(c,d,c); D X(a,b,c)=X(a,X(a,b,c),X(a,c,c)).
question_text_status: Author paraphrase with essential givens, options and text descriptions of diagrams; exact original wording/artwork remains at the anchored official source.
solution:
Approach: Use two basic majority rules: X(u,u,v)=u, and X(0,1,v)=v. Prove claimed identities by cases and reject others with one counterexample.
For B, if a=b then both sides equal a. If a≠b, the outer X(a,b,z) returns z, so the left side becomes X(a,b,c), exactly the right side. Thus B holds.
For D, X(a,c,c)=c. If a=c, both the left side and X(a,X(a,b,c),c) equal a. If a≠c, X(a,b,c)=b, and the right side becomes X(a,b,c)=b. Thus D also holds.
A is not an associative law: choose (a,b,c,d,e)=(0,0,0,1,1). The left side is X(0,0,1)=0, whereas the right side is X(0,1,1)=1.
C fails for (a,b,c,d)=(0,1,1,1). Its left side is X(0,1,1)=1; its right side is X(0,1,0) AND X(1,1,1)=0 AND 1=0.
Therefore select B,D. Equality on a few examples cannot establish an identity, which is why the true cases require a complete case argument.

subject: 01-digital-logic
question_text: The four-bit two’s-complement encoding of −6 is 1010. Which wider encodings still represent −6? A eight-bit 10001010; B eight-bit 11111010; C sixteen-bit 1000000000001010; D sixteen-bit 1111111111111010.
question_text_status: Author paraphrase with essential givens, options and text descriptions of diagrams; exact original wording/artwork remains at the anchored official source.
solution:
Approach: Extend the sign bit, not zeros, when widening a signed two’s-complement representation.
In w bits, a word with leading bit 1 represents its unsigned value minus 2^w. The four-bit word 1010 has unsigned value 10, so 10−16=−6. To preserve that signed value when adding high-order bits, copy the leading 1 into every new position.
For eight bits this gives 11111010, with unsigned value 250 and signed value 250−256=−6. For sixteen bits it gives 1111111111111010, with unsigned value 65530 and signed value 65530−65536=−6. Therefore B and D are correct.
A has unsigned value 138 and thus signed value −118. C has unsigned value 32778 and thus signed value −32758. Merely retaining a single leading 1 and inserting zeros is not valid sign extension; it changes the negative weight of the leading bit without compensating through the new high bits.

subject: 04-data-structures
question_text: For a BST storing n distinct integers, assess: A “The maximum length of a path from the root node to any other node is (n−1).” B inorder traversal is always sorted. C worst-case search takes O(log₂ n). D every BST is a Min-Heap. Select all true statements. A’s wording is retained because it has a material quantifier ambiguity.
question_text_status: Author paraphrase with essential givens, options and text descriptions of diagrams; exact original wording/artwork remains at the anchored official source.
solution:
Approach: Separate guarantees for every individual tree from the largest possible height among all n-node BSTs.
Inorder traversal visits the left subtree, root, then right subtree. By the BST ordering invariant all left keys are smaller and all right keys are larger. Applying that reasoning recursively produces sorted order, so B is unconditionally true.
Any root-to-node path contains at most n nodes, hence at most n−1 edges. A completely skewed BST attains this bound. Under the intended “maximum possible over all BSTs” interpretation, A is true and the official answer is A,B. Literally, however, A says that each tree’s maximum root path IS n−1. A balanced three-node BST has height 1 rather than 2, so under that reading A is false and only B survives.
C is false because search follows a root-to-node path and may take Θ(n) in a skewed BST; balancing is not promised. D is false because a BST need not be complete, and its left child can be smaller than its root, violating min-heap order.
Keep the official A;B for scoring while explicitly warning about A’s wording. The mathematical distinction must not be hidden by replacing “is” with “at most”.
derived_answer: A;B under upper-bound interpretation; B under literal per-tree equality

subject: 02-computer-organization-architecture
question_text: Two independent multiplexers feed an ALU. Mux_A selects either 32-bit register RA or a 32-bit immediate; Mux_B selects either 32-bit register RB or another 32-bit immediate. The ALU writes a 32-bit register RZ. Which are supported? A two register operands; B one register and one immediate; C two immediate operands; D only one-register/one-immediate operations.
question_text_status: Author paraphrase with essential givens, options and text descriptions of diagrams; exact original wording/artwork remains at the anchored official source.
solution:
Approach: Enumerate independent multiplexer settings instead of assuming the instruction formats of a familiar processor.
Selecting RA at Mux_A and RB at Mux_B gives two register operands, so A is supported. Selecting RA and the B-side immediate, or the A-side immediate and RB, gives one register and one immediate; B is supported. Selecting the immediate input at both multiplexers gives two immediate operands, so C is supported as well.
All selected values are 32 bits and can be delivered simultaneously to the ALU, whose result goes to RZ. No data connection in the shown partial datapath forces a mux to choose a register merely because the other mux chose an immediate.
Thus select A,B,C. D is false because its word “only” excludes the other two combinations. This is a claim about the available datapath connections, not proof that a particular instruction-set encoding actually exposes every such combination.

subject: 06-theory-of-computation
question_text: A regular language L is accepted by an n-state NFA. Which statements are false? A L may also have an NFA with fewer than n states; B L may have a DFA with fewer than n states; C some DFA for L has at most 2^n states; D every DFA for L has more than 2^n states.
question_text_status: Author paraphrase with essential givens, options and text descriptions of diagrams; exact original wording/artwork remains at the anchored official source.
solution:
Approach: Apply subset construction and distinguish “may” from a guaranteed reduction.
When determinizing an NFA, a DFA state records the set of NFA states that can currently be active. An n-element set has 2^n subsets, so the construction uses at most 2^n states, including the empty subset if needed. Unreachable subsets can be removed. This proves C and directly contradicts D, making D the false statement.
The NFA in the premise is not required to be minimal. For example, an automaton for all strings can be padded with redundant states although a one-state accepting automaton already recognizes that language. Therefore A and B describe genuine possibilities for a nonminimal supplied NFA.
They do not assert that every n-state NFA can be reduced, nor a strict reduction at n=1 in the conventional nonempty-state model. The exponential bound is an upper bound that can be necessary for some languages, not a claim that every language needs exponentially many DFA states.
